t: How to approach any coding problem: the interview method
sum: A repeatable seven-step method for a coding round: restate, clarify, examples, brute force, find the bottleneck, pick a pattern, code, test — and how to talk while you do it.
why:
Picture two candidates given the same problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of two numbers that add up to the target. The first one recognises it, says "hash map", types a solution in four minutes in silence, and announces "done". The interviewer asks "what if the array can be empty?" and the code crashes. They ask "why a hash map?" and get "it's the standard approach". The second candidate spends two minutes asking whether the array is sorted, whether there is always an answer and whether the same element can be used twice; works one example on the whiteboard; says the obvious double loop is O(n²); notices that for every number the inner loop is just searching for one specific value; and concludes that a hash map turns that search into a constant-time lookup. They code it in six minutes, then trace it on their example and on an empty array. The second candidate took longer and gets the stronger score.

That surprises many people, because they think a coding round is a test of whether you know the answer. It is not. Interviewers usually score you on four separate dimensions: problem solving (did you find a good approach and can you justify it), coding (is the code correct, clean and idiomatic), verification (did you test it and find your own bugs) and communication (could the interviewer follow your thinking and work with you). Knowing the answer helps only the first, and only if you can explain it.

Without a method, three things go wrong under pressure. You freeze when you do not recognise the problem, because there is no next step to fall back on. You rush into code with a half-formed idea and have to rewrite it. And you finish with code you have never checked, so the interviewer finds the bug instead of you. A method fixes all three: it always gives you a next move, it makes you choose an approach before you type, and it builds testing into the end.

This lesson gives you that method — seven steps you can use on every problem in this track — and the reasoning behind each one. It also introduces the idea that drives all the later lessons: most efficient solutions are a brute force with one kind of repeated work removed, and each pattern is a standard way of removing one kind of repeated work.
primer:
The mental model: a doctor's consultation, not a quiz

A good way to think about a coding round is a doctor seeing a patient. A doctor does not hear "my chest hurts" and immediately write a prescription. They ask questions (where, since when, what makes it worse), examine the patient, form a first diagnosis, rule out the dangerous possibilities, decide on a treatment, and then check whether it worked. A doctor who prescribed instantly might sometimes be right, but you would not trust them, and they would be badly wrong whenever the case was unusual. The interviewer is watching for the same thing: a process that is reliable on problems you have never seen, not a lucky guess on one you have.

The analogy breaks in one place. A real doctor works alone; in an interview the "patient" — the interviewer — knows the answer and wants you to succeed. They will answer questions, give hints, and tell you when you are going down a wrong path, but only if they can follow what you are doing. That is why communication is a full quarter of the score.

The seven steps

Here is the whole method at a glance. Each step is explained in detail in the next section.

  1. Understand. Restate the problem in your own words and ask clarifying questions.
  2. Examples. Work two or three small inputs by hand, including at least one edge case.
  3. Brute force. Say the simplest correct solution and its complexity.
  4. Optimise. Find the repeated work in the brute force and choose the pattern that removes it.
  5. Agree. Summarise the approach and complexity and get a nod before coding.
  6. Code. Write it top-down, with clear names, talking through decisions.
  7. Verify. Trace the code by hand on your example and on the edge cases; fix bugs out loud.

Notice the shape of the timeline. Roughly the first twenty minutes involve no code at all. Beginners find this uncomfortable, because typing feels like progress. But a correct approach agreed in minute 18 usually becomes correct code by minute 35, while an unexamined idea typed in minute 4 often becomes a rewrite in minute 25 and unfinished code at the end.

The steps are not a rigid script. On an easy problem steps 3 and 4 may take thirty seconds together; on a hard one you may loop between steps 2 and 4 several times. What matters is that you always know which step you are in, so that you always have a next move.

If you remember one sentence from this primer, make it this: the optimal solution is usually the brute force with one kind of repeated work removed. Step 4 — find the repetition, pick the pattern that removes it — is where the rest of this track lives.
body:
Step 1 — Understand: restate and clarify

Start by saying the problem back in your own words: "So I get an unsorted list of integers and a target, and I return the two indices whose values add to the target." This takes ten seconds and catches misunderstandings that would otherwise cost you the round, such as returning values when the interviewer wanted indices.

Then ask clarifying questions. Problems are often underspecified on purpose, and the missing details change the solution. A short checklist covers almost everything:

  • Size. How large can the input be? (This decides the complexity you need — see the next lesson, al2.)
  • Values. Can numbers be negative, zero or very large? Are strings ASCII or Unicode? Can there be duplicates?
  • Shape. Is the input sorted? Can it be empty? Is a graph connected, directed, possibly cyclic?
  • Output. What exactly do I return — indices or values, one answer or all, in what order? What if there is no answer?
  • Environment. Can I modify the input? Is it a stream I see once, or all in memory?

You do not need to ask all of them every time; ask the ones whose answers would change your approach. For Two Sum, "is it sorted?" matters (sorted input allows a two-pointer solution with no extra memory), "can the same element be used twice?" matters, and "is there always exactly one answer?" decides what you return otherwise. Write the answers down where you and the interviewer can see them.

Step 2 — Examples: work it by hand

Before thinking about algorithms, solve two or three small inputs yourself. Choose them deliberately: one normal case, one that exercises a tricky rule, and one edge case. For Two Sum with target 9:

  • [2, 7, 11, 15] → indices [0, 1], a normal case.
  • [3, 3] → [0, 1], duplicates that together form the answer.
  • [5] → no answer, which tests what you return.

Examples do two jobs. They confirm you and the interviewer agree on the expected output before any code exists. And — this is the part beginners miss — the way you solve the example by hand is often the algorithm. When you look at [2, 7, 11, 15] and target 9, your eye sees 2 and immediately looks for 7. That "look for the complement" move is the hash-map solution. Pay attention to what your brain does on an example; it is usually smarter than your first formal idea.

Make examples big enough to be representative. An example of length 2 hides most bugs. Five to eight elements, not sorted, with a duplicate, is a good default.

Step 3 — Brute force: the simplest correct solution

Now say the most direct solution that is definitely correct, and its cost. For Two Sum: "Try every pair with two nested loops and return the first pair that sums to the target. That is O(n²) time and O(1) extra space." Big-O notation describes how the work grows as the input grows: O(n²) means doubling n roughly quadruples the work. (The next lesson, al2, teaches how to compute it and how to match it to the input size.)

Do not code the brute force unless the interviewer asks or you are completely stuck. Saying it takes one minute and earns three things: proof that you understood the problem, a correct fallback if nothing better appears, and — most importantly — a concrete object to optimise. It is much easier to improve a specific slow algorithm than to invent a fast one from nothing.

Step 4 — Optimise: find the repeated work, then the pattern

Look at the brute force and ask: what does it compute again and again? In the Two Sum double loop, the inner loop asks, for a fixed a[i], "is there a j with a[j] == target − a[i]?" That is a search for one specific value, repeated n times, and each search costs O(n). A structure that answers "have I seen this value, and where?" in constant time is a hash map. Replace the inner loop with a lookup and the whole thing becomes O(n) time and O(n) space.

That move — name the repeated work, then name the tool that does it cheaply — is the core skill of the whole track. Here is the table to internalise. Each row is a later lesson.

The brute force repeatedly…Pattern that removes itLesson
sums or counts over a rangeprefix sums, difference arraysal3
searches for a specific value or counthash map / hash setal4
checks pairs in a sorted arraytwo pointersal5
rescans an overlapping contiguous rangesliding windowal6
tries every candidate answer in orderbinary search (on the answer)al7
looks back for the nearest bigger/smaller elementmonotonic stackal8
finds the minimum or maximum of a changing setheapal10

Two more questions help when nothing jumps out. First, what if the input were sorted? Many problems become easy on sorted input, and sorting costs only O(n log n). Second, what is the best conceivable runtime? If you must at least read every element, you cannot beat O(n); if your answer is O(n log n) and the problem needs nothing like sorting, look for an O(n) idea.

If you are stuck, go back to step 2 with a new example, chosen to be bigger or more awkward. Solve it by hand, slowly, and write down what you are keeping track of in your head. Those things you track — "the largest value so far", "the last place I saw this letter" — are your variables and data structures.

Step 5 — Agree before coding

Summarise in two or three sentences: "I'll scan once, keeping a map from value to index. For each number I check whether target minus it is already in the map; if so I return both indices, otherwise I store the current one. O(n) time and O(n) space. Does that sound good?" This is a cheap checkpoint. If the interviewer wanted something else — constant space, or all pairs — you find out now, not after coding. Interviewers frequently say at this point "great, go ahead" or "can you do it without extra memory?"; both are useful.

Step 6 — Code: top-down, readable, narrated

Write the code in the order you would explain it. Start with the function signature and the main loop; if a piece is fiddly, call a helper function with a good name and write it afterwards (for example in_bounds(r, c) or merge(left, right)). Use names that carry meaning (seen, need, left) rather than a, b, tmp. Before a loop, say its invariant — the statement that stays true every time around — because most loop bugs are invariant bugs.

def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                       # value -> index of an earlier element
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        need = target - x
        if need in seen:            # invariant: seen holds nums[0..i-1]
            return [seen[need], i]
        seen[x] = i                 # store after checking: no reuse of i
    return []                       # agreed: empty list when no pair

Notice the small decisions, each spoken aloud: check before storing so an element cannot pair with itself; store the first index of a duplicate value is fine because we return as soon as a pair is found; return an empty list for no answer, as agreed in step 1. Narrate decisions like these, not keystrokes.

Step 7 — Verify: trace, then edge cases

Do not say "done" when you finish typing. Take your step-2 example and trace the code, writing the variables down as you go:

ixneedneed in seen?seen after
027no{2: 0}
172yes → return [0, 1]—

Then the edge cases: [3, 3] — at i = 0, 6 − 3 = 3 is not yet in seen, store it; at i = 1, 3 is there, return [0, 1]. Correct, and it confirms the "check before storing" decision matters. [5] — the loop runs once, finds nothing, returns []. Empty list — the loop never runs, returns []. Finally restate the complexity.

When you find a bug during the trace, say so plainly, explain the cause, make the smallest fix, and re-trace the part you changed. Finding your own bug is scored as a positive; it is exactly the verification skill the rubric looks for.

A second walk-through: a problem you do not recognise

The method earns its keep on problems you have not memorised. Take: "Given a list of daily temperatures, for each day return how many days you must wait for a warmer temperature, or 0 if none." Restate: for each index, the distance to the next strictly larger value to its right. Clarify: can there be up to 10⁵ days (yes), are temperatures integers (yes), what about equal temperatures (not warmer, keep waiting). Example: [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73] → [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]. Brute force: for each day scan right until a warmer one, O(n²) — 10¹⁰ steps at n = 10⁵, too slow.

Now the optimise step. Solve the example by hand and watch what you track. Walking left to right, days 71 and 69 are "still waiting"; when 72 arrives it answers 69 and then 71, but not 75. The waiting days always form a decreasing run of temperatures, and a new warmer day answers the most recent waiting days first. "Most recent first" is a stack. So: keep a stack of indices still waiting; for each new day, pop while the top is colder and record the distance; then push the new day. Each index is pushed and popped once, so O(n) total. You have just derived the monotonic stack (lesson al8) without knowing its name — which is the point of the method.

How to talk: communication as a skill

The communication dimension is not about talking constantly. It is about keeping the interviewer able to follow and help you. Three habits do most of the work. Signpost: "I'm going to handle the empty case first, then the main loop." Explain decisions: "I'm using a deque here because I pop from the front." Announce silence: "Let me think about the boundary for thirty seconds." When you are stuck, think out loud about what you have tried and why it fails — that is when interviewers give hints, and they can only give a useful hint if they know where you are.
deep:
Why the brute-force-then-optimise route works so often

Most interview problems are designed by taking a natural brute force and asking for something faster. The fast solution therefore almost always reuses information the brute force throws away. The double loop in Two Sum recomputes "where is the complement?" from scratch for every i, even though the elements before i never change. Prefix sums reuse the sum of a[0..i−1] instead of re-adding it. Dynamic programming reuses answers to subproblems. Monotonic stacks reuse the fact that some elements can never be the answer again. When you look at a brute force and ask "what am I throwing away that I could keep?", you are asking the question the problem setter designed the problem around.

The best conceivable runtime as a target

The best conceivable runtime is the lowest complexity that any solution could possibly have, usually because it must at least read the input or write the output. Printing all subsets of n elements cannot be faster than O(2ⁿ) because there are 2ⁿ of them; finding the maximum of an unsorted array cannot be faster than O(n) because any unread element could be the maximum. This gives you a stopping rule — if you are at the best conceivable runtime, stop optimising time and look at space or code clarity — and a direction: if you are at O(n log n) and the best conceivable is O(n), ask what is forcing the log factor (usually a sort or a heap) and whether you really need full order.

Recognition versus derivation

Pattern recognition is real and valuable — that is why the DSA list in this app is grouped by pattern. But there is a trap: recognition gives you the what without the why. Interviewers probe the why with variations: "now the array is a stream", "now values can be negative", "now return all pairs". A sliding-window solution to "longest subarray with sum ≤ k" works only because all values are non-negative (so extending the window never decreases the sum); a candidate who recognised it but did not derive it will not notice when a follow-up allows negatives and breaks the method. Each later lesson therefore names the precondition of its pattern — the property of the input that makes it valid. Saying it unprompted is one of the clearest strong signals in a coding round.

Invariants are how you write loops that are right the first time

An invariant is a sentence that is true at the start of every iteration of a loop. For binary search: "if the target exists, it lies in a[lo..hi]". For the two-sum map: "seen contains exactly the elements before i". If you state the invariant first, three things become mechanical: initialisation (make it true before the first iteration), the loop body (keep it true), and termination (when the loop stops, the invariant plus the stopping condition gives you the answer). Most off-by-one bugs come from an invariant that was never stated, so the code mixes two slightly different ones — for example half the code thinks hi is inclusive and half thinks it is exclusive.

Choosing a language and using its library well

Use the language you are fastest and most accurate in; for most interviews Python is a strong choice because the code is short and close to pseudocode. Know its standard tools cold: collections.Counter, defaultdict and deque, heapq (a min-heap), bisect (binary search on sorted lists), sorted(key=...), and functools.cache for memoisation. Also know their costs: list.pop(0) and x in some_list are O(n), slicing copies, and string concatenation in a loop can be quadratic. Using the library well is scored as code quality; using an O(n) call inside a loop by accident turns your O(n) solution into O(n²), and interviewers notice.

Follow-ups are the second half of the problem

Strong interviewers plan one or two follow-ups: a constraint change (stream instead of array, memory limit, very large values), a generalisation (k numbers instead of two), or a production angle (how would you test this, what if it ran on a thousand machines). Answering these well depends on the understanding you built while deriving the solution. Before you finish, it is worth asking yourself the obvious follow-up and mentioning it: "If the input didn't fit in memory, I'd …". That shows the senior habit of thinking past the immediate task.
prod:
In the interview room

This lesson's "production" is the interview itself — the real conditions you will perform under. The common failure modes are predictable, and each has a specific fix.

Coding too early. The symptom is a rewrite in the middle of the round. The cause is starting to type an idea that has not been checked against an example. The fix is the agreement step: never type until you can say the approach and its complexity in two sentences and the interviewer has nodded.

Silent struggle. The symptom is two or three minutes of silence. The interviewer cannot tell whether you are close to an insight or lost, so they cannot help, and the communication score drops. The fix is to think out loud about what you have tried and why it fails — that gives the interviewer an opening for a hint.

Over-engineering. Classes, generic helpers and exhaustive input validation for a 25-line problem. It costs time and hides the algorithm. Write a function, validate only what you agreed in step 1, and mention what production code would add rather than writing it.

Untested "done". The interviewer then traces your code and finds the bug, which moves credit from you to them. Always trace before saying you are finished.

Ignoring the time. In a 45-minute round with two problems, spending 35 minutes on the first one is a common way to fail. Ask at the start whether there will be more than one problem, and keep a rough clock: about 20 minutes per medium problem.

Online and remote variants

Many companies now run the first stage as an online assessment (OA): an automated test on a platform such as HackerRank or CodeSignal, typically two problems in 60–90 minutes, scored by hidden test cases. The method still applies, but compressed: read the constraints first (they tell you the complexity needed), write a brute force if you cannot see the optimal one quickly (partial credit from passing some tests is real), and test edge cases yourself because the hidden tests will. In live remote rounds on a shared editor, you usually cannot run code, so step 7 by hand is essential. Some companies now run rounds where an AI assistant is allowed; the same method applies, and the scoring shifts towards how well you specify, check and correct the assistant's output — steps 1, 2 and 7 matter even more.

Finally, panic after a bad first problem. Rounds are scored as a whole, and many offers include one shaky problem. Reset deliberately: take a breath, restate the next problem, and run the method from step 1.

How this maps to real engineering

The method is not interview theatre. Clarifying requirements, working examples, starting from a simple correct version, finding the bottleneck, agreeing on the design, writing readable code and testing it is how good engineers work on real tickets. Profilers in production play the role of step 4: they show you which repeated work dominates. That is why companies keep using this format; it is a small, timed version of the job.
myths: Interviewers only care whether the final code passes.

Most rubrics score four things separately: problem solving, coding, verification and communication. A candidate who reaches a correct optimal solution silently, after ten minutes of unexplained typing, often scores lower than one who reaches a near-optimal solution while explaining every decision and testing it by hand. The code is evidence; the reasoning is what is graded.
Saying the brute force first wastes time and makes you look weak.

Stating the brute force takes a minute and does three jobs: it proves you understood the problem, it gives you a correct fallback, and it shows exactly which repeated work the better solution must remove. Interviewers expect it. What looks weak is coding the brute force for fifteen minutes when you already know it is too slow.
If I recognise the problem from LeetCode I should jump straight to the known answer.

Jumping to a memorised answer without deriving it is easy to spot: you cannot explain why it works, you freeze when the interviewer changes one constraint, and you skip the edge cases the original problem did not have. Use recognition to choose a direction, then walk the reasoning out loud as if you were seeing it fresh.
Asking clarifying questions signals that you do not know the answer.

Real problems are underspecified on purpose. Interviewers deliberately leave out details — can values be negative, can the input be empty, are there duplicates — to see whether you notice. Two or three sharp questions in the first minutes are a positive signal; making silent assumptions that turn out wrong is a negative one.
Testing means running the code.

In most interviews you cannot run the code, or running it is not enough. Testing means tracing your code by hand on a small example, line by line, tracking the variables, and then checking the edge cases you listed earlier. That catches the off-by-one errors that a single happy-path run would miss.
lab:
Practise the method on one problem with a timer, and build the habit of testing a fast solution against a brute force — a technique called stress testing that you will reuse in every lesson.

  1. Set a 20-minute timer. Take Two Sum (or any problem from the DSA list you have not seen). Do steps 1–5 on paper, out loud, before writing code. Write the clarifying questions and your three examples down.
  2. Code the brute force and the optimised version in one file, stress.py: 
    import random

def brute(nums, target):
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)):
            if nums[i] + nums[j] == target:
                return True
    return False

def fast(nums, target):
    seen = set()
    for x in nums:
        if target - x in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(x)
    return False

for trial in range(20000):
    n = random.randint(0, 8)
    nums = [random.randint(-5, 5) for _ in range(n)]
    target = random.randint(-10, 10)
    if brute(nums, target) != fast(nums, target):
        print("MISMATCH", nums, target)
        break
else:
    print("all 20000 random tests agree")
  3. Run python stress.py. You should see "all 20000 random tests agree".
  4. Now plant a bug: in fast, move seen.add(x) above the if. Run again. The script prints a small failing input such as [3] 6 almost immediately — the element is paired with itself.

What this proves: small random inputs with a tiny value range find edge cases (duplicates, negatives, empty lists) far faster than hand-picked tests, and the failing case is small enough to trace by hand. Comparing booleans (does a pair exist?) instead of indices avoids false alarms when several answers are valid.
recap: A coding round is graded on problem solving, coding, verification and communication, not only on whether the code works.
Restate the problem in your own words and ask about input size, value ranges, duplicates, empty input and what to return when there is no answer.
Work two or three small examples by hand, including one edge case, before designing anything.
State the brute force and its complexity first; it proves understanding and shows which repeated work must be removed.

Find the bottleneck in the brute force and ask which pattern removes it: a hash map for repeated lookups, sorting plus two pointers for pairs, a window for contiguous ranges, a heap for repeated minimums, and so on.
Agree the approach and its complexity with the interviewer before writing code, then code top-down with clear names and helper functions.
Verify by tracing the code on a small example and then on each edge case, and fix bugs calmly and out loud.
Narrate decisions, not keystrokes: say what you are about to do and why, and keep the interviewer able to help you.
glossary: The most direct correct solution, usually trying every possibility. Often too slow, but a reliable starting point and a way to check faster solutions.
A character encoding with 128 characters (English letters, digits, punctuation). If input is ASCII-only, a fixed array of 128 counts can replace a hash map.
The part of a solution that dominates its running time, typically a loop that repeats work already done.
Exploring a graph level by level from a start node using a queue; taught in al16.
A question asked before solving to pin down missing details of the problem, such as input size or how to handle duplicates.
A stated limit on the input, such as 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, that tells you how fast the solution must be.
Exploring a graph by following one path as deep as possible before backtracking; taught in al16.
Data structures and algorithms: the subject of coding rounds, and of this track.
An input at the boundary of what is allowed — empty, a single element, all equal values, the maximum size, negative numbers — where code most often breaks.
A nudge from the interviewer. Taking a hint well (acknowledging it and building on it) is scored; ignoring it is a red flag.
A statement that is true every time the code reaches a certain point, such as 'everything left of i is already processed'. Writing it down makes loops easy to get right.
A bug where a loop or index goes one step too far or stops one step short, the most common bug in interview code.
An automated, timed coding test — often two problems in 60–90 minutes on HackerRank or CodeSignal — scored by hidden test cases.
A reusable solution shape — two pointers, sliding window, BFS, dynamic programming — that solves a whole family of problems.
The interviewer's scoring sheet: the dimensions you are graded on and what strong and weak look like for each.
How the extra memory a solution uses grows with input size.
How the number of steps a solution takes grows with input size, written in big-O notation such as O(n log n).
Running code by hand on a specific input, writing down the variable values after each step.
drill:
Run the method on an unseen problem

The interviewer says: "Given a string, return the first character that does not repeat anywhere in it." Go through steps 1–5 out loud. What do you ask, what examples do you use, what is the brute force, and what is the optimised plan?

Answer

Understand: restate it ("return the earliest character whose total count is one"). Ask: what to return if none (say an empty string or None — agree one); is it case-sensitive; ASCII or Unicode; how long can the string be? Examples: "leetcode" → "l"; "loveleetcode" → "v"; "aabb" → none; "" → none; "z" → "z". Brute force: for each position, scan the whole string counting that character; return the first with count 1 — O(n²) time, O(1) space. Optimise: the repeated work is counting the same character again and again; count every character once with a hash map (or a 26-slot array for lowercase ASCII) in one pass, then make a second pass in the original order and return the first character with count 1. O(n) time, O(k) space where k is the alphabet size. Agree: "Two passes: count with a Counter, then scan in order for count 1; O(n) time, O(alphabet) space." Verify: trace "loveleetcode": counts l2 o2 v1 e4 t1 c1 d1; the second pass hits l(2), o(2), v(1) → "v". Edge cases: empty string returns the agreed sentinel; "aabb" scans everything and returns it too. A likely follow-up is "the string is a stream and you must answer after each character" — keep counts plus an ordered structure of characters seen once (an OrderedDict or a queue with lazy removal).
qa: E
Walk me through how you approach a coding problem you have never seen.

I restate it in my own words and ask clarifying questions about input size, value ranges, duplicates and empty input. Then I work a couple of small examples by hand, state a brute-force solution with its complexity, and look for the repeated work that makes it slow. I pick the pattern that removes that work, confirm the approach and complexity with you, code it with clear names, and finally trace it on an example and the edge cases.

Follow-up: What do you do if you cannot see any better approach than brute force? — Say so, code the brute force cleanly so there is a working answer, then reason about the bottleneck out loud; interviewers often hint at that point.
E
Why state a brute-force solution before the optimal one?

It proves I understood the problem, gives a correct fallback, and makes the bottleneck visible. The optimised solution is usually the brute force with one repeated piece of work removed, so naming the brute force is the fastest path to the better one. It takes a minute, not fifteen.
E
What clarifying questions would you ask about 'find two numbers in an array that sum to a target'?

Is the array sorted? Can it contain negatives or duplicates? Is there always exactly one answer, and if not, what should I return? Do you want indices or values, and can I use the same element twice? How large can the array be? Each answer changes the solution: sorted input allows two pointers in O(1) space, unsorted suggests a hash map.
M
How do you decide which pattern a problem needs?

I look at the brute force and ask what it repeats. Repeated lookups suggest a hash map; repeated scans of a contiguous range suggest a sliding window or prefix sums; repeated 'smallest so far' suggest a heap; a sorted input or monotone yes/no answer suggests binary search; 'all combinations' suggests backtracking; overlapping subproblems suggest dynamic programming; relationships between items suggest a graph. The input size tells me what complexity I need, which narrows it further.

Follow-up: Give an example where two patterns both work. — Two Sum on a sorted array: a hash map is O(n) time and O(n) space, two pointers are O(n) time and O(1) space; I would mention both and pick two pointers.
M
You have written your solution. How do you test it without running it?

I trace it line by line on a small example, writing variable values as I go, and compare with the answer I worked out by hand earlier. Then I walk the edge cases I listed at the start — empty input, one element, all equal, negatives, maximum size — and ask what each line does with them. Most bugs show up at loop boundaries, so I check the first and last iteration specifically.
Follow-up: You find a bug during the trace — what then? — Say what the bug is, explain the fix, change the smallest amount of code, and re-trace just the part that changed.
M
The interviewer gives you a hint you do not understand. What do you do?

Acknowledge it and say what I think it means, then ask a targeted question: 'Do you mean sorting first so equal values are adjacent?' Silently ignoring a hint, or pretending to understand, is worse than asking. Hints are part of the evaluation; using one well costs far less than staying stuck.
M
How much should you talk while coding?

Enough that the interviewer always knows what I am doing and why: before each block I say what it is for, and I mention decisions such as the choice of data structure or a boundary condition. I do not narrate individual keystrokes. If I need to think silently, I say so — 'give me thirty seconds to think about the boundary' — so silence is not mistaken for being stuck.
M
You realise halfway through coding that your approach is wrong. What now?

Stop and say so immediately, explain why it fails with a concrete input, and propose the fix or new approach before changing code. Interviewers value catching your own error far more than they penalise the error itself. If time is short, I keep the working parts and change only what is needed.
M
How do you use the input constraints?

They tell me the complexity budget. A rough rule is that about 10⁸ simple operations fit in a second, so n ≤ 10⁵ means I need about O(n log n), n ≤ 20 allows O(2ⁿ), and n ≤ 500 allows O(n³). If the interviewer has not given constraints, I ask, because it decides whether brute force is already acceptable.
Follow-up: What if they say 'as large as possible'? — Then aim for linear or n log n time and mention memory: an O(n) extra array may matter if n is in the billions.
H
In the last ten minutes you have a working O(n²) solution and an idea for O(n log n) that is not coded. What do you do?

Make sure the O(n²) code is clean and verified first, because a correct solution beats a half-finished better one. Then explain the O(n log n) idea precisely — the data structure, the invariant and why it is correct — and code it only if there is clearly time. Describing the improvement well still earns most of the problem-solving credit.
H
How do you handle a problem that is ambiguous on purpose, like 'design an algorithm to deduplicate log lines'?

I turn it into a precise problem by asking about the definition of duplicate (exact match, or same after removing timestamps), whether order must be preserved, whether it fits in memory and whether it is a stream. Then I state my assumptions explicitly and solve that version, noting how the answer changes under the other assumptions, for example a hash set in memory versus external sorting or a probabilistic filter for a huge stream.

Follow-up: The data is too big for memory. — Hash each line into one of k bucket files so duplicates land in the same bucket, then deduplicate each bucket in memory; or accept a small false-positive rate with a Bloom filter.
H
What separates a 'strong hire' coding performance from a 'hire'?

Both reach a correct, efficient solution. A strong hire gets there with clear structure: precise clarifying questions, a brute force stated and dismissed quickly, an approach justified by the bottleneck, clean code that needed few fixes, and self-driven testing that found their own bugs. They also handle a follow-up variation fluently, because they understood why the solution works instead of remembering it.

t: Complexity analysis: big-O, constraints and choosing the algorithm
sum: How to count the work a solution does, express it in big-O, analyse loops, recursion and amortised operations, and read the input constraints to know which complexity the problem expects.
prereq: al1
The interview method: restate, examples, brute force, find the repeated work, pick a pattern, agree, code, verify.
why:
You have just written a solution in an interview. It is correct: you traced it on your examples and the edge cases. The interviewer nods and asks, "What's the time complexity?" You say "O(n)", because there is one for loop. They ask, "What about the in check inside it?" You realise the in is on a list, so each check scans the whole list, and the real cost is O(n²). With 10⁵ elements, that is the difference between a fraction of a second and several minutes.

The same gap appears in online assessments, but more brutally. The platform runs your code on hidden tests with up to 10⁵ or 10⁶ elements and a time limit of one or two seconds. A correct O(n²) solution passes the small tests and fails the large ones with "Time Limit Exceeded", and you get partial credit at best. The problem statement told you this would happen: the line 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ was a hint about which complexity was expected, if you knew how to read it.

Complexity analysis is the tool for both situations. It lets you predict, before you write or run anything, whether an approach is fast enough, and it lets you explain precisely why one solution beats another. It is also the language interviewers use in every round: "can you do better?" means "can you reach a lower complexity class?", and you cannot answer that without knowing which class you are in.

This lesson teaches you to count work: what big-O means and why it drops constants; how to analyse loops (including the nested loops that are secretly linear), recursion and amortised operations; how to measure memory; the hidden costs of common Python operations; and — the most practical skill of all — how to turn the input constraints into the target complexity before you design anything.
primer:
The mental model: counting steps as the input grows

Imagine you are looking for a friend's name in a printed phone book. One way is to read every name from the first page until you find it. Another is to open the book in the middle, see whether the name comes earlier or later in the alphabet, and repeat on the correct half. For a book with 1,000 names, the first method can take 1,000 looks; the second takes about 10. For a book with a million names, the first takes up to a million looks and the second about 20. The interesting thing is not the exact counts; it is how they grow. Making the book a thousand times bigger makes the first method a thousand times slower, and the second barely slower at all.

That is what complexity analysis captures: how the amount of work grows as the input grows. We count basic steps — a comparison, an addition, an array access, a hash lookup — as functions of the input size, usually called n. Then we keep only the part that dominates for large n.

Big-O in one paragraph

If an algorithm does 3n² + 10n + 50 steps, then for n = 1,000 the 3n² term is 3,000,000 and the rest is about 10,000: the n² term is everything. Big-O notation writes this as O(n²): it keeps the fastest-growing term and drops constant multipliers. Dropping the 3 is deliberate: constant factors depend on the machine, the language and the compiler, while the growth rate depends only on the algorithm. Formally, O(g(n)) is an upper bound — the work is at most a constant times g(n) once n is large enough — but in interviews people use it to mean "this is the growth class".

The classes you will meet, fastest to slowest

ClassNameTypical sourceSteps at n = 10⁶
O(1)constantarray index, hash lookup1
O(log n)logarithmicbinary search, heap push~20
O(n)linearone pass10⁶
O(n log n)linearithmicsorting, n heap operations~2 × 10⁷
O(n²)quadraticall pairs10¹²
O(2ⁿ)exponentialall subsetsastronomically many
O(n!)factorialall orderingseven more

A quick way to feel the difference: at a billion simple steps per second, an O(n log n) algorithm on a million items finishes in about 20 milliseconds, an O(n²) one takes about 17 minutes, and an O(2ⁿ) one on just 60 items would outlast the universe. The class is not a detail; it decides whether the program is usable at all.

Where the analogy breaks: the phone-book picture suggests only time matters. Memory has a complexity too — space complexity, how much extra memory grows with n — and many interview follow-ups ("can you do it in constant space?") are about that dimension instead.
body:
Counting a single loop

Start with the simplest case. This function looks at each element once and does constant work per element:

def total(a):
    s = 0
    for x in a:      # runs n times
        s += x       # O(1) each
    return s

The loop body runs n times and costs O(1) each time, so the total is O(n). The rule for sequential code is to add: two loops one after another are O(n) + O(n) = O(n). The rule for nested code is to multiply the number of times the inner body runs, which is where most mistakes happen.

Nested loops: count how many times the inner body runs

Two full nested loops over n elements run the inner body n × n = n² times: O(n²). A triangular loop, where the inner loop starts at the outer index, runs it (n−1) + (n−2) + … + 1 = n(n−1)/2 times. That is half as much, but half is a constant factor, so it is still O(n²).

Not every nested loop is quadratic. This is the key exception, and you will see it in every sliding-window and two-pointer solution:

left = 0
for right in range(n):              # n iterations
    add(a[right])
    while window_invalid():         # how many times in total?
        remove(a[left])
        left += 1

The inner while loop can run many times in one outer iteration, but each time it runs, left increases by one, and left never decreases and never exceeds n. So over the entire run, the inner body executes at most n times. Total work: n (outer) + n (inner, across all iterations) = O(n). The lesson: count the total number of executions of each line across the whole run, and look for a quantity that only moves in one direction. This technique has a name, the aggregate method, and it is the simplest kind of amortised analysis.

Logarithms: halving and doubling

A logarithm answers the question "how many times can I halve n before reaching 1?". log₂ 8 = 3 because 8 → 4 → 2 → 1. Any loop that halves (or doubles) a quantity each step runs O(log n) times:

i = n
while i > 1:
    i //= 2          # runs about log2(n) times

Binary search halves the search range each step, so it is O(log n). A balanced binary tree with n nodes has height about log₂ n, so walking from root to leaf is O(log n), which is why heap operations and balanced-tree lookups are O(log n). The base of the logarithm does not matter in big-O, because log₂ n and log₁₀ n differ only by a constant factor. Useful values to memorise: log₂ 10³ ≈ 10, log₂ 10⁶ ≈ 20, log₂ 10⁹ ≈ 30.

O(n log n) appears whenever you do a logarithmic operation for each of n elements (n heap pushes) or a linear amount of work at each of log n levels (merge sort). It is also the cost of comparison-based sorting, which cannot do better: there are n! possible orderings and each comparison at best halves the possibilities, so you need about log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n comparisons.

Recursion: the recursion tree

For a recursive function, draw the tree of calls, write the work done in each call (excluding its recursive calls), and add it all up. Take merge sort: a call on n elements does O(n) work merging and makes two calls on n/2 elements.

Compare the naive recursive Fibonacci: fib(n) calls fib(n-1) and fib(n-2) and does O(1) work itself. The tree branches twice at every level and has depth n, so it has roughly 2ⁿ nodes (more precisely about 1.6ⁿ). Exponential time comes from branching recursion whose branches recompute the same thing; memoisation (storing each answer the first time) collapses the tree to n distinct calls. That observation is the foundation of dynamic programming (al21).

A shortcut for divide-and-conquer recurrences of the form T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n) is the master theorem. You rarely need it formally in interviews; it is enough to know three results: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) is O(n log n) (merge sort); T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) is O(log n) (binary search); T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1) is O(n) (visiting every node of a balanced tree).

Amortised analysis: expensive sometimes, cheap on average

A Python list is a dynamic array: a block of memory with some spare capacity. Appending is cheap while there is spare room. When the block is full, the list allocates a larger block and copies everything — an O(n) operation. So is append O(1) or O(n)?

Both, depending on how you ask. A single append can be O(n). But because CPython grows the block proportionally (by roughly an eighth plus a little, so capacity keeps growing geometrically), each expensive copy of n elements is followed by on the order of n cheap appends before the next one. If the array doubled each time, the copies over n appends would total n/2 + n/4 + … ≤ n elements; with a smaller growth factor the total is a larger constant times n, but still O(n). So n appends cost O(n) in total, and the amortised cost per append is O(1). The same reasoning makes hash-table insertion amortised O(1) (occasional rehashing) and the sliding-window inner loop O(1) per step on average.

The growth must be proportional for this to work. If the array grew by a fixed 100 slots each time, a copy would happen every 100 appends, and the copies would total about n²/200 — quadratic.

Space complexity: what counts

Space complexity counts the extra memory the algorithm needs beyond the input, as a function of n. Three sources are easy to forget. The recursion stack: each active call holds a frame, so a recursion of depth d uses O(d) space even if the function allocates nothing. Implicit copies: a[1:] creates a new list of n−1 elements; a recursive function that passes slices therefore uses O(n²) memory in total across a chain of calls, where passing indices would use O(n). The output: by convention, memory for the answer itself is usually not counted, but say so.

Python also has a practical limit: the default recursion limit is 1,000 frames. A DFS on a path-shaped graph with 10⁵ nodes will crash with RecursionError. You can raise the limit with sys.setrecursionlimit, but the robust fix is an explicit stack.

Reading the constraints: the most useful table in this track

A typical machine runs roughly 10⁸ simple operations per second in compiled languages; pure Python manages about 10⁷. Problem setters choose input limits so that the intended complexity fits in about a second. So you can work backwards from the constraint to the algorithm before designing anything:

Largest nExpected complexityUsually means
≤ 10–12O(n!) or O(n · n!)try all permutations
≤ 20–25O(2ⁿ) or O(n · 2ⁿ)all subsets, bitmask DP, backtracking
≤ 100–500O(n³)triple loops, Floyd–Warshall, interval DP
≤ 2,000–5,000O(n²)all pairs, 2D DP
≤ 10⁵–10⁶O(n log n) or O(n)sort, heap, binary search, hashing, two pointers, linear DP
≥ 10⁸, or "up to 10¹⁸"O(log n) or O(1)binary search on the answer, math formula, fast power

This works in both directions. If n ≤ 20 in a problem about choosing items, the setter is telling you exponential search is fine — do not waste time looking for a polynomial algorithm. If n ≤ 10⁵, an O(n²) idea is a dead end before you start. In a live interview without written constraints, ask: "Roughly how big can the input be?" The answer is a hint.

Putting it together: analysing a complete solution

Here is how to analyse a realistic solution line by line, the way you would say it in an interview. The task: return the k most frequent words in a list of n words, ties broken alphabetically.

from collections import Counter
import heapq

def top_k(words, k):
    counts = Counter(words)                         # (1)
    return heapq.nsmallest(k, counts,               # (2)
                           key=lambda w: (-counts[w], w))

Line (1) hashes each word once. If the average word length is L, hashing costs O(L) per word, so building the counter is O(n·L) time and O(u·L) space, where u is the number of distinct words. Line (2) keeps a heap of size k while scanning the u distinct words; each push or pop is O(log k), so it is O(u log k) time and O(k) extra space. Total: O(n·L + u log k) time, O(u·L) space. In an interview you would usually treat L as a small constant and say "O(n + u log k), which is O(n log k) in the worst case where all words are distinct". Notice three habits: naming every variable that matters (n, u, k, L), justifying each term by the operation that causes it, and simplifying only at the end, saying what assumption the simplification makes.

Compare the alternative of sorting all distinct words by (−count, word): O(u log u). When k is much smaller than u, the heap is better; when k is close to u, they are the same. Saying that trade-off unprompted is the kind of answer that separates "knows big-O" from "uses big-O to choose".

Hidden costs: library operations that are not O(1)

Your algorithm's complexity is only as good as the operations it uses. These Python operations look cheap but cost O(n) (or more):

OperationCostCheap alternative
x in some_listO(n)x in some_set — O(1) average
lst.pop(0), lst.insert(0, x)O(n)collections.deque — O(1) at both ends
lst[a:b]O(b − a) copypass indices instead
s += piece in a loopcan be O(n) eachcollect pieces, then "".join(parts)
min(lst), sum(lst), lst.index(x)O(n)maintain a running value or a heap
sorted(lst)O(n log n)sort once outside the loop
hashing a string key of length kO(k)hash short keys, or cache

The pattern to watch for is one of these inside a loop over n elements. That is how a correct O(n) design becomes an O(n²) implementation.
deep:
Big-O, big-Omega and big-Theta: say what you mean

Strictly, big-O is only an upper bound: binary search is O(n) too, because log n ≤ n, even though that is a useless statement. Big-Omega (Ω) is a lower bound, and big-Theta (Θ) means both — the growth is pinned down exactly up to constants. In conversation and interviews, "O" is used to mean Θ, and that is fine. Where the distinction matters is lower bounds for problems: "any comparison sort is Ω(n log n)" and "finding the maximum of an unsorted array is Ω(n)" are statements about every possible algorithm, and they tell you when to stop trying to optimise.

Worst, average and expected cases

Quicksort is Θ(n log n) on average but Θ(n²) in the worst case, when each pivot is the smallest or largest element (for example, a naive first-element pivot on already-sorted input). Hash tables are O(1) expected per operation but O(n) worst case if many keys collide. "Expected" usually means averaged over the algorithm's own randomness (a random pivot, a random hash seed), which makes the guarantee hold for every input with high probability, rather than averaged over some assumed distribution of inputs. That is why Python randomises the hash of strings per process: it stops an attacker crafting colliding keys to force the worst case. When an interviewer asks about a hash-map solution, "O(n) expected" is the precise phrase.

Amortised analysis beyond the aggregate method

The aggregate method adds up total cost over a sequence and divides. A more flexible view is the potential method, which treats cheap operations as saving credit for future expensive ones. For the dynamic array, charge each append 3 units: 1 pays for the write and 2 are saved; when a resize copies the elements, the saved credit pays for the copies. You will not be asked to do potential-function proofs in coding interviews, but the intuition — "cheap operations prepay for rare expensive ones, and the expensive one cannot happen again until enough cheap ones have occurred" — is how you justify union-find's near-constant operations, monotonic stack pops, and the sliding-window inner loop.

When n is not the only variable

Many problems have several size parameters, and collapsing them into one hides the real cost. A grid is R × C; a graph has V vertices and E edges; a string problem has text length n and pattern length m; a list of words has k words of average length L. Report complexity in all of them: BFS is O(V + E), not O(n); building a trie is O(total characters), not O(k). This matters because the parameters can be wildly different: a graph with 10⁵ vertices might have 10⁵ edges (sparse) or 10¹⁰ edges (dense), and an algorithm that is O(V²) is fine for the dense case and terrible for the sparse one.

Pseudo-polynomial complexity

The coin-change DP runs in O(n · amount). That looks polynomial, but it is polynomial in the value of amount, not in the number of digits needed to write it. If amount is 10⁹, the table has 10⁹ entries — too many — even though the input is tiny. Such algorithms are called pseudo-polynomial. Recognising them matters in interviews because a follow-up such as "what if amount is up to 10⁹?" means the DP no longer works and you need a different idea (math, greedy with proof, or meet-in-the-middle).

Constants and the memory hierarchy

Two O(n) algorithms can differ by 10–100× in practice. Sequential array scans run at memory bandwidth because the CPU prefetches the next cache line; pointer-chasing through a linked list or a hash table with scattered entries waits for main memory on each step (about 100 ns, versus about 1 ns for a cache hit). In Python the gap is between operations that run in C (built-ins like sum, sorted, set intersection, slicing) and operations interpreted bytecode by bytecode. This is why "O(n) in Python with a tight interpreted loop" can lose to "O(n log n) using sorted()". Mention it when relevant; it shows you know where big-O stops being the whole story, and it is the reason performance engineers measure before and after every optimisation instead of trusting the analysis alone.
prod:
In the interview room

Interviewers ask for complexity after almost every solution, and they listen for three things. First, both time and space, unprompted. Second, the right variables — "O(R·C) for the grid" or "O(V + E)", not a vague "O(n)". Third, a justification in one sentence: "each cell is pushed onto the queue at most once, and each push does four neighbour checks". A bare answer with no reasoning invites the follow-up "why?", and a wrong reason is worse than none.

The most common mistakes are predictable. Calling a sliding window O(n²) because of the nested loop (it is O(n) by the aggregate argument). Calling a hash-map solution O(1) space (the map holds up to n entries). Forgetting the recursion stack (a recursive DFS on a 10⁵-node chain is O(n) space and, in Python, a crash). Forgetting the cost of sorting at the start (a two-pointer solution on unsorted input is O(n log n), not O(n)). And missing hidden O(n) calls inside loops.

In online assessments

Online assessment platforms show you the constraints and run hidden tests with the largest allowed inputs. Read the constraints before reading the examples. If your idea's operation count at the maximum n is above about 10⁸ (10⁷ in Python), it will time out; rethink before coding. If you cannot find the intended complexity, submit the brute force anyway — partial credit for passing the small tests is common — then improve it. Also watch input reading: reading 10⁶ numbers with repeated input() calls in Python can itself take a second; use sys.stdin.read().split() or the platform's fast template.

When the interviewer asks "can you do better?", answer with the class you are aiming for and why it is plausible: "the best conceivable is O(n) because every element must be read; the log factor comes from sorting, and I only need the k largest, so a heap of size k gives O(n log k)". That shows you are reasoning about where the cost comes from, not guessing at tricks. And when you genuinely believe you are optimal, say so with the lower-bound argument; interviewers sometimes ask "can you do better?" precisely to see whether you can defend an optimal answer.

In real systems

Complexity mistakes are a classic source of production incidents, because test data is small and production data is not. A request handler that does an O(n²) de-duplication works fine with 100 items in staging and takes minutes with 50,000 items for one large customer. Regular-expression engines with backtracking can take exponential time on crafted inputs (the "ReDoS" class of incidents, such as Cloudflare's global outage in July 2019, caused by a regex with catastrophic backtracking). Hash-flooding attacks, which send many colliding keys to make a server's hash tables degrade to linear scans, are why languages randomised their hash functions around 2011–2012. The habit this lesson builds — asking "what happens when n is a thousand times bigger?" — is the same habit that prevents those incidents.
myths: O(n) is always faster than O(n log n) or O(n²).

Big-O describes growth as n becomes large and ignores constant factors. For n = 20, an O(n²) loop doing 400 cheap steps can beat an O(n) algorithm that does 50 expensive hash operations per element. That is why real sort functions switch to insertion sort for small slices. In interviews the asymptotic class matters most, but say 'for large n'.
Two nested loops always mean O(n²).

It depends on how many times the inner loop body runs in total. In a sliding window, the inner while loop moves the left pointer, which only ever moves forward, so across the whole run it executes at most n times: the total is O(n) despite the nesting. Count total work, not indentation levels.
A hash map lookup is O(1), full stop.

It is O(1) on average, assuming a good hash function and a table that resizes. In the worst case, when many keys collide, a lookup can degrade to O(n), and hashing a key of length k costs O(k) itself — hashing a string of 10⁵ characters is not free. For interviews 'expected O(1)' is the right phrase.
Recursion is slow, so iterative solutions are always better.

A recursive solution has the same asymptotic time as the iterative one that does the same work. What changes is space: each active call uses a stack frame, so recursion of depth d costs O(d) memory, and Python's default recursion limit (1,000) can make deep recursion crash. The fix is to convert deep recursions to an explicit stack, not to avoid recursion in general.
Space complexity only counts data structures you create.

It also counts the recursion stack and any copies you make implicitly, such as slicing a list (a[1:] copies n−1 elements) or building strings by concatenation. A 'constant space' recursive tree traversal actually uses O(h) space, where h is the height of the tree.
lab:
Measure complexity instead of trusting it, and see a hidden O(n) cost with your own eyes. Uses only the Python standard library.

  1. Save as growth.py: 
    import time, random
from collections import deque

def timed(f, n):
    t = time.perf_counter(); f(n); return time.perf_counter() - t

def list_membership(n):
    seen = []
    for i in range(n):
        if i in seen: pass       # O(n) scan each time
        seen.append(i)

def set_membership(n):
    seen = set()
    for i in range(n):
        if i in seen: pass       # O(1) average
        seen.add(i)

def pop_front_list(n):
    q = list(range(n))
    while q: q.pop(0)            # O(n) each

def pop_front_deque(n):
    q = deque(range(n))
    while q: q.popleft()         # O(1) each

for f in (list_membership, set_membership, pop_front_list, pop_front_deque):
    a, b = timed(f, 5_000), timed(f, 10_000)
    print(f"{f.__name__:18} n=5k {a:.4f}s  n=10k {b:.4f}s  ratio {b/a:.1f}")
  2. Run python growth.py. Look at the ratio column: doubling n should roughly double the time for an O(n) total (ratio ≈ 2) and roughly quadruple it for O(n²) (ratio ≈ 4).
  3. Expect list_membership to show a ratio near 4 and set_membership near 2. pop_front_list may look closer to linear at these sizes, because CPython's memmove is very fast; increase n to 100,000 and 200,000 for it and the quadratic ratio appears.
  4. Change one function to use slicing in a loop (q = q[1:]) and predict its ratio before running.

What this proves: the class shows up in how time scales, not in a single timing; and constant factors (C-level memmove) can hide a bad class at small n — which is exactly why tests on small data miss complexity bugs.
recap: Time complexity counts how the number of basic steps grows with input size; big-O keeps the fastest-growing term and drops constants.
Count total work across the whole run, not the nesting depth of loops: a pointer that only moves forward contributes O(n) in total.
For recursion, multiply the work per call by the number of calls, which a recursion tree makes visible; branching recursion without memoisation is usually exponential.
Amortised analysis averages the cost over a sequence of operations, which is why appending to a dynamic array is O(1) even though an occasional resize is O(n).
Space complexity includes extra data structures, copies, and the recursion stack.
About 10⁸ simple operations run in a second in C++ or Java and roughly 10⁷ in pure Python, so the input size tells you the complexity the problem expects.
n ≤ 10–12 suggests O(n!) , n ≤ 20 suggests O(2ⁿ), n ≤ 500 suggests O(n³), n ≤ 5,000 suggests O(n²), n ≤ 10⁶ suggests O(n log n) or O(n), and larger n suggests O(log n) or O(1) per query.
Know the real cost of library operations, because one hidden O(n) call inside a loop turns a linear solution quadratic.
glossary: The average cost per operation over a long sequence of operations, even if a few individual operations are expensive.
Describing behaviour as the input size grows towards infinity, ignoring small inputs and constant factors.
An upper bound on growth: f(n) is O(g(n)) if, beyond some size, f(n) is at most a constant times g(n).
A lower bound on growth: the algorithm needs at least this much work for large inputs.
A tight bound: growth is bounded above and below by the same function, up to constants.
The two basic ways to visit every node of a graph — level by level with a queue, or path by path with a stack or recursion. Both are O(V + E); taught in al16.
The memory region that holds one frame per active function call; deep recursion uses one frame per level.
The fixed multiplier that big-O ignores, such as doing 3n steps instead of n.
Small, very fast memory next to the processor that holds recently used data; reading from it takes about a nanosecond versus about 100 for main memory.
An array that grows automatically by allocating a larger block and copying when full, such as a Python list.
Solving a problem by combining stored answers to overlapping subproblems so each is computed once; taught in al21–al23.
The number of times n can be halved before reaching 1; log₂ of 10⁶ is about 20.
A formula that gives the running time of divide-and-conquer recurrences of the form T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n).
Caching the result of a function call so the same arguments are computed only once.
An equation that expresses a recursive algorithm's running time in terms of its running time on smaller inputs.
A drawing of every call a recursive function makes, used to add up the total work.
The cost on the most expensive input of a given size, versus the expected cost over typical or random inputs.
drill:
Read the constraints, choose the approach

Three problems, each with only its constraints shown. For each, say the complexity you are aiming for and the kind of technique it suggests. (a) "Given n ≤ 18 tasks and a compatibility matrix, find the largest set of mutually compatible tasks." (b) "Given an array of n ≤ 2 × 10⁵ integers, answer q ≤ 2 × 10⁵ queries for the sum of a[l..r]." (c) "Given a number n ≤ 10¹², find the smallest x such that x² ≥ n."

Answer

(a) n ≤ 18 means O(2ⁿ · n) ≈ 4.7 × 10⁶ is fine: enumerate all subsets as bitmasks (or backtrack with pruning) and check compatibility; the problem (maximum clique) has no known polynomial algorithm, and the constraint tells you none is expected. (b) Answering each query by looping over l..r is O(n · q) = 4 × 10¹⁰, far too slow. With 2 × 10⁵ of each, we want O(n + q) or O((n + q) log n). Since there are no updates, a prefix-sum array (al3) answers each query in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing: sum = pre[r+1] − pre[l]. If the array also changed between queries, a Fenwick tree (al27) would give O(log n) per operation. (c) n ≤ 10¹² means even O(n) is too slow, and O(√n) = 10⁶ is fine but there is better: the condition x² ≥ n is monotone in x (false, false, …, true, true), so binary search on x over [0, 10⁶] finds it in about 20 steps — O(log n). Use integer arithmetic (math.isqrt in Python) to avoid floating-point error near perfect squares.
qa: E
What is the time complexity of a loop from 1 to n with an inner loop from 1 to i?

The inner body runs 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2 times, which is O(n²). The triangular shape halves the work compared with a full n-by-n loop, but halving is a constant factor, so the class is still quadratic.
E
Why is binary search O(log n)?

Each step compares with the middle element and discards half of the remaining range. Starting from n elements, after k steps n/2ᵏ remain, and the search ends when that reaches 1, so k = log₂ n. For a million elements that is about 20 comparisons.
E
What is the space complexity of a recursive function that computes the depth of a binary tree?

O(h), where h is the height of the tree, because at any moment there is one stack frame per level on the current path. For a balanced tree h is about log n; for a degenerate tree that is a single chain, h = n, which is why deep recursion can overflow the stack.
M
Appending to a Python list is described as O(1). How, if the list sometimes has to be copied?

The list over-allocates: when it is full it grows by a proportion of its size, copies everything, and then has spare room for many cheap appends. Each resize costs O(n) but happens after Θ(n) appends, so the total cost of n appends is O(n) and the amortised cost per append is O(1). A single append can still be slow; the guarantee is about sequences.
Follow-up: Would growing by a fixed 100 slots each time work as well? — No: then a resize happens every 100 appends and n appends cost about n²/200 copies, which is O(n²) in total.
M
The constraints say n ≤ 10⁵. What complexity are they hinting at?

Around 10⁸ simple operations run in about a second in a compiled language, so O(n²) = 10¹⁰ is too slow, while O(n log n) ≈ 1.7 × 10⁶ is comfortable. So they want O(n log n) or O(n) — usually sorting, a heap, binary search, a hash map or a linear scan. In Python I would aim for O(n) or O(n log n) with small constants.
M
What is the time complexity of the naive recursive Fibonacci, and how do you fix it?

Each call makes two more calls, so the recursion tree has about φⁿ ≈ 1.6ⁿ nodes: exponential time. The same values are computed many times — fib(n−2) is computed both directly and inside fib(n−1). Memoising, or computing bottom-up, makes each value computed once, so O(n) time; keeping only the last two values makes the space O(1).
Follow-up: Can you do better than O(n)? — Yes, O(log n) with fast matrix exponentiation or the doubling formulas, because Fibonacci is a linear recurrence.
M
Your sliding-window code has a while loop inside a for loop. Why is it O(n) and not O(n²)?

The inner loop only advances the left pointer, and the left pointer never moves backwards, so over the entire run it moves at most n times. Adding the n iterations of the outer loop gives at most 2n steps in total. Complexity comes from counting total work, and here each element enters and leaves the window once.
M
Which common Python operations are secretly O(n)?

Membership in a list (x in lst), list.pop(0) and list.insert(0, x), slicing (it copies), list.index, max/min/sum over a list, string concatenation in a loop (each + may copy), and sorted() which is O(n log n). Using any of these inside a loop over n elements makes the loop quadratic. The fixes are a set for membership, a deque for front operations, and join for strings.
Follow-up: Is 'x in some_dict' O(n)? — No, it is an average O(1) hash lookup; only lists and tuples are scanned.
M
What is the complexity of merge sort, and how do you derive it?

T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n): split, sort both halves recursively, merge in linear time. The recursion tree has log₂ n levels and each level does O(n) total merging work, so O(n log n). Space is O(n) for the merge buffer plus O(log n) for the stack.
H
Give the complexity of generating all subsets of n elements, and explain why it cannot be improved.

There are 2ⁿ subsets, and copying each into the output costs up to n, so O(n·2ⁿ) time. It cannot be beaten because the output itself has that size; any algorithm must at least write it. This is an output-sensitive bound, and it is why n ≤ 20 in constraints signals an exponential solution is intended.
Follow-up: What if they only want the count of subsets with sum k? — Then we do not need to list them, and DP over sums gives O(n·k), which can be far smaller.
H
An algorithm is O(n log n) on average but O(n²) in the worst case. When does that matter?

Quicksort with a naive pivot is the classic example: sorted or adversarial input makes every partition maximally unbalanced. It matters when inputs can be adversarial (a public API, a judge with crafted tests) or when latency spikes are unacceptable. Mitigations are random pivots, median-of-three, or switching to heapsort past a recursion depth (introsort). Hash tables have the same issue with crafted collisions, which is why Python randomises string hashing.
H
How would you estimate whether your Python solution will pass a time limit before submitting?

Compute the dominant operation count from the complexity and the maximum input size, then use about 10⁷ simple Python operations per second as a budget. If I am within a factor of a few, reduce constants: avoid function calls in the hot loop, use built-ins (sum, sorted, set operations) that run in C, precompute, and read input in bulk. If I am off by orders of magnitude, constant tuning will not save it — I need a better algorithm.
