t: Arrays, prefix sums and difference arrays
sum: Precompute running totals so any range sum is one subtraction; combine with a hash map to count subarrays with a given sum; use difference arrays to apply many range updates in O(1) each; Kadane's scan for maximum subarray.
prereq: al1
Find the repeated work in the brute force and remove it with a pattern.
al2
n ≤ 10⁵ means aim for O(n) or O(n log n); count total work, not loop nesting.
why:
Suppose a shop keeps its daily revenue for the last year in an array of 365 numbers, and a dashboard lets managers ask "what was revenue between day 40 and day 95?" A simple implementation adds up the 56 numbers for each question. That is fine for one question. Now the dashboard is used by 2,000 store managers, each looking at 50 ranges, over ten years of data — and every question re-adds thousands of numbers that were already added for the previous question. The work is almost entirely repeated.

The same waste appears constantly in interview problems: "sum of a subarray", "how many subarrays sum to k", "apply these 10⁵ increments to ranges", "average of every window". The brute force recomputes a sum from scratch for each range, so it costs O(length) per range and O(n²) or worse overall. With n = 10⁵, that is 10¹⁰ operations and a guaranteed time-out.

The fix is one of the simplest and most useful ideas in algorithms: compute the running total once, and then any range is the difference of two running totals. Revenue from day 40 to 95 is "revenue up to day 95" minus "revenue up to day 39". Each question becomes one subtraction.

This lesson builds that idea and its relatives, in order: the prefix-sum array and its off-by-one-proof convention; prefix sums combined with a hash map to count subarrays with a target sum (one of the most-asked medium problems); the same trick with XOR and remainders; difference arrays, which run the idea backwards to make range updates cheap; 2D prefix sums for grids; and Kadane's algorithm for the maximum subarray, a neighbouring linear scan that is often grouped with them.
primer:
The mental model: the odometer

A car's odometer shows the total distance driven since the car was made. If you want to know how far you drove on a particular trip, you do not need a record of every kilometre; you note the odometer at the start and the end, and subtract. The odometer is a running total, and the trip distance is the difference of two running totals.

A prefix-sum array is an odometer for an array. For an array a, define pre[i] as the sum of the first i elements. Then the sum of any contiguous slice — any subarray a[l..r] — is the reading at the end minus the reading at the start: pre[r+1] − pre[l].

Two things in that picture are worth fixing in memory. First, pre has one more entry than a, and pre[0] = 0. This sentinel means a range that starts at index 0 needs no special case: its sum is pre[r+1] − pre[0]. Second, think of pre[i] as living on the boundary before element i. Then "sum from boundary l to boundary r+1" reads naturally, and the +1 stops being mysterious.

Building the array is one pass: pre[i+1] = pre[i] + a[i]. After that, every range sum is O(1). So q queries cost O(n + q) instead of O(n·q).

The idea generalises to any combining operation you can undo. Sums undo with subtraction. XOR undoes with XOR (x ^ x = 0), so prefix XORs give the XOR of any range. Counts are sums of 0/1 indicators, so "how many vowels in s[l..r]" is a prefix count. What does not work directly is max or min: knowing the maximum of the first 9 elements and of the first 3 does not tell you the maximum of elements 3 to 8. Those need other structures (al27).

It helps to see the cost difference concretely. With n = 100,000 and q = 100,000 queries, each covering on average half the array, the brute force adds about 5 × 10⁹ numbers — minutes in Python. The prefix version adds 100,000 numbers once and then does 100,000 subtractions: a fraction of a second. The answer is identical; only the repeated work is gone. This is the purest example of the principle from al1, "the optimal solution is the brute force with one kind of repeated work removed", and it is worth recognising the shape, because the same shape hides inside much harder problems.

The analogy breaks in one useful way: an odometer only goes forward, but you will also run the idea in reverse — storing differences so that a range update becomes two point changes. That is the difference array, covered below.
body:
Building and using a prefix array

The canonical code, with the invariant written as a comment so the indexing is never in doubt:

def build_prefix(a):
    pre = [0] * (len(a) + 1)
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        pre[i + 1] = pre[i] + x      # invariant: pre[i] = sum(a[:i])
    return pre

def range_sum(pre, l, r):            # inclusive l..r
    return pre[r + 1] - pre[l]

In Python, itertools.accumulate(a, initial=0) builds the same list in one line. Trace it on a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]: pre = [0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14]. The sum of a[1..3] is pre[4] − pre[1] = 9 − 3 = 6, which matches 1 + 4 + 1.

When you see "many range-sum queries on an array that does not change", this is the whole solution. It is also a building block inside many other solutions: average of every window of size k is (pre[i+k] − pre[i]) / k; "is there a subarray of length at least L with average at least x" subtracts x from every element and asks about prefix sums; "pivot index" asks for i where pre[i] equals total − pre[i+1].

The key upgrade: prefix sums plus a hash map

Now a harder question: how many subarrays have sum exactly k? The brute force tries all O(n²) pairs (l, r). With prefix sums each pair is O(1), but there are still n² pairs. Where is the repeated work?

Fix the right end r. A subarray a[l..r] has sum k exactly when pre[r+1] − pre[l] = k, i.e. when pre[l] = pre[r+1] − k. So for each r we are asking: "how many earlier prefix values equal one specific number?" That is a repeated search for a specific value — the signal for a hash map (al4). Keep a dictionary from prefix value to how many times it has appeared so far; then each r takes O(1).

def subarray_sum(a, k):
    count = {0: 1}          # the empty prefix: sum 0 seen once
    run = ans = 0
    for x in a:
        run += x                        # run = pre[r+1]
        ans += count.get(run - k, 0)    # earlier prefixes equal to run-k
        count[run] = count.get(run, 0) + 1
    return ans

Trace it on a = [1, 2, 1, -1, 2], k = 3:

xrunrun − kcount[run − k]anscount after
11−200{0:1, 1:1}
23011{0:1, 1:1, 3:1}
14112{…, 4:1}
−13013{…, 3:2}
25203{…, 5:1}

Three subarrays: [1, 2], [2, 1], and [1, 2, 1, −1]. Notice two decisions. The seed {0: 1} represents the empty prefix, so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted (the first hit, [1, 2], needed it). And we look up before recording the current prefix, so a subarray is never empty when k = 0.

This works with negative numbers, which is why it beats the sliding window here: a window needs "adding an element never decreases the sum", which only holds for non-negative values (al6).

Three variations use the same skeleton with a different value stored:

  • Longest subarray with sum k (or with equal 0s and 1s, after mapping 0 → −1 so the target is 0): store the first index of each prefix value instead of a count, seeded with {0: −1}. The longest subarray ending at r starts just after the earliest matching prefix.
  • Subarrays with sum divisible by k: two prefixes with the same remainder mod k differ by a multiple of k. Count remainders instead of values.
  • Subarrays with XOR equal to k: prefix XOR, and look up run ^ k, because XOR is its own inverse.

Difference arrays: cheap range updates

Now the opposite problem: you receive many updates "add v to every element of a[l..r]", and only at the end do you need the final array. Applying each update directly costs O(r − l + 1), so 10⁵ updates on 10⁵ elements is 10¹⁰ steps.

Turn the prefix idea around. Store a difference array d, where d[i] = a[i] − a[i−1] — how much the value changes at position i. The original array is the prefix sum of d. Adding v to a whole range a[l..r] changes only two differences: the value jumps up by v at l, and drops back by v at r + 1. Everything in between keeps the same differences.

def apply_updates(n, updates):          # updates: (l, r, v), inclusive
    d = [0] * (n + 1)                   # one extra slot for r + 1 = n
    for l, r, v in updates:
        d[l] += v
        d[r + 1] -= v
    out, run = [], 0
    for i in range(n):
        run += d[i]
        out.append(run)
    return out

Each update is O(1) and the rebuild is O(n), so the total is O(n + u) for u updates. This is the solution to "Corporate Flight Bookings" (seats booked on ranges of flights) and "Car Pooling" (passengers getting on at one stop and off at another: +p at pickup, −p at drop-off, and the running sum is the number on board — fail if it ever exceeds capacity). The same idea, with sorted event points instead of an array, becomes the sweep line in al11.

Prefix sums in two dimensions

For a grid, let P[r][c] be the sum of the rectangle from the top-left corner (0, 0) to (r−1, c−1), with an extra row and column of zeros as sentinels. Each cell is built from three neighbours:

P[r+1][c+1] = g[r][c] + P[r][c+1] + P[r+1][c] - P[r][c]

The rectangle above and the rectangle to the left overlap in the top-left block, which was added twice, so it is subtracted once. Querying a rectangle (r1, c1)–(r2, c2) uses the same inclusion–exclusion in reverse: take the big rectangle to (r2, c2), remove the strip above r1 and the strip left of c1, and add back their overlap, which was removed twice.

def rect(P, r1, c1, r2, c2):
    return P[r2+1][c2+1] - P[r1][c2+1] - P[r2+1][c1] + P[r1][c1]

Building is O(R·C) and each query is O(1). This solves "Range Sum Query 2D" directly, and it is the standard trick for "count something in every k×k sub-square" problems, such as image processing filters and "largest square of 1s with sum constraints".

Kadane's algorithm: the maximum subarray

"Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum" looks like a prefix-sum problem — maximise pre[r+1] − pre[l] — and that view works: scan r while tracking the minimum prefix seen so far. The more common formulation is Kadane's algorithm, which is really a tiny dynamic program. Let cur be the best sum of a subarray that ends exactly at the current index. For the next element x there are only two options: extend the previous best (cur + x) or start fresh at x. Take the larger:

def max_subarray(a):
    cur = best = a[0]
    for x in a[1:]:
        cur = max(x, cur + x)     # extend, or restart here
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

Trace [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]: cur goes −2, 1, −2, 4, 3, 5, 6, 1, 5 and best ends at 6, the subarray [4, −1, 2, 1]. Initialise from the first element rather than 0, or an all-negative array wrongly returns 0 (the empty subarray), unless the problem allows empty. The restart rule has a clean meaning: if the best subarray ending at the previous index has a negative sum, it can only hurt, so drop it.

Variants follow from the DP view. Maximum product subarray: a negative number turns the smallest product into the largest, so track both the max and min product ending here. Circular maximum subarray: the answer either does not wrap (plain Kadane) or wraps, in which case it equals total − (minimum subarray).

Prefix sums on strings and counts

Prefix sums are not only for numeric arrays. Any question of the form "how many X are in positions l..r" turns into prefix counts of a 0/1 indicator. For example, "for each query (l, r), how many vowels are in s[l..r]?" — build cnt[i+1] = cnt[i] + (s[i] in "aeiou"), and each query is cnt[r+1] − cnt[l]. If you need counts of all 26 letters for many ranges (say, "can s[l..r] be rearranged into a palindrome?"), keep 26 prefix arrays, or one prefix array of 26-element count vectors, or — the elegant version — a single prefix bitmask where bit c flips each time letter c appears. A range can be rearranged into a palindrome when at most one letter has an odd count, which is "the XOR of two prefix masks has at most one bit set". That turns a 26-letter count comparison into one XOR and a bit test (al24).

The general lesson: decide what quantity you would compute for a range in the brute force, check that it combines with an invertible operation, and store its running version.

Recognising the pattern

Reach for prefix techniques when you see: "sum/count/XOR of a subarray or range", "number of subarrays with property X" where X is about a sum, "many queries on a fixed array", "apply many range increments", or a grid with "sum of a rectangle". Check the precondition: the combine must be invertible (sum, count, XOR — not max/min), and for plain prefix arrays the data must not change between queries. If values change, move to a Fenwick tree (al27).

Before coding, run a short checklist that catches nearly every prefix bug. Is my prefix array one longer than the input, with a zero at the front? Is my range formula pre[r+1] − pre[l] for an inclusive range — and did I convert the problem's indexing (some problems give 1-based l and r) exactly once? For the hash-map version, did I seed the map with the empty prefix, and do I look up before I insert? For first-index maps, do I store only the first occurrence (for longest) or update every time (for shortest)? For difference arrays, is the array n + 1 long so that d[r+1] never goes out of bounds, and is the end of the range inclusive or exclusive in this problem? Five questions, thirty seconds, and they cover the mistakes interviewers see most often.

Practice in the DSA list: Range Sum Query — Immutable, Find Pivot Index, Product of Array Except Self, Maximum Subarray, Subarray Sum Equals K, Contiguous Array, Subarray Sums Divisible by K, Continuous Subarray Sum, Corporate Flight Bookings, Car Pooling, Range Sum Query 2D.
deep:
Why the hash map makes it linear: pairs become lookups

Many "count subarrays" problems are really "count pairs of prefixes (i, j) with i < j and some relation between pre[i] and pre[j]". When the relation is equality after a shift (pre[i] = pre[j] − k) or equality of a derived key (same remainder, same XOR), a hash map counts all such pairs in one pass: process j left to right and look up how many earlier i match. When the relation is an inequality — "count subarrays with sum at most k" with negative numbers — a hash map cannot help, because there is no single key to look up. Then you need the earlier prefixes kept in sorted order: a merge-sort count or a Fenwick tree over compressed prefix values, giving O(n log n). Recognising "equality → hash map, inequality → sorted structure" is a senior-level shortcut.

Remainders and the pigeonhole principle

"Is there a non-empty subarray whose sum is divisible by n?" — always yes for an array of n integers. There are n + 1 prefix sums (including pre[0]) but only n possible remainders mod n, so two prefixes share a remainder, and the subarray between them is divisible by n. This pigeonhole argument is the theory behind the remainder-map technique and occasionally appears as a "prove it" follow-up. It also explains a common trap: in languages like Java and C++, the remainder of a negative number is negative, so −1 % 5 is −1, not 4, and identical residues would be stored under different keys. Normalise with ((x % k) + k) % k.

Why this is O(n) time but O(n) space, and when space matters

The hash-map version stores up to n + 1 distinct prefix values. For an array of 10⁷ elements that is a dictionary of ten million entries — several hundred megabytes in Python. If the problem only needs existence ("is there a subarray with sum k?") and values are non-negative, a two-pointer window uses O(1) space. If values are bounded and small, a plain array indexed by prefix value (shifted to be non-negative) replaces the dictionary with something many times smaller and faster. Interviewers sometimes probe exactly this with "what if memory is tight?", and the answer depends on which precondition you can exploit.

Overflow and very large sums

Prefix sums grow. With 10⁵ values up to 10⁹, the total reaches 10¹⁴, which overflows 32-bit integers. Python integers are unbounded, so this never bites in Python, but in Java or C++ use 64-bit (long). If an answer is required modulo 10⁹ + 7, store prefixes mod p and compute range sums as (pre[r+1] − pre[l] + p) % p so the result is not negative. Mentioning overflow when you discuss a prefix solution is a good signal even in Python interviews, because it shows you know the code would be ported.

Higher-order differences and polynomial updates

A difference array handles "add a constant over a range". If an update adds an arithmetic progression (1, 2, 3, … over the range), take differences twice: a second-order difference array turns it into a constant number of point updates, and two prefix passes rebuild it. This generalises: adding a polynomial of degree k needs k + 1 levels of differences. It is rare in interviews but appears in harder online assessments ("add 1, 2, 3, … to a range"), and it shows the structure behind the trick: prefix sum and difference are inverse operations, like integration and differentiation.

Minimum-prefix view of the maximum subarray

Kadane's algorithm and prefix sums are two views of the same problem. The maximum subarray ending at r is pre[r+1] minus the smallest prefix before it. So scanning r while maintaining min_prefix gives best = max(best, pre[r+1] − min_prefix). This view generalises where Kadane's does not: "maximum subarray sum with length at least L" keeps the minimum over prefixes at least L positions back; "maximum subarray sum not exceeding k" needs the smallest prefix that is at least pre[r+1] − k, which requires a sorted structure and binary search — O(n log n). Knowing both views lets you adapt to whichever constraint the follow-up adds.

Static range queries beyond sums

For non-invertible operations on a static array, a sparse table precomputes the answer for every range whose length is a power of two, in O(n log n). A query for min(a[l..r]) takes two overlapping power-of-two blocks covering [l, r] and returns the min of the two, in O(1). Overlap is harmless because min and max are idempotent (min(x, x) = x); for sums, overlap would double-count, which is why sums use prefix arrays instead. When the array changes, both options give way to a segment tree, covered in al27.
prod:
In the interview room

Prefix techniques are graded on two things: whether you see that the brute force recomputes range sums, and whether your indices are exactly right. The most common failure is an off-by-one at the boundary — using pre[r] − pre[l] for an inclusive range, or forgetting the {0: 1} seed so subarrays starting at index 0 are missed. Write the invariant ("pre[i] is the sum of the first i elements") as a comment before writing the loop, and test the range that starts at index 0 and the one that ends at the last index specifically.

The second common failure is reaching for a sliding window on a sum problem with negative numbers. The window gives the right answer on the examples (which often have only positives) and wrong answers on hidden tests. Ask "can values be negative?" in step 1 of the method, and if they can, use prefix sums with a hash map.

Interviewers often extend the problem with a follow-up. "Now the array changes between queries" means a Fenwick tree. "Now return the subarray itself, not the count" means storing first indices instead of counts. "Now it is a stream" means the prefix-plus-hash-map version already works online, because it only looks backwards — say so.

Finally, expect the "explain it to me" probe. Interviewers ask "why do you seed the map with zero?" or "why do you look up before inserting?" to check that you derived the solution rather than memorised it. The best answers tie each line back to the equation pre[l] = pre[r+1] − k: the seed is the l = 0 case, and the order of operations guarantees l ≤ r so the subarray is non-empty. Candidates who can say that in one sentence each come across as fluent; candidates who say "that is how the template goes" invite a harder follow-up.

On online assessments, prefix sums are a frequent "hidden" requirement: the problem looks like a simple loop, but the constraints (n and q both up to 10⁵ or 2 × 10⁵) make the per-query loop time out. Read the constraints before you design, and if you see many queries over a static array, build the prefix array first.

In real systems

Prefix sums are everywhere once you look for them. Databases and analytics engines precompute cumulative aggregates so dashboards can answer arbitrary date ranges instantly — the revenue example from the start of the lesson. Image processing uses 2D prefix sums under the name summed-area table or integral image; the Viola–Jones face detector (2001) used them to compute thousands of rectangle features per image in constant time each, which is what made real-time face detection practical on early-2000s hardware. Time-series systems store cumulative counters (Prometheus counters are monotonically increasing running totals) and compute rates as differences between two samples — exactly the odometer model, with the same pitfall: when a counter resets because a process restarts, the difference goes negative and must be handled. Difference arrays appear in scheduling and capacity planning: booking systems record "+1 at check-in, −1 at check-out" and a running sum gives occupancy on every day.
myths: Prefix sums only help when the array never changes.

Plain prefix sums do need a static array, because one update changes every later prefix. But the idea extends: a Fenwick tree (al27) keeps prefix sums under point updates in O(log n), and a difference array handles many range updates followed by one rebuild. Static is the simple case, not the only one.
Sliding window and prefix-sum-with-hash-map solve the same problems.

A shrinking sliding window for 'subarray with sum k' only works when all values are non-negative, because then growing the window never decreases the sum. With negative numbers the window has no monotone rule for when to shrink, and you need prefix sums plus a hash map, which work for any integers.
You need a 1-based array for prefix sums.

You need a prefix array one longer than the input, with pre[0] = 0 meaning 'sum of nothing'. That extra slot is what removes the special case for ranges starting at index 0; the input itself stays 0-based. Mixing the two conventions is the classic off-by-one bug.
Kadane's algorithm is a greedy trick you just have to memorise.

Kadane's is a one-variable dynamic program: best[i] = max(a[i], best[i−1] + a[i]), the best subarray that ends exactly at i. Seeing it that way explains it and lets you adapt it to variants such as maximum product (track both max and min) or circular arrays.
Counting subarrays with sum k needs the prefix values to be stored in order.

Only the counts of each prefix value seen so far matter, not their order or positions, because every earlier prefix equal to current − k pairs with the current index. A dictionary from prefix value to count is enough, and seeding it with {0: 1} handles subarrays that start at index 0.
lab:
Verify the prefix-plus-hash-map solution against brute force, including negative numbers, and see why a sliding window fails on them.

  1. Save as prefix_lab.py: 
    import random

def brute(a, k):
    return sum(1 for l in range(len(a)) for r in range(l, len(a))
               if sum(a[l:r+1]) == k)

def prefix_hash(a, k):
    count, run, ans = {0: 1}, 0, 0
    for x in a:
        run += x
        ans += count.get(run - k, 0)
        count[run] = count.get(run, 0) + 1
    return ans

def window(a, k):                 # only valid for non-negative a
    ans = left = s = 0
    for right, x in enumerate(a):
        s += x
        while s > k and left <= right:
            s -= a[left]; left += 1
        if s == k and left <= right: ans += 1
    return ans

for neg in (False, True):
    bad = 0
    for _ in range(3000):
        a = [random.randint(-3 if neg else 0, 3) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 8))]
        k = random.randint(-3, 6)
        assert prefix_hash(a, k) == brute(a, k), (a, k)
        bad += window(a, k) != brute(a, k)
    print("negatives" if neg else "non-negative", "window wrong on", bad, "of 3000")
  2. Run python prefix_lab.py. The assertion never fires: the hash-map version matches brute force in both modes.
  3. Look at the window counts. The window is wrong on many cases even without negatives, because this simple version undercounts when zeros allow several valid starting points; with negatives it is wrong much more often.

What this proves: the prefix-plus-hash-map method is correct for any integers, while a window needs strictly positive values (or extra care with zeros) to be correct for "sum exactly k". A random stress test finds that in seconds, which is why you should run one whenever you adapt a template.
recap: A prefix-sum array stores pre[i] = sum of the first i elements, with pre[0] = 0, so the sum of a[l..r] is pre[r+1] − pre[l] in O(1).
Building the prefix array is one O(n) pass; it turns q range-sum queries from O(n·q) into O(n + q).
Subarray sum equals k becomes 'how many earlier prefixes equal current − k?', answered by a hash map of prefix counts seeded with {0: 1}; this works with negative numbers.
The same trick works with any invertible combine: prefix XOR, prefix counts, or prefix sums modulo k for divisibility.
A difference array records +v at the start of a range and −v just after its end, so each range update is O(1); one prefix-sum pass then reconstructs the final array.
Two-dimensional prefix sums use inclusion–exclusion: the rectangle sum is P[r2+1][c2+1] − P[r1][c2+1] − P[r2+1][c1] + P[r1][c1].
Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum subarray in O(n) by tracking the best sum ending at each position.
Prefix arrays need a static array; with point updates use a Fenwick or segment tree instead.
glossary: Adjacent in the array with no gaps; a subarray is contiguous, a subsequence need not be.
An array d where d[i] = a[i] − a[i−1]; adding v to d[l] and subtracting v from d[r+1] adds v to the whole range a[l..r] after a prefix sum.
Solving a problem by building answers to subproblems from earlier stored answers; Kadane's algorithm is a one-variable DP. Taught in al21.
Data structures and algorithms; the DSA list in this app groups practice problems by pattern.
A structure that supports prefix sums and point updates in O(log n) each; taught in al27.
Adding and subtracting overlapping regions so each cell is counted exactly once, used for 2D prefix sums.
An operation you can undo, like addition (undo with subtraction) or XOR (undo with XOR). Prefix tricks need it to extract a range from two prefixes.
An O(n) scan that finds the maximum-sum subarray by tracking the best sum ending at each index.
The running total of an array up to a position; pre[i] is the sum of the first i elements.
A request for information, such as 'what is the sum of a[3..9]?'; problems often ask many queries on one array.
An operation that changes every element in an interval, such as 'add 5 to a[2..7]'.
A value updated as you scan an array, such as the sum so far.
An extra value, like pre[0] = 0 or a seeded {0: 1}, that removes a special case at the boundary.
A contiguous slice a[l..r] of an array.
Exclusive or: a bitwise operation where x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, so it is its own inverse.
drill:
Diagnose the bug

A candidate writes this to count subarrays with sum k and it fails the test a = [3], k = 3 (expected 1, returns 0). Find the bug, explain it in one sentence, and fix it.

def count(a, k):
    seen, run, ans = {}, 0, 0
    for x in a:
        run += x
        seen[run] = seen.get(run, 0) + 1
        ans += seen.get(run - k, 0)
    return ans
Answer

There are two bugs. First, seen is not seeded with {0: 1}, so the empty prefix is missing and no subarray starting at index 0 can be found — that is why [3] with k = 3 returns 0. Second, the current prefix is recorded before the lookup; when k = 0 this counts the current prefix against itself, i.e. an empty subarray, so every index adds at least one spurious match. The fix is to initialise seen = {0: 1} and swap the two lines so the lookup happens before the insert. A good way to explain it out loud: "pre[l] must come from strictly earlier positions, including the empty prefix at position 0".

Choose the technique

A hotel has 10⁵ bookings, each (check-in day, check-out day), over a 365-day year. Find the maximum number of rooms occupied on any night. Which technique, what complexity, and what is the one boundary decision you must ask about?

Answer

Difference array over days: +1 at check-in, −1 at check-out, then a prefix sum gives occupancy each night and the answer is its maximum. O(bookings + days) time, O(days) space. The boundary question: does a guest occupy the room on the check-out night? Normally not — a stay [in, out) occupies nights in..out−1 — so the −1 goes at index out, not out + 1. If days were up to 10⁹ instead of 365, the array would be too large; sort the 2·10⁵ events instead and sweep them, which is the sweep-line technique of al11.
qa: E
How do you answer many range-sum queries on a fixed array quickly?
Build a prefix array with pre[0] = 0 and pre[i+1] = pre[i] + a[i] in one O(n) pass. Then the sum of a[l..r] inclusive is pre[r+1] − pre[l], O(1) per query. Total O(n + q) instead of O(n·q).
E
Why does the prefix array have length n + 1?

pre[i] means the sum of the first i elements, and 'the first 0 elements' sum to 0. That extra slot means a range starting at index 0 uses pre[0] = 0 with no special case. It also keeps the formula pre[r+1] − pre[l] uniform.
E
Explain Kadane's algorithm.

Scan once keeping cur, the best sum of a subarray that ends at the current index, and best, the best seen anywhere. At each element, cur = max(x, cur + x): either extend the previous subarray or start fresh here, whichever is larger. best = max(best, cur). O(n) time, O(1) space; initialise with the first element so all-negative arrays work.
M
Count the subarrays whose sum is exactly k, where values can be negative.

Keep a running prefix sum and a hash map from prefix value to how many times it has occurred, seeded with {0: 1}. At each index, the subarrays ending here with sum k correspond to earlier prefixes equal to current − k, so add count[current − k] to the answer, then record the current prefix. O(n) time and space.

Follow-up: Why not a sliding window? — With negative values, extending the window can decrease the sum, so there is no rule for when to move the left pointer; the window only works for non-negative arrays.
M
How would you apply a million 'add v to a[l..r]' updates to an array of a million elements?

Use a difference array: for each update add v at d[l] and subtract v at d[r+1], which is O(1). After all updates, a prefix sum over d reconstructs the final array in O(n). Total O(n + updates) instead of O(n · updates).
M
Find the longest subarray with equal numbers of 0s and 1s.

Map 0 to −1 so the condition becomes 'sum is zero'. A subarray a[l..r] has sum zero exactly when two prefix sums are equal, so store the first index at which each prefix value appears (seed {0: −1}) and at each index compare with that first occurrence. Store only the first index, because we want the longest span. O(n).
M
Count subarrays whose sum is divisible by k.

Two prefixes with the same remainder mod k bound a subarray whose sum is divisible by k. So count prefix remainders in a map seeded with {0: 1} and add the count of the current remainder each step. In languages where % can return negatives, normalise with ((p % k) + k) % k; Python's % is already non-negative for positive k.
Follow-up: Now the subarray must have length at least 2. — Store the first index of each remainder instead of counts, and check that the gap is at least 2.
M
How do 2D prefix sums work?

P[r][c] holds the sum of the rectangle from (0,0) to (r−1,c−1). Build it with P[r+1][c+1] = grid[r][c] + P[r][c+1] + P[r+1][c] − P[r][c]. The sum of a rectangle with corners (r1,c1) and (r2,c2) is P[r2+1][c2+1] − P[r1][c2+1] − P[r2+1][c1] + P[r1][c1]: subtract the strip above and the strip to the left, then add back the corner subtracted twice.
M
Compute the product of all elements except self without division.

Two passes: a left-to-right prefix product where out[i] holds the product of everything before i, then a right-to-left pass multiplying in a running suffix product. Division would fail with zeros; the prefix/suffix version handles them naturally. O(n) time, O(1) extra space besides the output.
H
Maximum subarray sum in a circular array.

Either the best subarray does not wrap, which is plain Kadane's, or it wraps, in which case it is the total minus the minimum subarray (the part left out). Compute both with Kadane's for max and for min. The answer is max(maxSub, total − minSub), except when all numbers are negative, where total − minSub would be 0 for an empty subarray, so return maxSub.

Follow-up: Why does the wrap case equal total minus the minimum subarray? — A wrapping subarray's complement is a contiguous non-wrapping subarray, so maximising the kept part means minimising the removed part.
H
Given many queries 'how many elements in a[l..r] equal x', with up to 10⁵ queries and values up to 10⁵, what would you do?

If the number of distinct x queried is small, a prefix count array per value answers each query in O(1). In general that is too much memory, so store for each value the sorted list of its positions and answer with two binary searches (bisect) for the count of positions in [l, r] — O(log n) per query and O(n) memory total.
H
When is a prefix technique not applicable, and what do you use instead?

When the combine operation is not invertible, like max or min: you cannot get max(a[l..r]) from two prefix maxima. Then use a sparse table for static arrays (O(1) queries after O(n log n) preprocessing) or a segment tree for arrays that change. Also when the array changes between queries: use a Fenwick tree for sums with point updates.

t: Hashing and frequency counting: sets, maps and canonical keys
sum: Turn repeated searches into O(1) lookups: sets for membership, maps for value→index and counts, canonical keys for grouping, and the classic tricks — complement lookup, sequence starts, last-seen index, bijections and meet-in-the-middle counting.
prereq: al1
The optimal solution is usually the brute force with one kind of repeated work removed.
al2
Hash lookups are O(1) expected, O(n) worst case; hashing a key of length k costs O(k).
al3
Prefix sums plus a hash map count subarrays with a target sum in O(n).
why:
An engineer is asked to find which user IDs appear more than once in a log of 200,000 sign-ups. The first version compares every entry with every other entry: about 2 × 10¹⁰ comparisons. In Python that takes hours. A colleague rewrites it in five lines: walk through the log once, and for each ID ask "have I seen this before?" using a set. It finishes in a tenth of a second. Nothing clever happened to the logic; the only change is that the question "have I seen this?" went from scanning everything seen so far to a single lookup.

That question — have I seen this value, where, and how many times? — is the most common kind of repeated work in interview problems. Two Sum asks it for the complement of every element. Anagram problems ask it for every letter. "First unique character", "longest consecutive sequence", "contains duplicate within k", "group the anagrams", "count pairs with difference k", "isomorphic strings": all of them have a brute force that searches again and again, and all of them become linear when each search is replaced by a hash lookup.

Hashing is therefore the first optimisation to try in step 4 of the method. It is also a building block inside later patterns: sliding windows track counts in a map (al6), graph searches track visited nodes in a set (al16), and dynamic programming caches answers in a map (al21). Getting fluent with it pays off everywhere.

This lesson covers what a hash table actually does and what it costs; the three roles a hash structure plays (membership, position, count); the canonical-key idea for grouping; and a set of classic tricks — complement lookup, starting only from sequence starts, last-seen indices, two-way maps for bijections, and meet-in-the-middle counting — each with a worked trace.
primer:
The mental model: a coat check

At a theatre coat check, you hand over your coat and get a numbered ticket. When you come back, the attendant does not search through every coat on every rack; they read your number and go straight to that hook. A hash table works the same way. A hash function turns a key (a number, a string, a tuple) into an integer, the table uses that integer to pick a slot called a bucket, and the value is stored there. Looking the key up later recomputes the same hash and goes straight to the same bucket. No scanning, so the cost does not grow with the number of stored items.

The analogy breaks in one important way. Coat-check tickets are unique, but hash values are not: two different keys can land in the same bucket, which is called a collision. The table must handle it — by storing several entries per bucket or by probing for another free slot — and then compare the actual keys to find the right one. With a good hash function and a table that grows as it fills, collisions are rare and short, so operations are O(1) on average (expected). With a terrible hash function, or keys chosen by an attacker to collide, everything lands in one place and each operation degrades to O(n).

Three roles, two structures

In Python you use two hash structures: a set stores keys only, and a dict stores key → value pairs. Interview problems use them in three roles, and naming the role makes the design obvious:

  • Membership — "have I seen x?" — a set. Duplicate detection, visited nodes, "is the complement present?".
  • Position — "where did I see x?" — a dict from value to index (first, last, or all). Two Sum, "nearest duplicate", longest subarray with a property.
  • Count — "how many times have I seen x?" — a dict from value to count, usually collections.Counter. Anagrams, top-k frequent, majority element, window character counts.

A useful habit is to say the role and the key out loud as part of step 4: "the inner loop searches for target − x, so I want a map from value to index, keyed by value". Once you can say that sentence, the code almost writes itself, and the interviewer hears that you chose the structure for a reason rather than out of habit.

It is also worth knowing what a hash structure cannot do. It has no order: you cannot ask a set for "the smallest element greater than x" or "all keys between 10 and 20" without scanning everything. Questions like those need sorting, binary search (al7), a heap (al10) or a balanced search tree. If a follow-up adds an ordering requirement to a hashing problem, that is your cue to switch structures.

Whenever your brute force has an inner loop that answers one of those three questions, a hash structure replaces it, and the solution usually drops from O(n²) to O(n).
body:
Membership: the set

The simplest use: detect a duplicate. Walk the array once; before adding each value, check whether it is already in the set.

def has_duplicate(a):
    seen = set()
    for x in a:
        if x in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(x)
    return False

O(n) expected time, O(n) space. Compare the two alternatives you should mention: the double loop (O(n²) time, O(1) space) and sorting then comparing neighbours (O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space with an in-place sort). Choosing between them is a time–memory trade-off, and saying so is part of a strong answer.

A set also gives fast set algebra: a & b (intersection), a | b (union), a - b (difference). "Find the common elements of two arrays" is set(a) & set(b), O(n + m).

Position: value → index, and the complement trick

Two Sum is the template for the position role, and it introduces the complement idea. For each element x, the partner we need is target − x. Instead of searching for it, we look it up among the elements already passed:

def two_sum(a, target):
    where = {}                         # value -> index, for a[0..i-1]
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        if target - x in where:
            return [where[target - x], i]
        where[x] = i
    return []

The same move solves many "pair" problems once you write down what the partner must be. "Count pairs with difference k": the partner of x is x − k or x + k. "Count pairs whose sum is divisible by 60" (song durations): the partner of remainder r is remainder (60 − r) % 60, so count remainders in a map. "Find a pair of equal values at most k apart": store the last index of each value, and check i − last[x] ≤ k.

Which index to store depends on the question. For "longest" questions you want the first occurrence (to maximise the distance); for "nearest" or "within k" questions you want the last. For "all pairs" you store a count or a list.

Count: frequency maps

A frequency map answers "how many times does each value occur?" in one pass. Python's Counter does it in one line, and also gives most_common(k).

from collections import Counter
def is_anagram(s, t):
    return len(s) == len(t) and Counter(s) == Counter(t)

def first_unique(s):
    c = Counter(s)                 # pass 1: count everything
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):     # pass 2: in original order
        if c[ch] == 1:
            return i
    return -1

The two-pass shape is common: count everything first, then make a second pass that uses the counts. When the alphabet is small and known — lowercase English letters — a list of 26 integers indexed by ord(ch) - ord('a') does the same job faster and with fixed memory, and some interviewers like to see that you know it.

Counting also gives quick tests of feasibility. "Can the letters of magazine build note?" — every count in Counter(note) must be at most the count in Counter(magazine); in Python, not (Counter(note) - Counter(magazine)). "Can this string be rearranged into a palindrome?" — at most one letter may have an odd count.

Grouping by a canonical key

"Group these words into anagram groups" asks you to put items into the same bucket exactly when they are equivalent. The trick is to compute a canonical key: a value that is identical for equivalent items and different for non-equivalent ones. Then a defaultdict(list) does the grouping.

from collections import defaultdict
def group_anagrams(words):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for w in words:
        key = [0] * 26
        for ch in w:
            key[ord(ch) - 97] += 1
        groups[tuple(key)].append(w)   # list -> tuple: hashable
    return list(groups.values())

Trace it on ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]: "eat", "tea" and "ate" all produce the count tuple with a, e and t equal to 1, so they share a key; "tan" and "nat" share another; "bat" is alone. Two choices of key are common. The sorted word ("".join(sorted(w))) is simplest but costs O(L log L) per word of length L. The count tuple costs O(L) plus a fixed 26. Both must be hashable: a Python list cannot be a key, because it could change after insertion and break the table, so convert it to a tuple.

Canonical keys appear well beyond anagrams. "Group strings that are shifts of each other" ("abc", "bcd", "xyz"): key = the tuple of differences between consecutive letters mod 26. "Find duplicate subtrees": key = a serialisation of each subtree. "Group points on the same line through the origin": key = the reduced fraction (dy/g, dx/g) with a sign convention. The question to ask is always "what representation is equal exactly when the items should be grouped?"

Starting only from the start: Longest Consecutive Sequence

"Given an unsorted array, find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers, in O(n)." Sorting gives O(n log n), so the O(n) requirement is a hint to use a set. Put every number in a set, and then for each number count upward while the next number is present. The danger is that this counts the same run many times: in the run 1, 2, 3, 4, starting from 1 counts 4, from 2 counts 3, and so on — O(n²) on one long run.

The fix is to only start counting from numbers that are the start of a run: x is a start exactly when x − 1 is not in the set.

def longest_consecutive(a):
    s = set(a)
    best = 0
    for x in s:
        if x - 1 not in s:             # x starts a run
            y = x
            while y + 1 in s:
                y += 1
            best = max(best, y - x + 1)
    return best

Iterating over the set (not the array) also handles duplicates for free. This "only start from the start" trick is a small instance of a general idea: when a nested loop could revisit the same elements, find a condition that assigns each element to exactly one outer iteration.

Two-way maps: bijections

"Are 'egg' and 'add' isomorphic?" — can each character of s be replaced consistently to get t, with no two characters mapping to the same one? A single map s→t checks consistency in one direction only. With s = "ab", t = "cc", the map {a: c, b: c} is consistent, yet two characters map to c, so the strings are not isomorphic. You need a second map t→s, and both must agree at every position. The same structure solves "Word Pattern" (pattern letters ↔ words). Whenever a problem says "one-to-one" or "bijection", plan for two maps.

Meet in the middle: counting with half-sums

"Given four arrays of length n ≤ 200, count tuples with A[i] + B[j] + C[k] + D[l] = 0." The brute force is O(n⁴) = 1.6 × 10⁹. Split the four arrays into two pairs. Count every possible a + b in a Counter (n² = 40,000 sums). Then for every c + d, the matching first halves are those summing to −(c + d), and the Counter tells you how many in O(1). Total O(n²). This is the complement trick applied to sums of groups rather than single elements, and it is called meet in the middle. The same idea turns subset-sum on 40 items from 2⁴⁰ (about 10¹²) into two lists of 2²⁰ (about 10⁶) sums each.

Composite keys: Sudoku and grids

Keys can be tuples, which lets one set track several facts. To validate a Sudoku board, every digit may appear once per row, column and 3×3 box. Store keys such as ("row", r, d), ("col", c, d) and ("box", r // 3, c // 3, d) in one set; if any key is already present when you add it, the board is invalid. Grid problems often use a set of (r, c) tuples for visited cells, which is clearer than a 2D boolean array when the grid is sparse or unbounded.

Counting without a map: the majority element

Sometimes a count can be kept with O(1) memory. "Find the element that appears more than n/2 times" can be solved with a Counter (O(n) space), but the Boyer–Moore majority vote does it with two variables: a candidate and a counter. Walk the array; if the counter is 0, adopt the current element as candidate; then add 1 if the element equals the candidate and subtract 1 otherwise. Each non-majority element can cancel at most one majority element, and the majority has more than half, so it survives as the final candidate. Trace [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]: the candidate goes 2 (count 1, 2), then 1 and 1 bring it to 0, the next 1 becomes the candidate, 2 cancels it, and the last 2 becomes the candidate with count 1 — answer 2. If the majority is not guaranteed to exist, a second pass must verify the candidate's count. Mentioning this after giving the Counter solution is a good way to answer "can you do it in O(1) space?".

Hashing, sorting or a plain array?

Three tools answer "count or find equal things", and choosing well is part of the score. A plain array indexed by value is the fastest when values are small non-negative integers or characters from a known alphabet: no hashing, no collisions, perfect cache behaviour. A hash map handles arbitrary keys in O(1) expected per operation but uses more memory per entry and gives no order. Sorting costs O(n log n), but afterwards equal items are adjacent and order-based follow-ups ("the k closest", "the next larger") become easy. A simple rule: if the key space is small and dense, use an array; if keys are arbitrary and you need one pass, use a hash map; if you need order or must save memory, sort.

Recognising the pattern

Reach for hashing when the brute force's inner loop searches for a specific value, a specific count, or "something equivalent to this". Signals in the problem statement: "duplicate", "unique", "frequency", "anagram", "pair that sums to", "group", "first non-repeating", "seen before", "O(n)" required on unsorted input. Then name the role — membership, position or count — and the key. If the key is not obvious, ask what makes two items "the same" for this problem.

Practice in the DSA list: Two Sum, Valid Anagram, Contains Duplicate II, Isomorphic Strings, Group Anagrams, Longest Consecutive Sequence, 4Sum II, Valid Sudoku, Subarray Sum Equals K (al3), Insert Delete GetRandom O(1).
deep:
How CPython's dict actually works

CPython's dict and set use open addressing: there is one array of slots, and when a key's preferred slot is taken, the table probes other slots in a pseudo-random sequence derived from the hash until it finds the key or an empty slot. Since Python 3.6 the dict is split into a compact array of entries kept in insertion order plus a sparse index table that holds positions into it — which is why iteration follows insertion order (guaranteed by the language from 3.7) and why dicts use less memory than they used to. The table resizes when it is about two-thirds full, so probes stay short; each resize rehashes everything, costing O(n), but resizes are geometric, so insertion is amortised O(1) (the dynamic-array argument from al2). Deletion leaves a "dummy" marker so probe sequences are not broken, which is why a dict that has had many deletions can be larger than its contents suggest.

Hashability and the equality contract

The rule that makes hash tables correct is: if a == b then hash(a) == hash(b). The table relies on it to look in the right bucket. That is why mutable objects such as lists are unhashable: if you inserted a list and then appended to it, its hash would change, and the entry would become unreachable. Tuples are hashable only if everything inside them is. Custom classes can define __eq__ and __hash__ together (dataclasses with frozen=True do this automatically). A classic bug is defining __eq__ without __hash__: Python then sets __hash__ to None and the objects cannot be put in sets. Another subtle one: 1 == 1.0 == True in Python, and they hash equally, so a dict treats them as the same key.

Worst cases and hash flooding

Expected O(1) assumes the keys do not collide systematically. In December 2011, researchers showed at the 28C3 conference that web frameworks in many languages could be knocked over by a single HTTP request containing thousands of form fields whose names were chosen to collide in the language's string hash; parsing the request into a hash table became quadratic and pinned a CPU for minutes. Languages responded by randomising string hashing per process (Python made it the default in 3.3 and later switched to the SipHash function). In interviews, the relevant takeaways are: say "O(1) expected"; know that integer keys in Python hash to themselves, so adversarial integer inputs can still collide on some judges; and know that sorting has no such worst case, which occasionally makes it the safer choice.

The hidden cost of big keys

Hashing a key costs time proportional to its size. Using whole substrings as keys — for example, putting every substring of length L into a set to find repeats — costs O(L) per substring, so O(n·L) overall, which is O(n²) when L is proportional to n. CPython caches the hash of a string object after computing it once, but every new slice is a new object. The professional fix is a rolling hash, which updates the hash of a sliding window in O(1) when one character leaves and one enters; it is the core of Rabin–Karp and is covered in al26. A cheaper fix for small alphabets is to encode each window as an integer (two bits per DNA letter, for instance) and update it with shifts.

Probabilistic cousins: when exactness is too expensive

A hash set of a billion URLs needs tens of gigabytes. Two structures trade exactness for memory and come up in system-design follow-ups. A Bloom filter uses a bit array and several hash functions: inserting sets k bits; a query says "definitely not present" if any bit is 0, or "probably present" otherwise — no false negatives, a tunable false-positive rate, about 10 bits per element for 1%. A Count-Min sketch keeps a small table of counters indexed by several hashes and answers frequency queries with a bounded overestimate. If an interviewer extends a hashing problem with "now the data does not fit in memory", mentioning partitioning by hash into files (so equal keys land in the same file) and these sketches shows the senior-level next step.
prod:
In the interview room

Hashing questions are usually where interviewers check fundamentals quickly, so fluency matters. The common mistakes are: using a list for membership (if x in seen_list), which silently makes the solution O(n²); using a list as a dict key and hitting TypeError: unhashable type; inserting before checking in complement problems, so an element pairs with itself; and claiming O(1) space for a solution that stores up to n entries. Say the space cost unprompted — "O(n) extra for the map" — and, if relevant, offer the sorting alternative with its O(1) extra space.

Expect the "why" probes on the clever ones. For Longest Consecutive Sequence, interviewers almost always ask why the nested loop is not quadratic; the answer is the aggregate argument (each number is counted by exactly one run, the one starting at its smallest element). For isomorphic strings, they ask why one map is not enough; have the "ab" → "cc" counterexample ready. For Group Anagrams, they ask about the complexity of the key; know that the sorted key is O(L log L) and the count key O(L).

A frequent follow-up is a constraint change that breaks hashing: "the input is a stream of a billion items and you have 1 GB of memory". Talk through partitioning (hash each item to one of k files so duplicates land together, then process each file in memory), approximate structures (a Bloom filter for membership, Count-Min for frequencies), or sorting externally.

Finally, keep an eye on what you return. Many hashing problems ask for indices, and storing values instead of indices (or the first index when the problem wants the last) is an easy way to produce plausible but wrong output. Re-read the "Output" answers from step 1 of the method before you code, and test one case where the same value appears twice.

In real systems

Hash tables are the most used data structure in production software. Caches (Memcached, Redis, an in-process functools.lru_cache) are hash maps with an eviction policy. Database hash joins build a hash table on the smaller table and probe it with rows from the larger one, turning an O(n·m) nested-loop join into O(n + m). Payment and messaging APIs store idempotency keys in a hash map so a retried request is recognised and not executed twice. Deduplication in data pipelines hashes each record (often a content hash such as SHA-256) into a set or a key-value store. Distributed systems spread keys over servers with consistent hashing, so adding a server only moves a small fraction of keys. The interview patterns — membership, position, count, canonical key — map directly onto these uses: a cache is membership plus value, a hash join is the complement trick at table scale, and deduplication is a canonical key.
myths: Any value can be a dictionary key.

Keys must be hashable, which in Python means immutable in the parts that affect equality. Lists, sets and dicts cannot be keys because changing them after insertion would change their hash and lose the entry. Convert to a tuple, a frozenset, or a string first — for example tuple(sorted(word)) or a tuple of 26 counts.
A hash set solution is always better than sorting.

Hashing gives O(n) expected time but uses O(n) extra memory, has worse cache behaviour and no ordering. Sorting is O(n log n) but can work in place and makes 'neighbours' adjacent, which some follow-ups need. For 10⁵ items both are fast; when memory is tight or output must be ordered, sorting can win. Say which trade-off you are making.
Dictionaries in Python are unordered.

Since Python 3.7 the language guarantees that dicts preserve insertion order. Sets do not guarantee any order. If you rely on dict order in an interview, say so, because in other languages (Java's HashMap, C++'s unordered_map) iteration order is effectively arbitrary.
Counter and defaultdict are 'cheating' in interviews.

They are standard library and interviewers expect fluent candidates to use them. What matters is that you know what they cost (Counter(s) is O(n)) and could write the plain-dict version if asked. Using them makes code shorter and less error-prone, which is part of the coding score.
Longest Consecutive Sequence with a set is O(n²) because of the inner while loop.

The inner loop only starts from numbers that are the start of a run (x − 1 not in the set), and each number is visited by exactly one such inner loop. So the total inner work across the whole run is n, and the algorithm is O(n) — the same aggregate argument as the sliding window.
lab:
Compare the set-based Longest Consecutive Sequence against a sort-based version on random data, and see what happens without the "start of run" check.

  1. Save as hash_lab.py: 
    import random, time

def by_sort(a):
    if not a: return 0
    b = sorted(set(a)); best = cur = 1
    for i in range(1, len(b)):
        cur = cur + 1 if b[i] == b[i-1] + 1 else 1
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

def by_set(a, check_start=True):
    s, best = set(a), 0
    for x in s:
        if check_start and x - 1 in s:
            continue
        y = x
        while y + 1 in s: y += 1
        best = max(best, y - x + 1)
    return best

for _ in range(2000):
    a = [random.randint(-10, 10) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 12))]
    assert by_sort(a) == by_set(a) == by_set(a, False), a
print("all variants agree on small inputs")

big = list(range(20000)); random.shuffle(big)
for f, kw in ((by_sort, {}), (by_set, {}), (by_set, {"check_start": False})):
    t = time.perf_counter(); f(big, **kw)
    print(f.__name__, kw, f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.3f}s")
  2. Run python hash_lab.py. The first line confirms all three versions give the same answers on random small inputs.
  3. Look at the timings on one long run of 20,000 consecutive numbers. The sort and the checked set version finish in milliseconds; the unchecked version counts every suffix of the run, about 2 × 10⁸ lookups, and takes far longer.

What this proves: correctness tests on small random inputs cannot see a complexity bug — all three versions agree — but a single adversarial large input exposes it immediately. When you remove a check "because the answer is the same", time it on the worst case.
recap: When the brute force repeatedly searches for a specific value, a hash set or map turns each search into an O(1) expected lookup.
Use a set for 'have I seen it?', a map from value to index for 'where did I see it?', and a map from value to count for frequency questions.
Two Sum is the template: for each element, look up its complement among elements already seen, then insert the element.
Group items by a canonical key that is equal exactly when the items should be grouped, such as the sorted letters or the letter-count tuple for anagrams.
Longest Consecutive Sequence is O(n) by only starting a count from numbers whose predecessor is absent.
Bijection checks need two maps, one in each direction; meet-in-the-middle counting stores all half-sums in a map to cut O(n⁴) to O(n²).
Keys must be hashable: use tuples or frozensets, never lists.
Hash operations are O(1) expected but O(n) worst case and cost O(k) to hash a key of length k; hash maps also cost O(n) memory.
glossary: A one-to-one pairing in both directions: every item maps to exactly one partner and no two items share a partner.
A slot in a hash table where entries whose hashes point there are stored.
A standard representation chosen so that two items get the same key exactly when they belong together, such as the sorted letters of a word for anagrams.
Two different keys whose hashes point to the same bucket; the table must store both and tell them apart by comparing keys.
The value that, combined with the current one, gives the target — for Two Sum, target − x.
Python's collections.Counter: a dict subclass that counts hashable items.
Python's collections.defaultdict: a dict that creates a default value (like an empty list or 0) for a missing key.
A map from each distinct value to the number of times it occurs.
A function that turns a key into an integer, used to pick a bucket; equal keys must produce equal hashes.
An object with a hash that never changes during its lifetime and that can be compared for equality; in Python, immutable built-ins like int, str and tuple.
The ratio of stored entries to buckets; tables resize when it passes a threshold to keep lookups fast.
Splitting a search into two halves, enumerating each half separately, and combining them with a lookup, to turn O(n⁴) into O(n²) or O(2ⁿ) into O(2^(n/2)).
A hash-table design where colliding entries are stored in other slots of the same array, found by probing; CPython's dict and set use it.
drill:
Design under a changed constraint

You solved "find all duplicate emails in a list" with a set. The interviewer now says: the list has 5 billion emails (about 150 GB) and your machine has 16 GB of memory. How do you find the duplicates exactly?

Answer

A single in-memory set will not fit, so partition first. Stream the input once and write each email to one of, say, 64 bucket files chosen by hash(email) mod 64. Equal emails always hash to the same bucket, so every duplicate pair ends up in the same file, and each file is about 150 / 64 ≈ 2.3 GB — small enough to deduplicate with an in-memory set (or to sort). Process the files one at a time and output the duplicates. Cost: two passes over the data, O(n) expected time, and disk I/O dominates. If a bucket is still too large (a very common email), split it again with a different hash seed. Mention the alternatives: an external sort followed by a linear scan for equal neighbours (also two to three passes, deterministic, no hash worst case), or a Bloom filter in front for a fast approximate first pass if a small false-positive rate is acceptable — but the question said "exactly", so the Bloom filter can only pre-filter, with a second exact check on its "maybe" answers.
qa: E
Check whether an array contains a duplicate.

Scan once with a set: if the current value is already in the set, return true; otherwise add it. O(n) expected time and O(n) space. The alternative is to sort and compare neighbours, O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space if sorting in place is allowed.
E
Solve Two Sum in O(n).

Keep a map from value to index of elements already seen. For each element x at index i, if target − x is in the map, return its index and i; otherwise store x → i. Checking before storing prevents pairing an element with itself. O(n) time and space.
E
Are two strings anagrams?

Compare their character counts: Counter(s) == Counter(t), or a 26-slot array for lowercase letters, after checking the lengths match. O(n) time and O(alphabet) space. Sorting both and comparing is O(n log n) and simpler but slower.
M
Group a list of words into anagram groups.

Map each word to a canonical key that is identical for anagrams, and append the word to a list under that key in a defaultdict(list). The key can be the sorted word as a tuple or string (O(L log L) per word) or a tuple of 26 letter counts (O(L) per word). Return the dict's values.
Follow-up: Which key is faster for long words? — The count tuple: O(L) instead of O(L log L), at the cost of a fixed 26-element tuple per word.
M
Find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers in an unsorted array in O(n).

Put all numbers in a set. For each number x whose predecessor x − 1 is not in the set, x starts a run: count upward while x + 1, x + 2, … are in the set. Each number is counted once by the run that contains it, so the total work is O(n). Sorting would give O(n log n).
Follow-up: Why skip numbers whose predecessor exists? — Without that check, every number starts its own count and a run of length n costs n + (n−1) + … = O(n²).
M
Given an array and k, is there a pair of equal values at most k indices apart?

Keep a map from value to the last index where it appeared. At each index i, if the value is in the map and i − last ≤ k, return true; then update the last index to i. O(n) time. A variant keeps only the last k values in a set as a sliding window, giving O(min(n, k)) space.
M
How do you decide whether two strings are isomorphic (characters can be consistently replaced)?

Keep two maps, s→t and t→s. For each position, if s[i] already maps to something other than t[i], or t[i] already maps to something other than s[i], return false; otherwise record both mappings. One map is not enough: 'ab' and 'cc' would pass with only s→t, because a→c and b→c are both allowed by a single map.
M
Count tuples (i, j, k, l) from four arrays with A[i] + B[j] + C[k] + D[l] = 0.

Meet in the middle: count every sum a + b in a Counter (n² entries), then for each c + d add count[−(c + d)]. O(n²) time and space instead of O(n⁴). The same idea solves 'subset sum for n = 40' by enumerating 2²⁰ sums for each half.
M
Validate a partially filled 9×9 Sudoku board.

Keep three collections of seen keys: (row, digit), (col, digit) and (box, digit), where box = (r // 3, c // 3). For each filled cell, if any of its three keys is already present, the board is invalid; otherwise add them. One pass over 81 cells, O(1) for a fixed board size. Encoding all three as tuples in a single set also works, e.g. ('r', r, d).
H
Hash maps are O(1). Why might a hash-based solution time out on a judge?

Three reasons. Worst-case collisions: adversarial keys that collide degrade lookups to O(n), which is why Python randomises string hashes per process. Expensive keys: hashing a long string or a large tuple costs O(k), so using whole substrings as keys can make an 'O(n)' solution O(n²). And constant factors: dict operations are far slower than array indexing, so for small integer keys an array of counts can be several times faster.
Follow-up: How would you hash many substrings cheaply? — Use a rolling hash (al26) so each substring's hash is computed in O(1) from the previous one.
H
Design a data structure that supports insert, delete and getRandom in O(1).

Keep a list of values and a map from value to its index in the list. Insert appends and records the index. Delete swaps the element with the last one in the list, updates the moved element's index in the map, pops the last element and deletes the map entry. getRandom picks a random index into the list. The swap-with-last trick is what makes delete O(1) without leaving holes.
H
When would you choose sorting over hashing for grouping or duplicate detection?

When memory is tight (in-place sorting needs O(1) extra versus O(n) for a table), when the output must be ordered anyway, when the data is too large for memory (external sort then a linear scan works on disk, a hash table does not), or when keys are not easily hashable but are comparable. Hashing wins when you need a single pass, streaming input, or O(n) time on large in-memory data.
