t: Two pointers: opposite ends, read/write and merging
sum: Use two indices that move in a coordinated way so each step safely rules out many candidates: pair sums on sorted arrays, 3Sum, container and rain-water problems, in-place compaction, Dutch national flag partitioning and merging sorted sequences.
prereq: al2
A loop whose pointers only move forward does O(n) total work; sorting costs O(n log n).
al4
Two Sum on unsorted input uses a hash map of complements: O(n) time and O(n) space.
why:
You have a sorted list of 100,000 product prices and a gift card worth exactly 500. Is there a pair of products that uses the card exactly? The brute force checks every pair — about five billion of them. A hash map of complements (al4) does it in one pass, but uses memory for 100,000 entries and ignores the fact that the list is already sorted. There is a better way that uses the order: put one finger on the cheapest product and one on the most expensive. If the two together cost less than 500, the cheapest product is hopeless — even with the most expensive item it falls short — so move the left finger up. If they cost more, the most expensive item is hopeless — even with the cheapest it overshoots — so move the right finger down. Every step eliminates one product for good, and the fingers meet after at most 100,000 steps, using no extra memory.

That is the two-pointer technique: two indices that move through a sequence according to a rule that guarantees each move only throws away candidates that cannot be the answer. It turns pair-checking O(n²) loops into O(n) scans and in-place problems into single passes with O(1) memory.

It shows up in three shapes. Opposite ends: pointers start at both ends and move towards each other (pair sums, palindromes, container and rain-water problems). Same direction: a read pointer scans and a write pointer marks where kept elements go (removing duplicates, moving zeros, partitioning). Two sequences: one pointer per sorted input (merging, intersections, subsequence checks). Fast and slow pointers on linked lists are a fourth shape covered in al9.

This lesson teaches each shape with a worked trace and, more importantly, the safe-move argument behind it — the one or two sentences that prove the method correct. Interviewers ask for that argument often, because it separates candidates who understand the pattern from those who have only seen it.
primer:
The mental model: eliminating rows and columns

Think of all possible pairs (i, j) with i < j as the cells of a triangle-shaped grid: row i, column j. The brute force visits every cell. Two pointers stands at one cell, (l, r), and asks one question. On a sorted array with a target sum, the answer to "is a[l] + a[r] too small, too big or exact?" lets it rule out an entire row or column at once:

  • Too small: every pair in row l to the left of r has a smaller or equal sum (because a[j] ≤ a[r] for j ≤ r), so the whole rest of row l is too small. Eliminate the row: l += 1.
  • Too big: every pair in column r below l has a larger or equal sum, so the whole column is too big. Eliminate the column: r −= 1.

That picture is the whole idea, and it generalises: whenever the candidates form a grid in which the values are monotonic along both directions (increasing as you go right and down), you can start at a corner and walk a staircase, discarding a row or a column at each step. Searching a matrix whose rows and columns are both sorted works the same way.

The same-direction version uses a different model: a conveyor belt with an inspector. The read pointer is the belt bringing every item past; the write pointer is the end of the "kept" pile. Each item is inspected once; kept items are placed at the write position and the pile grows by one. Everything before the write pointer is final. Nothing ever moves backwards, so it is one pass.

A third, quieter model is worth naming because it explains why two pointers is fast at all: neither pointer ever moves backwards. In the opposite-ends version, l only increases and r only decreases, so together they make at most n moves. In the same-direction version, the read pointer makes n moves and the write pointer at most n. That monotonic movement is what turns a loop that looks like it might be quadratic into a linear one — the same aggregate argument as in al2. If you ever find yourself resetting a pointer to an earlier position, you are no longer doing two pointers, and the complexity argument no longer holds.

Where the models break: neither tells you which rule makes a move safe for a given problem. That rule is problem-specific — sortedness for pair sums, "the shorter wall limits the area" for containers, "the kept prefix is final" for compaction — and finding it is the real work. The body of the lesson shows the rule for each classic problem.
body:
Opposite ends I: pair sum on a sorted array

def two_sum_sorted(a, target):
    l, r = 0, len(a) - 1
    while l < r:                      # pairs need two distinct indices
        s = a[l] + a[r]
        if s == target:
            return [l, r]
        if s < target:
            l += 1                    # a[l] too small for every partner <= r
        else:
            r -= 1                    # a[r] too big for every partner >= l
    return []

The comments are the safe-move argument, and you should say them while coding. The loop does at most n − 1 iterations because each one moves a pointer inward. O(n) time, O(1) space. The condition is l < r because a pair needs two different indices.

A counting variant shows the power of the elimination view. "How many pairs have sum less than target?" — when a[l] + a[r] < target, a[l] works with every index from l + 1 to r (they are all at most a[r]), so add r − l in one step and move l. When the sum is too big, move r. Still O(n) after sorting.

Opposite ends II: palindromes

Checking whether a string reads the same backwards is the simplest opposite-ends problem: compare s[l] and s[r], and move both inward while they match. The interview version adds noise — "ignore non-alphanumeric characters and case" — which tests careful pointer handling:

def is_palindrome(s):
    l, r = 0, len(s) - 1
    while l < r:
        while l < r and not s[l].isalnum(): l += 1
        while l < r and not s[r].isalnum(): r -= 1
        if s[l].lower() != s[r].lower():
            return False
        l += 1; r -= 1
    return True

The inner skipping loops repeat the l < r guard; without it, a string of only punctuation would run a pointer off the end. A follow-up, "Valid Palindrome II" (may delete at most one character), branches once at the first mismatch: check whether s[l+1..r] or s[l..r−1] is a palindrome. That is still O(n), because the branch happens once.

Fix one, two-pointer the rest: 3Sum

"Find all unique triplets that sum to zero." The brute force is O(n³). Sort the array; then for each index i, the problem "find pairs in a[i+1..] summing to −a[i]" is exactly sorted pair sum, O(n). That gives O(n²) overall. The harder part is uniqueness: the input can contain duplicates, and the output must not. Sorting makes duplicates adjacent, so skip them in two places.

def three_sum(a):
    a.sort()
    out = []
    for i in range(len(a) - 2):
        if a[i] > 0: break                     # smallest is positive: no zero sum
        if i > 0 and a[i] == a[i - 1]: continue  # same fixed value as before
        l, r = i + 1, len(a) - 1
        while l < r:
            s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r]
            if s < 0: l += 1
            elif s > 0: r -= 1
            else:
                out.append([a[i], a[l], a[r]])
                l += 1; r -= 1
                while l < r and a[l] == a[l - 1]: l += 1   # skip equal lefts
    return out

Trace on [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4], sorted to [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]. i = 0 (−4): needs pairs summing to 4; the pointers find none. i = 1 (−1): needs 1; l at −1, r at 2 → sum 0, record [−1, −1, 2]; move both and skip; l at 0, r at 1 → sum 0, record [−1, 0, 1]. i = 2 is −1 again, equal to a[1], so skip it — this is what prevents [−1, 0, 1] being recorded twice. i = 3 (0): needs 0 from [1, 2], none. Result: [[−1, −1, 2], [−1, 0, 1]].

The general form is kSum: fix k − 2 elements with nested loops (each skipping duplicates), and two-pointer the last two. That is O(n^(k−1)). For 4Sum, O(n³).

Opposite ends III: Container With Most Water

Given wall heights h, choose two walls to hold the most water: area = (r − l) × min(h[l], h[r]). The brute force tries all pairs. Start with the widest container, l = 0 and r = n − 1, and ask which pointer to move. Suppose h[l] < h[r]. Any container that keeps wall l and pairs it with a wall further in has smaller width and height still capped at h[l] — so it cannot beat the current area. Every candidate involving wall l has been dominated; discard it by moving l. The rule: always move the shorter wall.

def max_area(h):
    l, r, best = 0, len(h) - 1, 0
    while l < r:
        best = max(best, (r - l) * min(h[l], h[r]))
        if h[l] < h[r]: l += 1
        else: r -= 1
    return best

When the heights are equal, moving either is safe: any container keeping one of them is narrower and still capped at that height. This is a nice example where the array is not sorted, yet the problem has its own monotonic structure that makes the move safe.

Opposite ends IV: Trapping Rain Water

Water above position i rises to the lower of the tallest wall on its left and the tallest on its right: water[i] = min(maxL[i], maxR[i]) − h[i]. A clear O(n)-space solution precomputes both arrays. The two-pointer version removes the arrays by noticing that you do not need both maxima exactly — only the smaller one. Keep left_max (tallest seen from the left so far) and right_max. If h[l] < h[r], then somewhere on the right there is a wall at least h[r], which is taller than h[l]; so for position l the limiting side is the left, and its water is left_max − h[l]. Process l and move it. Otherwise process r symmetrically.

def trap(h):
    l, r = 0, len(h) - 1
    left_max = right_max = water = 0
    while l < r:
        if h[l] < h[r]:
            left_max = max(left_max, h[l])
            water += left_max - h[l]
            l += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, h[r])
            water += right_max - h[r]
            r -= 1
    return water

On [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1] this returns 6. It is one of the most-asked hard problems precisely because the safe-move argument is subtle; practise saying it in two sentences. (A monotonic-stack solution exists too, al8.)

Same direction: read and write pointers

"Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place and return the new length." The read pointer i visits every element; the write pointer w marks the end of the kept prefix. The invariant: a[0..w−1] holds the unique values seen so far, in order.

def remove_duplicates(a):
    if not a: return 0
    w = 1                                # a[0] is always kept
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        if a[i] != a[w - 1]:             # new value: keep it
            a[w] = a[i]
            w += 1
    return w

The same skeleton solves "move zeros to the end" (keep non-zeros, then fill the tail with zeros), "remove all occurrences of val", and "keep at most two copies of each value" (compare with a[w − 2] instead of a[w − 1]). The output is stable — kept elements stay in their original order — because the write pointer only receives elements in scan order.

Three pointers: the Dutch national flag

"Sort an array of 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass" (Sort Colors). Keep three regions: a[0..lo−1] are 0s, a[lo..mid−1] are 1s, a[hi+1..] are 2s, and a[mid..hi] is unexamined. Look at a[mid]:

def sort_colors(a):
    lo, mid, hi = 0, 0, len(a) - 1
    while mid <= hi:
        if a[mid] == 0:
            a[lo], a[mid] = a[mid], a[lo]; lo += 1; mid += 1
        elif a[mid] == 1:
            mid += 1
        else:
            a[mid], a[hi] = a[hi], a[mid]; hi -= 1   # do not advance mid

The asymmetry is the whole difficulty. After swapping a 2 to the back, the value that arrives at mid came from the unexamined region, so it must be examined before mid moves. After swapping a 0 to the front, the value arriving at mid came from the 1s region (or is the same element), so mid can advance. Trace [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0] by hand once and the rule will stick; the result is [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]. This three-way partition is also how quicksort handles many equal keys efficiently.

Two sequences: merging

With two sorted sequences, one pointer each, repeatedly take the smaller head and advance that pointer. That is the merge step of merge sort, and it powers "merge two sorted lists", "intersection of two sorted arrays" (advance the smaller; record when equal), and "is s a subsequence of t" (advance in t always, in s only on a match).

A classic twist: "merge nums2 into nums1, where nums1 has enough empty slots at the end". Merging from the front would overwrite elements of nums1 you have not read yet. Merge from the back instead: compare the last real elements, write the larger one into the last slot, and move left. The write position is always at or beyond the read position in nums1, so nothing unread is overwritten.

Greedy pairing: boats

"Each boat carries at most two people and a weight limit; find the minimum number of boats." Sort the weights. The heaviest person must take a boat; the best partner for them is the lightest person, because if the lightest cannot fit with them, nobody can. So: if a[l] + a[r] ≤ limit, both go (l++, r−−); otherwise the heaviest goes alone (r−−). Count a boat each step, and loop while l <= r so a final single person is counted. This is two pointers driven by a greedy exchange argument (al12).

Recognising the pattern

Reach for two pointers when: the input is sorted, or sorting is allowed and does not lose information you need; the problem asks about pairs or triplets with a sum or difference condition; it asks for in-place modification with O(1) extra space; it involves a palindrome or symmetric comparison; or it involves merging or intersecting sorted sequences. Then ask: what makes a move safe? If you can state it, you have the algorithm.

Practice in the DSA list: Valid Palindrome, Two Sum II, Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array, Move Zeroes, 3Sum, 4Sum, Container With Most Water, Sort Colors, Boats to Save People, Trapping Rain Water.
deep:
The general correctness argument

Every opposite-ends algorithm has the same proof shape. Define the candidate set as all pairs (i, j) with l ≤ i < j ≤ r. The invariant is: "if an answer exists, it lies in the current candidate set" (or, for optimisation problems, "the best answer outside the current set has already been recorded"). Each move removes one row or one column from the set, and the safe-move argument shows that nothing removed could be a better answer. When l meets r the set is empty, so every answer has been found or dominated. Saying "each move discards a row or column of the pair grid, and I can show nothing discarded could win" is a complete correctness proof in an interview.

Why sorting is sometimes not allowed

Sorting destroys the original positions. If the problem asks for indices (classic Two Sum), you must either sort (value, index) pairs — O(n log n) time and O(n) space, no better than hashing — or use a hash map. If the problem is about contiguous subarrays (sums of subarrays, windows), sorting changes which elements are adjacent and breaks the problem entirely; those need prefix sums (al3) or sliding windows (al6), not opposite-ends pointers. The question to ask before sorting is: "does the answer depend on the original order?"

Staircase search in sorted matrices

The pair-grid picture becomes literal in "search a matrix where every row and every column is sorted". Start at the top-right corner: if the value is larger than the target, the whole column below is larger, so move left; if smaller, the whole row to the left is smaller, so move down. At most R + C steps. The same staircase idea finds "the k-th smallest element in a sorted matrix" when combined with binary search on the value (count how many entries are ≤ x by walking the staircase in O(R + C)), which is a good example of patterns composing (al7).

Two pointers and the merge family

The two-sequence merge is one of the most important operations in computing. Merge sort's merge step, external sorting (merge sorted runs from disk), database sort-merge joins, and the compaction step of log-structured storage engines (merging sorted files of keys) are all the same loop: advance the pointer at the smaller head. Generalising to k sequences needs a heap to find the smallest of k heads (al10). Recognising that "merge k sorted lists" is two-sequence merging plus a heap is a standard interview step.

Floyd's algorithm on arrays: functional graphs

"Find the duplicate number" (n + 1 values in the range 1..n, read-only array, O(1) space) looks like a hashing problem but forbids the memory. View the array as a function f(i) = a[i]. Starting from index 0 and following f repeatedly must eventually repeat a value (pigeonhole), so the path is a "rho" shape: a tail leading into a cycle. Two different indices map to the duplicate value, which makes the duplicate the entrance of the cycle. Floyd's algorithm finds it: move slow by one step and fast by two until they meet inside the cycle; then restart one pointer from the beginning and move both by one step; they meet exactly at the entrance. The proof is a short distance argument (the tail length equals the distance from the meeting point to the entrance, modulo the cycle length), and it is covered with linked lists in al9. It is a favourite hard follow-up because it combines a pigeonhole argument, a graph view of an array and two pointers.

Invariants with three regions

The Dutch flag generalises to any "partition into k groups in one pass" with k − 1 boundaries plus a scan pointer, but its real value is as a model of reasoning with region invariants. Write the regions as a picture ("0s | 1s | unknown | 2s") and for each case of the scanned value, ask which region boundary moves and whether the element that arrives at the scan position has been examined. Bugs in partition code — including the famous one where quicksort degenerates on many equal keys — come from getting that question wrong. Interviewers who ask Sort Colors are usually checking exactly this reasoning.
prod:
In the interview room

Two-pointer code is short, so interviewers judge it on precision. The typical failures are: an infinite loop because some branch forgets to move a pointer; an off-by-one in the loop condition (l < r versus l <= r) — decide by asking whether a single element can be an answer on its own; duplicate triplets in 3Sum because only one of the two skip points is handled; and index errors in the inner skipping loops because the l < r guard is missing. Test with an array of all equal values and with a two-element array; those two inputs catch most of these bugs.

The second thing interviewers look for is the justification. "Why do you move the left pointer here?" is the most common follow-up for this pattern. Prepare one-sentence arguments: sorted pair sum ("a[l] is too small even with the largest remaining partner"), container ("any container keeping the shorter wall is narrower and no taller"), rain water ("the other side has a taller wall, so this side's maximum decides"). A memorised solution without the argument tends to fall apart when the interviewer changes the problem slightly.

Finally, know when not to use it. If the input is unsorted and you must return original indices, offer the hash-map solution first. If the problem is about contiguous ranges, you probably want a sliding window (al6), which is a same-direction two-pointer specialised for windows.

A good way to practise is to say the safe-move argument before writing the loop, as part of step 5 of the method ("I'll start at both ends; if the sum is too small, the left element is too small for every remaining partner, so I advance it"). If you cannot state the argument, that is a signal that the two-pointer idea may be wrong for this problem — perhaps it needs a hash map, a window or a different order — and it is far cheaper to find that out before coding than after.

On online assessments, two-pointer problems often hide behind constraints: an array of 10⁵ elements with a pair or triplet condition, and a memory limit that makes a hash map of all pairs impossible. Sorting plus two pointers is usually the intended solution there.

In real systems

The merge loop is everywhere in data infrastructure. Database engines implement sort-merge joins: when both inputs are sorted on the join key (often because an index provides that order), the join walks both with one pointer each, advancing the smaller key, in a single pass. External sorting — sorting data much larger than memory — writes sorted runs to disk and then merges them with a pointer per run. Log-structured merge (LSM) storage engines such as RocksDB and Cassandra continuously compact sorted files by merging them, dropping overwritten and deleted keys along the way — a read pointer per file and a write pointer for the output, exactly the compaction pattern from this lesson. Version-control and diff tools merge sorted lists of file paths to find added and removed files. In each case the reason is the same as in the interview: one pass, sequential reads (which disks and caches love), and constant extra memory per input.
myths: Two pointers only works on sorted arrays.

The opposite-ends version needs an order (sorted values, or a property like 'the shorter wall limits the water') that tells you which pointer to move. The same-direction version — read and write pointers for in-place compaction, fast and slow pointers — works on any array. What every version needs is a rule that makes each move safe.
Moving the pointer at the smaller value in Container With Most Water is a heuristic that happens to work.

It is provably correct. The area is limited by the shorter wall, and any container that keeps that shorter wall and moves the other one inward is narrower and no taller, so it can never be better. Moving the shorter wall therefore discards only candidates that cannot win.
3Sum with two pointers needs a set to remove duplicate triplets.

If the array is sorted, duplicates are adjacent, so you skip them directly: skip a fixed element equal to the previous one, and after finding a triplet, advance both pointers past equal values. That produces each unique triplet exactly once with no extra memory.
Two pointers is always better than a hash map.

On already-sorted input it wins: O(n) time and O(1) space. On unsorted input you must sort first, which costs O(n log n) and loses the original indices, so for a problem like Two Sum that returns indices a hash map is the better fit. Choose based on whether order exists or is cheap to create.
The loop condition is always left < right.

It depends on whether the two pointers may refer to the same element. For pair problems the elements must be distinct, so left < right. For binary-search-like loops or palindrome checks where the middle element needs no check, left < right is also right; but for problems where a single element can form an answer by itself (such as boats where one person can go alone), left <= right is needed so the last person is counted.
lab:
Stress-test your 3Sum against a brute force that uses a set of sorted tuples, focusing on duplicates.

  1. Save as two_ptr_lab.py: 
    import random
from itertools import combinations

def brute(a):
    return sorted({tuple(sorted(t)) for t in combinations(a, 3) if sum(t) == 0})

def three_sum(a):
    a = sorted(a); out = []
    for i in range(len(a) - 2):
        if i and a[i] == a[i-1]: continue
        l, r = i + 1, len(a) - 1
        while l < r:
            s = a[i] + a[l] + a[r]
            if s < 0: l += 1
            elif s > 0: r -= 1
            else:
                out.append((a[i], a[l], a[r])); l += 1; r -= 1
                while l < r and a[l] == a[l-1]: l += 1
    return out

for _ in range(5000):
    a = [random.randint(-4, 4) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 9))]
    assert three_sum(a) == brute(a), a
print("3Sum matches brute force on 5000 random arrays")
  2. Run it. The assertion should never fail. The tiny value range (−4..4) guarantees many duplicates, which is where 3Sum bugs live.
  3. Delete the line if i and a[i] == a[i-1]: continue and run again. The script fails quickly on an input with a repeated fixed value, showing a duplicated triplet.
  4. Restore it and delete the inner while l < r and a[l] == a[l-1] line instead. Predict the failing input before running.

What this proves: both duplicate-skipping points are necessary, and random tests with a small value range expose duplicate bugs that hand-picked examples usually miss.
recap: Two pointers replaces a pair-checking double loop with two indices that move so that each step rules out a whole row or column of candidate pairs.
On a sorted array, if a[l] + a[r] is too small, a[l] cannot pair with anything to its right of l that is at most r, so l moves right; if too large, r moves left.
3Sum sorts, fixes one element and runs two pointers on the rest, skipping duplicates, for O(n²) time and O(1) extra space.
Container With Most Water moves the pointer at the shorter wall, because no container that keeps the shorter wall can be larger.
Read/write pointers compact an array in place: the write pointer marks the end of the kept prefix and only advances when an element is kept.
The Dutch national flag uses three pointers to partition into three groups in one pass.
Merging two sorted sequences advances the pointer at the smaller head; filling from the back merges in place when the destination has room at the end.
Every two-pointer solution rests on an invariant and a safe-move argument; say both out loud.
glossary: Partitioning an array into three groups (such as less than, equal to and greater than a pivot) in one pass with three pointers; named by Edsger Dijkstra.
The proof that a pointer move only discards candidates that cannot be the answer.
Two pointers moving through a sequence at different speeds, used for cycle detection and finding middles; detailed in al9.
Modifying the input directly using only O(1) extra memory.
A statement that holds before and after every iteration of a loop, used to argue correctness.
Log-structured merge tree: a storage-engine design that writes sorted files and periodically merges (compacts) them, used by RocksDB and Cassandra.
Combining two sorted sequences into one sorted sequence by repeatedly taking the smaller head.
Always moving in one direction; two-pointer indices are monotonic, which is why the total work is linear.
Rearranging an array so elements satisfying a condition come before those that do not.
Here, simply an index into an array or a reference into a list, not a memory address.
A same-direction technique where one index scans every element and another marks where the next kept element should be written.
Preserving the original relative order of elements that are kept or equal.
A group of three elements, as in 3Sum.
drill:
Prove the move, then extend

An interviewer asks: "In Container With Most Water, prove that moving the shorter wall never skips the optimal container. Then: what changes if the area formula were (r − l) × max(h[l], h[r])?"

Answer

Proof: suppose h[l] ≤ h[r]. Every container that uses wall l together with some wall j where l < j < r has width j − l < r − l and height min(h[l], h[j]) ≤ h[l] = min(h[l], h[r]). So its area is strictly smaller than the current one. Therefore no container involving wall l and a wall inside the current range can beat what we have already recorded, and wall l can be discarded. Each step discards one wall, so after n − 1 steps every container has been considered or dominated. With max instead of min: the argument breaks. A taller inner wall can now increase the height, and moving the shorter wall no longer dominates anything — in fact the widest container that includes the single tallest wall is optimal: the answer is max over the tallest wall t of max(t − 0, n − 1 − t) × h[t]. The lesson for the interview: the two-pointer rule is a consequence of the problem's structure (here, min), and when the structure changes, re-derive the rule rather than reusing the code.
qa: E
Check whether a string is a palindrome, ignoring non-alphanumeric characters and case.

Put one pointer at each end. Skip characters that are not alphanumeric on both sides, compare the lowercased characters, and move both pointers inward while they match. Return false at the first mismatch. O(n) time and O(1) space, without building a cleaned copy.
E
Find two numbers in a sorted array that sum to a target.

Start with l at 0 and r at the end. If a[l] + a[r] equals the target, return them; if the sum is too small, move l right to increase it; if too large, move r left. Each step discards one element that cannot be in any valid pair, so it is O(n) time and O(1) space.
E
Move all zeros to the end of an array in place, keeping the order of the other elements.

Use a write pointer w starting at 0. Scan with i; whenever a[i] is non-zero, write it to a[w] and increment w (or swap a[i] and a[w]). After the scan, everything before w is the non-zero elements in order; fill the rest with zeros. One pass, O(1) extra space, stable.
M
Explain why moving the left pointer is safe in sorted Two Sum when the sum is too small.

If a[l] + a[r] is smaller than the target, then a[l] plus any element at index at most r is also too small, because a[r] is the largest of those. So a[l] cannot be part of any pair with the remaining candidates, and we can discard it. The symmetric argument justifies moving r when the sum is too large.
Follow-up: How does this look on the grid of all pairs? — Each move eliminates a whole row or column of the upper-triangular grid, which is why n moves cover all n²/2 pairs.
M
Solve 3Sum: find all unique triplets that sum to zero.

Sort the array. For each index i, skip it if a[i] equals a[i−1]; then run two pointers on the range after i looking for pairs summing to −a[i]. When a triplet is found, record it and move both pointers past any equal values. Stop early when a[i] > 0. O(n²) time, O(1) extra space apart from sorting and output.
Follow-up: What about 4Sum? — Add one more fixed loop with the same duplicate skipping: O(n³). In general kSum is O(n^(k−1)).
M
Container With Most Water: why move the shorter wall?

The area is width times the shorter height. If we kept the shorter wall and moved the taller one inward, the width would shrink and the height would still be capped by the shorter wall, so the area cannot increase. Every container that pairs the shorter wall with something further in is therefore no better than the current one, and we can discard that wall. One pass, O(n).
M
Sort an array of 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass.

Dutch national flag: keep lo, mid and hi. Everything before lo is 0, between lo and mid is 1, after hi is 2. Look at a[mid]: if 0, swap with a[lo] and advance both; if 1, advance mid; if 2, swap with a[hi] and decrement hi without advancing mid, because the swapped-in value has not been examined yet. Stop when mid passes hi.
M
Merge two sorted arrays where the first has enough empty space at the end.

Fill from the back. Pointers at the last real element of each array and at the last slot of the first array; place the larger of the two candidates at the write slot and move that pointer. Filling from the back never overwrites an unread element of the first array. When the second array is exhausted, the rest is already in place. O(m + n), O(1) extra.
M
Count the pairs in an array whose sum is less than a target.

Sort, then l at 0 and r at the end. If a[l] + a[r] < target, then a[l] pairs successfully with every index from l+1 to r, so add r − l at once and move l right; otherwise move r left. Counting a whole block in one step is what keeps it O(n) after the O(n log n) sort.
H
Trapping Rain Water in O(1) extra space.

Water above position i is min(max left of i, max right of i) − height[i]. With two pointers, keep left_max and right_max. If height[l] < height[r], the right side has a wall at least height[r] > height[l], so the water at l depends only on left_max: add left_max − height[l] (after updating left_max) and move l. Otherwise do the symmetric step on the right. O(n) time, O(1) space.

Follow-up: Why is it safe to use only left_max for position l? — Because some wall on the right is at least as tall as height[r], which exceeds the left side, so the minimum of the two maxima is determined by the left.
H
Given an array of n + 1 integers in the range 1..n with exactly one repeated value, find it without modifying the array and in O(1) extra space.

Treat the array as a function i → a[i]; because values are in 1..n, following it from index 0 eventually enters a cycle, and the cycle's entrance is the duplicate (two indices point to it). Use Floyd's fast and slow pointers to find a meeting point inside the cycle, then reset one pointer to the start and move both one step at a time; they meet at the entrance. O(n) time, O(1) space.
H
When would you choose two pointers over a hash map, and vice versa, for pair problems?

Two pointers when the input is already sorted or must be sorted anyway, when O(1) extra space matters, or when you need counts of pairs satisfying an inequality (which hashing cannot do directly). A hash map when the input is unsorted and original indices must be returned, when the data arrives as a stream, or when sorting would dominate the cost. Saying the trade-off in those terms is what interviewers want.

t: Sliding window: fixed, growing–shrinking and counting windows
sum: Maintain a contiguous window and update it incrementally as it slides, instead of recomputing each range: fixed-size windows, longest and shortest valid windows, counting subarrays with at-most-k tricks, and the monotonic deque for window maximums.
prereq: al3
Prefix sums answer range sums in O(1) and handle negative numbers; windows do not.
al4
Counters and dicts track frequencies of the elements inside a window.
al5
Same-direction pointers that only move forward give O(n) total work.
why:
A fitness app shows "your best 7-day step streak": the largest total over any 7 consecutive days in the last year. The obvious code takes every starting day, adds up the next 7 values, and keeps the maximum — 365 × 7 additions, which is fine. Then product asks for a 30-day version over five years of minute-level heart-rate data, about 2.6 million values with a 43,200-value window. Now the obvious code does about 10¹¹ additions, and almost all of them are repeated: the window starting at minute 1,001 shares 43,199 values with the window starting at minute 1,000.

Moving the window by one position only changes two things: one value enters on the right, and one value leaves on the left. If you keep the current window's total, the next total is old total + entering value − leaving value — two operations instead of 43,200. That is the sliding window: keep a summary of a contiguous range and update it incrementally as the range moves.

Interviews use the idea constantly, usually in a stronger form where the window's size is not fixed. "Longest substring without repeating characters", "smallest subarray with sum at least target", "longest substring with at most k distinct characters", "minimum window containing all the characters of t" — each asks for the best contiguous range satisfying a condition. The brute force checks all O(n²) ranges, often with O(n) work each. A window that grows on the right and shrinks on the left visits each element at most twice and solves them in O(n).

This lesson builds the pattern from the fixed-size case to the variable "longest" and "shortest" templates, the counting trick for "number of subarrays with at most / exactly k", and the monotonic deque for window maximums. Just as important, it teaches the precondition that makes windows correct — monotonic validity — so you can tell when a window will silently give wrong answers and you need prefix sums instead.
primer:
The mental model: an inchworm

Picture an inchworm crawling along a ruler. Its head (the right pointer) reaches forward to grab the next mark; its tail (the left pointer) follows behind. The worm's body is the window: everything between tail and head. The worm never crawls backwards, and it never jumps — the head moves forward one mark at a time, and the tail moves forward only when the body must get shorter. Because both ends only move forward along a ruler of length n, the whole journey takes at most 2n moves, no matter how the body stretches and contracts along the way.

The worm also carries a small notebook: the window's summary. It might be the sum of the marks inside, a count of each letter, or the number of distinct letters. When the head grabs a new mark, the worm updates the notebook for one element entering; when the tail lets go, it updates it for one element leaving. Neither update looks at the rest of the window. That is where the speed comes from.

Three kinds of window

Almost every window problem is one of three types, and naming the type tells you the template:

  • Fixed size k: slide one step at a time; add the entering element, remove the leaving one. Example: maximum sum of k consecutive elements.
  • Variable, longest valid: grow the head every step; while the window is invalid, shrink the tail; then record the length. Example: longest substring without repeats.
  • Variable, shortest valid: grow the head every step; while the window is valid, record its length and shrink the tail. Example: smallest subarray with sum at least target.

Where the analogy breaks: a real inchworm can always shrink safely. A sliding window is only correct if shrinking never throws away something you would need later. That requires the condition to be monotonic: for "longest" problems, if a window is invalid then every bigger window containing it is invalid too (a substring with a repeat still has the repeat if you extend it). If the condition is not monotonic — sums with negative numbers are the classic case — a window gives wrong answers, and you need a different tool. Checking monotonicity takes ten seconds and is the single most important habit in this lesson.

Here is the cost comparison that justifies the effort. For "longest substring without repeating characters" on a string of 10⁵ characters, the brute force checks about 5 × 10⁹ substrings, each needing a scan to test for repeats. The window version makes at most 2 × 10⁵ pointer moves with an O(1) dictionary update each. That is the difference between hours and milliseconds, achieved without any clever data structure — only by refusing to forget what the previous window already knew.

One more framing helps when you are deciding between windows and other tools: a window answers questions about contiguous ranges. If the problem allows picking elements that are not next to each other ("subsequence", "subset", "any k elements"), it is not a window problem, however similar the wording looks.
body:
Fixed-size windows

def max_sum_k(a, k):
    s = sum(a[:k])
    best = s
    for r in range(k, len(a)):
        s += a[r] - a[r - k]          # one in, one out
        best = max(best, s)
    return best

Trace a = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], k = 3: the first window sums to 8; sliding gives 8 − 2 + 1 = 7, then 7 − 1 + 3 = 9, then 9 − 5 + 2 = 6. Best 9 ([5, 1, 3]). O(n) time instead of O(n·k).

The summary does not have to be a sum. "Find all anagrams of p in s" uses a fixed window of length m = len(p) whose summary is the character counts. Comparing two Counters at each step costs O(alphabet); a sharper version keeps one dictionary diff of (window count − p count) per character and an integer bad = how many characters have a non-zero difference. Each add or remove changes one character's difference, and you adjust bad when that difference becomes or stops being zero. When bad == 0, the window is an anagram. That is O(1) per step and O(n) overall, and it is the same "track how many constraints are currently satisfied" idea that powers Minimum Window Substring below.

Variable window, longest valid: the template

def longest_valid(a):
    left = 0
    best = 0
    # summary = ...                    # e.g. counts, sum, distinct
    for right, x in enumerate(a):
        add(x)                          # head moves: update summary
        while not valid():              # shrink until valid again
            remove(a[left])
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

Every "longest" problem fills in three blanks: what the summary is, how add and remove update it, and what valid means. Correctness rests on monotonic validity: if a[l..r] is invalid, then a[l'..r] for any l' < l is also invalid, so once the tail passes position l it never needs to come back. Complexity: each element is added once and removed at most once, so O(n) total, plus the cost of the summary updates.

Longest substring without repeating characters

Summary: a set (or counts) of the characters in the window. Valid: no character appears twice. When the head adds a character that is already present, shrink until its earlier copy leaves.

def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    last = {}                          # char -> last index seen
    left = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last and last[ch] >= left:
            left = last[ch] + 1        # jump past the earlier copy
        last[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

This version jumps the tail directly instead of stepping it, using the last-seen index map from al4. The guard last[ch] >= left matters: a character last seen before the current window is not a repeat inside it, and jumping to it would move the tail backwards. Trace on "abcabcbb":

rightchlast[ch] beforeleft afterwindowbest

Answer 3. O(n) time, O(alphabet) space.

"At most k" conditions

A large family of problems has the shape "longest window with at most k of something": at most k zeros (Max Consecutive Ones III: you may flip k zeros), at most 2 distinct values (Fruit Into Baskets), at most k distinct characters. The summary is a count — zeros in the window, or a Counter plus its number of keys — and valid means the count is at most k. Each is the template with a two-line summary.

Longest Repeating Character Replacement is the cleverest member. You may replace k characters to make the window all one letter. A window can be made uniform when length − maxfreq ≤ k, where maxfreq is the count of its most frequent letter: you keep the majority letter and replace the rest. So valid = (right − left + 1) − maxfreq ≤ k.

def character_replacement(s, k):
    count = {}
    left = maxfreq = best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        count[ch] = count.get(ch, 0) + 1
        maxfreq = max(maxfreq, count[ch])
        while (right - left + 1) - maxfreq > k:
            count[s[left]] -= 1
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

Notice that maxfreq is never decreased when the tail moves, so it can become stale (higher than the true maximum in the window). That is deliberate and safe: the answer can only grow when some window achieves a higher maxfreq than before, and a stale value only prevents shrinking below a length we have already achieved. With an alphabet of 26 you could also recompute the max exactly in O(26) per step; mentioning both shows understanding.

Variable window, shortest valid

For "shortest" problems the loop shape flips: record inside the while loop, because you want to keep shrinking as long as the window stays valid.

def min_subarray_len(target, a):        # all a[i] > 0
    left = s = 0
    best = float("inf")
    for right, x in enumerate(a):
        s += x
        while s >= target:               # valid: record, then try smaller
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            s -= a[left]
            left += 1
    return 0 if best == float("inf") else best

Monotonicity here is the reverse: if a window is valid (sum ≥ target), every larger window containing it is valid too, because values are positive. So once you have shrunk past a position, the windows you skipped could only have been longer.

Minimum Window Substring

The famous hard version: the smallest window of s that contains every character of t, counting multiplicity. The summary is a window Counter, plus two numbers that make the validity check O(1): required = how many distinct characters t needs, and formed = how many of them currently meet their required count.

from collections import Counter
def min_window(s, t):
    need = Counter(t)
    required, formed = len(need), 0
    have = {}
    left, best = 0, (float("inf"), 0, 0)
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        have[ch] = have.get(ch, 0) + 1
        if ch in need and have[ch] == need[ch]:
            formed += 1                       # this char just became satisfied
        while formed == required:             # valid: record and shrink
            if right - left + 1 < best[0]:
                best = (right - left + 1, left, right)
            out = s[left]
            have[out] -= 1
            if out in need and have[out] < need[out]:
                formed -= 1                   # just became unsatisfied
            left += 1
    n, l, r = best
    return "" if n == float("inf") else s[l:r + 1]

On s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC" the head first reaches a valid window at "ADOBEC"; shrinking removes A and invalidates it; the head continues until "DOBECODEBA" is valid again, shrinking gives "CODEBA"; later "BANC" (length 4) is found, which is the answer. The key details are incrementing formed only when a count reaches the need exactly (not every time the character is seen) and decrementing only when it drops below. O(|s| + |t|).

Counting subarrays: the r − l + 1 trick

"How many subarrays have at most k distinct values?" After the shrink step, the window a[left..right] is the longest valid window ending at right. Every shorter window ending at right — starting at left, left + 1, …, right — is also valid (monotonicity again). That is right − left + 1 subarrays, so add that each step.

"Exactly k" is harder because validity is not monotonic in that form: shrinking can go from exactly k to k − 1. The standard trick turns it into two monotonic problems: exactly(k) = atMost(k) − atMost(k − 1). Every subarray with exactly k distinct values is counted in the first term and not the second. This solves "Subarrays with K Different Integers" and "Count Number of Nice Subarrays" (exactly k odd numbers) in O(n).

The maximum of every window: monotonic deque

"Return the maximum of every window of size k." A running sum works because subtraction undoes addition, but there is no way to "un-max". Recomputing each window is O(n·k). The insight: when a new element x arrives, every older element smaller than or equal to x can never be the maximum of any future window — x is newer (stays in the window longer) and at least as large. So keep a deque of indices whose values are strictly decreasing from front to back:

from collections import deque
def max_sliding_window(a, k):
    dq, out = deque(), []                 # indices, values decreasing
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while dq and a[dq[-1]] <= x:      # dominated: will never be max
            dq.pop()
        dq.append(i)
        if dq[0] <= i - k:                # front left the window
            dq.popleft()
        if i >= k - 1:
            out.append(a[dq[0]])          # front is the max
    return out

This is a monotonic deque, the queue cousin of the monotonic stack (al8). The same structure gives sliding window minimums and appears inside DP optimisations ("jump game with maximum score in the last k steps").

Choosing the summary: a short catalogue

Most of the design work in a window problem is choosing the summary, so it helps to have a catalogue. A running sum answers sum and average conditions. A count of one kind of element (zeros, vowels, odd numbers) answers "at most k of X". A Counter plus its number of keys answers "at most k distinct". A Counter plus a satisfied-constraints count answers "contains all of t" and anagram questions. A last-seen index map answers "no repeats" and lets the tail jump. A monotonic deque answers maximum and minimum. A sorted structure or two heaps answers medians and order statistics. When a new problem arrives, ask which of these the validity check needs, and whether it can be updated in O(1) (or O(log k)) when one element enters or leaves. If no summary can be updated incrementally, the problem is probably not a window problem.

Recognising the pattern — and its limit

Reach for a sliding window when the problem asks about a contiguous subarray or substring, the words are "longest", "shortest", "maximum/minimum sum of size k", "at most k", "contains all", or "number of subarrays where…", and the condition is monotonic. Before coding, test monotonicity in one sentence: "if this window is invalid, is every bigger one invalid too?" If the answer is no — typically because values can be negative — use prefix sums with a hash map (al3), or prefix sums with a sorted structure for inequalities.

Practice in the DSA list: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock, Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, Longest Repeating Character Replacement, Permutation in String, Find All Anagrams in a String, Max Consecutive Ones III, Fruit Into Baskets, Minimum Size Subarray Sum, Minimum Window Substring, Subarrays with K Different Integers, Sliding Window Maximum.
deep:
Monotonic validity, stated precisely

Let P(l, r) mean "the window a[l..r] satisfies the condition". The longest-window template is correct when P is closed under shrinking: if P(l, r) holds then P(l', r') holds for every l ≤ l' ≤ r' ≤ r. Equivalently, if a window is invalid, every window containing it is invalid. Then for each right end r, the valid left ends form a suffix [L(r), r], and L(r) never decreases as r increases — which is exactly why the tail only moves forward. The shortest-window template needs the opposite: P closed under growing. Writing this down once makes it easy to classify new problems: "no repeated characters" is closed under shrinking; "sum ≥ target with positive values" is closed under growing; "sum exactly k" is neither, which is why it needs prefix sums or the at-most trick.

Why the stale maximum is correct

In Longest Repeating Character Replacement, let M be the maxfreq variable. It equals the largest frequency any window has had so far, which is at least the true frequency in the current window. The loop keeps length − M ≤ k, so the window length is at most M + k. Because M only increases, the window length never decreases below the best seen: when the true frequency is lower than M, the window simply slides (head and tail both advance by one) at the best length found so far. The recorded best only increases when M increases, and at that moment M is the true frequency of the newly added character in the current window, so the window is genuinely valid. That is a complete argument, and interviewers who know the problem sometimes ask for it.

Windows on time rather than indices

In production the window is often defined by time: "requests in the last 60 seconds", "errors in the last 5 minutes". The data structure is the same — a deque of (timestamp, value) pairs with a running summary — but the tail condition becomes "pop while front timestamp ≤ now − window". The difference from index windows is that events can be bursty, so the deque can grow large; production systems then switch to approximations: fixed buckets (one counter per second, summed over the last 60) or the sliding-window counter, which weights the previous fixed window's count by how much of it still overlaps. Recognising that an interview window problem and a rate limiter are the same structure is a good bridge into system-design follow-ups.

Window summaries that need more than O(1)

Some window questions need an order statistic: the median of each window, or "is there a pair within the window whose difference is at most t?" (Contains Duplicate III). The summary must then support insert, delete and an ordered query. Options are a balanced search tree or a sorted list (O(log k) per operation with the third-party sortedcontainers, or bisect.insort at O(k) per insert in plain Python), two heaps with lazy deletion for the median (al10), or bucketing by value range for the difference question (bucket width t + 1 means two values in the same bucket always qualify, so only neighbouring buckets need checking). The window logic stays the same; only the summary changes.

Two strings, one window

Several problems slide a window over one string while comparing it with a fixed second string (anagrams, permutation in string, minimum window). The unifying trick is to keep a count of how many constraints are currently satisfied rather than re-comparing whole count tables. Each add or remove changes one character's count, which can satisfy or break at most one constraint, so the satisfied-count changes by at most one per step. This "maintain the number of satisfied constraints incrementally" idea also appears in stream processing and in database incremental view maintenance, and it is what makes these solutions O(n) rather than O(n·alphabet).

When the window should be replaced by binary search

For "longest subarray with sum ≤ k" with only positive values, the window gives O(n). An alternative is binary search on the length (al7): for a candidate length L, check with a fixed window whether any window of length L qualifies. That is O(n log n) and worse here, but it is the right fallback when validity is monotonic in the length but the window's left end cannot be advanced incrementally — for example, when the check involves a hash of the window's contents (longest duplicate substring, al26).
prod:
In the interview room

Window problems are among the most common mediums, so interviewers see the same bugs again and again. The top ones: recording the answer in the wrong place (inside the shrink loop for a longest problem, or outside it for a shortest problem); moving the tail backwards when jumping with a last-seen map (missing the last[ch] >= left guard); updating formed every time a needed character is added instead of only when its count reaches the requirement exactly; forgetting to delete zero-count keys from a Counter when the problem counts distinct keys (len(counter) then over-reports); and an off-by-one in the window length (right − left + 1). Say the three blanks of the template — summary, add/remove, valid — before coding, and test with a string where every character is the same and one where all are distinct.

The most valuable sentence you can say is the monotonicity check: "this works because values are non-negative, so a window that is too big stays too big as it grows". It shows you know when the pattern applies. Interviewers often follow up by removing the precondition ("now values can be negative"), and the candidate who stated it immediately says "then the window breaks; I'd switch to prefix sums with a hash map".

For the deque problem, expect "why is it O(n)?" — each index is appended once and popped at most once, from either end — and "why pop elements less than or equal to the new one, not just less than?" (equal older elements are dominated too: the new one leaves the window later).

On online assessments, window problems are frequently disguised: "the longest period of days where the total rainfall stayed under X", "the smallest number of consecutive deliveries covering all product types", "for each hour, the busiest server in the last 10 minutes". Translate the story into "contiguous range + monotonic condition + summary" and the template applies directly.

In real systems

Sliding windows are a core primitive in networking and streaming. TCP's flow control is literally a sliding window over the byte stream: the sender may have a window's worth of unacknowledged bytes in flight, and the window slides forward as acknowledgements arrive (net4). Rate limiters at API gateways use sliding-window logs or counters to enforce "N requests per rolling minute" without the burst-at-the-boundary problem of fixed windows; Cloudflare has described its sliding-window counter approximation publicly. Stream processors such as Apache Flink and Kafka Streams offer tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding (fixed, overlapping) and session (gap-based) windows, and compute aggregates incrementally exactly like the running sum here. Monitoring systems compute moving averages and rolling percentiles over time windows to smooth noisy metrics and trigger alerts. The interview skill — choose a summary that updates in O(1) per event — is precisely what makes those systems cheap at millions of events per second.
myths: Sliding window works for any 'subarray with sum k' problem.

A shrinking window needs a monotonic rule: adding an element must never make an invalid window valid again by shrinking later, and removing one must never break a valid one in the wrong direction. With non-negative numbers, sums only grow as the window grows, so the rule holds. With negatives it does not, and you need prefix sums with a hash map instead (al3).
The nested while loop makes sliding window O(n²).
The left pointer only moves forward and at most n times over the whole run, so the inner loop's total work is O(n). Each element enters the window once and leaves at most once.
In Longest Repeating Character Replacement you must recompute the maximum frequency when the window shrinks.

You do not. The answer only improves when a window has a larger max frequency than any seen before, so keeping a stale, too-high maxfreq never produces a wrong larger answer; it just stops the window from shrinking as eagerly. This keeps the solution O(n) without rescanning the counts.
For 'exactly k distinct' you can shrink whenever the count exceeds k and count the windows with exactly k.

That misses windows: for a fixed right end, the valid left ends with exactly k distinct form a range, not a single point, and the simple window only sees one of them. The reliable trick is exactly(k) = atMost(k) − atMost(k − 1), where each atMost is a standard window.
A window must always be represented by a set of its elements.

Use whatever summary the validity check needs: a running sum, a count of zeros, a Counter of characters, the number of distinct characters, or a deque of candidate maxima. Choosing the smallest summary that can be updated in O(1) per add and remove is the design step.
lab:
Stress-test two window solutions against brute force, including the repeated-character edge cases that break hand-rolled versions.

  1. Save as window_lab.py: 
    import random
from collections import Counter

def brute_longest(s):
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(s)):
        for j in range(i, len(s)):
            if len(set(s[i:j+1])) == j - i + 1:
                best = max(best, j - i + 1)
    return best

def window_longest(s):
    last, left, best = {}, 0, 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last and last[ch] >= left:
            left = last[ch] + 1
        last[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

def brute_exact(a, k):
    return sum(1 for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i, len(a))
               if len(set(a[i:j+1])) == k)

def at_most(a, k):
    cnt, left, total = Counter(), 0, 0
    for right, x in enumerate(a):
        cnt[x] += 1
        while len(cnt) > k:
            cnt[a[left]] -= 1
            if cnt[a[left]] == 0: del cnt[a[left]]
            left += 1
        total += right - left + 1
    return total

for _ in range(3000):
    s = "".join(random.choice("abc") for _ in range(random.randint(0, 10)))
    assert window_longest(s) == brute_longest(s), s
    a = [random.randint(1, 3) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 10))]
    k = random.randint(1, 3)
    assert at_most(a, k) - at_most(a, k - 1) == brute_exact(a, k), (a, k)
print("window solutions match brute force")
  2. Run it; expect the final message.
  3. Remove the condition and last[ch] >= left and run again: a string like "abba" fails, because the tail jumps backwards to the old "a".
  4. Remove the del cnt[...] line: the at-most count becomes wrong, because len(cnt) still counts characters whose count fell to zero.

What this proves: the two classic window bugs are invisible on inputs without repeats, and a three-letter alphabet in random tests finds them immediately.
recap: A sliding window keeps a contiguous range and updates a summary in O(1) as elements enter on the right and leave on the left, instead of recomputing every range.
Fixed-size windows add a[r] and remove a[r − k] each step; variable windows grow the right end and shrink the left end while the window is invalid.
For longest-valid problems, shrink until valid and then record; for shortest-valid problems, record and shrink while still valid.
The method needs monotonic validity: if a window is invalid, every larger window containing it is also invalid (or the reverse for shortest problems).
Each element enters and leaves the window at most once, so the total work is O(n) despite the nested loop.
Count subarrays with at most k of something by adding r − l + 1 at each right end; exactly k equals atMost(k) minus atMost(k − 1).
A monotonic deque of indices gives the maximum (or minimum) of every window in O(n) total.
If values can be negative or the condition is not monotonic, use prefix sums with a hash map instead.
glossary: Constant average cost per step over the whole run, even if some steps do more work.
Counting subarrays with exactly k of a property as count(at most k) minus count(at most k − 1).
A double-ended queue that supports adding and removing at both ends in O(1); Python's collections.deque.
Building answers from stored answers to smaller subproblems; some DP transitions take the max over the last k states, which a monotonic deque speeds up. Taught in al21.
A window whose length k is given; it slides by one element per step.
A deque whose values are kept in decreasing (or increasing) order, so its front is the window's maximum (or minimum).
The property that makes windows work: once a window is invalid, growing it cannot make it valid, so the left end never needs to move back.
Two counts used in Minimum Window Substring: how many distinct characters must be satisfied, and how many currently are.
Advancing the left pointer to remove elements from the window.
The information kept about the window (sum, counts, distinct count, deque) that lets validity be checked in O(1).
A window that satisfies the problem's condition, such as having no repeated characters or a sum at least the target.
A window whose size changes: it grows on the right and shrinks on the left to stay valid.
A contiguous range a[l..r] of an array or string under consideration.
drill:
Is it a window?

For each problem, decide whether a shrinking sliding window is correct, and if not, what to use. (a) Longest subarray whose product is less than k, all values positive. (b) Longest subarray with sum exactly k, values may be negative. (c) Shortest subarray with sum at least k, values may be negative. (d) Number of subarrays whose product is less than k, positive values.

Answer

(a) Yes: with positive values the product only grows as the window grows, so "product < k" is closed under shrinking. Grow right, multiply; while product ≥ k, divide by the left value and advance. (b) No: negatives break monotonicity. Use prefix sums with a map from prefix value to its first index; at each r, look up pre[r+1] − k (al3). (c) No for a plain window, because with negatives shrinking can increase the sum. Use prefix sums with a monotonic deque of increasing prefix values: for each r, pop from the front while pre[r+1] − pre[front] ≥ k (recording the length), and pop from the back while the back's prefix is ≥ pre[r+1] (it can never be a better left end). This is O(n) and is LeetCode's "Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K". (d) Yes, with the counting trick: after shrinking so the product is below k, every subarray ending at r and starting in [left, r] qualifies, so add r − left + 1. Handle k ≤ 1 separately (no positive product is below 1 or 0).
qa: E
Find the maximum sum of any k consecutive elements.
Sum the first k elements, then slide: for each new right index r, add a[r] and subtract a[r − k], tracking the maximum. O(n) time and O(1) space, versus O(n·k) for recomputing each window.
E
Best time to buy and sell a stock once: why is it a window problem?

Scan days as the right end and keep the minimum price seen so far as the best left end. The profit for selling today is price − min_so_far; track the maximum. It is a window whose left end jumps to any new minimum, O(n) time and O(1) space.
M
Longest substring without repeating characters.

Grow the window on the right; if the new character is already in the window, shrink from the left until it is not (or jump left to one past its last index stored in a map). Record the window length after each step. Each character enters and leaves once, so O(n) time and O(alphabet) space.

Follow-up: Why must the jump use max(left, last[c] + 1)? — The stored last index may be before the current left end, from a character already removed; jumping back would re-include removed characters.
M
Longest repeating character replacement: you may change k characters.

A window can be made uniform if its length minus the count of its most frequent character is at most k. Grow the right end, update counts and maxfreq; while length − maxfreq > k, remove the left character and advance. Record the length. maxfreq can be left stale when shrinking, because only a larger maxfreq can produce a longer answer.
Follow-up: Is the answer still correct with a stale maxfreq? — Yes; the window never shrinks below the best length found so far, and it only grows when a genuinely higher frequency appears.
M
Smallest subarray with sum at least target, all values positive.

Grow the right end adding to the sum; while the sum is at least target, record the length and remove the left element. Positive values make validity monotonic, so O(n). If values could be negative, use prefix sums with a monotonic deque instead.
M
Find all start indices of anagrams of p in s.

Fixed window of length len(p). Keep counts of the window and compare with counts of p, or better, keep a single 'difference' counter and the number of characters whose difference is non-zero. Slide by adding s[r] and removing s[r − m], updating that number; record r − m + 1 whenever it is zero. O(n) time.
M
Count subarrays with at most k distinct integers, then exactly k.
For at most k: standard window that shrinks when distinct > k; every window ending at r with left end in [l, r] is valid, so add r − l + 1. For exactly k: atMost(k) − atMost(k − 1). Both O(n).
M
Max consecutive ones if you may flip at most k zeros.
The window is valid while it contains at most k zeros. Grow right, count zeros; while zeros > k, shrink left. Record the length. O(n) time, O(1) space.
H
Minimum window substring: smallest window of s containing all characters of t with multiplicity.

Count need = Counter(t) and track formed, the number of distinct characters whose requirement is currently met. Grow right; when a character's window count reaches its need, formed++. While formed equals the number of distinct needed characters, record the window if smaller, then remove the left character, decrementing formed if it drops below need, and advance. O(|s| + |t|).
Follow-up: How do you return the substring itself? — Store the best (length, left, right) and slice once at the end.
H
Sliding window maximum for every window of size k.

Keep a deque of indices whose values are in decreasing order. For each new index, pop from the back while the back's value is at most the new value (they can never be a maximum again), push the new index, pop the front if it has left the window, and the front is the current maximum. Each index is pushed and popped once: O(n).
Follow-up: Sliding window median? — Two heaps with lazy deletion, or a sorted container: O(n log k).
H
Why does a shrinking window fail for 'longest subarray with sum at most k' when values can be negative, and what do you do?

Validity is no longer monotonic: adding a negative number can turn an invalid window valid again, so after shrinking past an element you might have needed it later. Use prefix sums: for each right end you want the smallest l with pre[l] ≥ pre[r+1] − k. Keep the candidates for l in a structure that supports that search — a monotonic stack of increasing prefix maxima with binary search gives O(n log n).
H
Design a rate limiter that allows at most N requests in any rolling 60-second window.

A sliding-window log keeps a deque of timestamps per user: on each request, pop timestamps older than now − 60 s from the front, allow if fewer than N remain and append now. It is exact but stores up to N timestamps per user. A sliding-window counter approximates with two fixed-minute counters weighted by overlap, using O(1) memory. The deque version is the interview sliding-window pattern applied to time instead of indices.
