t: Binary search: boundaries, rotated arrays and searching on the answer
sum: Binary search as 'find the first index where a monotone predicate becomes true': one template with an invariant, lower and upper bounds, rotated arrays and peaks, and binary search on the answer for capacity, speed and split problems.
prereq: al2
Halving a range each step takes log₂ n steps; about 30 steps cover 10⁹ values.
al5
An invariant that holds every iteration plus a safe-move argument proves a pointer algorithm correct.
why:
A delivery company needs to pick the size of truck for a route. It has 500 packages to deliver in order, a deadline of 5 days, and trucks that come in any capacity. Too small a truck and the packages take more than 5 days; too large and the company wastes money. What is the smallest capacity that meets the deadline? There is no obvious formula. The brute force tries capacity 1, then 2, then 3, simulating the deliveries each time, until one works. If the answer is a capacity of 400,000 kg, that is 400,000 simulations.

But there is structure here. If a capacity works, every larger capacity also works; if a capacity fails, every smaller one fails too. The answers line up as "fail, fail, fail, …, work, work, work". Finding the boundary in such a sequence is exactly what binary search does: try the middle capacity; if it works, the answer is there or smaller; if not, it is larger. Each simulation halves the range of possible answers, so about 19 simulations find the boundary among 400,000 candidates.

Most people meet binary search as "find a number in a sorted array", and that is part of it. The bigger idea — and the one interviewers lean on in medium and hard problems — is that binary search finds the boundary of any monotone yes/no question. Koko eating bananas, shipping capacity, splitting an array to minimise the largest part, placing routers as far apart as possible, finding a peak, searching a rotated array: all are binary search once you see the monotone predicate.

Binary search is also famously easy to get subtly wrong. This lesson therefore gives one template with a written invariant that handles every case, then applies it to boundaries (lower and upper bounds), rotated arrays and peaks, binary search on the answer, real-valued searches, and the hardest classic, the median of two sorted arrays.
primer:
The mental model: the guessing game, and the line of lights

In the number-guessing game ("I'm thinking of a number from 1 to 100; I'll say higher or lower"), the best strategy is to guess the middle. Each answer rules out half of the remaining numbers, so you never need more than 7 guesses for 100 numbers, or 30 for a billion. That is binary search's power: the work grows with the logarithm of the size.

A more useful picture for interviews is a long row of lights. Every light is either off or on, and all the off lights come before all the on lights. You want to find the first light that is on, but checking a light costs something (an array read, or a whole simulation). Check the middle light. If it is on, the first on-light is here or to the left; if off, it is to the right. Each check halves the stretch where the boundary can be.

That is the reframe that makes binary search reliable: stop thinking "find x" and start thinking "find the first index where pred is true". A monotone predicate is a yes/no question that is false up to some point and true from then on. For "find x in a sorted array", the predicate is a[i] ≥ x: the first true is where x is (if it exists) or where it would be inserted. For the delivery trucks, the predicate is "capacity c finishes within 5 days". The loop is identical; only the predicate changes.

Where the analogy breaks: the guessing game assumes you are told "higher" or "lower" directly. In real problems you have to construct the predicate, prove it is monotone, and pick bounds that certainly contain the answer. Those three steps — predicate, monotonicity, bounds — are where the thinking goes; the loop itself should be automatic.

A second example makes the reframe concrete. "Find the last occurrence of 7 in a sorted array" sounds like a different problem from "find the first occurrence". In the predicate view it is not: the last 7 sits just before the first element that is greater than 7, so search for the first true of a[i] > 7 and step back one. Every boundary question on sorted data — first, last, count, floor, ceiling, insertion point — becomes "first true of the right predicate, possibly minus one". You no longer need a separate variant of the loop for each question, which is exactly where most bugs come from.

Finally, keep the cost model in mind. Binary search makes about log₂(range) predicate checks. If each check is O(1) (an array read), the whole search is O(log n). If each check is an O(n) simulation, the search is O(n log range). Both are usually tiny compared with trying every candidate.
body:
The one template

Use this template for every binary search. It finds the first index in [lo, hi) where a monotone predicate is true, returning hi if there is none.

def first_true(lo, hi, pred):
    # invariant: pred is False on [orig_lo, lo), True on [hi, orig_hi)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2      # lo <= mid < hi
        if pred(mid):
            hi = mid              # mid might be the first True
        else:
            lo = mid + 1          # first True is to the right of mid
    return lo                     # lo == hi: the boundary

Why it is correct: the invariant says everything left of lo is false and everything from hi onwards is true (with hi starting one past the end, meaning "assume true"). When pred(mid) is true, mid could be the first true, so we keep it by setting hi = mid. When false, mid and everything left of it are false, so lo = mid + 1. Because mid is strictly less than hi, every iteration shrinks the interval, so the loop terminates, and when lo == hi the invariant pins the boundary exactly. There is no "found it, return early" case to get wrong.

The two ways people break binary search are both avoided here. Infinite loops come from setting lo = mid (when hi = lo + 1, mid = lo and nothing changes); this template never does that. Off-by-one errors come from mixing inclusive and exclusive bounds; this template uses one convention, the half-open interval [lo, hi).

Lower bound, upper bound, and finding a target

On a sorted array, two predicates cover almost everything:

  • Lower bound: first index with a[i] ≥ x — first_true(0, n, lambda i: a[i] >= x), the same as bisect.bisect_left(a, x).
  • Upper bound: first index with a[i] > x — bisect.bisect_right(a, x).

From these: x is present if lower bound < n and a[lower] == x. The first occurrence of x is the lower bound; the last occurrence is upper bound − 1; the number of occurrences is upper − lower. "The largest element ≤ x" is at upper − 1; "the smallest element ≥ x" is at lower. Trace a = [1, 2, 2, 2, 5, 7], x = 2: lower bound = 1, upper bound = 4, so 2 occurs 4 − 1 = 3 times at indices 1..3. For x = 3: both bounds are 4, so it is absent and would be inserted at index 4.

In Python you should use bisect in real code and say so, but interviewers usually want you to write the loop once to show you can. Since Python 3.10, bisect functions accept a key argument, which helps when searching a list of tuples.

Searching a sorted matrix and other index spaces

If a matrix's rows are sorted and each row starts after the previous row ends, it is a sorted array of R·C elements written row by row. Binary search on a virtual index k in [0, R·C), reading the element at matrix[k // C][k % C]. That is O(log(R·C)). (If only rows and columns are sorted separately, use the staircase walk from al5 instead.)

The index space can be anything ordered: days, timestamps, versions. The Time-Based Key-Value Store keeps, for each key, a list of (timestamp, value) appended in increasing time order; get(key, t) needs the last entry with timestamp ≤ t, which is bisect_right(times, t) − 1.

Rotated sorted arrays

A rotated sorted array, such as [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], is a sorted array cut once with the halves swapped. It is not sorted, but it has a property that keeps binary search alive: whatever mid you pick, at least one of the halves [lo, mid] and [mid, hi] is sorted, because the single "drop" can only be in one of them.

Find the minimum. Compare a[mid] with the last element of the current range. If a[mid] > a[hi], the drop — and so the minimum — is to the right of mid. Otherwise the range mid..hi is sorted and the minimum is at mid or to its left. That is a monotone predicate: "a[i] ≤ a[last]" is false on the left part and true on the right part.

def find_min(a):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] > a[hi]:
            lo = mid + 1          # drop is right of mid
        else:
            hi = mid              # mid..hi sorted: min at mid or left
    return a[lo]

Trace [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]: lo = 0, hi = 6, mid = 3 (7 > 2) → lo = 4; mid = 5 (1 ≤ 2) → hi = 5; mid = 4 (0 ≤ 1) → hi = 4. Answer a[4] = 0.

Search for a target. At each step, decide which half is sorted by comparing a[lo] with a[mid], then check whether the target falls inside the sorted half's range. If it does, search there; otherwise search the other half.

def search_rotated(a, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] == x: return mid
        if a[lo] <= a[mid]:                    # left half sorted
            if a[lo] <= x < a[mid]: hi = mid - 1
            else: lo = mid + 1
        else:                                  # right half sorted
            if a[mid] < x <= a[hi]: lo = mid + 1
            else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1

This one uses the closed-interval style with an early return, because "find x" naturally ends when it is found; both styles are fine as long as you do not mix them. Duplicates break the "which half is sorted" test when a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi]; the fix is to shrink lo and hi by one, which makes the worst case O(n).

Peaks: binary search without sortedness

"Find any peak" (an element larger than its neighbours, with the outside treated as −∞) in O(log n). Look at a[mid] and a[mid + 1]. If a[mid] < a[mid + 1], the values rise to the right; following the rise must eventually hit a peak, because the array ends with −∞. So a peak exists in (mid, hi]. Otherwise, a peak exists in [lo, mid]. The invariant is "a peak exists in [lo, hi]", and each step keeps it while halving the range. This is a good example to remember because it shows that the requirement is not sortedness but a guarantee about which half still contains an answer.

Binary search on the answer

Now the delivery-truck problem from the start. The general recipe has four steps:

  1. Identify the answer as a number in a known range: a speed, a capacity, a distance, a time.
  2. Write the feasibility check: "given candidate answer x, can the task be done?" Usually a greedy pass in O(n).
  3. Prove monotonicity: if x is feasible, is every larger x feasible (for minimisation)? State why.
  4. Choose bounds: lo where it is certainly infeasible or the smallest legal value, hi where it is certainly feasible. Then run the template.

Koko eating bananas: piles of bananas, h hours, Koko eats at most k bananas per hour from one pile. Find the minimum k to finish. Check(k): hours = Σ ceil(p / k) ≤ h. Monotone: a faster speed never takes more hours. Bounds: k from 1 to max(piles) (at max, each pile takes one hour, the least possible).

def min_eating_speed(piles, h):
    def ok(k):
        return sum((p + k - 1) // k for p in piles) <= h   # ceil without floats
    lo, hi = 1, max(piles)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if ok(mid): hi = mid
        else: lo = mid + 1
    return lo

Trace piles = [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8: lo = 1, hi = 11. mid = 6: hours 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 6 ≤ 8, ok → hi = 6. mid = 3: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 > 8 → lo = 4. mid = 5: 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 ok → hi = 5. mid = 4: 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 ok → hi = 4. Answer 4. Complexity O(n log max(pile)).

The same recipe solves a whole family:

  • Capacity to ship within D days: candidates from max(weight) to sum(weights); greedy check counts days.
  • Split array largest sum (minimise the largest of k contiguous parts): candidates from max(a) to sum(a); greedy check counts parts.
  • Magnetic force / aggressive cows (place m items maximising the minimum gap): here larger answers are harder, so the predicate is "gap d is achievable" and you want the last true — use first_true on "d is not achievable" and subtract one, or flip the comparison.
  • Minimum days to make m bouquets: candidates are days; check counts bouquets formed from flowers bloomed by that day.

The tell-tale signs in a problem statement are "minimum maximum", "maximum minimum", "smallest x such that…", "at least / at most within a limit", and constraints with a huge value range (up to 10⁹) but moderate n.

Binary search on real numbers

"Find the square root of x to six decimal places" or "find the minimum time such that…" with real-valued answers. The template changes slightly: there is no "+1", so loop a fixed number of times (100 iterations halve the range by 2¹⁰⁰, far beyond double precision) or until hi − lo is below the tolerance.

def sqrt_real(x, iters=100):
    lo, hi = 0.0, max(1.0, x)
    for _ in range(iters):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        if mid * mid >= x: hi = mid
        else: lo = mid
    return hi

For integer square roots, use the integer template (or math.isqrt) and avoid floating point entirely, because float rounding near perfect squares gives off-by-one answers for large inputs.

Choosing between the closed and half-open styles

You will see two styles in the wild. The closed style keeps the target in [lo, hi] inclusive, loops while lo ≤ hi, and updates with mid ± 1; it suits "find x and return early". The half-open first-true style used in this lesson keeps the boundary in [lo, hi), loops while lo < hi, and updates with hi = mid or lo = mid + 1; it suits every boundary question and search on the answer. Both are correct. The danger is mixing them — a closed-style loop condition with half-open updates is the source of most infinite loops and missed elements. Pick one as your default (the first-true style covers more problems), and switch to the other only deliberately.

Recognising the pattern

Reach for binary search when: the input is sorted or rotated-sorted; the problem asks for a first/last position, count or insertion point; a constraint makes O(n) too slow for a single query (O(log n) needed); or the answer is a number and "is x good enough?" is monotone. Then state the predicate, why it is monotone, and the bounds, before writing the loop.

Practice in the DSA list: Binary Search, Find First and Last Position, Search a 2D Matrix, Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array, Search in Rotated Sorted Array, Find Peak Element, Time Based Key-Value Store, Koko Eating Bananas, Capacity To Ship Packages, Magnetic Force Between Two Balls, Split Array Largest Sum, Median of Two Sorted Arrays.
deep:
Proving the feasibility check is monotone

Search on the answer is only correct if feasibility is monotone, and interviewers increasingly ask you to justify it. The argument is usually a one-line "relaxation" proof: any schedule that works with capacity c also works with capacity c + 1, because every day's load that fit under c also fits under c + 1. For maximisation problems the argument flips: if items can be placed with minimum gap d, they can be placed with any smaller gap, using the same placement. When you cannot find such an argument, be suspicious — for example, "number of distinct values in the window is at most k" is monotone in the window size, but "number of distinct values equals k" is not, and a binary search over it would silently skip answers.

The greedy check must be optimal for the fixed answer

The feasibility check usually greedily packs elements in order ("start a new day when the next package would overflow"). That greedy is only valid if it uses the minimum number of days for that capacity. For contiguous splits it is: the exchange argument says that delaying a cut never helps, because a part that could have taken one more element and did not only pushes more load onto later parts. When the order is not fixed (you may reorder packages), greedy packing becomes bin packing, which is NP-hard, and binary search on the answer no longer has a cheap check. Spotting that difference — contiguous versus arbitrary assignment — is a senior-level observation.

Median of two sorted arrays: binary search on a partition

The hard classic searches over a cut position rather than a value. Cut the shorter array A at i (i elements on the left) and the other array B at j = (m + n + 1) // 2 − i, so the two left parts together contain half the elements (the extra one when the total is odd). The cut is correct exactly when every left element is ≤ every right element, which reduces to two comparisons: A[i − 1] ≤ B[j] and B[j − 1] ≤ A[i]. If A[i − 1] > B[j], i is too far right; if B[j − 1] > A[i], i is too far left — a monotone condition over i, so binary search finds it in O(log min(m, n)). Use −∞ and +∞ for the elements just outside the arrays so empty sides need no special code. Then the median is max(left maxima) for odd totals, or the average of max(left maxima) and min(right minima) for even totals. Explaining it as "binary search on where to cut A, with B's cut determined by the half-size constraint" is the clear version interviewers hope to hear.

Ternary search and unimodal functions

When a function increases and then decreases (unimodal), you can find its maximum by comparing two interior points m1 < m2: if f(m1) < f(m2), the maximum is right of m1; otherwise it is left of m2. Each step discards a third of the range. For integer domains it is usually simpler and as fast to binary search the predicate "f(i) < f(i + 1)", which is true on the rising part and false on the falling part — exactly the peak-finding argument. Ternary search is mostly useful on real-valued convex functions (minimising a cost over a continuous parameter).

Exponential search for unbounded ranges

If you do not know an upper bound — searching an infinite sorted stream, or a predicate over all positive integers — first find one by doubling: check 1, 2, 4, 8, … until the predicate is true at 2ᵏ, then binary search within [2ᵏ⁻¹, 2ᵏ]. Total cost O(log answer), not O(log of some huge guess). The same doubling idea is behind "galloping" in Timsort's merge, which Python's own sort uses to merge runs quickly when one run's elements mostly come before the other's.

Binary search inside other algorithms

Binary search often appears as a component. The O(n log n) longest increasing subsequence keeps an array tails[k] = the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1; tails is sorted, and each new element replaces the lower bound of itself in it (al21). Sweep-line and interval problems binary search sorted event lists. "Count pairs with distance ≤ d" plus binary search on d finds the k-th smallest pair distance. Recognising binary search as a building block — "I need the first element ≥ x in a sorted structure that I maintain" — is how you get O(n log n) solutions to problems that look quadratic.
prod:
In the interview room

Binary search is where interviewers watch for precision under pressure. The failures they see most are infinite loops (lo = mid with the lower middle), returning the wrong boundary (the last false instead of the first true), off-by-one bounds for search on the answer (starting lo at 0 when a speed of 0 divides by zero, or hi too small so the true answer is outside the range), and the classic overflow in languages with fixed-size integers. Avoid all of them by saying the template, the predicate, and the bounds out loud before writing any code: "first true of 'speed k finishes within h hours', k from 1 to max pile, which is always feasible".

Testing binary search by hand has a standard checklist: empty array; one element (present and absent); target smaller than everything; target larger than everything; target equal to the first and last element; many duplicates of the target. For search on the answer, test the smallest and largest possible answers. Five minutes of this catches almost every bug.

Interviewers also probe recognition. A strong signal is spotting search on the answer from the shape "minimise the maximum" before the interviewer hints at it, and justifying monotonicity in one sentence. A weak signal is trying a DP or a greedy guess on Split Array Largest Sum without noticing the monotone structure.

Online assessments love search on the answer because it rewards recognition: the problem is phrased as an optimisation with a story ("minimum number of hours", "largest possible minimum distance"), the constraints allow values up to 10⁹, and a straightforward simulation is O(n) per candidate. If you catch yourself writing a loop over every candidate answer, stop and ask whether feasibility is monotone.

In real systems

The most famous production binary search bug: in 2006 Joshua Bloch reported that the binary search in Java's standard library (and the mergesort in many libraries) computed (low + high) / 2, which overflows when the array has more than about a billion elements. The bug had been in the JDK for nine years and in the textbook it was copied from for longer; the fix is low + (high − low) / 2 or an unsigned shift. It is the canonical example of a "correct" algorithm failing at scale. Binary search is also a daily debugging tool: git bisect binary searches commit history for the change that introduced a bug — with 1,000 commits since the last good build, about 10 test runs find the culprit. The same idea bisects configuration changes, dependency versions, or the size of input that makes a service fall over. Inside databases, B-tree indexes binary search the sorted keys within each page on the way down the tree, and time-series databases binary search block indexes to find the blocks covering a time range. Capacity planning tools effectively search on the answer: "what is the smallest instance count that keeps p99 latency under 200 ms at this load?", found by load-testing candidates chosen by bisection.
myths: Binary search only works on sorted arrays.

It works on any search space where a yes/no predicate is monotone — false, false, …, true, true. A sorted array is one example (predicate: a[i] ≥ x), but so are 'can we ship everything in D days with capacity c?' and 'is there a peak to the right of i?'. Recognising a monotone predicate is the real skill.
Binary search is easy, so bugs are unlikely.

Binary search is notoriously easy to get subtly wrong: infinite loops when lo = mid, off-by-one on inclusive versus exclusive bounds, and missing the last element. Jon Bentley reported that most professional programmers he tested could not write a correct one, and Java's library version had an integer-overflow bug for nine years. Use one template with a written invariant every time.
mid = (lo + hi) // 2 is always safe.

In Python, yes, because integers do not overflow. In Java or C++, lo + hi can overflow a 32-bit int for large arrays; use lo + (hi − lo) / 2. Also, with lo = mid updates you need the upper middle (lo + hi + 1) // 2 or the loop never terminates when hi = lo + 1.
Search on the answer is a different algorithm from binary search.

It is the same algorithm applied to a range of candidate answers instead of array indices. The predicate is 'is answer x feasible?', computed by a greedy or linear check, and it must be monotone in x. The total cost is the cost of the check times log(range).
Rotated sorted array search is O(log n) even with duplicates.

With duplicates, a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi] gives no information about which half is sorted, so the algorithm can only shrink by one element. The worst case becomes O(n), for example an array of all equal values with one different element.
lab:
Check the template against bisect on random data, and Koko's binary search against a linear scan of candidate speeds.

  1. Save as bs_lab.py: 
    import random, bisect

def first_true(lo, hi, pred):
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if pred(mid): hi = mid
        else: lo = mid + 1
    return lo

def koko_bs(piles, h):
    ok = lambda k: sum((p + k - 1) // k for p in piles) <= h
    return first_true(1, max(piles), ok)

def koko_linear(piles, h):
    k = 1
    while sum((p + k - 1) // k for p in piles) > h: k += 1
    return k

for _ in range(5000):
    a = sorted(random.randint(0, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 10)))
    x = random.randint(-1, 10)
    assert first_true(0, len(a), lambda i: a[i] >= x) == bisect.bisect_left(a, x)
    assert first_true(0, len(a), lambda i: a[i] > x) == bisect.bisect_right(a, x)
    piles = [random.randint(1, 30) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 6))]
    h = random.randint(len(piles), 40)
    assert koko_bs(piles, h) == koko_linear(piles, h), (piles, h)
print("template, bisect and Koko all agree")
  2. Run it and expect the final message.
  3. Change lo = mid + 1 to lo = mid and run again: the script hangs on the first interval of length 2 where the predicate is false at mid. Press Ctrl+C.
  4. Change Koko's lower bound from 1 to 0 and run: a ZeroDivisionError appears as soon as a search probes speed 0.

What this proves: the template is exactly bisect_left / bisect_right with the right predicate, and the two most common bugs — a non-shrinking update and a bad bound — fail loudly on small random inputs. Note that h is kept at least the number of piles, because fewer hours than piles is infeasible at any speed.
recap: Frame every binary search as finding the first position where a monotone predicate becomes true.
Use one template: lo and hi bracket the boundary, mid = (lo + hi) // 2, if pred(mid) then hi = mid else lo = mid + 1, stop when lo == hi.
Lower bound is the first index with a[i] ≥ x and upper bound the first with a[i] > x; their difference counts occurrences of x, and Python's bisect_left and bisect_right implement them.
In a rotated sorted array, one half around mid is always sorted; check whether the target lies in that sorted half to decide which way to go.
Binary search on the answer applies when 'x is feasible' is monotone in x: search the range of possible answers with a greedy feasibility check.
The cost of search on the answer is O(check × log(range)), for example O(n log(max value)).
On real numbers, iterate a fixed number of times or until the interval is smaller than the required precision.
Test every binary search on empty input, one element, the target at both ends, and a target that is absent.
glossary: Searching a range of candidate answers for the smallest (or largest) feasible one, using a feasibility check as the predicate.
Python's standard-library module for binary search on sorted lists: bisect_left, bisect_right, insort.
Solving a problem from stored answers to smaller subproblems; taught in al21–al23.
A function that answers 'can the task be done with answer x?', usually by a greedy pass in O(n).
A range [lo, hi) that includes lo and excludes hi; its length is hi − lo.
A statement that holds before and after every iteration, such as 'the boundary lies in [lo, hi]'.
The first index whose value is greater than or equal to x; equivalently the insertion point that keeps equal elements to the right.
A yes/no function over an ordered space that is false up to some point and true from then on (or the reverse).
A class of problems for which no polynomial-time algorithm is known; bin packing is one. If a check is NP-hard, search on the answer gives no shortcut.
An element strictly greater than its neighbours.
A sorted array cut at some point with the two parts swapped, such as [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2].
Searching for the maximum of a unimodal function by comparing two interior points and discarding a third of the range.
Increasing then decreasing (or the reverse), with a single peak.
The first index whose value is strictly greater than x.
drill:
Recognise and set up search on the answer

"You have n routers to place on a straight street at given candidate positions (sorted, up to 10⁵ of them, coordinates up to 10⁹). Place exactly m routers to maximise the minimum distance between any two." Describe the predicate, why it is monotone, the bounds, the check, and the complexity.

Answer

The answer is a distance d. Predicate: "we can place m routers with every gap at least d". Monotone in the decreasing direction: if gap d is achievable, any smaller gap is achievable with the same placement, so the predicate is true, true, …, true, false, false. We want the last true. Using the first-true template, search for the first d where it is not achievable and subtract one; or write the mirrored template with mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2 and lo = mid on success. Bounds: d from 0 (always achievable) to (max − min) // (m − 1) + 1 (cannot be achievable, since m − 1 gaps cannot all exceed the total span divided by m − 1). Check: greedy — place the first router at the first position, then place each next router at the first position at least d beyond the last placed one; feasible if you place m. The greedy is optimal because placing a router as early as possible never reduces the room for later ones. Complexity: O(n) per check and about 30 checks for a 10⁹ range, so O(n log(range)) ≈ 3 × 10⁶ steps.
qa: E
Write binary search for a target in a sorted array and give its complexity.

Keep lo and hi; take mid; if a[mid] equals the target return it; if smaller, search the right half (lo = mid + 1); otherwise the left half (hi = mid − 1). Stop when lo > hi and return −1. Each step halves the range, so O(log n) time and O(1) space.
E
How do you find the insertion position of x in a sorted array?

That is the lower bound: the first index with a[i] ≥ x, or n if none. Search with pred(i) = a[i] ≥ x over [0, n): if pred(mid) then hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1; return lo. In Python, bisect.bisect_left(a, x).
E
Count how many times x occurs in a sorted array in O(log n).
Occurrences = upper bound − lower bound: bisect_right(a, x) − bisect_left(a, x). Both are binary searches, so O(log n) total, regardless of how many copies there are.
M
Search in a rotated sorted array with distinct values.

At each step, one of the halves [lo, mid] or [mid, hi] is sorted, which you can tell by comparing a[lo] with a[mid]. If the left half is sorted and the target lies between a[lo] and a[mid], go left; otherwise go right. Symmetrically if the right half is sorted. O(log n).
Follow-up: With duplicates? — When a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi] you cannot tell which half is sorted, so shrink both ends by one; worst case O(n).
M
Find the minimum of a rotated sorted array.

Compare a[mid] with a[hi]. If a[mid] > a[hi], the minimum is to the right of mid, so lo = mid + 1; otherwise it is at mid or to the left, so hi = mid. When lo == hi it is the minimum. Comparing with a[hi] rather than a[lo] avoids a special case for unrotated arrays.
M
Find a peak element in O(log n) when the array is not sorted.

Compare a[mid] with a[mid + 1]. If a[mid] < a[mid + 1], the slope goes up to the right, and since a[n] is treated as −∞ there must be a peak on the right: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise there is a peak at mid or to the left: hi = mid. The predicate 'a[i] > a[i + 1]' is not globally monotone, but the invariant 'a peak exists in [lo, hi]' is maintained.
M
Koko eats bananas: piles and h hours; find the minimum eating speed.

Feasibility of speed k is monotone: if k works, any larger speed works. Binary search k over [1, max(pile)], checking feasibility with sum(ceil(p / k)) ≤ h in O(n). The first feasible k is the answer. O(n log max(pile)).
Follow-up: Why is the upper bound max(pile)? — At that speed every pile takes one hour, which is the minimum possible per pile, so no larger speed helps.
M
Capacity to ship packages within D days.

Search capacity c over [max(weight), sum(weights)]: below the max a package cannot be shipped, and the sum ships everything in one day. Feasibility: greedily load packages in order, starting a new day when the next would exceed c, and check days ≤ D. Monotone because a bigger ship never needs more days. O(n log(sum)).
M
What is the time-based key-value store problem and how does binary search solve it?

set(key, value, timestamp) with increasing timestamps, and get(key, t) returns the value with the largest timestamp ≤ t. Store per key a list of (timestamp, value), which stays sorted because timestamps increase. get does bisect_right on the timestamps and takes the element before the insertion point. set is O(1), get O(log n).
H
Split an array into k contiguous parts minimising the largest part sum.

Binary search the answer S over [max(a), sum(a)]. Feasibility: greedily cut a new part whenever adding the next element would exceed S, and check parts ≤ k. A larger S never needs more parts, so feasibility is monotone. O(n log(sum)). The same structure solves 'minimum days to make m bouquets' and 'aggressive cows' (maximise the minimum gap, searching for the last feasible value).
Follow-up: Is there a DP solution? — Yes, O(k·n²) over (parts, prefix), which is far slower; binary search on the answer exploits the monotone structure.
H
Find the median of two sorted arrays in O(log(min(m, n))).

Binary search a cut position i in the shorter array; the cut in the other is j = (m + n + 1)/2 − i so the left parts together hold half the elements. The cut is correct when A[i−1] ≤ B[j] and B[j−1] ≤ A[i]. If A[i−1] > B[j], move i left; otherwise right. The median comes from the maxima of the left parts and minima of the right parts, with ±∞ sentinels at the edges.
H
How do you avoid infinite loops and off-by-one errors in binary search?

Pick one template and state its invariant. With pred monotone false→true and the answer in [lo, hi]: mid = (lo + hi) // 2, then hi = mid if pred(mid) else lo = mid + 1. The range strictly shrinks because mid < hi, and the loop ends when lo == hi at the first true. If you need the last false instead, it is lo − 1. Never mix lo = mid with the lower middle.

t: Stacks and monotonic stacks: matching, parsing and next-greater problems
sum: Use a stack whenever the most recent unfinished thing is the one to resolve next: bracket matching, expression evaluation and nested decoding; then the monotonic stack for next greater/smaller elements, spans, the largest rectangle and contribution counting.
prereq: al2
Each element pushed once and popped at most once gives O(n) total work despite a nested while loop.
al6
A monotonic deque keeps candidates in sorted order and pops dominated elements.
why:
A code editor checks brackets as you type. You write foo(bar[1], {x: (2 and it underlines the line, because the parenthesis you most recently opened has not been closed. To decide whether a closing bracket is legal, the editor only cares about one thing: which bracket was opened most recently and is still open. Once that bracket is closed, the one opened before it becomes the most recent. That "most recent unfinished thing first" order is exactly what a stack provides: you add (push) and remove (pop) only at the top.

That order shows up in a surprising number of interview problems. Matching brackets, evaluating arithmetic, decoding nested strings like 3[a2[c]], undoing operations, simplifying file paths, and every recursive algorithm (the call stack is a stack) all resolve the most recent open item first.

A second, cleverer use is the monotonic stack. "For each day, how many days until a warmer one?" has a brute force that, for every day, scans forward — O(n²) on a year of hourly readings. But think about which days are still waiting for an answer as you scan: they form a decreasing sequence of temperatures, and when a warm day arrives it answers the most recent waiting days first. That is a stack again, and keeping it ordered gives an O(n) solution to a whole family: next greater element, previous smaller element, stock spans, the largest rectangle in a histogram, trapping rain water, and sums over all subarrays.

This lesson covers both halves: the classic stack problems (matching, evaluation, nesting, min stack) and the monotonic stack, including the two hard classics interviewers love — Largest Rectangle in Histogram and Sum of Subarray Minimums — with full traces and the reasoning that makes each step safe.
primer:
The mental model: a stack of plates, and people looking along a line

A stack is a pile of plates: you put a plate on top, and you take the top plate off. You never pull one from the middle. That is LIFO — last in, first out. In Python, a list is a stack: append pushes, pop removes the top, and stack[-1] peeks. All three are O(1).

For the monotonic stack, a different picture helps. Imagine people standing in a line, all facing right, each wanting to know who is the first taller person ahead of them. Walk along the line from left to right, keeping a group of "people still waiting for an answer". When a new person arrives, everyone waiting who is shorter than the newcomer has their answer — it is the newcomer — and leaves the group. Who leaves first? The most recent waiters, because they are standing right next to the newcomer. And the group that remains is always ordered from tallest (waited longest) to shortest (most recent): whenever someone joins, everyone shorter has just left, so the newcomer is the shortest member. The group is a stack, sorted by height.

Two facts make this fast. Each day joins the waiting group once and leaves it at most once, so the total work is O(n). And once a day leaves, it is never needed again, because its question has been answered. The stack holds only the candidates that could still matter, kept in sorted (monotonic) order.

Where the analogy breaks: real people looking along a line see over shorter people, so "who is the first taller person ahead" is answered by eyesight in parallel. The algorithm has to discover the answer by scanning, and the order in which answers are discovered — most recent first — is what forces the stack. If the question were "the first taller person ahead that arrived earliest", the structure would be different. Always check that "most recent unresolved first" matches the question before reaching for a stack.

It is worth seeing what the stack saves. The brute force for "next warmer day" scans forward from every day, so a year of hourly data (8,760 readings) on a long cooling trend costs tens of millions of comparisons, and a million readings would cost on the order of 10¹¹. The stack version does at most two operations per reading — one push and one pop — so a million readings take a couple of million steps. The answers are identical; the stack simply refuses to compare a day against readings that can no longer be its answer.

There is also a simple test for whether a problem is a stack problem at all: if you processed the items by hand, would you ever need to "go back" to the item you saw most recently and finish it? Brackets, nested decoding, waiting days and histogram bars all pass that test. If instead you need the oldest item first (tasks in arrival order), you want a queue, and if you need the smallest or largest item regardless of when it arrived, you want a heap (al10).
body:
Matching: valid parentheses

def is_valid(s):
    pairs = {")": "(", "]": "[", "}": "{"}
    stack = []
    for ch in s:
        if ch in "([{":
            stack.append(ch)
        else:
            if not stack or stack[-1] != pairs[ch]:
                return False          # closer with no matching opener
            stack.pop()
    return not stack                  # leftover openers are unmatched

Three failure conditions, and the code checks each: a closer arriving with an empty stack ("())"), a closer that does not match the most recent opener ("([)]"), and openers left over at the end ("(("). A counter is enough when there is one bracket type, but "([)]" shows why several types need the stack: counts are balanced, order is not.

Variations follow the same shape. "Minimum additions to make valid" counts unmatched closers during the scan plus leftover openers at the end. "Longest valid parentheses" pushes indices instead of characters, with a sentinel index −1 at the bottom marking the position before the current valid run; the length of a valid run is i − stack[-1].

Evaluation: postfix and calculators

Postfix notation (Reverse Polish notation) writes the operator after its operands: 2 1 + 3 * means (2 + 1) × 3. It needs no brackets and evaluates with one stack: push numbers; on an operator, pop two, apply, push the result.

def eval_rpn(tokens):
    st = []
    for t in tokens:
        if t in "+-*/":
            b, a = st.pop(), st.pop()          # right operand pops first
            if t == "+": st.append(a + b)
            elif t == "-": st.append(a - b)
            elif t == "*": st.append(a * b)
            else: st.append(int(a / b))        # truncate toward zero
        else:
            st.append(int(t))
    return st[0]

Two details catch people: the right operand is popped first, so a − b must use them in the reverse pop order; and many problems specify truncation toward zero, which in Python is int(a / b), not a // b (floor division rounds −7 // 2 to −4).

For ordinary infix expressions with + and − and parentheses (Basic Calculator), you do not need full parsing. Keep a running result, the current number being read, and the current sign. On "+" or "−", fold sign * number into the result and set the new sign. On "(", push the outer (result, sign) and start fresh; on ")", finish the inner result, pop the outer pair, and combine: result = outer_result + outer_sign * inner_result. The stack depth equals the bracket nesting depth. Adding * and / with precedence uses the classic pattern of pushing signed terms and multiplying or dividing the top term immediately when * or / appears, then summing the stack at the end.

Nesting: decoding strings

"Decode 3[a2[c]]" to accaccacc. Every "[" opens a new context that must be finished before the outer one continues — the stack pattern. Push the outer context (the string built so far and the repeat count) on "[", and restore it on "]".

def decode_string(s):
    stack, cur, num = [], "", 0
    for ch in s:
        if ch.isdigit():
            num = num * 10 + int(ch)            # multi-digit counts
        elif ch == "[":
            stack.append((cur, num)); cur, num = "", 0
        elif ch == "]":
            prev, k = stack.pop()
            cur = prev + cur * k
        else:
            cur += ch
    return cur

Trace 3[a2[c]]: read 3; "[" pushes ("", 3); "a" → cur = "a"; read 2; "[" pushes ("a", 2), cur = ""; "c" → cur = "c"; "]" pops ("a", 2) → cur = "a" + "cc" = "acc"; "]" pops ("", 3) → cur = "accaccacc". The same push-context, pop-and-combine shape solves "simplify a Unix path" (push directory names, pop on ".."), "parse nested lists", and "count atoms in a chemical formula".

Min stack

"Design a stack with push, pop, top and getMin all in O(1)." The minimum changes only on push and pop, and the stack's history is exactly what pop restores. So store, with each element, the minimum of the stack at the moment it was pushed:

class MinStack:
    def __init__(self): self.st = []                 # (value, min_so_far)
    def push(self, x):
        m = x if not self.st else min(x, self.st[-1][1])
        self.st.append((x, m))
    def pop(self): self.st.pop()
    def top(self): return self.st[-1][0]
    def getMin(self): return self.st[-1][1]

Popping automatically "restores" the previous minimum, because the element below carries the minimum as it was before. This idea — store a summary of everything below with each stack entry — also gives O(1) max stacks and is the basis of the two-stack queue with O(1) minimum.

The monotonic stack template: next greater element

For each index, find the next index to the right with a strictly greater value. Keep a stack of indices whose values are decreasing from bottom to top. These are the indices still waiting for an answer.

def next_greater(a):
    ans = [-1] * len(a)
    st = []                                  # indices, values decreasing
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while st and a[st[-1]] < x:          # x answers every smaller waiter
            ans[st.pop()] = i
        st.append(i)
    return ans                               # -1: no greater element

Why the stack stays decreasing: we only push i after popping everything smaller than a[i], so a[i] is at most everything below it. Why popped elements are safe to discard: their answer has just been found, and the first greater element to the right is unique. Why it is O(n): each index is pushed once and popped at most once.

Trace Daily Temperatures, [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73] (the answer is i − popped index):

itemppopped (answer)stack after (temps)
073—[73]
17473 → 1[74]
27574 → 1[75]
371—[75, 71]
469—[75, 71, 69]
57269 → 1, 71 → 2[75, 72]
67672 → 1, 75 → 4[76]
773—[76, 73]

Answers: [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]. The four variants — next greater, next smaller, previous greater, previous smaller — differ only in the comparison and the scan direction (or in reading the stack top before pushing: after popping, the stack top is the previous greater-or-equal element of the current index). For a circular array, loop i over 2n and use i % n, pushing only in the first pass.

Spans and fleets: absorbing what you pop

Online Stock Span asks, for each new price, how many consecutive days up to and including today had a price at most today's. Keep a stack of (price, span). For a new price, pop every entry with price ≤ today's and add its span to today's span; then push (price, span). A popped day can never stop a future span, because today is at least as high and more recent — so it is safe to absorb it. Amortised O(1) per day.

Car Fleet: cars at different positions heading to a target, each with a speed; a faster car that catches a slower one ahead must slow down and they form a fleet. Sort by position, closest to the target first, and compute each car's arrival time if unobstructed. Walking from the front, a car whose arrival time is no greater than the fleet in front catches up and merges; otherwise it starts a new fleet. A stack of fleet times (always increasing from front to back) makes this explicit; its size is the answer.

Largest Rectangle in Histogram

Given bar heights, find the largest rectangle that fits under the histogram. For any bar used as the rectangle's height, the rectangle extends left and right until it meets a lower bar. So the answer is max over i of heights[i] × (next smaller index − previous smaller index − 1). A monotonic stack finds both boundaries in one pass: keep indices with increasing heights; when a lower bar arrives at index i, it is the next smaller bar for every taller bar on the stack, and after popping one, the new stack top is that bar's previous smaller bar.

def largest_rectangle(h):
    st, best = [], 0
    for i, x in enumerate(h + [0]):            # sentinel flushes the stack
        while st and h[st[-1]] > x:
            height = h[st.pop()]
            left = st[-1] if st else -1         # previous smaller index
            best = max(best, height * (i - left - 1))
        st.append(i)
    return best

The sentinel 0 at the end forces every remaining bar to be popped and measured, so no special code is needed after the loop. "Maximal Rectangle" in a binary matrix reduces to this: for each row, build heights[c] = number of consecutive 1s ending at this row in column c, and run the histogram algorithm. O(R·C).

Contribution counting: Sum of Subarray Minimums

"Return the sum of min(sub) over every contiguous subarray." There are O(n²) subarrays. Turn the sum around: instead of asking "what is each subarray's minimum?", ask "for each element, in how many subarrays is it the minimum?". Element i is the minimum of every subarray that starts after its previous smaller element and ends before its next smaller element. If left[i] is the number of choices for the start and right[i] the number of choices for the end, then a[i] contributes a[i] × left[i] × right[i].

Duplicates need care. In [2, 2], the subarray [2, 2] has two equal minimums; if both claim it, it is counted twice. The fix is to break ties on one side only: use "previous strictly smaller" for the left boundary and "next smaller or equal" for the right. Then a subarray with several equal minimums is credited only to the leftmost of them. Both boundaries come from monotonic stacks in O(n), so the whole sum is O(n). The same technique gives the sum of subarray maximums, and their difference gives "sum of subarray ranges".

Greedy with a monotonic stack: Remove K Digits

"Remove k digits from the number '1432219' to make it as small as possible." The leftmost digits matter most. Scanning left to right, if the current digit is smaller than the previous kept digit, removing the previous one makes the number smaller (a larger digit in a more significant position is replaced). Keep an increasing stack: while k > 0 and the top is greater than the current digit, pop and decrement k; then push. Leftover k removes from the end (the tail is increasing, so its last digits are the largest). For 1432219, k = 3: keep 1; 4; 3 pops 4; 2 pops 3; 2; 1 pops 2; 9 — result 1219. Strip leading zeros, and return "0" if nothing remains.

Recognising the pattern

Use a plain stack when the problem has nesting or "most recent unmatched": brackets, expressions, decoding, paths, undo, or converting recursion to iteration. Use a monotonic stack when the question is about the nearest greater or smaller element in some direction, spans or "how far until", rectangles bounded by the shortest bar, or sums over all subarrays of a min or max. Decide the comparison for equal values before coding.

Practice in the DSA list: Valid Parentheses, Min Stack, Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation, Decode String, Asteroid Collision, Daily Temperatures, Next Greater Element II, Online Stock Span, Car Fleet, Remove K Digits, Basic Calculator, Largest Rectangle in Histogram, Sum of Subarray Minimums.
deep:
Why popped elements are never needed again

Every monotonic-stack solution rests on one of two arguments for why a popped element is never needed again. The first is answered: in next greater element, when a new element x pops an index j, x is the first element to the right of j that is greater, so j's question is settled and it leaves for good. The second is dominated: for problems where elements are popped not because they are answered but because something better has arrived — the sliding-window maximum deque, stock span, remove-k-digits — the argument is: the newer element is at least as good for every future query (larger and later), so the older one can never be the answer again. Stating which of the two arguments applies ("answered" or "dominated") is the cleanest way to justify the algorithm in an interview.

Strict versus non-strict comparisons

With distinct values, < and ≤ give identical results. With duplicates they give different, well-defined answers: popping on a[top] < x finds the next strictly greater element, while popping on a[top] <= x finds the next greater-or-equal. For the histogram, either works, because equal bars yield the same maximal rectangle (one of them computes it correctly, the other a smaller one, and the maximum is unaffected). For contribution counting, the choice is load-bearing: exactly one side must be strict so that each subarray is assigned to exactly one minimum. When an interviewer asks "what about duplicates?", this is the answer they want.

Trapping rain water, the stack way

Al5 solved Trapping Rain Water with two pointers by computing water column by column. The monotonic stack computes it layer by layer: keep a decreasing stack of bar indices; when a taller bar arrives at i, pop the top j (the bottom of a basin); the new top k is the left wall; the water above j fills a rectangle of width i − k − 1 and height min(h[k], h[i]) − h[j]. Each pop adds one horizontal slab. Both methods are O(n); the stack version generalises to questions about the basins themselves (how many, their widths), which the two-pointer version cannot answer.

Cartesian trees and range minimum queries

The previous-smaller and next-smaller relationships define a tree: each element's parent is the larger of its previous-smaller and next-smaller neighbours. This is the Cartesian tree of the array, and the monotonic stack builds it in O(n). Its root is the minimum, and the minimum of any range a[l..r] is the lowest common ancestor of l and r in the tree. That connection is how theoretical range-minimum-query structures achieve O(n) preprocessing and O(1) queries, and it explains why so many range-min problems (histogram, subarray minimums) have stack solutions: they are traversing the Cartesian tree implicitly.

The shunting-yard algorithm

Full infix expressions with precedence (2 + 3 × 4) and brackets are parsed with Dijkstra's shunting-yard algorithm (1961): an output queue and an operator stack. Numbers go to the output. An operator pops operators of higher (or equal, for left-associative) precedence from the stack to the output before being pushed. "(" is pushed; ")" pops to the output until the matching "(". At the end, the remaining operators are popped. The output is postfix, which the RPN evaluator above computes. Knowing this exists, and that "Basic Calculator II/III" are simplified versions of it, is enough for interviews; writing it fully takes about 25 lines.

Two stacks make a queue

A queue (first in, first out) can be built from two stacks: push onto an "in" stack; to pop, if the "out" stack is empty, move everything from "in" to "out" (reversing the order), then pop from "out". Each element is moved at most once, so every operation is amortised O(1). Combined with the min-stack trick, this gives a queue with O(1) minimum — another route to the sliding-window minimum. It is a common warm-up question and a neat demonstration of amortised reasoning.

Stacks and recursion

Every recursive function runs on the call stack, which pushes a frame (arguments, local variables, return address) per call and pops it on return. Converting recursion to iteration means managing that stack yourself: push the arguments of pending calls and loop while the stack is non-empty. It matters in Python because the default recursion limit is 1,000 frames: a recursive depth-first search on a 10⁵-node path crashes, an iterative one does not. When post-order work is needed (do something after children finish), push a marker or a (node, state) pair so the node is revisited after its children — the same trick as the "enter/exit" events in iterative tree traversals (al14).
prod:
In the interview room

Stack problems are judged on edge cases and invariants. The common failures: popping from an empty stack (a closer before any opener, an operator with too few operands); forgetting the leftover stack at the end (unmatched openers, bars never popped — which the sentinel fixes); getting operand order wrong for − and /; using floor division where truncation is required; and, for monotonic stacks, storing values when the problem needs distances (store indices — you can always read the value from the array). Test with an empty input, a single element, all equal values, strictly increasing and strictly decreasing inputs; increasing and decreasing are the two extremes of stack behaviour (nothing popped until the end versus everything popped immediately).

Interviewers almost always ask about complexity because of the nested loop: answer with the push-once-pop-once argument in one sentence. For the histogram, expect "walk me through why the width is i − stack[-1] − 1", and for Sum of Subarray Minimums, "how do you handle duplicates?". Having those explanations ready is what makes a hard problem look comfortable.

A good habit is to say which stack you are building before coding: "a stack of indices with strictly decreasing values, popped when a warmer day arrives; each pop answers the popped day". That single sentence fixes the content (indices), the order (decreasing), the comparison (strict), and the meaning of a pop (answered) — the four decisions that otherwise get made inconsistently in the middle of the code.

Online assessments often wrap monotonic stacks in a story — "for each building, how many buildings to its right can it see?", "for each order, the next order with a higher price", "the largest billboard that fits under a skyline". The tell is the phrase "the next / previous / nearest ... larger / smaller", or a request to sum something over every contiguous range. Translate the story into "nearest greater or smaller in a direction" and pick the variant.

In real systems

Stacks are built into how computers run programs. The call stack holds one frame per active function call, which is why infinite recursion ends in a stack overflow (in Python, a RecursionError when the interpreter's limit is reached). CPython and the Java virtual machine are stack machines: bytecode instructions push and pop operands on an evaluation stack — dis.dis on any Python function shows instructions like LOAD_FAST (push) and BINARY_OP (pop two, push one), the same pattern as the RPN evaluator. Compilers and interpreters parse expressions and nested blocks with stacks (shunting-yard, or recursive descent, which uses the call stack). Editors and design tools implement undo and redo as two stacks: an action pushes onto undo; undoing pops it and pushes onto redo; any new action clears redo. Browsers keep back and forward history the same way. And monotonic-stack logic appears in financial software computing spans and running highs, and in skyline and layout algorithms that need "the nearest taller element".
myths: A monotonic stack is a special data structure.

It is an ordinary stack with one rule about what you push: before pushing, pop everything that breaks the order. The power comes from the observation that popped elements can never be the answer for anything later, not from the structure.
The while loop inside the for loop makes monotonic stack solutions O(n²).
Every index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once over the entire run, so the total number of pops is at most n. The whole algorithm is O(n).
For next-greater problems it does not matter whether you pop on < or ≤.

With duplicates it matters. Popping on ≤ makes an equal later element count as 'greater or equal', and contribution-counting problems like Sum of Subarray Minimums double-count subarrays unless one side uses strict comparison and the other non-strict. Decide what 'greater' means for equal values before coding.
Valid Parentheses only needs a counter.

A counter works for a single bracket type. With several types, '([)]' has balanced counts but is invalid because the brackets close in the wrong order. You need a stack to remember which bracket is the most recent unmatched one.
Stacks are only for parsing problems.

They also model anything with a 'most recent first' structure: undo history, recursion (every recursive function can be rewritten with an explicit stack), depth-first search, backtracking, and the monotonic-stack family of nearest-greater and histogram problems.
lab:
Stress-test the histogram and subarray-minimum solutions against brute force, with many duplicate values.

  1. Save as stack_lab.py: 
    import random

def hist_brute(h):
    return max([min(h[i:j+1]) * (j - i + 1) for i in range(len(h))
                for j in range(i, len(h))], default=0)

def hist_stack(h):
    st, best = [], 0
    for i, x in enumerate(h + [0]):
        while st and h[st[-1]] > x:
            height = h[st.pop()]
            left = st[-1] if st else -1
            best = max(best, height * (i - left - 1))
        st.append(i)
    return best

def summin_brute(a):
    return sum(min(a[i:j+1]) for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i, len(a)))

def summin_stack(a, strict_left=True):
    n = len(a); left = [0]*n; right = [0]*n; st = []
    for i in range(n):                      # previous strictly smaller
        while st and (a[st[-1]] >= a[i] if strict_left else a[st[-1]] > a[i]):
            st.pop()
        left[i] = i - (st[-1] if st else -1); st.append(i)
    st = []
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):          # next smaller or equal
        while st and a[st[-1]] > a[i]: st.pop()
        right[i] = (st[-1] if st else n) - i; st.append(i)
    return sum(a[i] * left[i] * right[i] for i in range(n))

for _ in range(3000):
    a = [random.randint(0, 4) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 9))]
    assert hist_stack(a) == hist_brute(a), a
    assert summin_stack(a) == summin_brute(a), a
print("histogram and subarray minimums match brute force")
bad = sum(summin_stack(a, False) != summin_brute(a)
          for a in ([random.randint(0, 2) for _ in range(6)] for _ in range(1000)))
print("both sides non-strict: wrong on", bad, "of 1000 inputs")
  2. Run it and expect the match message.
  3. Look at the last line: when both comparisons allow equality, subarrays with repeated minimums are counted twice and many inputs come out wrong.

What this proves: the stack solutions are exact, and the tie-breaking rule in contribution counting is not optional — small value ranges, which force duplicates, expose it immediately.
recap: A stack is last-in, first-out: push and pop at the same end in O(1), which a Python list does with append and pop.
Use a stack when the most recent unresolved item must be resolved first: matching brackets, nested structures, undo, and recursion.
Expression problems keep operands and pending operators or signs on stacks and resolve them when a closing bracket or lower-precedence operator arrives.
A min stack stores the minimum so far alongside each value, so getMin is O(1).
A monotonic stack keeps indices whose values are increasing or decreasing; when a new element breaks the order, each popped index has just found its next greater or smaller element.
Largest Rectangle in Histogram pops a bar when a lower bar arrives; the popped bar's rectangle spans from the new stack top to the current index.
Contribution counting multiplies, for each element, the number of subarrays where it is the minimum, using previous-smaller and next-smaller distances with one strict and one non-strict comparison.
Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so monotonic stack algorithms are O(n).
glossary: Bounding the total cost of a sequence of operations, such as at most n pops over the whole run, rather than each step separately.
Computing a sum over all subarrays by asking, for each element, in how many subarrays it plays a role, and adding those contributions.
Last in, first out: the most recently added item is the first removed.
A stack that also returns its minimum in O(1), usually by storing the running minimum with each element.
A stack whose elements are kept in increasing or decreasing order by popping any element that would break the order before pushing.
For each position, the first element to its right that is larger than it.
Writing operators after their operands, like 3 4 + 2 *; it needs no brackets and is evaluated with a stack. Also called Reverse Polish notation (RPN).
Another name for postfix notation, in which operators follow their operands.
For each position, the nearest element to its left that is smaller than it.
Add to the top, remove from the top, and look at the top without removing it.
An extra value added at the start or end (such as a bar of height 0) so the last elements are processed without special-case code.
Dijkstra's stack-based algorithm for converting an infix expression with precedence and brackets into postfix order.
For a stock price, the number of consecutive days up to today with price at most today's.
A collection where items are added and removed only at one end, the top.
drill:
Explain a hard one cleanly

An interviewer gives you Largest Rectangle in Histogram, accepts your O(n) stack solution, and asks: "Prove that every candidate rectangle that could be the answer is measured at some point, and tell me what changes if bars can have height 0."

Answer

The optimal rectangle has some height H, which must equal the height of its shortest bar, say bar j (otherwise it could be made taller). Its left edge must be just after the previous bar lower than h[j], and its right edge just before the next bar lower than h[j] — otherwise it could be extended. So the optimum is "bar j's maximal rectangle" for some j, and it suffices to measure the maximal rectangle of every bar. The algorithm does exactly that: bar j is popped when the first lower bar to its right arrives at index i (its right boundary), and after popping, the stack top is the nearest bar to its left that is lower or equal (the stack holds increasing heights, so everything between that top and j was popped earlier by j or by bars taller than j, which means it is at least h[j] tall). The width i − top − 1 is therefore j's maximal width. With equal heights, one of the equal bars may measure a slightly short width, but the other measures the full one, so the maximum is still correct. The sentinel 0 makes sure every bar is popped. Height-0 bars need no change: they pop everything taller, contribute area 0 themselves, and act as natural separators.
qa: E
Check whether a string of (), [] and {} is valid.

Scan left to right; push opening brackets; on a closing bracket, the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opener, which you pop. At the end the stack must be empty. O(n) time and space. A map from closer to opener keeps the code short.
E
Evaluate an expression in Reverse Polish notation.

Push numbers. On an operator, pop the right operand then the left, apply the operator, and push the result. The final stack holds the answer. Mind the order for − and /, and truncate division toward zero if the problem says so (int(a / b) in Python, not a // b).
E
Design a stack that returns its minimum in O(1).

Store pairs (value, min so far) on one stack, where min so far is min(value, previous top's min). push, pop, top and getMin are all O(1). Alternatively keep a second stack of minimums and push to it only when the new value is ≤ its top.
M
Daily Temperatures: for each day, how many days until a warmer one?

Keep a stack of indices with decreasing temperatures. For each day i, while the stack top is colder than today, pop it and set its answer to i − top. Then push i. Days left on the stack never get a warmer day and keep answer 0. Each index is pushed and popped once, so O(n).
M
Next greater element in a circular array.
Run the monotonic stack over 2n indices using i % n, pushing indices only during the first pass. The second pass lets elements near the end find greater elements at the start. O(n) time and space.
M
Decode a string like 3[a2[c]].

Keep a stack of (string built so far, repeat count) frames. On a digit, accumulate the number; on '[', push the current string and count and reset them; on ']', pop and set current = previous + current × count; on a letter, append. Nested brackets are handled because each '[' saves the outer context.
M
Car Fleet: cars at positions with speeds heading to a target; how many fleets arrive?

Sort cars by position descending (closest to the target first) and compute each car's arrival time. Walk them in that order with a stack of fleet arrival times: if a car's time is no greater than the fleet ahead's time, it catches up and joins; otherwise it forms a new fleet. The number of fleets is the stack size. O(n log n) for sorting.
M
Online Stock Span: for each new price, how many consecutive days up to today had price at most today's?

Keep a stack of (price, span). For a new price, start span = 1 and pop while the top's price is ≤ the new price, adding each popped span. Push (price, span). Popped days are absorbed because no future query can stop at them. Amortised O(1) per call.
M
Remove k digits from a number to make it as small as possible.

Greedy with a monotonic increasing stack: for each digit, while k > 0 and the stack top is greater than the digit, pop it (removing a larger digit earlier in the number helps most) and decrement k. Push the digit. If k remains, remove from the end. Strip leading zeros and return '0' if empty. O(n).
H
Largest rectangle in a histogram.

Keep a stack of indices with increasing heights, and append a sentinel bar of height 0. When a bar lower than the top arrives, pop the top: its rectangle has that height and extends from just after the new stack top to just before the current index, so width = i − stack[-1] − 1 (or i if the stack is empty). Track the maximum. Each bar is pushed and popped once: O(n).
Follow-up: Maximal rectangle of 1s in a binary matrix? — Build a histogram of consecutive 1s ending at each row and run this algorithm per row: O(R·C).
H
Sum of the minimums of all subarrays.

For each element, count the subarrays in which it is the minimum: left = distance to the previous strictly smaller element, right = distance to the next smaller-or-equal element, both found with monotonic stacks. Its contribution is a[i] × left × right. The strict/non-strict split ensures each subarray with several equal minimums is credited to exactly one of them. O(n).
Follow-up: Sum of (max − min) over all subarrays? — Compute the sum of maximums the same way and subtract the sum of minimums.
H
Implement a basic calculator with +, −, parentheses and spaces.

Scan once keeping result, the current number and the current sign. On + or −, add sign × number to result and set the new sign. On '(', push (result, sign) and reset result to 0 and sign to +1. On ')', finish the inner result, then pop and combine: result = popped_result + popped_sign × inner. O(n) time, stack depth equals bracket nesting.
