t: Linked lists: pointer surgery, dummy heads and fast/slow pointers
sum: How to manipulate singly linked lists without losing nodes: dummy heads, in-place reversal, merging, fast and slow pointers for middles and cycles (with Floyd's proof), gap pointers, and the composite problems built from them.
prereq: al5
Two pointers moving at coordinated speeds; Floyd's idea was previewed for 'find the duplicate number'.
al2
Recursion depth costs O(depth) stack space; Python's default limit is 1,000 frames.
why:
Linked lists are rarely the best data structure in real code, so why do interviews ask about them so often? Because they test something specific: whether you can manipulate references precisely, without losing data, while keeping several moving parts in your head. Reverse a list, and if you reassign one pointer in the wrong order, the rest of the list becomes unreachable and is gone. Remove a node and forget the case where it is the head, and the function returns the wrong list. These are exactly the kind of small, careful, state-tracking steps that real systems code — memory allocators, caches, schedulers, parsers — is full of.

Linked lists also carry a few genuinely beautiful ideas that reappear elsewhere. Two pointers moving at different speeds can find the middle of a list in one pass, detect a cycle using constant memory, and even find exactly where the cycle starts. A dummy node before the head turns half a dozen special cases into none. And the hardest list problems — reorder a list, reverse in groups of k, sort a list — turn out to be compositions of three or four basic moves.

This lesson builds those moves one at a time: the node model and safe traversal; the dummy head; in-place reversal with a full trace; merging; fast and slow pointers for middles and cycles, including the proof behind Floyd's algorithm; gap pointers for "n-th from the end"; and then the composite problems. Along the way it covers when a linked list is the right structure at all, and why, in practice, it usually is not.
primer:
The mental model: train cars and couplings

Picture a train. Each car carries some cargo (the value) and has a coupling that hooks onto the next car (the next pointer). The engine is the head. To reach the tenth car, you walk from the engine through nine couplings — there is no way to jump straight to car ten. To insert a car between cars 4 and 5, you only need to change two couplings: unhook 4 from 5, hook 4 to the new car, and hook the new car to 5. Nothing else moves. That is the trade-off of a linked list compared with an array: insertion and removal at a known place is cheap, but finding a place means walking.

In code, a node is a tiny object:

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

The list is just a reference to its first node. The last node's next is None. Walking the list is a loop: node = head; while node: ...; node = node.next.

The one rule that prevents almost every linked-list bug: before you change a coupling, keep hold of whatever it was attached to. If you unhook car 4 from car 5 without anyone holding car 5, cars 5 onwards roll away and are lost. In code, that means saving nxt = curr.next before reassigning curr.next.

Where the analogy breaks: a real train has one engine, but a linked list can be shared — two lists may merge into a common tail, or a list can loop back on itself (a cycle) so that walking never ends. Real trains do not form loops; buggy linked lists do, and several interview problems are about detecting exactly that.

It helps to have the costs side by side. Reading the k-th element: O(1) in an array, O(k) in a list. Inserting or deleting at the front: O(n) in an array (everything shifts), O(1) in a list. Inserting or deleting next to a node you already hold: O(n) in an array, O(1) in a list (O(1) for deletion only if it is doubly linked or you hold the predecessor). Appending at the end: amortised O(1) in a dynamic array, O(1) in a list if you keep a tail reference. Memory: an array stores the elements contiguously; a list adds a reference (or two) per element and scatters the nodes. Interview problems on lists are designed around the column where lists win — rearranging nodes without copying — and they forbid the shortcut of copying values into an array, which is why constraints like "O(1) extra space" appear so often.

Finally, a note on vocabulary. In Python there are no raw memory pointers; "pointer" in linked-list problems just means a variable that refers to a node. Assigning a = b makes a refer to the same node as b — it does not copy the node. Keeping that distinction in mind (moving a reference versus changing a node's next) is half of getting these problems right.
body:
The dummy head

Many list operations might change the first node: removing all nodes with a given value (what if the head has it?), merging two lists (which head comes first?), partitioning around a value. Without care, each needs a special case for the head. A dummy node removes the special case: create a placeholder node whose next is the real head, do the operation as if every real node had a predecessor, and return dummy.next.

def remove_elements(head, val):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    while prev.next:
        if prev.next.val == val:
            prev.next = prev.next.next     # unlink; prev stays put
        else:
            prev = prev.next
    return dummy.next

Notice that when a node is removed, prev does not advance: the new prev.next has not been checked yet. That small detail is a classic bug source.

Reversal, iteratively

Reversing a list in place is the single most important list operation, because it appears inside many harder problems. Three references walk the list: prev (the already-reversed part), curr (the node being flipped), and a temporary nxt (the rest of the list, saved before flipping).

def reverse(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next        # 1. save the rest
        curr.next = prev       # 2. flip this arrow
        prev = curr            # 3. advance prev
        curr = nxt             # 4. advance curr
    return prev                # new head

Trace on 1 → 2 → 3 → None:

stepprevcurrnxtlinks after
startNone1—1→2→3
1122None←1, 2→3
2233None←1←2, 3
33NoneNoneNone←1←2←3

Return prev = 3, the new head. O(n) time, O(1) space. Practise until you can write those four lines without thinking; then variants follow. "Reverse the sublist from position m to n" walks to the node before m, reverses n − m + 1 nodes with the same loop, and reconnects both ends.

A recursive version exists: reverse the rest, then make the next node point back to the current one (head.next.next = head; head.next = None). It is elegant but uses O(n) stack frames and fails on long lists in Python, so present the iterative one by default.

Merging two sorted lists

Merging uses the dummy head and a tail pointer that always points to the last node of the merged result:

def merge(a, b):
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:
            tail.next, a = a, a.next
        else:
            tail.next, b = b, b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b             # attach the leftover
    return dummy.next

No new nodes are created; existing nodes are re-linked. Using <= keeps the merge stable (equal values from a come first). This is the merge step of merge sort, and "merge k sorted lists" is the same loop with a heap choosing the smallest of k heads (al10).

Fast and slow pointers: the middle

Move slow one node per step and fast two. When fast reaches the end, slow has covered half the distance — the middle. One pass, no length needed.

def middle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    return slow     # odd length: exact middle; even: second middle

For 1→2→3→4→5, slow ends at 3. For 1→2→3→4, at 3 (the second middle). If you need the first middle — for example to cut a list into two halves for merge sort — use while fast.next and fast.next.next, which stops slow one node earlier on even lengths.

Fast and slow pointers: cycles (Floyd's algorithm)

If a list has a cycle, walking it never reaches None. To detect one with O(1) memory, run the same two pointers. Without a cycle, fast hits None. With a cycle, both pointers eventually enter it; from then on, fast gains exactly one node on slow per step, so the gap shrinks by one each step and they must meet — fast cannot "jump over" slow.

Finding where the cycle starts needs a second phase. Let the tail before the cycle have a nodes, the cycle have c nodes, and the meeting point be b nodes into the cycle. When they meet, slow has walked a + b steps and fast 2(a + b). Fast has also done some whole number k of extra laps: 2(a + b) = a + b + k·c, so a + b = k·c, which means a = k·c − b. Read that equation as a walk: starting from the meeting point and walking a steps around the cycle lands at (b + a) mod c = 0 — the cycle's start. And walking a steps from the head also lands at the cycle's start. So:

def cycle_start(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:                 # phase 1: they meet in the cycle
            p = head
            while p is not slow:         # phase 2: both move one step
                p, slow = p.next, slow.next
            return p                     # the cycle's first node
    return None                          # no cycle

This is the same algorithm that finds the duplicate in an array of n + 1 values in 1..n (al5), where the array defines the next pointers.

Gap pointers: n-th from the end

To remove the n-th node from the end in one pass, keep two pointers exactly n + 1 nodes apart. Start both at a dummy before the head, move fast n + 1 steps, then move both until fast is None. Now slow is the node just before the target, which is what you need to unlink it: slow.next = slow.next.next. Starting at the dummy makes "remove the head" (n equals the length) work with no special case.

Composite problems

Harder list problems are usually two or three of the moves above, glued together. Recognising the pieces is the skill.

  • Reorder List (L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln−1 …): find the middle, cut, reverse the second half, then merge by alternating nodes.
  • Palindrome Linked List in O(1) space: find the middle, reverse the second half, compare the halves node by node, and (politely) reverse it back.
  • Sort List in O(n log n): merge sort — split at the middle (first-middle variant), sort both halves, merge.
  • Reverse Nodes in k-Group: repeat "check k nodes exist, reverse k nodes, reconnect" with a pointer to the node before each group.

Reverse in k-groups is the hardest of these to get right, because of the reconnection. For each group: remember group_prev (the node before the group) and the group's first node first; reverse k nodes, which leaves prev at the new group head and curr at the node after the group; then set group_prev.next = prev (link to the new head) and first.next = curr (the old first node is now the group's tail and must link onward); finally move group_prev = first. Drawing the four nodes involved before writing the code makes it straightforward.

Rearranging by building sub-lists

A family of medium problems — Partition List (all nodes less than x before the rest, keeping order), Odd Even Linked List (all odd-position nodes, then all even-position nodes), splitting a list into k parts — shares one robust technique: walk the list once and append each node to the end of one of several new lists, each with its own dummy head and tail pointer, then stitch the lists together.

def partition(head, x):
    small = s_tail = ListNode()
    large = l_tail = ListNode()
    while head:
        if head.val < x:
            s_tail.next = head; s_tail = head
        else:
            l_tail.next = head; l_tail = head
        head = head.next
    l_tail.next = None              # crucial: cut the old link
    s_tail.next = large.next        # stitch
    return small.next

The line l_tail.next = None is the one people forget. The last node placed in the large list still points to whatever followed it in the original list — possibly a node now in the small list — which creates a cycle. Whenever you rebuild lists from existing nodes, terminate every tail explicitly.

Removing duplicates from a sorted list is the same "keep or skip" idea in its simplest form: walk with one pointer, and while the next node has the same value, skip it with curr.next = curr.next.next; only advance when the next value differs. The "remove all nodes that have duplicates" variant needs a dummy head and a prev pointer, because whole runs — possibly including the head — disappear.

Two more classics

Intersection of two lists. Two lists may share a common tail. Pointer a walks list A and then switches to B's head; pointer b walks B and then switches to A's head. If A's own part has length x, B's own part y, and the shared tail z, each pointer walks x + z + y nodes before reaching the intersection a second time, so they arrive together. If there is no intersection, both reach None together after x + y steps. O(m + n) time, O(1) space, no lengths needed.

Copy List with Random Pointer. Each node has an extra random reference to any node or None, and you must deep-copy the list. The straightforward way is a dict from each original node to its copy: one pass creates the copies, a second wires copy.next = map[orig.next] and copy.random = map[orig.random]. The O(1)-space way interleaves: insert each copy right after its original (A → A' → B → B' …), then orig.next.random = orig.random.next sets every copy's random pointer, and a final pass separates the two lists.

Add Two Numbers. Digits are stored in reverse order, so the lists can be added like grade-school addition from the least significant digit: walk both, add digits and the carry, create a node for the units digit, carry the tens. Keep going while either list has nodes or the carry is non-zero, so 5 + 5 produces 0 → 1.

Recognising the pattern

Linked-list problems announce themselves, so recognition is about choosing the move: anything that may change the head → dummy node; "reverse" anywhere → the four-line loop; "middle", "half" or "cycle" → fast and slow pointers; "from the end" → gap pointers; two sorted lists → merge. For anything else, ask which combination of those it is.

Practice in the DSA list: Reverse Linked List, Merge Two Sorted Lists, Linked List Cycle, Intersection of Two Linked Lists, Remove Nth Node From End, Reorder List, Add Two Numbers, Copy List with Random Pointer, Sort List, Reverse Nodes in k-Group, Merge k Sorted Lists (al10), LRU Cache (al28).
deep:
Why fast must gain exactly one step

Floyd's argument relies on the relative speed being 1: once both pointers are in the cycle, the distance from slow forward to fast decreases by exactly one each iteration (fast moves two, slow one), so it reaches zero — they cannot pass each other without meeting. With speeds 1 and 3 the gap shrinks by 2 per step and can skip over zero when the cycle length and gap are odd and even in the wrong combination, so meeting is not guaranteed on the first lap. The time bound is also clean: slow enters the cycle after a steps and is caught within c more steps, so detection is O(a + c) = O(n). Brent's algorithm is an alternative that moves only one pointer and teleports the other at powers of two; it does fewer next-pointer evaluations and is used in Pollard's rho factorisation, but Floyd's is the one interviewers expect, and the one whose second phase gives the cycle start so neatly.

Doubly linked lists and why LRU caches use them

A singly linked list cannot remove a node in O(1) unless you also hold its predecessor, because the predecessor's next must change. A doubly linked list stores prev as well, so given any node you can unlink it in O(1): node.prev.next = node.next; node.next.prev = node.prev. Combine it with a hash map from key to node and you get an LRU cache: the map finds a node in O(1), the list moves it to the front in O(1) on access, and evicting the least recently used item pops the back in O(1). Two sentinel nodes (a dummy head and a dummy tail) remove every edge case. This design is covered in detail in al28 and is exactly how Python's OrderedDict is implemented in its pure-Python version.

Memory layout: why arrays usually win

Big-O hides the most important practical fact about linked lists: their nodes are scattered in memory. An array's elements are adjacent, so the CPU loads 64-byte cache lines containing many elements and prefetches the next ones; a list traversal follows a reference to an arbitrary address at each step, which may cost a main-memory access of around 100 ns instead of about 1 ns. In Python the gap is smaller (everything is a reference to a heap object anyway), but a Python list of ints still beats a chain of node objects by a wide margin, and uses far less memory per element (8 bytes for the reference versus a full object with a dict or slots for each node). That is why Python's collections.deque is implemented as a doubly linked list of blocks of 64 elements: it keeps O(1) operations at both ends while getting most of the cache benefit of arrays.

Recursion on lists and the stack

Many list operations have elegant recursive forms — reverse, merge, remove elements, check palindrome with a "front pointer" carried through recursion. Each uses one stack frame per node, so O(n) space, and in Python a list of more than about 1,000 nodes raises RecursionError. In interviews, write the iterative version by default and mention the recursive one as an alternative. If you do use recursion (merge is the most natural), say "this is O(n) stack space; for long lists I'd make it iterative".

Skip lists: linked lists with express lanes

A skip list adds "express lane" pointers on top of a sorted linked list: each node is promoted to the next level with probability one half, so level k has about n/2ᵏ nodes. Search starts at the top level and drops down whenever the next node would overshoot, giving O(log n) expected time for search, insert and delete — like a balanced tree, but with simpler code and easy concurrent implementations. Redis uses skip lists for its sorted sets, and LevelDB and RocksDB use them for their in-memory tables. If an interviewer asks how to make a sorted linked list searchable in O(log n), a skip list is the answer they are fishing for.
prod:
In the interview room

Linked-list rounds are graded heavily on correctness under edge cases, because the code is short and the bugs are predictable. The ones interviewers see most: losing the rest of the list by reassigning next before saving it; dereferencing None (fast.next.next when fast.next is None); forgetting to return dummy.next and returning the old head instead; advancing prev after a deletion, which skips a node; and creating an accidental cycle by not setting the last node's next to None after reordering — which makes the interviewer's test harness hang. Test every solution on an empty list, a single node, two nodes, and a case that changes the head.

A strong habit is to draw the nodes and arrows before coding the tricky part — for reversal in k-groups or reorder, draw the four or five nodes around the operation, write the new arrows, then translate each arrow into one assignment, in an order that never loses a reference. Interviewers like seeing this because it is how careful engineers work, and it makes your code much more likely to be right first time.

Expect the Floyd follow-ups: "why do they meet?" (relative speed one), "why does the second phase find the start?" (a ≡ c − b mod c), and "what is the complexity?" (O(n) time, O(1) space). Being able to sketch the a, b, c picture in thirty seconds turns a memorised trick into an understood algorithm.

On online assessments and in shared editors, you often have to build test lists yourself. Write two small helpers first — one that turns a Python list into a linked list and one that turns a linked list back into a Python list with a length limit (so an accidental cycle prints a truncated list instead of hanging). They take a minute and make every later test a one-liner, and interviewers read them as a sign of an experienced engineer.

In real systems

Linked lists live where O(1) insertion and removal at a known position matter more than traversal speed. Operating-system kernels use them constantly: the Linux kernel's list_head is an intrusive circular doubly linked list (the links are embedded inside the objects themselves, so no separate node allocation is needed) used for run queues, open files, timers and device lists. Memory allocators keep free lists of available blocks, linked through the free blocks' own memory. LRU caches — in databases' buffer pools, in CDN edge caches, in functools.lru_cache — use a hash map plus a doubly linked list. Hash tables that resolve collisions by chaining keep a short linked list per bucket. Python's OrderedDict (pure-Python version) and deque (blocks) are linked structures. Elsewhere, arrays have largely replaced linked lists because of caches; Bjarne Stroustrup's well-known talk on "vector versus list" showed a vector outperforming a list even for insertion-heavy workloads at large sizes, because finding the insertion point dominates and arrays find it much faster.
myths: Linked lists are faster than arrays for insertion, so they are generally faster.

Inserting at a known node is O(1) in a list and O(n) in an array, but finding that node is O(n) in a list. And walking a list touches scattered memory, so each step can miss the CPU cache, while arrays are read sequentially. In practice arrays (Python lists) win for almost everything except frequent insertion and deletion at positions you already hold a reference to.
You need the length of the list to find the n-th node from the end.

Two pointers with a gap of n do it in one pass: advance the first pointer n steps, then move both until the first reaches the end. The second is then n nodes from the end. Computing the length first works too but takes two passes.
Floyd's cycle detection finds where the cycle starts because the pointers meet there.

They usually meet somewhere inside the cycle, not at its start. Finding the start needs a second phase: reset one pointer to the head and move both one step at a time; they meet at the start. The proof is a short distance argument.
A dummy head node is a hack.

It is a standard technique that removes the special case of changing the head. Any operation that might delete or replace the first node — removing elements, merging, partitioning — becomes uniform when there is always a node before the first real one.
Recursive list reversal is as good as iterative.

Both are O(n) time, but recursion uses O(n) stack frames, and Python raises RecursionError at the default limit of about 1,000 frames. For lists that can be long, the iterative three-pointer version with O(1) space is the one to write.
lab:
Build lists from Python lists, run the core operations, and check Floyd's algorithm on lists with cycles of every shape.

  1. Save as list_lab.py: 
    import random

class Node:
    def __init__(self, v, nxt=None): self.val, self.next = v, nxt

def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals): head = Node(v, head)
    return head

def to_list(h, limit=100):
    out = []
    while h and len(out) < limit: out.append(h.val); h = h.next
    return out

def reverse(h):
    prev = None
    while h: h.next, prev, h = prev, h, h.next
    return prev

def cycle_start(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            p = head
            while p is not slow: p, slow = p.next, slow.next
            return p
    return None

for _ in range(2000):
    vals = list(range(random.randint(0, 12)))
    assert to_list(reverse(build(vals))) == vals[::-1]
    if vals:
        nodes, h = [], build(vals)
        while h: nodes.append(h); h = h.next
        k = random.randint(-1, len(nodes) - 1)       # -1: no cycle
        if k >= 0: nodes[-1].next = nodes[k]
        got = cycle_start(nodes[0])
        assert got is (nodes[k] if k >= 0 else None)
print("reverse and cycle_start correct on 2000 random lists")
  2. Run it and expect the final message. Each trial builds a list and, most of the time, links the tail back to a random node to form a cycle — including a self-loop on the last node and a cycle through the whole list.
  3. Note the one-line reverse: h.next, prev, h = prev, h, h.next. Python evaluates the whole right side first, so the old h.next is saved automatically. Rewrite it as three separate assignments in that order and watch it break.

What this proves: the second phase of Floyd's algorithm lands exactly on the cycle's first node for every tail length and cycle length, and the "save before overwrite" rule is what makes reversal correct.
recap: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a reference to the next node; you reach a node only by walking from the head.
Before reassigning a next pointer, save the reference you are about to overwrite, or the rest of the list is lost.
A dummy node placed before the head makes operations that might change the head uniform; return dummy.next at the end.
Iterative reversal walks once with prev, curr and next pointers and runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.
Fast and slow pointers find the middle (slow ends there when fast reaches the end) and detect cycles (they meet if and only if there is a cycle).
After Floyd's pointers meet, restarting one from the head and moving both by one step makes them meet at the cycle's start.
A gap of n between two pointers finds the n-th node from the end in one pass.
Many hard list problems are compositions: find the middle, reverse a part, and merge or compare the parts.
glossary: A situation where following next pointers eventually returns to a node already visited, so the walk never reaches None.
A list whose nodes also have a reference to the previous node, allowing O(1) removal of a node you hold a reference to.
A CPU cache is small fast memory near the processor; a CDN (content delivery network) caches web content near users. Both commonly evict with LRU.
A placeholder node placed before the real head, also called a sentinel, so the head can be changed like any other node.
Two references moving through a list at two speeds, usually two steps and one step per iteration.
The tortoise-and-hare cycle-detection method: fast and slow pointers meet inside a cycle if one exists, and a second phase finds the cycle's start.
The first node of a list; the list is usually passed around as a reference to its head.
Rearranging nodes by changing their next pointers rather than creating new nodes.
Least recently used: an eviction policy that removes the item not accessed for the longest time; implemented with a hash map plus a doubly linked list (al28).
One element of a linked list: a value plus a reference to the next node (and in a doubly linked list, the previous one).
The value of next in the last node, marking the end of the list.
A variable that refers to a node; in Python every variable holding an object is a reference to it.
The last node of a list, whose next is None.
Walking the list from the head, following next until None.
drill:
Compose the moves

"Given a linked list, check whether it is a palindrome in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, and leave the list unchanged when you return." Describe the steps and the edge cases.

Answer

Step 1: find the first middle with fast and slow pointers (loop while fast.next and fast.next.next), so for 1→2→2→1 slow stops at the first 2 and for 1→2→3→2→1 at 3. Step 2: reverse the list starting at slow.next — that is the second half — with the iterative loop, keeping a reference to the reversed head. Step 3: walk p from the head and q from the reversed head, comparing values while q is not None; any mismatch means not a palindrome (record the result rather than returning immediately). Step 4: reverse the second half again and reattach it with slow.next = the re-reversed head, restoring the original list, then return the result. Edge cases: empty list and single node are palindromes (handle before step 1, or check that the loop does nothing harmful); for odd lengths the middle node stays with the first half and is never compared, which is correct. Complexity: O(n) time — four linear passes at most — and O(1) extra space. Mention the simpler O(n)-space alternative (copy values into an array and compare with its reverse) and why the interviewer's constraint rules it out.
qa: E
Reverse a singly linked list.

Walk once with three references: prev starts at None, curr at the head. For each node, save nxt = curr.next, point curr.next back to prev, then advance prev = curr and curr = nxt. When curr is None, prev is the new head. O(n) time, O(1) space.
E
Merge two sorted linked lists.

Create a dummy node and a tail pointer. While both lists are non-empty, attach the smaller head to tail.next, advance that list and the tail. Attach whatever remains. Return dummy.next. O(m + n) time and O(1) extra space, reusing the existing nodes.
E
Detect whether a linked list has a cycle.

Move slow one step and fast two steps per iteration. If fast reaches None, there is no cycle. If there is a cycle, fast enters it and gains one node per step on slow, so they must meet. O(n) time and O(1) space; a hash set of visited nodes also works with O(n) space.
M
Find the node where a cycle begins.

Run Floyd's algorithm until slow and fast meet. Then move one pointer back to the head and advance both one step at a time; the node where they meet is the cycle's start. If the tail before the cycle has length a and the meeting point is b steps into a cycle of length c, then a ≡ c − b (mod c), which is why the second phase lines up.
Follow-up: How do you find the cycle length? — From the meeting point, keep one pointer still and walk the other until it returns, counting steps.
M
Remove the n-th node from the end in one pass.

Use a dummy node before the head. Move fast n + 1 steps ahead of slow (both starting at the dummy), then move both until fast is None. slow is now just before the node to remove, so set slow.next = slow.next.next. The dummy handles removing the head itself.
M
Find the middle of a linked list.

Move slow by one and fast by two while fast and fast.next exist. When the loop ends, slow is at the middle; for even lengths it is the second of the two middle nodes. To get the first middle instead, loop while fast.next and fast.next.next exist.
M
Reorder a list L0 → L1 → … → Ln into L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln−1 → ….

Three steps, each a basic technique: find the middle with fast and slow pointers and cut the list there; reverse the second half; then merge the two halves by alternating nodes. O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
M
Add two numbers stored as linked lists with digits in reverse order.

Walk both lists together with a carry, creating a node for (a + b + carry) % 10 and setting carry to the quotient. Continue while either list has nodes or carry is non-zero. A dummy head simplifies building the result. O(max(m, n)).
M
Deep-copy a list where each node also has a random pointer.

Either keep a dict from original node to its copy (two passes: create copies, then wire next and random through the dict), using O(n) space; or interleave copies after each original node, set copy.random = original.random.next, and then separate the two lists, using O(1) extra space.
M
Find the node where two singly linked lists intersect.

Walk pointer a through list A then list B, and pointer b through B then A. Each walks a + c + b nodes in total (where c is the shared tail), so they reach the intersection at the same time, or both reach None together if there is none. O(m + n) time, O(1) space.
H
Reverse nodes in groups of k.

Use a dummy and a pointer group_prev to the node before the current group. Check that k nodes exist ahead; if not, stop. Reverse those k nodes with the standard loop, then reconnect: group_prev.next becomes the new group head and the old group head (now the group tail) points to the next group. Move group_prev to that tail and repeat. O(n) time, O(1) space.
Follow-up: What if the last partial group should also be reversed? — Remove the 'k nodes exist' check and reverse whatever remains.
H
Sort a linked list in O(n log n) time.

Merge sort fits lists well: split at the middle with fast and slow pointers, sort each half recursively, and merge. Merging lists needs no extra array, so space is O(log n) for recursion; a bottom-up version that merges runs of size 1, 2, 4, … achieves O(1) extra space. Quicksort is a poor fit because it needs random access for good pivots.

t: Heaps and priority queues: top-k, two heaps, k-way merge and scheduling
sum: How a binary heap keeps the minimum available in O(1) with O(log n) updates, how to use Python's heapq, and the patterns built on it: top-k with a size-k heap, the running median with two heaps, merging k sorted streams, and greedy scheduling.

Merging two sorted lists by repeatedly taking the smaller head.
why:
A hospital emergency department does not treat patients in arrival order. A nurse assigns each arriving patient a priority, and whenever a doctor becomes free, the most urgent waiting patient goes next. Patients keep arriving and leaving, so the "most urgent" one keeps changing. If the department kept the waiting list fully sorted, every arrival would mean re-sorting; if it kept the list unsorted, every time a doctor became free someone would scan the whole list. Neither is good when hundreds of patients pass through.

That situation — a collection that keeps changing, where you repeatedly need only the best element — is what a priority queue handles, and a binary heap is how it is almost always built. A heap gives you the minimum (or maximum) instantly and lets you insert or remove in O(log n) time. For a million elements, that is about 20 steps per operation instead of a million.

Interview problems use heaps in a handful of recognisable patterns. Top-k: the k largest, closest, or most frequent items among n, in O(n log k) — far better than sorting when k is small. Two heaps: the median of a stream, maintained as numbers arrive. K-way merge: combining k sorted lists or streams. Greedy scheduling: meeting rooms, CPU task order, choosing projects, reorganising strings — always "pick the best available option now", where a heap holds the options. Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm (al20) is also a heap at its core.

This lesson explains how a heap works inside (because interviewers sometimes ask you to implement one, and because knowing the mechanics explains the costs), how to use Python's heapq correctly, and each of the patterns above with a worked example.
primer:
The mental model: a company org chart where every boss outranks their reports

Imagine an organisation chart drawn as a tree, with one rule: every manager is more senior (here, "smaller", for a min-heap) than the people who report to them. Nothing is said about how two colleagues on the same level compare, or about cousins in different departments. But the rule alone guarantees one thing: the person at the top of the chart is the most senior of everyone. That is a heap: a tree where each parent is no larger than its children, which puts the minimum at the root.

The heap is kept as a complete binary tree — each manager has at most two reports, and the levels fill left to right with no gaps. That shape keeps the tree's height at about log₂ n, and it lets the whole tree live in a plain array with no pointers at all: the root is index 0, and the children of index i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2; the parent of i is (i − 1) // 2.

Two operations keep the rule true. To push, put the new element in the next free spot at the bottom and let it "climb": while it is smaller than its parent, swap them. To pop the minimum, take the root, move the last element into the root's place, and let it "sink": while it is larger than its smaller child, swap them. Each walks at most the height of the tree, so both are O(log n). Peeking at the minimum is just reading index 0.

Where the analogy breaks: in a real organisation you might ask "who is the third most senior person?" and expect the chart to tell you. A heap cannot answer that cheaply. It only knows the top. If you need arbitrary order queries (the k-th smallest, everything between two values), use a sorted structure instead. A heap's strength is exactly and only "give me the best one, repeatedly, while things change".

It is also worth fixing the vocabulary. A priority queue is the abstract idea: a collection you can add items to, each with a priority, and from which you can always remove the highest-priority item. A binary heap is one concrete way to build it. Other implementations exist — a sorted list (cheap removal, expensive insertion), an unsorted list (cheap insertion, expensive removal), a balanced search tree (both O(log n), more memory and more general) — but the heap wins for the common case because it is compact, simple and fast. In interviews, "priority queue" and "heap" are used interchangeably.

That narrow strength is also why a heap beats full sorting in so many problems. If you need the 10 largest numbers out of a billion, sorting all billion does far more work than necessary; a heap that only ever holds 10 candidates does about a billion cheap comparisons and a few log₂ 10 ≈ 3-step adjustments. Paying only for the order you actually use is the recurring theme of this lesson.
body:
Inside the heap: push and pop, traced

Start from the heap array [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5, 9] in the figure. Push 0: append it at index 7, whose parent is (7 − 1) // 2 = 3 (value 7). 0 < 7, swap → index 3; parent is index 1 (value 3), swap → index 1; parent is index 0 (value 1), swap → index 0. Result: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 7]. Three swaps for a heap of 8: log₂ 8 = 3.

Pop from that: return 0, move the last element (7) to the root: [7, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9]. Sift down: children of 0 are 1 and 2; the smaller child is 1, and 7 > 1, so swap → [1, 7, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9]. Children of index 1 are indices 3 and 4 (values 3 and 4); smaller is 3, 7 > 3, swap → [1, 3, 2, 7, 4, 5, 9]. Index 3 has no children; stop. Always swap with the smaller child, or the heap rule would break between the two children.

def sift_up(h, i):
    while i > 0 and h[(i - 1) // 2] > h[i]:
        p = (i - 1) // 2
        h[i], h[p] = h[p], h[i]
        i = p

def sift_down(h, i):
    n = len(h)
    while True:
        smallest, l, r = i, 2 * i + 1, 2 * i + 2
        if l < n and h[l] < h[smallest]: smallest = l
        if r < n and h[r] < h[smallest]: smallest = r
        if smallest == i: return
        h[i], h[smallest] = h[smallest], h[i]
        i = smallest

Interviewers occasionally ask you to implement a heap from scratch; those two functions plus push (append, sift up) and pop (swap root with last, pop last, sift down the root) are the whole thing. heapify — turning an arbitrary array into a heap — calls sift_down on every non-leaf index from (n // 2) − 1 down to 0, and costs O(n), not O(n log n) (the deep layer explains why).

Using heapq correctly

Python's heapq works on an ordinary list and is always a min-heap:

import heapq
h = []
heapq.heappush(h, 5); heapq.heappush(h, 1); heapq.heappush(h, 3)
h[0]                      # 1, peek
heapq.heappop(h)          # 1
heapq.heapify(data)       # in place, O(n)
heapq.heappushpop(h, x)   # push then pop, faster than two calls
heapq.nlargest(k, data)   # convenience top-k
heapq.nsmallest(k, data, key=...)

Three practical rules prevent most bugs. Max-heap: push −x and negate on the way out. Priorities with payloads: push tuples (priority, item); tuples compare element by element, so the priority decides. Ties: if two priorities are equal, Python compares the next field, and if that is an object without ordering (a ListNode, a dict), you get TypeError: '<' not supported. Insert a tie-breaker that is always comparable — an index or an increasing counter: (priority, count, item). The heapq documentation recommends exactly this.

Pattern 1: top-k with a size-k heap

"Find the k largest elements" (or the k-th largest). Keep a min-heap holding the k largest seen so far. Its root is the smallest of those k — the current k-th largest, and the threshold a newcomer must beat.

def kth_largest(nums, k):
    h = []
    for x in nums:
        heapq.heappush(h, x)
        if len(h) > k:
            heapq.heappop(h)          # drop the smallest of k+1
    return h[0]

Trace nums = [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2: the heap goes [3] → [2, 3] → push 1, pop 1 → [2, 3] → push 5, pop 2 → [3, 5] → push 6, pop 3 → [5, 6] → push 4, pop 4 → [5, 6]. Root 5 is the 2nd largest. Cost O(n log k) time and O(k) memory, which beats sorting (O(n log n)) when k is small, and works on a stream that never ends — "Kth Largest Element in a Stream" is this function split into a constructor and an add method.

The same shape answers many questions by changing the key. K closest points to the origin: keep the k smallest distances, so use a max-heap of size k (push (−distance², point)) and pop the farthest whenever it grows past k. Top k frequent elements: count with a Counter, then keep a min-heap of size k over (count, value) pairs.

Two alternatives are worth naming. Quickselect partitions around a random pivot and recurses into one side only, finding the k-th largest in O(n) average time — faster, but O(n²) worst case and not suitable for streams. Bucket sort fits frequencies: counts are between 1 and n, so make an array of n + 1 lists indexed by count and read from the top; that is O(n) for top-k frequent.

Pattern 2: two heaps for the running median

"Numbers arrive one at a time; after each, report the median." Sorting after every insert is O(n log n) each. Instead split the numbers into two halves: a max-heap lo holding the smaller half and a min-heap hi holding the larger half. Keep every element of lo ≤ every element of hi, and keep the sizes equal or lo one larger. Then the median is lo's top (odd count) or the average of both tops (even count).

class MedianFinder:
    def __init__(self):
        self.lo, self.hi = [], []          # lo: max-heap via negation
    def add(self, x):
        heapq.heappush(self.lo, -x)
        heapq.heappush(self.hi, -heapq.heappop(self.lo))  # move lo's max up
        if len(self.hi) > len(self.lo):                   # rebalance
            heapq.heappush(self.lo, -heapq.heappop(self.hi))
    def median(self):
        if len(self.lo) > len(self.hi):
            return -self.lo[0]
        return (-self.lo[0] + self.hi[0]) / 2

The "push into lo, move lo's max to hi, rebalance" sequence is a neat way to avoid comparing x with the tops by hand: it guarantees the ordering invariant (lo's max ends up no larger than hi's min) and the size invariant in three lines. The sliding-window median adds removals, which a heap cannot do directly; the standard fix is lazy deletion — record elements to delete in a counter and discard them when they reach a top.

Pattern 3: k-way merge

"Merge k sorted lists." Merging two lists takes the smaller of two heads; merging k lists needs the smallest of k heads, repeatedly — a priority queue of size k.

def merge_k_lists(lists):
    h = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]
    heapq.heapify(h)
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while h:
        val, i, node = heapq.heappop(h)
        tail.next = node; tail = node
        if node.next:
            heapq.heappush(h, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
    return dummy.next

Each of N total nodes is pushed and popped once in a heap of size at most k: O(N log k). The index i is the tie-breaker that stops Python from comparing two ListNodes. The same structure solves "smallest range covering one element from each of k lists" (also track the current maximum among the heads; the range is [heap min, current max]), "k-th smallest element in a sorted matrix" (rows are k sorted lists), and "find k pairs with the smallest sums" (a heap of candidate index pairs, expanded lazily). It is also how external sorting merges sorted runs from disk.

Pattern 4: greedy scheduling

Many problems have the shape "at each moment, choose the best available option", where options become available over time. Sort the inputs by when they become available, and keep the available options in a heap keyed by "best".

Meeting Rooms II (minimum rooms needed): sort meetings by start; keep a min-heap of end times for meetings in progress. For each meeting, if the earliest end is ≤ its start, that room is free — pop it. Push the new meeting's end. The largest heap size during the sweep is the answer. For [[0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20]]: push 30; at 5, earliest end 30 > 5, push 10 (two rooms); at 15, earliest end 10 ≤ 15, pop it, push 20 (still two). Answer 2.

Single-Threaded CPU: tasks have an enqueue time and a processing time; the CPU, when idle, picks the available task with the shortest processing time (ties by index). Sort by enqueue time; keep a min-heap of (processing time, index) for tasks that have arrived; when the heap is empty, jump the clock to the next enqueue time.

IPO: you have capital w and may complete at most k projects, each needing some capital and giving a profit. Sort projects by required capital. Each round, push the profits of every project you can now afford into a max-heap, then take the largest profit. Taking the best affordable project is safe because capital only grows, so anything affordable now stays affordable later.

Reorganize String / Task Scheduler: always place the most frequent remaining character (or task) that is not blocked. A max-heap of counts plus a small queue or "held-back" slot for the item that just ran implements it. For Task Scheduler there is also a closed-form answer, (f − 1)(n + 1) + m capped below by the number of tasks, where f is the maximum frequency and m how many tasks share it — worth deriving once by drawing the frames.

Heap, sort or quickselect? A quick decision table

SituationBest toolCost
Top k of static data, k smallsize-k heapO(n log k), O(k) memory
Top k of static data, need only the k-th value, fastest averagequickselectO(n) average, O(n²) worst
Top k of a stream that never endssize-k heapO(log k) per element
Need everything in order oncesortO(n log n)
Repeated min/max while inserting and removingheapO(log n) per operation
Arbitrary rank or range queries under updatesbalanced tree / FenwickO(log n) per operation
Top k by frequency, counts bounded by nbucket sortO(n)

Naming the alternatives and picking one for a stated reason ("the input is a stream, so quickselect is out") is exactly the kind of judgement interviewers score under problem solving.

Recognising the pattern

Reach for a heap when you repeatedly need the minimum or maximum of a collection that changes: "k largest / smallest / closest / most frequent", "median of a stream", "merge k sorted", "schedule", "earliest finishing", "most profitable available", "next event in time order", or a shortest path with weights. If you need the extreme only once, a single scan is enough; if you need full order once, sort. A heap is for repeated extremes under change.

Practice in the DSA list: Kth Largest Element in an Array, Kth Largest Element in a Stream, K Closest Points to Origin, Top K Frequent Elements, Meeting Rooms II (al11), Task Scheduler, Reorganize String, Single-Threaded CPU, Find Median from Data Stream, Merge k Sorted Lists, IPO, Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists.
deep:
Why heapify is O(n)

Bottom-up heapify calls sift_down on each non-leaf node. A node at height h (distance from the bottom) sifts down at most h levels. In a complete tree of n nodes, about n/2 nodes are leaves (height 0, no work), n/4 have height 1, n/8 height 2, and so on. The total work is at most n·(1/4·1 + 1/8·2 + 1/16·3 + …) = n·Σ h/2^(h+1) = n. Intuitively, the expensive sifts happen only near the root, where there are very few nodes. Pushing elements one at a time does the opposite — most elements are inserted at the bottom and may climb the full height — which is why it is O(n log n). This is a classic "explain the analysis" question.

Heapsort, and why it is rarely used

Heapify, then pop n times placing each popped element at the end of the array: that sorts in O(n log n) worst case with O(1) extra memory — heapsort. It beats quicksort's worst case and mergesort's memory, yet libraries rarely use it as the main sort because its memory access pattern jumps around the array (index i to 2i + 1), which is cache-unfriendly, and it is not stable. Its main production role is as the fallback in introsort: when quicksort's recursion gets too deep (a sign of bad pivots), switch to heapsort to guarantee O(n log n).

Decrease-key, lazy deletion and Dijkstra

Dijkstra's algorithm needs to lower a node's tentative distance when a shorter path is found ("decrease-key"). A textbook indexed heap tracks each element's position so it can sift it up in O(log n). heapq has no such operation, so Python implementations push a new (distance, node) entry and skip stale entries when they are popped ("if d > dist[node]: continue"). This is lazy deletion: the heap may hold up to E entries instead of V, so operations cost O(log E) = O(log V²) = O(2 log V), the same order. It is simpler and usually faster in practice. The same trick handles "remove an arbitrary element" for sliding-window medians and for task cancellation in schedulers.

Tie-breaking and stability

Heaps are not stable: two elements with equal priority can come out in either order. When order among equals matters — first-come-first-served among equal priorities, or a required tie rule like "smallest index first" in Single-Threaded CPU — encode it in the key: (priority, arrival_counter, item). The counter also prevents comparisons between payloads that are not orderable. For max-heaps with tie rules, be careful which fields you negate: for "largest profit, then smallest index", push (−profit, index).

d-ary heaps and other variants

A d-ary heap gives each node d children instead of two. The tree is shallower (log_d n levels), so sift up is cheaper, while sift down compares d children per level. When pushes and decrease-keys outnumber pops — as in Dijkstra on dense graphs — a 4-ary heap is often faster, and the Go runtime uses a 4-ary heap for its timers. Fibonacci heaps achieve amortised O(1) decrease-key, giving Dijkstra O(E + V log V) in theory, but their constant factors make them slower in practice than a binary or d-ary heap. For interviews, knowing that the binary heap is the practical default, and why, is enough. If asked to design a priority queue that supports changing priorities efficiently, describe an indexed heap: alongside the array, keep a dict from item to its array position, and update it on every swap, so decrease-key can find the item in O(1) and sift it in O(log n).

When a heap is the wrong tool

If you need the k-th element under arbitrary insertions and deletions, or range queries ("how many values between a and b"), a heap cannot help; use a balanced search tree (or sortedcontainers.SortedList), a Fenwick tree over compressed values (al27), or an order-statistics tree. If the priorities are small integers, a bucket queue (an array of lists indexed by priority) gives O(1) operations. And if you only need the top k once over static data, sorted(data)[-k:] is simpler and fine unless n is very large; say so before reaching for a heap to show you choose tools by need.
prod:
In the interview room

Heap solutions are short, so the bugs are in the details. The most common: forgetting that heapq is a min-heap (pushing positive values when you need the largest first); negating on the way in but not on the way out; pushing tuples whose second field is not comparable and crashing on ties; popping from an empty heap; and using a heap of size n when a heap of size k was the point (O(n log n) instead of O(n log k), and O(n) memory). Another subtle one is modifying an element in place after pushing it — the heap does not know and its order breaks. Treat heap entries as immutable and push new ones.

Interviewers often follow up on complexity choices: "why O(n log k) and not O(n log n)?", "could you do better than a heap?" (quickselect or bucket sort), and "what if the data is a stream?" (the size-k heap still works; quickselect does not). For the median, the follow-up is usually "now support removal" (lazy deletion) or "what if all numbers are integers between 0 and 100?" (a counting array with a running pointer gives O(1) per operation).

For scheduling problems, the follow-up is a proof: "why is picking the earliest-ending room or the most profitable affordable project optimal?". Have a one-sentence exchange argument ready: if an optimal plan chose something else at that moment, swapping in the greedy choice does not make it worse.

On online assessments, heap problems often come disguised as simulations: "servers process requests; when a server is free it takes the oldest highest-priority request", "workers finish jobs at different times; find when the last job finishes". Simulating time step by step is too slow when times go up to 10⁹; the fix is an event-driven simulation where a heap of (time, event) pairs lets you jump directly to the next interesting moment.

In real systems

Priority queues are built into a lot of infrastructure. Event loops keep timers in a min-heap keyed by expiry time: libuv, the library under Node.js, stores timers in a binary min-heap, and each loop iteration looks at the root to know how long it may sleep. Search engines collect the top-k results with a bounded heap — Apache Lucene's PriorityQueue keeps the k best-scoring documents while scoring millions, discarding anything below the current k-th score, exactly the size-k pattern from this lesson. Network routers and OSPF-style routing protocols run Dijkstra's algorithm with a priority queue to compute shortest paths. Job schedulers and message brokers (for example, priority queues in RabbitMQ) order work by priority. Streaming analytics compute "top-k trending items" over windows with heaps combined with approximate counters. Discrete-event simulators — used to model networks, factories and queues — are a priority queue of future events processed in time order. When an interviewer asks how you would build "a service that returns the 10 most popular products in the last hour", a size-k heap over counts is the core of the answer.
myths: A heap keeps its elements sorted.

A heap only guarantees that every parent is no larger than its children (for a min-heap), which puts the minimum at the root. The rest of the array is only partially ordered; printing it does not give sorted output. To get sorted order you must pop repeatedly, which is heapsort.
To find the k largest elements you need a max-heap.

The efficient way uses a min-heap of size k: keep the k largest seen so far, with the smallest of them at the root, and replace the root whenever a larger element arrives. That costs O(n log k) and O(k) memory. A max-heap of all n elements works too but costs O(n + k log n) time and O(n) memory.
Building a heap from n elements costs O(n log n).

heapify builds it bottom-up in O(n). Most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a short distance; the total work sums to less than 2n swaps. Pushing n elements one at a time is O(n log n), so prefer heapify when you have the data up front.
Python's heapq can be a max-heap if you pass a flag.

heapq is always a min-heap. For a max-heap, push negated keys (−x) for numbers or tuples with a negated first element. For objects that are not numbers, wrap them in a class whose __lt__ is reversed, or push (−priority, tie_breaker, item).
A heap can find or delete any element in O(log n).

Only the root is cheap to find. Finding an arbitrary element is O(n), so deletion of arbitrary elements is usually done by lazy deletion: mark it as removed and discard it when it reaches the root. Indexed heaps that track positions support O(log n) decrease-key, but heapq does not.
lab:
Check the median finder against sorting, and compare the size-k heap with full sorting for top-k.

  1. Save as heap_lab.py: 
    import heapq, random, statistics, time

class MedianFinder:
    def __init__(self): self.lo, self.hi = [], []
    def add(self, x):
        heapq.heappush(self.lo, -x)
        heapq.heappush(self.hi, -heapq.heappop(self.lo))
        if len(self.hi) > len(self.lo):
            heapq.heappush(self.lo, -heapq.heappop(self.hi))
    def median(self):
        if len(self.lo) > len(self.hi): return -self.lo[0]
        return (-self.lo[0] + self.hi[0]) / 2

for _ in range(500):
    mf, seen = MedianFinder(), []
    for _ in range(random.randint(1, 30)):
        x = random.randint(-5, 5); mf.add(x); seen.append(x)
        assert mf.median() == statistics.median(seen), seen
print("two-heap median matches statistics.median")

def topk_heap(a, k):
    h = []
    for x in a:
        if len(h) < k: heapq.heappush(h, x)
        elif x > h[0]: heapq.heapreplace(h, x)
    return sorted(h, reverse=True)

a = [random.random() for _ in range(2_000_000)]
for name, f in (("heap", lambda: topk_heap(a, 10)),
                ("sort", lambda: sorted(a, reverse=True)[:10])):
    t = time.perf_counter(); r = f(); print(name, f"{time.perf_counter()-t:.2f}s")
  2. Run it. The first message confirms the median after every insertion, including many duplicates and negative numbers.
  3. Compare the timings. The heap version mostly does one comparison per element (x > h[0] is usually false once the heap holds large values); sorting does O(n log n) work in C. Depending on your machine, the C-level sort can be competitive at this size despite its worse complexity — note which wins and by how much.

What this proves: the two-heap invariant gives exact medians; and asymptotic advantage (n log k versus n log n) competes with constant factors (Python loop versus C sort), which is worth saying in an interview when you choose between them.
recap: A priority queue gives fast access to the smallest (or largest) element of a changing collection; a binary heap implements it with O(1) peek and O(log n) push and pop.
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array: children of index i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and every parent is at most its children in a min-heap.
Push appends and sifts up; pop moves the last element to the root and sifts down; heapify builds a heap in O(n).
Python's heapq is a min-heap; negate keys for a max-heap and use (priority, counter, item) tuples to break ties and avoid comparing items.
For the k largest of n items, keep a min-heap of size k: O(n log k) time and O(k) memory.
The running median keeps a max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half, balanced so their sizes differ by at most one.
Merging k sorted lists keeps one head per list in a heap and repeatedly pops the smallest: O(N log k) for N total elements.
Greedy scheduling problems use a heap to always pick the best available option, such as the earliest-ending meeting or the most profitable affordable project.
glossary: A complete binary tree stored in an array where each parent is ordered relative to its children; the standard priority-queue implementation.
A binary tree with every level full except possibly the last, which is filled from the left; it maps onto an array with no gaps.
Rearranging an array into a heap in place, bottom-up, in O(n).
Python's standard-library module of heap functions operating on a plain list as a min-heap.
Merging k sorted sequences into one by repeatedly taking the smallest current head, using a heap of size k.
Marking an element as removed and discarding it only when it reaches the top of the heap, instead of searching for it.
A heap whose root is the largest (max-heap) or smallest (min-heap) element.
An abstract collection that supports inserting items with priorities and removing the highest-priority item.
Open Shortest Path First: an internet routing protocol in which each router runs Dijkstra's algorithm with a priority queue.
A selection algorithm that partitions like quicksort but recurses into one side only, finding the k-th smallest in O(n) on average.
Moving an element down the heap, swapping it with its smaller child, until both children are no smaller.
Moving an element up the heap, swapping it with its parent, until the parent is no larger.
The problem of finding the k largest (or smallest, or most frequent) items in a collection or stream.
Keeping the lower half of the data in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap to read the median in O(1).
drill:
Design with a heap

"Design a service that, at any moment, returns the 10 most frequently searched queries in the last 60 minutes. There are about 5,000 searches per second." Sketch the data structures and the costs, and say what you would approximate if memory were tight.

Answer

Keep per-minute buckets: a ring of 60 dictionaries, each mapping query → count for that minute, plus a running dictionary total[query] = count over the last 60 minutes. On each search, increment the current minute's bucket and total (O(1)). When a minute rolls over, subtract the expiring bucket's counts from total (deleting zero entries) and reuse the bucket — amortised O(1) per search. To answer top-10, run a size-10 min-heap over total's items: O(u log 10) for u distinct queries in the window, which may be hundreds of thousands, so cache the answer and recompute every few seconds rather than per request. That is accurate but stores every distinct query in the hour. If memory is tight, replace exact counts with a Count-Min sketch (fixed memory, slight overestimates) and keep a small heap of candidate heavy hitters (the "top-k with sketch" approach used in streaming systems), or use the Space-Saving algorithm, which tracks only m counters and guarantees to contain every query whose frequency exceeds N/m. Mention the trade-off: exactness versus memory, and recompute-on-read versus maintain-on-write.
qa: E
What are the costs of heap operations?

Peek at the minimum O(1); push O(log n); pop the minimum O(log n); build from n elements with heapify O(n). Searching for or deleting an arbitrary element is O(n), because the heap only orders parents relative to children.
E
Find the k-th largest element in an array.

Keep a min-heap of size k while scanning: push each element and pop when the size exceeds k. At the end the root is the k-th largest. O(n log k) time, O(k) space. Quickselect gives O(n) average time and O(1) extra space but O(n²) worst case without a random pivot.
E
How do you use heapq as a max-heap?
Push negated values and negate again when popping: heappush(h, −x), −heappop(h). For tuples, negate the priority field: (−priority, tiebreak, item). heapq has no max-heap flag.
M
Top k frequent elements.

Count with a Counter in O(n), then keep a min-heap of (count, value) of size k over the distinct values: O(n + u log k), where u is the number of distinct values. Alternatively bucket sort by frequency: an array of lists indexed by count, read from the highest count down, which is O(n).
Follow-up: Which is better? — Bucket sort is O(n) but uses an array of size n + 1; the heap is better when k is small and u is large, and it works on streams.
M
Find the median of a data stream.

Keep a max-heap for the lower half (store negatives in heapq) and a min-heap for the upper half. Insert into the lower heap, move its maximum to the upper heap, and if the upper heap becomes larger, move its minimum back. The median is the lower heap's top (odd count) or the average of both tops. O(log n) per insert, O(1) per median.
M
Meeting Rooms II: the minimum number of rooms for a set of intervals.

Sort meetings by start time and keep a min-heap of end times of meetings in progress. For each meeting, if the earliest-ending one has finished (its end ≤ this start), pop it to reuse its room; then push this meeting's end. The heap's maximum size is the answer. O(n log n).
Follow-up: Without a heap? — Sort starts and ends separately and sweep with two pointers, counting +1 at a start and −1 at an end: the maximum running count is the answer.
M
K closest points to the origin.

Keep a max-heap of size k keyed by distance (push (−d², x, y)); when it exceeds k, pop the farthest. At the end the heap holds the k closest. Compare squared distances to avoid square roots. O(n log k).
M
Task scheduler with cooldown n between identical tasks: minimum total time.

Greedy formula: let f be the highest task frequency and m the number of tasks with that frequency; the answer is max(len(tasks), (f − 1)(n + 1) + m). A simulation with a max-heap of remaining counts and a queue of tasks cooling down gives the same answer and also produces the schedule.
M
Reorganize a string so no two adjacent characters are equal.

Count characters and push (−count, char) into a max-heap. Repeatedly pop the most frequent character that differs from the previous one, append it, and push the previous character back if it still has count left. If the heap empties while a character is held back, it is impossible; that happens when some count exceeds (n + 1) // 2.
H
Merge k sorted linked lists.

Push (value, list index, node) for each list head into a min-heap. Pop the smallest, append it to the result, and push its next node if any. Each of the N nodes is pushed and popped once in a heap of size at most k, so O(N log k). The list index breaks ties so nodes are never compared directly.
Follow-up: Another approach? — Divide and conquer: merge lists in pairs, log k rounds of O(N) merging, also O(N log k) and O(1) extra space.
H
IPO: start with capital w, pick at most k projects each with a capital requirement and profit, maximising final capital.

Sort projects by required capital. Repeat k times: push the profits of all newly affordable projects (requirement ≤ current capital) into a max-heap, then pop the largest profit and add it to the capital. If the heap is empty, stop. Each project is pushed once: O(n log n + k log n). The greedy is optimal because taking the most profitable affordable project never reduces future options.
H
Smallest range covering at least one element from each of k sorted lists.

Keep a min-heap with one current element per list and track the current maximum among them. The range [heap min, current max] covers all lists; record it if it is smaller. Pop the minimum and push the next element of that list, updating the maximum. Stop when any list is exhausted. O(N log k).
