t: Intervals and the sweep line: merge, insert, select and count overlaps
sum: Sort intervals to make overlaps local: merging and inserting, the greedy that keeps the most non-overlapping intervals, intersections of two lists, meeting rooms via events or a heap, booking calendars, and sweep lines with coordinate compression.
prereq: al3
Difference arrays: +v at a start and −v after an end, then a running sum.
al5
Two pointers over two sorted sequences, advancing the one that ends first.
al10
A min-heap of end times tracks meetings in progress.
why:
A team calendar has 40 people, each with a list of meetings for the week, and you are asked: "when can all 40 meet for an hour?" Or: "how many rooms does the building need so that no meeting is double-booked?" Or: "a booking system receives reservations one by one — reject any that clash with an existing one". These are interval problems. Each meeting is a range on the time line, and the questions are about how the ranges overlap.

The brute force compares every interval with every other: with 10⁵ meetings that is 5 × 10⁹ comparisons, and many questions (merge everything that overlaps, transitively) are awkward even then. The fix is almost always the same first step: sort. Once intervals are sorted by start, an interval can only overlap the ones just before it, so a single left-to-right scan replaces the all-pairs comparison. The whole problem becomes O(n log n) for the sort and O(n) for the scan.

What changes from problem to problem is the sort key and what the scan keeps. Merging keeps the current block. Choosing the most non-overlapping intervals sorts by end instead, for a reason worth understanding. Counting how many intervals are active at once turns each interval into two events — a start and an end — and sweeps over them. Comparing two lists of intervals walks them with two pointers. And the booking-calendar problem keeps intervals in sorted order as they arrive.

This lesson works through each of those shapes with traces, the greedy proofs behind the sort-by-end choice, the boundary questions (do touching intervals overlap?) that cause most bugs, and the sweep-line technique that generalises to the famous skyline problem.
primer:
The mental model: a time line and a sweeping hand

Draw every interval as a bar on a horizontal time line. Now imagine a vertical line — a sweep line — moving from left to right across the picture. As it moves, it touches some bars. Most of the time nothing interesting happens; the set of touched bars changes only when the line reaches the start or the end of some bar. Those are the events. Any question about overlaps — how many bars are touched at once, where the free gaps are, which bars merge into one block — can be answered by stopping only at the events, in sorted order, and updating a small amount of state.

That one picture contains most of the lesson. The merged blocks are the stretches where the count is above zero: [1, 6] and [7, 11]. The maximum overlap is the highest point of the count, 3 — the number of meeting rooms needed. The free time is where the count is zero: before 1, between 6 and 7, after 11. Different problems read different features off the same sweep.

The second thing to fix in your mind is the overlap test. Two intervals [a, b] and [c, d] overlap exactly when each starts before the other ends: a ≤ d and c ≤ b. The opposite — they do not overlap — is "one ends before the other starts": b < c or d < a. If you ever find yourself writing four cases ("c inside [a, b], or d inside, or …"), stop and use the two-comparison test instead.

Where the analogy breaks: on a picture, touching bars look like they meet, but whether they overlap depends on meaning. A meeting from 1 to 2 and another from 2 to 3 can use the same room; a closed numeric range [1, 2] and [2, 3] share the point 2. This boundary decision — closed intervals, where touching counts, or half-open intervals [a, b), where it does not — changes ≤ to < in the code and changes the order of events at equal times. It is the most common source of wrong answers in interval problems, so it is the first clarifying question to ask.

A final framing that ties this lesson to earlier ones: the sweep's running count is exactly the difference-array idea from al3, applied to sorted event points instead of every index. When coordinates are small and dense, a difference array is simplest; when they are large or sparse, sort the events. Same idea, different storage.
body:
Merging overlapping intervals

Sort by start. Then each interval either overlaps the block you are building (it starts at or before the block's end) or begins a new block. Overlap is transitive along the sorted order, so one pass suffices.

def merge(intervals):
    intervals.sort(key=lambda iv: iv[0])
    out = []
    for s, e in intervals:
        if out and s <= out[-1][1]:            # overlaps the current block
            out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)    # extend (max: it may be inside)
        else:
            out.append([s, e])
    return out

Trace [[1, 5], [3, 6], [8, 11], [7, 9], [4, 5]] sorted to [[1, 5], [3, 6], [4, 5], [7, 9], [8, 11]]: start [1, 5]; [3, 6] overlaps → [1, 6]; [4, 5] overlaps but ends earlier → still [1, 6] (this is why you need max, not just "take e"); [7, 9] starts after 6 → new block; [8, 11] overlaps → [7, 11]. Result [[1, 6], [7, 11]], matching the figure. Change <= to < if touching intervals should stay separate.

Inserting into a sorted list

If the existing intervals are already sorted and non-overlapping, inserting one new interval does not need a sort. Walk once in three phases: copy everything that ends before the new interval starts; absorb everything that overlaps it, widening the new interval to cover them; copy the rest.

def insert(intervals, new):
    out, i, n = [], 0, len(intervals)
    s, e = new
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < s:        # entirely before
        out.append(intervals[i]); i += 1
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= e:       # overlapping
        s = min(s, intervals[i][0]); e = max(e, intervals[i][1]); i += 1
    out.append([s, e])
    out.extend(intervals[i:])                   # entirely after
    return out

O(n). The two loop conditions are the overlap test split in half: "ends before the new one starts" and "starts before the new one ends".

Selecting non-overlapping intervals: sort by end

"Remove the minimum number of intervals so the rest do not overlap." Flip it: keep the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals; the answer is n minus that. This is the classic activity selection problem, and its greedy rule is: sort by end, and take every interval that starts at or after the end of the last one taken.

def erase_overlap_intervals(intervals):
    intervals.sort(key=lambda iv: iv[1])
    kept, last_end = 0, float("-inf")
    for s, e in intervals:
        if s >= last_end:            # compatible (touching allowed here)
            kept += 1; last_end = e
    return len(intervals) - kept

Why the end, not the start? Among all intervals, the one that finishes first leaves the most room for everything after it. The exchange argument: take any optimal selection; its first interval ends no earlier than the greedy's first choice (which ends earliest of all). Swap it for the greedy's choice — the rest of the optimal selection still fits, because the greedy interval ends even sooner — so there is an optimal solution that agrees with the greedy's first step. Repeat for the remaining intervals. Sorting by start fails on [[1, 100], [2, 3], [4, 5]]: it would take [1, 100] first and block both short meetings.

Minimum arrows to burst balloons is the same algorithm in disguise. Sort balloons by end, shoot at the first balloon's end (the latest point that still hits it, so it hits as many others as possible), skip every balloon that starts at or before that point, and repeat. The number of arrows equals the maximum number of pairwise disjoint balloons.

Intersecting two interval lists

Given two lists of disjoint, sorted intervals, return their intersection. Two pointers, one per list (al5). The overlap of the current pair is [max(starts), min(ends)], non-empty if its start ≤ its end. Then advance the pointer whose interval ends first: it cannot overlap anything later in the other list, because those start later still.

def interval_intersection(A, B):
    i = j = 0; out = []
    while i < len(A) and j < len(B):
        lo = max(A[i][0], B[j][0]); hi = min(A[i][1], B[j][1])
        if lo <= hi: out.append([lo, hi])
        if A[i][1] < B[j][1]: i += 1
        else: j += 1
    return out

Counting overlaps: events, or a heap

"Minimum number of meeting rooms" is "maximum number of intervals active at the same time". Two equivalent methods.

Sweep with events. Turn each meeting into two events, (start, +1) and (end, −1). Sort them, and walk with a running count; the maximum count is the answer. The order of events at the same time encodes the boundary decision: for meetings, an end at 10 and a start at 10 should not need two rooms, so process the end first — sorting tuples (time, delta) does that automatically because −1 < +1.

def min_rooms(intervals):
    events = []
    for s, e in intervals:
        events.append((s, 1)); events.append((e, -1))
    events.sort()                      # at equal time, -1 (end) before +1
    cur = best = 0
    for _, d in events:
        cur += d; best = max(best, cur)
    return best

Heap of end times. Sort meetings by start and keep a min-heap of the end times of meetings currently using rooms (al10). For each meeting, if the earliest end is ≤ its start, that room is free — pop it; then push the new end. The heap size never shrinks below what is needed, and its peak is the answer. The heap version is useful when you also need to know which room each meeting gets.

A third variant uses two sorted arrays — all starts, all ends — and two pointers: walk the starts; if the next start is before the earliest unused end, allocate a room; otherwise reuse one by advancing the end pointer. It is the sweep without building tuples.

Booking calendars: intervals arriving one at a time

"My Calendar I": bookings arrive online; accept a booking [s, e) only if it does not overlap any accepted one. Keep accepted bookings sorted by start (a list maintained with bisect, or a balanced tree). For a new booking, find where it would go; it is valid if the previous booking ends at or before s and the next booking starts at or after e — only the two neighbours can conflict, because the stored bookings do not overlap each other.

import bisect
class MyCalendar:
    def __init__(self): self.starts, self.ends = [], []
    def book(self, s, e):
        i = bisect.bisect_right(self.starts, s)
        if i > 0 and self.ends[i - 1] > s: return False   # previous overlaps
        if i < len(self.starts) and self.starts[i] < e: return False  # next overlaps
        self.starts.insert(i, s); self.ends.insert(i, e)
        return True

The search is O(log n); Python list insertion is O(n), which is fine for the problem's limits, and a balanced tree (or sortedcontainers.SortedList) makes it O(log n). "My Calendar II" (allow double but not triple bookings) and "III" (report the maximum overlap after each booking) switch to the sweep: keep a sorted map from time to delta, add +1 at s and −1 at e, and sweep it to compute the running maximum — O(n) per booking, acceptable for small n, or a segment tree with lazy propagation for large n (al27).

The skyline problem: a sweep with a heap

Buildings are rectangles [left, right, height] on a common ground line; output the outline's key points, where the maximum height changes. Sweep x from left to right. The state is the multiset of heights of buildings covering the current x; the answer changes when the maximum of that multiset changes. A max-heap holds the active heights; ended buildings are removed lazily (keep their right edge in the heap entry and pop entries whose right edge is ≤ x before reading the top).

import heapq
def get_skyline(buildings):
    events = sorted({l for l, r, h in buildings} | {r for l, r, h in buildings})
    res, live, i, n = [], [], 0, len(buildings)     # live: (-height, right)
    buildings.sort()
    for x in events:
        while i < n and buildings[i][0] <= x:        # add buildings starting here
            heapq.heappush(live, (-buildings[i][2], buildings[i][1])); i += 1
        while live and live[0][1] <= x:               # drop ended buildings
            heapq.heappop(live)
        h = -live[0][0] if live else 0
        if not res or res[-1][1] != h:
            res.append([x, h])
    return res

Processing all buildings that start at x before reading the maximum, and dropping all that end at x, handles the tricky equal-coordinate cases (a building ending exactly where a taller one starts, or two buildings starting together) without hand-crafted event ordering. O(n log n).

Coordinate compression

When interval endpoints go up to 10⁹ but there are only 10⁵ intervals, there are at most 2 × 10⁵ distinct coordinates that matter. Sort the distinct endpoints and replace each by its rank (rank = {x: i for i, x in enumerate(sorted(set(points)))}). Now a difference array or a segment tree of size 2 × 10⁵ works. Be careful with what the gaps mean: between compressed coordinates i and i + 1 lies a real stretch of length points[i + 1] − points[i], which matters if you are measuring total covered length rather than counting.

Free time and gaps

"Employee Free Time" gives each person's busy intervals (sorted) and asks for the finite stretches when everyone is free. The answer is the complement of the union of all busy intervals: merge everything, then read the gaps between consecutive merged blocks. If there are k people with N intervals in total, flattening and sorting is O(N log N); a k-way merge with a heap (one pointer per person, al10) produces the intervals in start order in O(N log k) without a full sort, and you can merge on the fly. "Find a common one-hour slot for all attendees within working hours" is the same idea plus a final filter on gap length and a clip to [9:00, 17:00). Representing the working-hours boundary as two extra "busy" intervals — before 9:00 and after 17:00 — is a neat way to avoid special cases at the ends.

Recognising the pattern

Interval problems mention ranges, meetings, bookings, schedules, segments, coverage, or "overlap". Decide three things first: does touching count as overlapping; what to sort by (start for merging and inserting, end for selecting and arrows); and what state the scan keeps (current block, last end, running count, heap of ends, or an ordered set). Then the code is a sort and a loop.

Practice in the DSA list: Merge Intervals, Insert Interval, Non-overlapping Intervals, Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons, Interval List Intersections, Meeting Rooms II, My Calendar I, Car Pooling (al3), The Skyline Problem.
deep:
Which greedy problems sort by end, and why

Activity selection (maximum non-overlapping), minimum arrows, and "minimum points to stab all intervals" are the same problem and all sort by end. The proof is the exchange argument given in the body, and it hinges on one property: among intervals compatible with what you have taken so far, the earliest-ending one is never worse than any other choice, because it constrains the future least. Weighted activity selection (each interval has a value, maximise the total) breaks the greedy — a long, valuable interval can beat several short cheap ones — and needs dynamic programming: sort by end, and for each interval i take max(dp[i − 1], value[i] + dp[p(i)]) where p(i) is the last interval ending before i starts, found by binary search. That is O(n log n) and a common follow-up.

Interval graph colouring equals maximum overlap

"Minimum rooms" is graph colouring on an interval graph (intervals are vertices, overlaps are edges). Colouring general graphs is NP-hard, but interval graphs are special: the minimum number of colours equals the size of the largest clique, which is the maximum number of intervals sharing a point. The sweep computes that clique size, and the heap-based assignment (give each meeting the room that frees up earliest) constructs a colouring with exactly that many colours. It is a nice example of structure turning an intractable problem into an O(n log n) one, and it explains why the greedy room assignment is optimal.

Half-open intervals as a design choice

Many systems standardise on half-open intervals [start, end): Python's range and slicing, C++ iterators, time ranges in calendars and databases. The benefits are concrete: the length is end − start with no +1; consecutive intervals [a, b) and [b, c) tile a range without overlap or gap; and an empty interval is simply start == end. Adopting half-open intervals in interval code removes most off-by-one errors: the overlap test becomes a < d and c < b, and events at the same time sort ends before starts. When a problem gives closed intervals of integers, you can convert to half-open by adding one to every end.

Beyond one dimension: rectangle union and sweep with a segment tree

"Total area covered by a set of axis-aligned rectangles" is the 2D generalisation. Sweep a vertical line across x; events are the left and right edges of rectangles. Between consecutive events, the covered area is (Δx) × (total covered length on the y-axis). Maintaining that covered y-length as y-intervals are added and removed needs a segment tree over compressed y-coordinates that stores, per node, a cover count and the covered length — O(n log n) overall. This is the canonical "sweep line plus a data structure" problem, and recognising it as such (rather than rasterising the plane) is the senior insight.

Counting pairs of overlapping intervals

"How many pairs of intervals overlap?" looks quadratic but is O(n log n). Sort by start and sweep; when an interval starts, every interval currently active overlaps it, so add the active count before incrementing it. With a heap of end times (or two sorted arrays of starts and ends and binary search: the number of intervals that start before my end minus those that end before my start), each interval contributes in O(log n). This "count at the moment of arrival" trick turns many pair-counting problems into a single sweep, and it is the same idea as counting subarrays at each right end in al6.

Interval trees and stabbing queries

If intervals are stored long-term and you must answer "which intervals contain point x?" or "which overlap [a, b]?" many times, sorting once and scanning per query is O(n). An interval tree — a balanced search tree keyed by start, where each node also stores the maximum end in its subtree — answers overlap queries in O(log n + k) for k results, because whole subtrees whose maximum end is before a can be skipped. Databases use related structures (R-trees for spatial data, GiST indexes in PostgreSQL support range types with overlap operators), and genome browsers use them to find features overlapping a region. In interviews, describing the augmentation ("store the max end per subtree to prune") is usually enough.
prod:
In the interview room

Interval questions are judged heavily on boundary handling, so ask the clarifying question out loud: "if one meeting ends at 10 and another starts at 10, is that a conflict?" Then make the code consistent with the answer: ≤ or < in the overlap test, and the order of events at equal times. The other frequent bugs are: forgetting max when extending a merged block (an interval contained in the current block would shrink it); sorting by the wrong key for selection problems; mutating the input list when the caller did not expect it (sort a copy if in doubt); and assuming the input is sorted when it is not. Test with an empty list, a single interval, nested intervals, touching intervals, and identical intervals.

For the greedy ones, expect "why does sorting by end work?". Answer with the exchange argument and the counterexample for sorting by start; it takes thirty seconds and is exactly what the question is probing. For Meeting Rooms II, interviewers often accept either the heap or the event sweep, then ask for the other — knowing both, and that they compute the same maximum clique, is a strong signal.

Interval problems also appear in online assessments with large coordinates (up to 10⁹) where a candidate's instinct is to build an array over the time line. Read the constraints: if coordinates are large but n is moderate, sort events or compress coordinates instead.

A useful meta-habit: before coding, sketch two or three intervals on a number line, including a nested pair and a touching pair, and run your planned rule on the sketch. Interval bugs are visual, and a ten-second drawing catches most of them before they reach the code.

In real systems

Calendar and scheduling software is interval logic end to end: free/busy computation merges every attendee's busy intervals and returns the gaps, and room-booking systems check new reservations against neighbours exactly like My Calendar. Cloud schedulers and batch systems track reserved capacity over time as a sweep of +resources and −resources events. In genomics, tools such as bedtools merge, intersect and subtract millions of genomic intervals (genes, reads, variants) using sorted sweeps — the merge in this lesson is literally bedtools' core operation. Databases support range types and exclusion constraints (PostgreSQL can enforce "no two bookings for the same room overlap" with a GiST index), and time-series and log stores prune data by time ranges, merging overlapping retention and compaction windows. Network stacks track received byte ranges — TCP selective acknowledgements report which ranges have arrived, and the receiver merges ranges as gaps fill. In each case the engineering lesson is the interview lesson: sort first, then sweep, and be explicit about endpoints.
myths: You should always sort intervals by start time.

Sort by start for merging and inserting, because you want to extend the current block as long as the next interval begins inside it. Sort by end for selecting the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals (or the minimum arrows), because the interval that finishes first leaves the most room for the rest. The sort key follows from the greedy argument.
Two intervals overlap if one's start lies inside the other.

Checking only 'does c lie inside [a, b]?' misses the case where [c, d] starts before a and covers it, such as [3, 4] and [1, 10]. The clean test is symmetric: [a, b] and [c, d] overlap exactly when a ≤ d and c ≤ b — each starts before the other ends (use < for half-open intervals).
Meeting Rooms II needs a heap.

A heap of end times works, but so does a sweep: sort all start times and all end times separately and walk them with two pointers, adding a room at each start and freeing one at each end that is not later than the start. The maximum count is the answer, in O(n log n) with plain arrays.
Touching intervals like [1, 2] and [2, 3] always overlap.

It depends on the problem. For closed intervals of numbers they share the point 2; for meetings, one ending at 2 and the next starting at 2 do not conflict. Ask, and encode the answer consistently in the comparison (≤ versus <) and in the order of events at equal times.
Sweep line only works when coordinates are small.

The sweep processes sorted event points, not every coordinate, so it works with coordinates up to 10⁹ or real numbers. Only the difference-array version needs a dense array; with large coordinates you sort the events or compress the coordinates to their ranks first.
lab:
Verify merge and minimum rooms against brute-force definitions on random intervals, including touching ones.

  1. Save as interval_lab.py: 
    import random, heapq

def merge(iv):
    out = []
    for s, e in sorted(iv):
        if out and s <= out[-1][1]: out[-1][1] = max(out[-1][1], e)
        else: out.append([s, e])
    return out

def covered_points(iv):                 # brute force on integer points
    return sorted({x for s, e in iv for x in range(s, e + 1)})

def rooms_sweep(iv):                    # half-open meetings [s, e)
    ev = sorted([(s, 1) for s, e in iv] + [(e, -1) for s, e in iv])
    cur = best = 0
    for _, d in ev: cur += d; best = max(best, cur)
    return best

def rooms_brute(iv):
    return max([sum(s <= t < e for s, e in iv) for t in range(0, 25)], default=0)

for _ in range(3000):
    iv = []
    for _ in range(random.randint(0, 7)):
        s = random.randint(0, 20); iv.append([s, s + random.randint(0, 4)])
    m = merge([x[:] for x in iv])
    assert covered_points(m) == covered_points(iv)
    assert all(m[i][1] < m[i+1][0] for i in range(len(m) - 1))
    meetings = [x for x in iv if x[1] > x[0]]
    assert rooms_sweep(meetings) == rooms_brute(meetings), meetings
print("merge and rooms agree with brute force")
  2. Run it; expect the final message. The merge check confirms two things: the merged blocks cover exactly the same integer points, and consecutive blocks are separated by a gap.
  3. Change the event sort so starts come before ends at the same time (sort by (t, -d)). The room count now disagrees with the brute force whenever one meeting ends exactly when another starts.

What this proves: the boundary convention lives in two places — the ≤ in merge and the event order in the sweep — and random tests with small coordinates hit touching endpoints constantly.
recap: Sorting intervals makes overlaps local: after sorting by start, an interval can only overlap the block immediately before it.
Two intervals [a, b] and [c, d] overlap exactly when a ≤ d and c ≤ b; decide up front whether touching endpoints count.
Merge intervals by sorting on start and extending the last merged interval's end while the next start is not beyond it.
To keep the most non-overlapping intervals, sort by end and greedily take each interval that starts after the last taken end; the number removed is n minus that count.
Two sorted interval lists intersect with two pointers: the overlap is [max of starts, min of ends], and you advance whichever interval ends first.
The maximum number of simultaneous intervals comes from a sweep over +1 start and −1 end events, or from a min-heap of end times.
With large coordinates, sort the event points or compress coordinates to ranks instead of building a dense array.
Each interval problem is a sort followed by a linear scan, so O(n log n) time is typical.

An interval [a, b] that includes both endpoints.
Replacing large or sparse coordinates by their rank in sorted order so they can index a small array.
A point on the sweep line where something changes, such as an interval starting (+1) or ending (−1).
A proof technique for greedy algorithms: show that any optimal solution can be changed into the greedy one without getting worse.
An interval [a, b) that includes a but not b; consecutive half-open intervals touch without overlapping.
A contiguous range of values given by a start and an end.
A graph whose vertices are intervals and whose edges join overlapping intervals; colouring it optimally is easy, unlike general graphs.
A balanced search tree augmented with maximum end values, answering 'which stored intervals overlap this query?' in O(log n + k).
Combining overlapping intervals into one interval spanning them all.
Sharing at least one point (or, for half-open intervals, a non-empty range).
The outline formed by a set of rectangular buildings, described by the points where the maximum height changes.

drill:
Weighted scheduling: when the greedy breaks

"Each job has [start, end, profit]. Choose non-overlapping jobs to maximise total profit (touching allowed). n ≤ 5 × 10⁴." Why does the sort-by-end greedy fail, and what is the O(n log n) solution?

Answer

The greedy maximises the number of jobs, not their profit: with [1, 10, 100], [1, 2, 1], [3, 4, 1], it takes the two short jobs (profit 2) instead of the long one (profit 100). Use dynamic programming over jobs sorted by end. Let ends be the sorted end times and dp[i] the best profit using the first i jobs. For job i (0-based) with start s and profit p, find j = bisect_right(ends, s) — the number of jobs that end at or before s, which are all compatible with it. Then dp[i + 1] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + p): skip job i, or take it plus the best compatible prefix. The answer is dp[n]. Sorting is O(n log n) and each step does one binary search, so O(n log n) total, O(n) memory. This "sort by end + binary search for the last compatible job" is a pattern worth recognising; it reappears in problems like "maximum number of events you can attend with values".
qa: E
Merge all overlapping intervals.

Sort by start. Keep a result list; for each interval, if it starts at or before the last result's end, extend that end to the maximum of both ends; otherwise append it. O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n) for the scan.
E
Can a person attend all meetings?
Sort by start and check that each meeting starts at or after the previous one ends. Any start earlier than the previous end is a conflict. O(n log n).
E
When do two intervals overlap?

[a, b] and [c, d] overlap when a ≤ d and c ≤ b — each starts before the other ends. Use strict < for half-open intervals or when touching endpoints should not count. The intersection, if non-empty, is [max(a, c), min(b, d)].
M
Insert a new interval into a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals.

Three phases in one pass: copy every interval that ends before the new one starts; merge every interval that overlaps the new one into it, taking the minimum start and maximum end; then copy the rest. O(n), no sort needed because the input is already sorted.
M
Minimum number of intervals to remove so the rest do not overlap.

Equivalent to keeping the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals. Sort by end; keep an interval if it starts at or after the end of the last kept one. The answer is n minus the number kept. Sorting by end is optimal because finishing earliest leaves the most room.
Follow-up: Why not sort by start? — A long interval that starts early would be kept and block many short ones; [1, 100], [2, 3], [4, 5] shows it.
M
Minimum arrows to burst balloons given as horizontal intervals.

Sort by end. Shoot an arrow at the first balloon's end; it bursts every balloon starting at or before that point. Move to the first balloon starting after the arrow, shoot at its end, and repeat. This is activity selection: the number of arrows equals the maximum number of pairwise disjoint balloons.
M
Intersections of two sorted lists of disjoint intervals.

Two pointers i and j. The candidate overlap is [max(starts), min(ends)]; if its start is ≤ its end, record it. Then advance the pointer whose interval ends first, because it cannot overlap anything further in the other list. O(m + n).
M
Meeting Rooms II: minimum rooms needed.

Sort starts and ends separately. Walk the starts; for each start, if the earliest unused end is ≤ the start, a room frees up (advance the end pointer), otherwise allocate a new room. The number of rooms allocated is the answer. Or use a min-heap of end times. Both O(n log n).
Follow-up: How would you also return which room each meeting uses? — Use a heap of (end time, room id) and a heap or list of free room ids.
M
Design a calendar that rejects double bookings (My Calendar I).

Keep booked intervals sorted by start. For a new [s, e), find its position with bisect; it conflicts if the previous booking ends after s or the next booking starts before e. Insert if no conflict. O(log n) to find plus O(n) to insert into a Python list, or O(log n) with a balanced tree or SortedList.
M
Find the free time common to all employees, given each one's sorted busy intervals.

Flatten all busy intervals, sort by start, and merge them. The gaps between consecutive merged intervals are the common free times. A heap-based k-way merge avoids the full sort when there are many employees: O(N log k).
H
The skyline problem.

Create events: each building contributes a start (x, height) and an end (x, height). Sweep x in order, keeping a max-heap of active heights (with lazy deletion of ended buildings, or a sorted multiset). After processing all events at an x, if the maximum height differs from the last emitted height, emit (x, max). Order events at equal x carefully: starts before ends, taller starts first, shorter ends first. O(n log n).
H
Given up to 10⁵ intervals with coordinates up to 10⁹, find the point covered by the most intervals.

Sweep over events: (start, +1) and (end, −1), sorted by coordinate, with −1 before +1 at the same coordinate if intervals are half-open (or +1 first if closed). Track the running count and its maximum, remembering the coordinate. O(n log n) and O(n) memory, independent of the coordinate range — no dense array needed.

Follow-up: Same question but online, with intervals added one at a time and queries in between? — Coordinate-compress all endpoints up front if known, and use a segment tree with lazy range add and max query; otherwise a balanced tree keyed by coordinate.

t: Greedy algorithms: choosing locally, proving globally
sum: When taking the best-looking option at each step is provably optimal, how to prove it with exchange and stays-ahead arguments, how to find the right sort key, and the classic greedy problems — jumps, gas stations, partitions, pairing, candy — plus how to spot when greedy fails.
prereq: al1
State a brute force first; it doubles as a checker for a faster idea.
al10
Heaps keep the best available option at hand while options change.
al11
Activity selection: sort by end and take compatible intervals, proved by an exchange argument.
why:
A cashier giving change for 63 cents in US coins does not think hard: take as many quarters as fit (two, 50 cents), then dimes (one, 60), then pennies (three). Six coins, and it is the fewest possible. At each step the cashier takes the biggest coin that fits and never reconsiders. That is a greedy algorithm: make the choice that looks best right now, commit to it, and move on.

Now imagine a country whose coins are 1, 3 and 4 cents, and you need 6 cents. The same strategy takes a 4, then a 1, then another 1 — three coins. But two 3-cent coins would do. The greedy choice (the 4) looked best locally and ruined the global answer. Nothing in the problem statement warned you; the coins just happened to be arranged so that greed fails.

That is the whole story of greedy algorithms in interviews. When they work, they are the simplest and fastest solutions available — often a sort and a single scan. Interval scheduling, jump games, gas stations, partitioning strings, pairing people into boats, assigning tasks, Huffman compression and the shortest-path and spanning-tree algorithms of later lessons are all greedy. But a greedy idea is easy to invent and easy to get wrong, and the examples in a problem statement rarely expose the failure. Interviewers know this, which is why "why is that correct?" is the standard follow-up to any greedy solution.

This lesson teaches both halves: the classic greedy problems with traces, and the two proof techniques — the exchange argument and the stays-ahead argument — that let you justify a greedy in a sentence or two. It also shows how to derive the right sort key instead of guessing, how "greedy with regret" uses a heap to undo bad choices, and how to test a greedy against brute force when you cannot find a proof.
primer:
The mental model: hiking in fog

Imagine hiking up a mountain in thick fog. You can only see a few metres around you, so you take the steepest step upwards each time. On a smooth hill with a single summit, this gets you to the top. On a rugged mountain with several peaks, it may strand you on a small hilltop while the real summit is elsewhere — and since you never walk downhill, you cannot recover. A greedy algorithm is that hiker: it looks only at the immediate choice, takes the best one, and never backtracks. Whether that works depends entirely on the shape of the problem.

The property that makes the "smooth hill" case work has a name: the greedy-choice property. Some locally best choice is always part of some optimal solution. If that holds at every step, and the remaining problem after the choice is a smaller version of the same problem (optimal substructure), the greedy is correct. If it fails even once, the greedy can be wrong.

Two ways to prove a greedy

You do not need formal proofs in interviews, but you do need a convincing two-sentence argument. Almost every greedy proof is one of two kinds.

Exchange argument. Take any optimal solution that differs from the greedy one. Find the first place they differ, and swap the optimal solution's choice there for the greedy choice. Show the result is still feasible and no worse. Repeating the swap turns the optimal solution into the greedy one without losing anything, so the greedy is optimal. (This is how activity selection was proved in al11.)

Stays-ahead argument. Define a measure of progress — "the furthest index reachable", "the number of intervals selected so far", "the time at which the k-th task finishes". Show by induction that after every step the greedy's measure is at least as good as any other algorithm's after the same number of steps. Then at the end it is at least as good, which means optimal.

Where the hiking analogy breaks: real hikers can see ahead a little, and many greedy algorithms quietly use some lookahead or preprocessing — sorting all items first, or computing every letter's last occurrence — before making their irreversible choices. The defining feature of greedy is not ignorance of the future; it is never undoing a choice (except in the "regret" variant, which explicitly allows one kind of undo).

A practical consequence: when you propose a greedy in an interview, propose its proof shape at the same time. "I'll sort by deadline and take the earliest; I think an exchange argument works because swapping a later-deadline job for the earliest one can only make room." Even a sketch of the argument tells the interviewer you know greedy needs justification, and it often reveals a flaw before you have written any code.
body:
The shape of a greedy solution

Most greedy solutions have three parts: an order in which to consider items (often a sort), a rule for accepting or rejecting each item, and a running state that the rule checks. Activity selection is the archetype: order by end time, accept an interval if it starts after the last accepted end, state = last accepted end. When you meet a new optimisation problem, try to fill in those three blanks — and then try to break your rule with a small counterexample before coding.

Reachability: Jump Game I and II

Jump Game: from index i you may jump up to nums[i] steps; can you reach the last index? Track reach, the furthest index you can get to using the indices seen so far. Every index up to reach is reachable (you can always jump shorter), so the only question is whether reach ever falls behind the scan.

def can_jump(nums):
    reach = 0
    for i, step in enumerate(nums):
        if i > reach:
            return False          # stuck: i cannot be reached
        reach = max(reach, i + step)
    return True

On [3, 2, 1, 0, 4]: reach becomes 3, 3, 3, 3, then i = 4 > 3 — false. The stays-ahead measure is reach itself: no strategy can reach further than the maximum over all reachable indices of i + nums[i].

Jump Game II: the minimum number of jumps (the end is guaranteed reachable). A DP over positions is O(n²). The greedy view is breadth-first search by levels: the indices reachable with 0 jumps are [0, 0]; with 1 jump, [1, furthest from level 0]; with 2 jumps, everything up to the furthest point reachable from level 1; and so on. Each level is a contiguous range, so you only need its end.

def jump(nums):
    jumps = level_end = furthest = 0
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1):        # no jump needed from the last index
        furthest = max(furthest, i + nums[i])
        if i == level_end:                 # finished scanning this level
            jumps += 1
            level_end = furthest
    return jumps

Trace [2, 3, 1, 1, 4]: i = 0 → furthest 2, level end reached → jumps 1, level_end 2; i = 1 → furthest 4; i = 2 → furthest 4, level end → jumps 2, level_end 4. Answer 2 (0 → 1 → 4).

A running-total argument: Gas Station

Stations on a circle; station i gives gas[i] and the trip to the next costs cost[i]. Find the starting station that lets you go all the way round, or −1. The brute force tries every start: O(n²). Two observations make it O(n).

First, if the total gas is less than the total cost, no start works; if it is at least the total cost, a start exists (a classic result; the problem also promises that a valid start, when one exists, is unique). Second, if you start at s and your tank first goes negative when leaving station i, then no station between s and i can be a valid start either: each of them was reached from s with a non-negative tank, so starting there with an empty tank is no better, and you would still run dry by i. So skip straight to i + 1.

def can_complete_circuit(gas, cost):
    if sum(gas) < sum(cost):
        return -1
    start = tank = 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
        if tank < 0:              # nobody from start..i works
            start, tank = i + 1, 0
    return start

Extending a part as far as necessary: Partition Labels

"Split a string into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part." Precompute the last index of every letter. Scan, keeping the current part's end as the furthest last occurrence of any letter seen in the part; when the scan reaches that end, the part can be closed — every letter in it has no occurrences later.

def partition_labels(s):
    last = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(s)}
    sizes, start, end = [], 0, 0
    for i, c in enumerate(s):
        end = max(end, last[c])
        if i == end:
            sizes.append(end - start + 1)
            start = i + 1
    return sizes

Closing each part at the earliest legal moment maximises the number of parts: any valid partition must extend a part at least to the last occurrence of every letter it contains, so the greedy's parts are as short as possible (stays ahead on "number of parts closed by position i").

Deriving the sort key: Two City Scheduling

2n people must be split evenly between cities A and B; person i costs a[i] to send to A and b[i] to B. Minimise the total. Start with everyone in B and ask what it costs to move a person to A: a[i] − b[i]. You must move exactly n people, so move the n with the smallest (most negative) differences. In code: sort by a − b, send the first half to A and the rest to B.

The general technique is worth learning: compare two adjacent items and ask when swapping them helps. If person x goes to A and y to B, swapping changes the cost by (a[y] + b[x]) − (a[x] + b[y]) = (a[y] − b[y]) − (a[x] − b[x]). The swap helps exactly when y's difference is smaller than x's, so the optimal assignment sends smaller differences to A. That calculation produced the sort key; it was not a guess.

The same derivation gives "Largest Number" (concatenate numbers to form the largest result): for two numbers a and b, a should come first when the string a + b is larger than b + a. Sorting with that comparator gives the optimal order. In Python: sorted(map(str, nums), key=functools.cmp_to_key(lambda x, y: -1 if x + y > y + x else 1)).

Always serve the smallest first: Hand of Straights

"Can the cards be divided into groups of W consecutive values?" The smallest remaining card cannot be in the middle or end of a group — nothing smaller is left — so it must start a group. Greedily start a group there, remove v, v + 1, …, v + W − 1, and repeat.

from collections import Counter
def is_n_straight_hand(hand, W):
    if len(hand) % W: return False
    count = Counter(hand)
    for v in sorted(count):
        need = count[v]
        if need:
            for x in range(v, v + W):
                if count[x] < need: return False
                count[x] -= need
    return True

Processing all copies of the smallest value at once (subtracting need from each of the next W values) keeps it O(n log n) for the sort plus O(distinct · W).

Two directions, two passes: Candy

Children stand in a line with ratings; each needs at least one candy, and a child with a higher rating than a neighbour must get more than that neighbour. Minimise the total. The constraint has two directions (left neighbour and right neighbour), and a single scan can only respect one. So do two passes: left to right, give each child one more than the left neighbour if rated higher, else 1; right to left, raise each child to one more than the right neighbour if rated higher. Taking the maximum at each child satisfies both directions with the least candy.

def candy(r):
    n = len(r); c = [1] * n
    for i in range(1, n):
        if r[i] > r[i - 1]: c[i] = c[i - 1] + 1
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
        if r[i] > r[i + 1]: c[i] = max(c[i], c[i + 1] + 1)
    return sum(c)

Ratings [1, 0, 2]: the first pass gives [1, 1, 2]; the second raises the first child to 2 → [2, 1, 2], total 5.

Pairing extremes: boats, cookies and arrays

A family of pairing problems is solved by sorting and matching extremes. Boats to save people (al5): the heaviest person pairs with the lightest if they fit, otherwise goes alone — if the lightest cannot share with the heaviest, nobody can. Assign cookies: give the smallest adequate cookie to the least demanding child. Array partition (maximise the sum of the min of each pair): sort and pair neighbours, so each pair's smaller element is as large as possible. Each has a one-line exchange argument: if an optimal pairing matched the extremes differently, swapping partners would not make it worse.

Fractional versus 0/1 knapsack

If items can be split (gold dust, bandwidth), the greedy is optimal: sort by value per unit weight and take as much as possible of the best, then the next. If items are indivisible (a laptop, a camera), the same greedy fails: capacity 10 with items (weight 6, value 6), (5, 5), (5, 5) — by value density all are equal, and greedy may take the 6 first and fit nothing else (value 6), while the two 5s give 10. The 0/1 knapsack needs dynamic programming (al22). This pair is the textbook demonstration that a tiny change in the problem flips greedy from optimal to wrong.

Greedy with regret

Sometimes the right greedy is "take everything tentatively, and when a constraint breaks, undo the worst choice so far". Course Schedule III: courses have a duration and a deadline; take as many as possible. Sort by deadline, add each course, and if the total time exceeds the current deadline, drop the longest course taken so far (a max-heap of durations finds it). Dropping the longest course keeps the count the same as dropping any other but frees the most time for the future. The same pattern solves "minimum number of refuelling stops" (pass stations, remember their fuel in a max-heap, and refuel from the biggest passed station only when you run out) and "IPO" (al10).

When the greedy is wrong: test it

If you cannot find a proof in a minute or two, test. Write a brute force (try all subsets or orders for n ≤ 8) and compare on a few thousand random small inputs. A counterexample appears in seconds when the greedy is wrong, and it is usually small enough to understand why — which often suggests the right approach (dynamic programming, or a different sort key). This is not cheating in an interview; describing it ("I'd validate this greedy against brute force on small cases") is a sign of engineering maturity.

Practice in the DSA list: Jump Game, Jump Game II, Gas Station, Partition Labels, Hand of Straights, Two City Scheduling, Candy, Non-overlapping Intervals and Minimum Arrows (al11), Boats to Save People (al5), IPO and Task Scheduler (al10), Remove K Digits (al8).
deep:
Why greedy works on some structures: matroids

There is a precise theory of when "sort by weight and take whatever keeps the set valid" is optimal. A matroid is a collection of "independent" sets with two properties: subsets of independent sets are independent, and if one independent set is larger than another, some element of the larger can be added to the smaller while keeping it independent (the exchange property). On any matroid, the greedy algorithm finds a maximum-weight independent set. The forests of a graph form a matroid, which is why Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm (sort edges, add if it does not create a cycle) is correct (al20). Sets of linearly independent vectors form a matroid too. Interviews will not ask you to prove matroid properties, but knowing the concept explains why some greedy algorithms are guaranteed and why problems that lack the exchange property (knapsack, coin change in general) are not.

The adjacent-swap method for scheduling

Many single-machine scheduling problems are solved by finding an order, and the order is found by comparing adjacent jobs. To minimise total completion time, put shorter jobs first (shortest processing time): swapping a longer job ahead of a shorter one delays the short one by more than it speeds up the long one. To minimise the maximum lateness, order by deadline (earliest deadline first). To minimise weighted completion time, order by processing time divided by weight (Smith's rule). Each rule comes from the same calculation: write the cost of "a then b" and "b then a", subtract, and read off the comparator. The comparator must be transitive for a sort to be valid; ratios and differences are, but some ad hoc comparators are not, which is a subtle source of wrong answers.

Greedy as an approximation

For NP-hard problems, greedy algorithms often give guaranteed approximations. For set cover — choose the fewest sets whose union covers everything — repeatedly picking the set that covers the most uncovered elements gives a solution within a factor of about ln n of optimal, and no polynomial algorithm can do much better unless P = NP. For scheduling jobs on m identical machines to minimise the finishing time, assigning each job to the least-loaded machine (with jobs sorted longest first) is within 4/3 of optimal. In system design follow-ups, "the exact problem is hard, but greedy gives a provable approximation" is a valuable thing to be able to say.

Huffman coding: a greedy with a heap

To compress text, give frequent symbols short bit codes and rare ones long codes, with no code being a prefix of another so decoding is unambiguous. Huffman's algorithm: put every symbol in a min-heap by frequency; repeatedly pop the two least frequent, merge them into a node whose frequency is their sum, and push it back; when one node remains, it is the root of the code tree. The exchange argument: in some optimal tree the two least frequent symbols are siblings at the deepest level, so merging them first is safe. It is optimal among prefix codes and runs in O(n log n). It remains in daily use inside DEFLATE (gzip, zlib, PNG) alongside LZ77.

Interval-style greedy versus heap-style greedy

Greedy algorithms come in two implementation styles, and recognising which one a problem needs saves time. Sort-and-scan greedies decide everything from a single fixed order: activity selection, partition labels, two-city scheduling, candy. Heap-driven greedies must repeatedly find the best option among a set that changes as the scan proceeds: IPO (affordable projects grow over time), course schedule III (drop the longest taken course), meeting rooms (earliest free room), Huffman (two smallest current frequencies). If the "best" option depends on choices already made, you need a heap or a balanced tree; if it depends only on the input, a sort is enough.

When a greedy is "almost" right

Some problems are greedy only after a transformation. Jump Game II becomes greedy once you see the BFS levels. Gas Station becomes greedy once you prove the skip argument. Task Scheduler has a closed form once you think in frames of size n + 1. Conversely, some problems look greedy and are not: "minimum number of coins" (DP), "longest increasing subsequence" (DP or patience sorting with binary search), "maximum profit with at most k transactions" (DP). A good habit is to state the property your greedy relies on and ask whether the problem guarantees it; if it does not, reach for dynamic programming before coding.
prod:
In the interview room

Greedy problems are where candidates most often give a confident wrong answer. The interviewer's follow-up "why is that optimal?" is not hostile; it is the main thing being tested. Have the argument ready in one of the two shapes: "suppose an optimal solution chose something else first; swapping in my choice keeps it feasible and no worse" (exchange), or "after every step, my reach / count / finishing time is at least as good as any other strategy's" (stays ahead). If you cannot form either, say so and propose validating against brute force, or switch to dynamic programming.

The common implementation bugs are small: off-by-one in Jump Game II (looping to the last index adds an extra jump), forgetting the total-gas check in Gas Station, using the wrong comparator direction in sort keys, and forgetting edge cases like a single element or all-equal ratings. And a classic recognition mistake: applying the coin-change greedy to arbitrary coin systems, or the fractional-knapsack greedy to 0/1 items.

Interviewers also like to change one constraint to see whether the greedy survives: weighted intervals instead of unweighted, indivisible items instead of divisible ones, "at most k transactions" instead of unlimited. When the greedy-choice property breaks, say so and pivot to DP; that pivot is a strong signal.

Finally, greedy solutions are often the shortest code in the round, which can make candidates rush. Slow down for the proof and for edge cases; a five-line correct greedy with a clear argument scores better than a five-line greedy that was simply lucky on the examples.

A practical technique when stuck between greedy and DP in the room: work out the answer by hand for three or four tiny inputs using both the greedy rule and exhaustive reasoning. If they always agree and you can articulate why, commit to the greedy; if you find a disagreement, you have both a counterexample and a strong hint about which extra state the DP needs.

On online assessments, greedy problems often hide behind large constraints (n up to 10⁵ with values up to 10⁹), which rule out DP over values and point to "sort, then one pass". If a DP you are considering has a dimension of size 10⁹, look for the greedy.

In real systems

Greedy algorithms run a surprising amount of infrastructure. Huffman coding sits inside gzip, zlib and PNG via DEFLATE (RFC 1951), and canonical Huffman codes appear in JPEG and many other formats. Network routing relies on Dijkstra's greedy shortest paths (OSPF and IS-IS link-state protocols), and network design uses minimum spanning trees. Load balancers often route each request greedily to the least-loaded or least-connections backend, and "power of two choices" (pick two random backends, send to the less loaded) is a famous greedy with provably good balance. Operating-system schedulers have used shortest-job-first and earliest-deadline-first rules; cluster schedulers place tasks greedily by resource fit. Ad auctions and recommendation re-ranking often use greedy selection with diversity constraints because exact optimisation is too slow at request time. The engineering lesson matches the interview one: greedy is fast and simple, and its correctness (or approximation quality) must be argued, not assumed.
myths: If a greedy works on the examples, it is correct.

Greedy ideas are easy to invent and often wrong on inputs the examples do not cover. Coin change with coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6 is the classic: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins) but 3 + 3 uses two. Either prove the greedy with an exchange or stays-ahead argument, or test it against a brute force on small random inputs.
Greedy and dynamic programming are unrelated.

Both rely on optimal substructure. Greedy additionally has the greedy-choice property: one specific choice can be made without looking at subproblems. When that property fails, the problem usually still yields to dynamic programming over all choices. Many DP problems have a greedy special case, such as unweighted versus weighted interval scheduling.
The sort key in a greedy is a matter of intuition.

It can usually be derived. Compare two adjacent items a and b in a candidate order and ask when swapping them helps; the condition becomes the comparator. For two-city scheduling that gives 'sort by cost difference'; for Largest Number it gives 'a + b > b + a'.
Greedy algorithms are always simple loops.

Many need a data structure to make the greedy choice efficiently: a heap for 'most profitable affordable project', a sorted map for 'smallest remaining card', a monotonic stack for 'remove the larger digit before a smaller one'. The greedy rule is simple; finding the chosen item quickly is where the engineering goes.
Jump Game II needs dynamic programming.

A DP over positions is O(n²). The greedy treats it as breadth-first search by levels: everything reachable with j jumps forms a contiguous range, and the next range ends at the furthest point reachable from it. One pass, O(n).
lab:
Catch a wrong greedy with a brute force, and confirm a right one.

  1. Save as greedy_lab.py: 
    import random
from itertools import product

def coins_greedy(coins, amount):
    n = 0
    for c in sorted(coins, reverse=True):
        n += amount // c; amount %= c
    return n if amount == 0 else None

def coins_dp(coins, amount):
    INF = float("inf"); dp = [0] + [INF] * amount
    for a in range(1, amount + 1):
        dp[a] = min((dp[a - c] + 1 for c in coins if c <= a), default=INF)
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] < INF else None

for coins in ([1, 5, 10, 25], [1, 3, 4], [1, 7, 10]):
    bad = [a for a in range(1, 60) if coins_greedy(coins, a) != coins_dp(coins, a)]
    print(coins, "greedy wrong for amounts:", bad[:6], "..." if len(bad) > 6 else "")

def jump_greedy(nums):
    jumps = end = far = 0
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
        far = max(far, i + nums[i])
        if i == end: jumps += 1; end = far
    return jumps

def jump_bfs(nums):                      # brute force: shortest path
    n, dist = len(nums), {0: 0}; frontier = [0]
    while frontier:
        nxt = []
        for i in frontier:
            for j in range(i + 1, min(n, i + nums[i] + 1)):
                if j not in dist: dist[j] = dist[i] + 1; nxt.append(j)
        frontier = nxt
    return dist.get(n - 1)

for _ in range(3000):
    nums = [random.randint(1, 3) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 10))]
    assert jump_greedy(nums) == jump_bfs(nums), nums
print("Jump Game II greedy matches BFS")
  2. Run it. For US-style coins the greedy is never wrong; for [1, 3, 4] it fails at 6 (and others); for [1, 7, 10] it fails at 14 (greedy 10 + 1×4 = five coins, optimal 7 + 7 = two).
  3. The second part confirms the Jump Game II greedy equals a true shortest-path search on random inputs (values ≥ 1 guarantee the end is reachable).

What this proves: a few lines of brute force settle whether a greedy idea is safe for the inputs you care about, and they produce the small counterexample you need to explain why it is not.
recap: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step and never revisits it; it is correct only when that choice can always be extended to an optimal solution.

Prove a greedy with an exchange argument (any optimal solution can be changed to agree with the greedy choice without getting worse) or a stays-ahead argument (after each step the greedy is at least as good as any other solution).
Derive sort keys by comparing two adjacent items and asking when swapping them improves the result.
Jump Game tracks the furthest reachable index; Jump Game II counts BFS-like levels of reachable ranges.
In Gas Station, if the total gas covers the total cost, the answer is the station just after the last point where the running tank went negative.
Two-city scheduling sorts by cost difference; Partition Labels extends each part to the furthest last occurrence of any letter in it.
Candy needs two passes, one for each direction of the neighbour constraints.
When no proof comes, test the greedy against brute force on small random inputs; a counterexample means you need dynamic programming or search.

A rule that decides which of two items should come first in a sort.

The compression format behind gzip, zlib and PNG, combining LZ77 back-references with Huffman coding.
Solving a problem by combining stored answers to overlapping subproblems; the fallback when greedy fails. Taught in al21–al23.
A proof that swaps part of an optimal solution for the greedy choice and shows the result is still optimal.
Satisfying all of the problem's constraints, whether or not it is optimal.
A knapsack variant where items can be split; greedy by value per weight is optimal, unlike the 0/1 version.
The property that some locally optimal choice is part of a globally optimal solution.
A greedy compression scheme that repeatedly merges the two least frequent symbols, producing an optimal prefix code.
A mathematical structure (independent sets with an exchange property) on which the greedy algorithm is always optimal.
The property that an optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems.
A technique where a greedy takes an option tentatively and later undoes the worst previous choice when a constraint is violated, usually with a heap.
A proof that the greedy solution is at least as good as any other after every step, so it is at least as good at the end.
drill:
Prove it or break it

For each greedy, say whether it is correct; give a proof sketch or a counterexample. (a) To minimise the number of platforms at a train station, sort trains by arrival and assign each to the platform that became free earliest. (b) To maximise the number of tasks finished before their deadlines (each task takes one unit of time), always do the task with the earliest deadline next. (c) To maximise total value in a knapsack of capacity W with indivisible items, take items in decreasing order of value until nothing fits.

Answer

(a) Correct. It is Meeting Rooms II: a new platform is opened only when every existing platform is occupied at this train's arrival, so at that moment the number of overlapping trains equals the number of platforms — no solution can use fewer (stays-ahead on platforms versus maximum overlap so far). (b) Correct, provided expired tasks are skipped. Process tasks in deadline order and schedule a task in the next free time slot only if that slot is still before its deadline; otherwise skip it. Exchange argument: if an optimal schedule does some task with a later deadline in a slot where the greedy put the earliest-deadline task, swapping them keeps both on time (the earlier-deadline task moves earlier or stays, the later one moves to a slot no later than the earlier task's deadline, which is before its own). A naive "earliest deadline next" that does not skip already-expired tasks wastes slots on them and can lose. (c) Wrong. Capacity 10, items (weight 10, value 10), (5, 6), (5, 6): greedy by value takes the 10-weight item for value 10, while the two 5-weight items give 12. Greedy by value density also fails in general (see the fractional versus 0/1 example). 0/1 knapsack needs dynamic programming over capacity (al22).
qa: E
Jump Game: can you reach the last index?

Scan once tracking reach, the furthest index reachable so far. At each index i, if i > reach you are stuck, return false; otherwise reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]). Return true if the scan finishes. O(n) time, O(1) space.
E
Assign cookies to children to maximise satisfied children, where child i needs a cookie of size at least g[i].

Sort both lists. Walk the cookies from smallest; give each to the least greedy unsatisfied child it can satisfy (two pointers). Using the smallest adequate cookie for the least demanding child leaves bigger cookies for harder cases. O(n log n).
E
What is the difference between greedy and dynamic programming?

Greedy commits to one choice per step based on a local rule and never reconsiders; DP considers all choices and combines the best answers to subproblems. Greedy is faster and simpler but only correct when the greedy-choice property holds; DP is correct more generally when subproblems overlap and have optimal substructure.
M
Jump Game II: minimum number of jumps to reach the end.

Treat it as BFS by levels. Keep the end of the current level and the furthest index reachable from it. Scan i from 0 to n − 2, updating furthest = max(furthest, i + nums[i]); when i reaches the current level's end, take a jump: jumps += 1 and the level end becomes furthest. O(n) time, O(1) space.

Follow-up: Why is this optimal? — All indices reachable in j jumps form a prefix range; the greedy computes exactly the boundary of each range, so the first range containing the last index gives the minimum j.
M
Gas Station: find the start index that lets you complete the circuit, or −1.

If total gas < total cost, return −1. Otherwise scan with a running tank; whenever it drops below zero at station i, no station from the current start up to i can be the start, so set start = i + 1 and reset the tank. Return start. O(n).

Follow-up: Why can you skip all stations between the old start and i? — Each of them was reached with a non-negative tank from the old start, so starting there with an empty tank is no better and also fails by i.
M
Partition Labels: split a string into as many parts as possible so each letter appears in at most one part.

Record the last index of each letter. Scan with the current part's end = max(end, last[c]); when the index reaches end, close the part and record its size. Each part is as small as it can be, so the number of parts is maximised. O(n).
M
Two City Scheduling: send n people to A and n to B minimising total cost.

Sort people by costA − costB; send the first n (most relatively cheaper for A) to A and the rest to B. Exchange argument: if a person sent to B has a smaller difference than one sent to A, swapping them reduces cost. O(n log n).
M
Hand of Straights: can the cards be split into groups of W consecutive values?

Count values. Repeatedly take the smallest remaining value v; it must start a group, so decrement v, v+1, …, v+W−1, failing if any is missing. Sorting the distinct values and processing them in order with the counter makes it O(n log n).
M
Give the coin change counterexample for greedy and explain when greedy works.

Coins [1, 3, 4], amount 6: greedy takes 4, 1, 1 (three coins) while 3, 3 needs two. Greedy works for canonical systems such as 1, 5, 10, 25, where taking the largest coin never prevents an optimal solution; for arbitrary systems, use dynamic programming over amounts.
H
Candy: children in a line with ratings; each gets at least one candy and a child with a higher rating than a neighbour gets more. Minimise candies.

Two passes. Left to right: if rating[i] > rating[i − 1], candy[i] = candy[i − 1] + 1, else 1. Right to left: if rating[i] > rating[i + 1], candy[i] = max(candy[i], candy[i + 1] + 1). Sum. Each pass enforces one direction of the constraint minimally; taking the max keeps both. O(n) time.
H
Course Schedule III: courses with durations and deadlines; take as many as possible.

Sort by deadline. Scan, adding each course's duration to the running time and pushing it into a max-heap. If the running time exceeds the current deadline, pop the longest course taken so far and subtract its duration. The heap size is the answer. This 'greedy with regret' is optimal because dropping the longest course frees the most time while losing only one course. O(n log n).
H
Largest Number: arrange non-negative integers to form the largest concatenation.

Sort with the comparator: a before b if str(a) + str(b) > str(b) + str(a). This comparator is derived from the two-item swap and is transitive, so a sort produces the optimal order. Join, and return '0' if the result starts with '0'. O(n log n · L) for numbers of length L.
Follow-up: Why not just sort strings descending? — '9' versus '91' works, but '3' and '30' fail: descending gives '303' while '330' is larger.
