t: Recursion and backtracking: subsets, permutations, combinations and constraint search
sum: How to think recursively, the choose–explore–unchoose template for exhaustive search, and the classic families — subsets, combinations, permutations, partitions, grid word search, N-Queens and Sudoku — with duplicate handling, pruning and complexity.
prereq: al2
Exponential complexity: 2ⁿ subsets and n! orderings; n ≤ 20 hints at exponential search; recursion uses one stack frame per level.
al8
Every recursive function runs on the call stack and can be rewritten with an explicit stack.
why:
"Generate every valid combination of n pairs of parentheses." "List all the ways to choose numbers from this list that add up to 7." "Solve this Sudoku." "Can this word be traced through adjacent letters on this grid?" These problems ask you to search through a huge space of possibilities — all subsets, all orderings, all placements — for the ones that satisfy some rules. There is no clever formula; the answer really does require trying possibilities. The question is how to try them systematically, so you never miss one, never repeat one, and abandon hopeless ones as early as possible.

That systematic search is called backtracking. You build a candidate solution one choice at a time; after each choice, you explore everything that can follow from it; when you have finished (or the choice turns out to be a dead end), you undo it and try the next option. It is how you would solve a maze with a piece of chalk: walk until you hit a dead end, back up to the last junction, take a different turn.

Backtracking is built on recursion, which many people find slippery at first, so this lesson starts there: how to write a recursive function you can trust. Then it introduces the choose–explore–unchoose template and applies it to each classic family — subsets, combinations, permutations, partitions, grid search, N-Queens and Sudoku — including the two techniques interviewers probe most: handling duplicate inputs without producing duplicate outputs, and pruning branches that cannot succeed.

These problems are recognisable from their constraints. If n is at most about 15 or 20, or the problem says "return all", the setter is telling you an exponential search is expected. Your job is to write it cleanly, explain its complexity, and prune it well.
primer:
Thinking recursively: trust the smaller call

A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. It has two parts: a base case, which is small enough to answer directly, and a recursive case, which reduces the problem and combines the answer. The mental trick that makes recursion easy is to trust the recursive call: assume it correctly solves the smaller problem, and only ask "given that, how do I solve this one?". Do not try to trace every level in your head.

For example, "how many subsets does a list of n elements have?" Base case: the empty list has one subset (the empty one). Recursive case: take the first element; every subset of the rest either gets it or not, so the count doubles: subsets(n) = 2 × subsets(n − 1). You never pictured all eight subsets of three elements; you trusted the smaller answer.

The mental model for backtracking: a maze with chalk

Searching all possibilities is like exploring a maze to find every exit. At each junction you have several corridors. You pick one, mark it with chalk, and keep going. If you reach an exit, you write it down. If you reach a dead end — or a place where the rules say you cannot possibly reach an exit — you walk back to the last junction, rub out the chalk, and try the next corridor. When every corridor at a junction has been tried, you back up further. You will visit every reachable place exactly once along each path, and the chalk marks mean you never walk in circles.

The maze is the decision tree: the root is "no choices made yet", each edge is one choice, and each leaf is a complete candidate. Backtracking walks this tree depth-first.

The template: choose, explore, unchoose

Almost every backtracking solution has the same skeleton:

def backtrack(state):
    if is_solution(state):
        record(copy of state)
        return                       # or continue, if solutions can extend
    for choice in choices(state):
        if not valid(state, choice):
            continue                 # prune
        apply(choice, state)         # choose
        backtrack(state)             # explore
        undo(choice, state)          # unchoose

Filling in the blanks — what the state is, what the choices are at each step, what makes a choice invalid, and when a state is a solution — is the whole design. "Unchoose" is what makes it backtracking: the state is shared and mutated in place, so every change must be reversed before trying the next option, leaving the state exactly as it was.

Where the maze analogy breaks: in a real maze, two different routes can lead to the same room, and a good explorer would notice. Plain backtracking does not — it may explore the same sub-situation many times via different paths. When that happens and the answer for a sub-situation does not depend on how you got there, memoisation turns the search into dynamic programming (covered in the deep layer and in al21).
body:
Subsets: two ways to see the same tree

Include/exclude. For each element in turn, branch twice: take it or skip it. Depth n, two branches per level, 2ⁿ leaves, each leaf a subset.

def subsets(nums):
    res, path = [], []
    def go(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            res.append(path[:]); return
        path.append(nums[i]); go(i + 1); path.pop()   # take nums[i]
        go(i + 1)                                      # skip nums[i]
    go(0)
    return res

Start-index loop. The figure's version: every node is a subset; from a node, extend with any element after the last one chosen.

def subsets(nums):
    res, path = [], []
    def go(start):
        res.append(path[:])                 # every node is an answer
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            path.append(nums[i])
            go(i + 1)
            path.pop()
    go(0)
    return res

Both produce 2ⁿ subsets. Copying each costs up to n, so the total is O(n·2ⁿ) time; the recursion depth is n. The start-index form generalises better, because combinations, combination sums and partitions all use it.

Notice path[:]. path is one list shared by the whole search; appending path itself would store a reference to that list, and by the end of the search every stored "subset" would be the same, empty list. This is the single most common backtracking bug.

Combinations and combination sums

Combinations (choose k of n) are the start-index subset search, recording only when the path has length k — and pruning when there are not enough elements left to reach k (if len(path) + (n − i) < k: break).

Combination Sum: candidates may be reused any number of times; find all combinations summing to a target. The state is the path and the remaining target. Two details make it work: recurse with i (not i + 1) so the same candidate can be chosen again, and sort the candidates so that once one is too large, all later ones are too, and the loop can stop.

def combination_sum(cands, target):
    cands.sort(); res, path = [], []
    def go(start, remain):
        if remain == 0:
            res.append(path[:]); return
        for i in range(start, len(cands)):
            if cands[i] > remain: break          # sorted: prune the rest
            path.append(cands[i])
            go(i, remain - cands[i])            # i, not i+1: reuse allowed
            path.pop()
    go(0, target)
    return res

Trace candidates [2, 3, 6, 7], target 7: from [], take 2 → remain 5 → take 2 → 3 → take 2 → 1 → 2 > 1, break; back, take 3 → 0, record [2, 2, 3]; … take 7 from [] → record [7]. Result [[2, 2, 3], [7]]. The start index is what prevents [2, 3, 2] and [3, 2, 2] from appearing as separate answers: within one path, indices never decrease.

Handling duplicates: skip equal values at the same depth

If the input contains duplicates — Subsets II with [1, 2, 2], or Combination Sum II where each candidate is used once — the plain search produces duplicate outputs: choosing the first 2 or the second 2 at the same position leads to identical subtrees. The fix: sort, then in the loop skip an element equal to the previous one at the same depth.

for i in range(start, len(nums)):
    if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
        continue          # same value already tried as this position's choice
    ...

The condition i > start is the key. At a given depth, the first copy of a value is tried; later copies would only repeat it. But deeper in the tree, after the first 2 has been chosen, the loop starts at the next index, where the second 2 is the first element — so it is allowed, and [2, 2] is produced exactly once. For [1, 2, 2], the subsets are [], [1], [1, 2], [1, 2, 2], [2], [2, 2].

Permutations: track what is used

Permutations use every element once in every order, so there is no start index; instead, any unused element may come next. Keep a used array.

def permute(nums):
    res, path, used = [], [], [False] * len(nums)
    def go():
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            res.append(path[:]); return
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            if used[i]: continue
            used[i] = True; path.append(nums[i])
            go()
            path.pop(); used[i] = False
    go()
    return res

n choices at depth 0, n − 1 at depth 1, …, so n! leaves and O(n·n!) work. For duplicates (Permutations II), sort and add: skip i if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i − 1] and not used[i − 1]. That rule means a second copy of a value can only be placed after the first copy has been placed, which forces equal values into a fixed relative order and removes the duplicates.

Pruning with constraints: Generate Parentheses

"All valid strings of n pairs of parentheses." A naive search generates all 2^(2n) strings of brackets and filters the valid ones. Better: never build an invalid prefix. A prefix stays valid if you add "(" while fewer than n have been used, and ")" while fewer closes than opens have been used.

def generate_parenthesis(n):
    res, path = [], []
    def go(open_, close):
        if len(path) == 2 * n:
            res.append("".join(path)); return
        if open_ < n:
            path.append("("); go(open_ + 1, close); path.pop()
        if close < open_:
            path.append(")"); go(open_, close + 1); path.pop()
    go(0, 0)
    return res

For n = 3 this produces exactly the 5 valid strings and visits only valid prefixes. The count is the n-th Catalan number, about 4ⁿ / n^1.5 — the search does work proportional to the output, which is the best possible. The general lesson: check constraints as early as possible, on partial solutions, not at the leaves.

Backtracking on a grid: Word Search

"Does the word exist in the grid as a path of adjacent cells, each used at most once?" Start a depth-first search from every cell; at depth k, the current cell must equal word[k]. The state includes which cells are on the current path, and that state must be restored when backing up.

def exist(board, word):
    R, C = len(board), len(board[0])
    def dfs(r, c, k):
        if k == len(word): return True
        if not (0 <= r < R and 0 <= c < C) or board[r][c] != word[k]:
            return False
        saved, board[r][c] = board[r][c], "#"          # choose: mark visited
        found = any(dfs(r + dr, c + dc, k + 1)
                    for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)))
        board[r][c] = saved                            # unchoose: restore
        return found
    return any(dfs(r, c, 0) for r in range(R) for c in range(C))

Overwriting the cell with "#" is a cheap visited marker that needs no extra set, and restoring it is the "unchoose". Forgetting the restore makes later searches from other starting cells see a corrupted board — a very common bug. Worst case O(R·C·4·3^(L−1)) for a word of length L: from each start, four first moves and at most three onward (you cannot go back). Simple pruning helps a lot in practice: if the board does not contain enough of each letter in the word, return false immediately; and searching from the end of the word when its last letter is rarer than its first shrinks the tree.

Partitioning: Palindrome Partitioning

"Return all ways to split a string into palindromes." The choices at each step are "where does the next piece end?". From start index s, for each end e ≥ s with s[s..e] a palindrome, take that piece and recurse from e + 1. Precomputing is_pal[i][j] (true if s[i..j] is a palindrome) with a small DP in O(n²) makes every check O(1). The output can have up to 2^(n−1) partitions (a string of identical letters), so the search is exponential by necessity.

Constraint search: N-Queens

Place n queens on an n×n board so none attack each other. Place one per row (two in a row would attack), so the choice at depth r is a column. A column conflicts if it is already used, or if a queen sits on the same diagonal. All cells on one diagonal share r − c; all cells on one anti-diagonal share r + c. Three sets give O(1) conflict checks:

def solve_n_queens(n):
    res, cols, diag, anti, place = [], set(), set(), set(), []
    def go(r):
        if r == n:
            res.append(["." * c + "Q" + "." * (n - c - 1) for c in place]); return
        for c in range(n):
            if c in cols or r - c in diag or r + c in anti: continue
            cols.add(c); diag.add(r - c); anti.add(r + c); place.append(c)
            go(r + 1)
            cols.remove(c); diag.remove(r - c); anti.remove(r + c); place.pop()
    go(0)
    return res

For n = 8 there are 92 solutions, and the search explores roughly 2,000 partial placements rather than 8⁸ ≈ 16.7 million, because conflicts are caught as soon as each queen is placed.

Sudoku: choose the most constrained cell

A Sudoku solver is backtracking over empty cells with digits as choices. Keep sets of used digits for each row, column and box (box index = (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3). The single most effective improvement is the MRV heuristic (minimum remaining values): at each step, fill the empty cell with the fewest legal digits. A cell with one option is forced (no branching), and a cell with zero options means the current branch is dead, which is discovered immediately rather than many levels later. With MRV and O(1) legality checks, typical puzzles solve in milliseconds; without it, hard puzzles can take much longer.

Complexity: count the tree

The cost of a backtracking search is (number of nodes in the explored tree) × (work per node). Useful reference counts: subsets 2ⁿ, permutations n!, combinations C(n, k), balanced parentheses the Catalan number, phone letters up to 4ⁿ. Add the cost of copying each solution (O(n)) and state the recursion depth (usually n, the solution length). For constraint searches like N-Queens and Sudoku there is no clean formula; say that the worst case is exponential and that pruning makes practical cases fast.

Returning one solution versus all solutions

Many problems only need to know whether a solution exists, or to return any one (Sudoku, Word Search). Then the recursive function returns a boolean, and as soon as a recursive call returns true, every level returns true immediately without trying further options — the search stops at the first success. Problems that ask for all solutions or a count must keep going after a success. Mixing the two — returning early from an "all solutions" search, or continuing after success in an existence check — is a frequent source of wrong or slow code, so decide which kind you are writing before you start.

Recognising the pattern

Backtracking fits when the problem says "all" (all subsets, permutations, combinations, partitions, paths, boards), when n is small (≤ 15–20), or when it asks for any solution to a puzzle with constraints. Before coding, write down the state, the choices, the pruning rule and the solution test, and decide how duplicates are handled.

Practice in the DSA list: Subsets, Subsets II, Combination Sum, Combination Sum II, Permutations, Letter Combinations of a Phone Number, Generate Parentheses, Word Search, Palindrome Partitioning, N-Queens, Sudoku Solver, Word Search II (al15).
deep:
Pruning: feasibility, bounds and ordering

Three kinds of pruning make backtracking practical. Feasibility pruning cuts a branch when the partial solution already violates a constraint (a queen under attack, a remaining sum below zero, more closing than opening brackets). Bound pruning cuts a branch when even the best possible completion cannot beat the best solution found so far — the basis of branch and bound for optimisation problems such as "the fewest coins" or "the shortest tour": if the current cost plus an optimistic estimate of the remainder already exceeds the best found, stop. Ordering does not cut branches by itself but changes which are explored first: trying the most constrained variable first (MRV) finds dead ends early, and trying the most promising value first finds good solutions early, which tightens bounds. Each pruning rule needs a one-sentence justification that it only removes hopeless branches.

From backtracking to dynamic programming

Consider Word Break ("can the string be split into dictionary words?"). Backtracking tries a first word, recurses on the rest, and backtracks on failure. On a string like "aaaa…ab" with dictionary {"a", "aa", "aaa"}, the same suffix is reached by many different splits of the prefix, and each time it is re-explored: exponential time. But the answer for a suffix does not depend on how the prefix was split. Caching the result per start index (functools.cache) collapses the search to n distinct subproblems with O(n) work each: O(n²). That transformation — notice repeated subproblems whose answers are path-independent, then memoise — is exactly how dynamic programming arises from recursion (al21). It does not apply when the state includes the whole path (Word Search's visited cells) or when you must output every solution.

Bitmasks as state

For small n, a set of chosen items can be a single integer whose bits mark membership. Subsets of n elements are just the integers 0 to 2ⁿ − 1, so they can be generated without recursion: [[nums[i] for i in range(n) if mask >> i & 1] for mask in range(1 << n)]. In permutation-like searches, a bitmask "used" set is hashable and cheap, which makes memoisation possible: "shortest path visiting all nodes" or "can we partition into k equal-sum subsets" memoise on (mask, …) and become bitmask DP with 2ⁿ·n states (al23, al24). N-Queens solvers use three bitmasks for columns and diagonals and find free positions with bit tricks, which is the fastest known simple implementation.

Meet in the middle

When n is around 40, 2⁴⁰ ≈ 10¹² is too many, but 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶ is fine. Split the items into two halves, enumerate all subset sums of each half by backtracking, sort one list, and for each sum in the other list binary search for the complement. This solves subset-sum-like problems for n ≈ 40 in O(2^(n/2) · n). It is a useful card to play when the constraint is slightly too large for plain backtracking.

Recursion depth and iterative backtracking

Backtracking depth is the solution length — at most n, often small — so the call stack is rarely a problem; Python's default limit of 1,000 is plenty for subset and permutation problems. Grid searches are the exception: a DFS that can wander through a large grid may recurse once per cell, and a 300×300 grid has 90,000 cells. For those, use an explicit stack (al8, al16). Also be aware that the cost of copying a path at every node, rather than only at solutions, can dominate; copy only when recording.

Generators and lazy search

In Python, a backtracking function can yield each solution instead of appending it to a list, and recursive calls use yield from. The caller then consumes solutions one at a time and can stop early (next(gen) for "any one solution"), and memory stays proportional to the recursion depth rather than the number of solutions. This is how itertools.permutations and combinations behave, and it is the right shape for searches whose full output would not fit in memory.

Exact cover and Dancing Links

N-Queens, Sudoku and many tiling puzzles are instances of exact cover: choose rows of a 0/1 matrix so every column is covered exactly once. Knuth's Algorithm X solves exact cover by backtracking, always branching on the column with the fewest options (MRV again), and his "Dancing Links" implementation stores the matrix as circular doubly linked lists so that removing and restoring rows and columns — the choose and unchoose steps — are O(1) pointer updates. It is a beautiful example of designing a data structure around the undo operation of backtracking.
prod:
In the interview room

Backtracking code is graded on three things: correctness of the state management, duplicate handling, and the complexity explanation. The frequent bugs: appending path instead of a copy; forgetting to undo a change (popping the path but not unmarking used, or not restoring a grid cell); recursing with i + 1 when reuse is allowed (or i when it is not); skipping duplicates without sorting first, or with i > 0 instead of i > start; and mutable default arguments (def go(path=[])) that leak between calls. Test with an empty input, a single element, and an input with duplicates.

Explain complexity by counting the tree: "there are 2ⁿ subsets, each copied in O(n), so O(n·2ⁿ) time, O(n) extra space for the recursion besides the output". For pruned searches, say the worst case and why pruning helps. Interviewers often ask how to speed up a slow backtracking solution; the answers are better pruning, better ordering (MRV), memoisation if subproblems repeat, or a different algorithm if the problem has more structure than the search exploits.

Be ready to write the same search iteratively or as a generator. Some interviewers ask for a generator that yields solutions lazily (yield path[:] inside the recursion, and yield from go(...) for recursive calls), which is how you would expose a search over a huge space without materialising everything in memory.

One more practical point: when an online assessment problem has n ≤ 20 and the obvious approach is exponential, write the backtracking cleanly first and only then optimise. A correct exponential solution that passes the given limits is the intended answer far more often than candidates expect.

When the search is slow in a live round and you have a few minutes, the highest-value improvements are almost always the same three: sort the choices so that failures happen early (largest numbers first, most constrained cell first), add a cheap feasibility check on partial solutions, and break symmetry (do not try equivalent choices twice, such as placing an item into two empty buckets). Say which one you are adding and why; interviewers value the reasoning as much as the speed-up.

In real systems

Backtracking search is the engine inside many practical tools. SAT solvers — which check whether a Boolean formula can be satisfied, and are used for hardware verification, package dependency resolution and planning — descend from the DPLL backtracking algorithm, enhanced with constraint propagation and clause learning. Package managers like pip's resolver and Debian's apt explore candidate versions and backtrack on conflicts. Constraint solvers for timetabling, staff rostering and logistics use backtracking with heuristics like MRV. Regular-expression engines in Python, Java and JavaScript use backtracking to match patterns, which is why some patterns take exponential time on adversarial inputs (catastrophic backtracking, the cause of real outages); engines like RE2 avoid backtracking entirely to guarantee linear time. Prolog's execution model is backtracking search. Even type inference and parsing with ambiguous grammars rely on it. The interview lessons — explicit state, careful undo, early pruning, smart ordering — are exactly the concerns of those systems.
myths: Backtracking is just brute force, so it is never the intended solution.

When the problem asks for all solutions (all subsets, all permutations, all valid boards), the output itself is exponential and backtracking is optimal up to the output size. When it asks for one solution under constraints (Sudoku, N-Queens), backtracking with good pruning is the standard approach. The constraints, such as n ≤ 15, usually say so.
You can append the current path to the results directly.
The path list is shared and mutated throughout the search, so appending it stores a reference that will later be emptied. Append a copy — path[:] or list(path) — at the moment you record a solution.
Sorting is optional when handling duplicates.

The standard 'skip a value equal to the previous one at the same depth' rule only works if equal values are adjacent, which requires sorting first. Without sorting you need a set of used values per recursion level.
Recursion is always slower than iteration.

A recursive function and its iterative equivalent do the same work; recursion adds function-call overhead and stack frames. For backtracking, recursion is the clearest way to express the search, and its depth is the size of a solution (at most n), so stack space is rarely a problem.
Pruning only changes speed, never correctness.

A pruning rule that is too aggressive cuts branches that contain valid solutions and silently produces wrong answers. Every pruning condition must be justified: it may cut only branches that provably cannot lead to a solution (or to a better one).
lab:
Check your backtracking generators against itertools and count how much pruning saves.

  1. Save as bt_lab.py: 
    import itertools, random

def subsets_ii(nums):
    nums = sorted(nums); res, path = [], []
    def go(start):
        res.append(tuple(path))
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]: continue
            path.append(nums[i]); go(i + 1); path.pop()
    go(0); return sorted(res)

def perms_ii(nums):
    nums = sorted(nums); res, path, used = [], [], [False] * len(nums)
    def go():
        if len(path) == len(nums): res.append(tuple(path)); return
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            if used[i] or (i and nums[i] == nums[i-1] and not used[i-1]): continue
            used[i] = True; path.append(nums[i]); go(); path.pop(); used[i] = False
    go(); return sorted(res)

for _ in range(500):
    a = [random.randint(1, 3) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 6))]
    want_sub = sorted({tuple(sorted(c)) for r in range(len(a) + 1)
                       for c in itertools.combinations(a, r)})
    assert subsets_ii(a) == want_sub, a
    assert perms_ii(a) == sorted(set(itertools.permutations(a))), a
print("subsets II and permutations II match itertools")

nodes = 0
def queens(n, r=0, cols=set(), d=set(), ad=set()):
    global nodes; nodes += 1
    if r == n: return 1
    return sum(queens(n, r + 1, cols | {c}, d | {r - c}, ad | {r + c})
               for c in range(n) if c not in cols and r - c not in d and r + c not in ad)
print("8-queens solutions:", queens(8), "nodes explored:", nodes, "vs 8^8 =", 8**8)
  2. Run it. The first line confirms both duplicate-handling rules produce exactly the distinct subsets and permutations.
  3. The second line prints 92 solutions and the number of partial placements explored — a couple of thousand, compared with 16,777,216 naive placements. (This version builds new sets instead of undoing, trading speed for simplicity; mutable default sets are safe here only because they are never mutated.)

What this proves: the duplicate rules are exact, and constraint checks on partial solutions shrink the search by orders of magnitude.
recap: A recursive function needs a base case and a recursive case that moves towards it; trust that the recursive call solves the smaller problem.
Backtracking builds a solution one choice at a time: choose, explore recursively, then unchoose to restore the state before trying the next option.
Subsets use include/exclude decisions or a loop from a start index; there are 2ⁿ subsets, so the search costs O(n·2ⁿ) including copying.
Combinations and combination sums pass a start index to avoid reordering; reuse of an element means recursing with the same index rather than the next.
Permutations track which elements are used; there are n! permutations, so the cost is O(n·n!).
With duplicate inputs, sort first and skip an element equal to its predecessor at the same depth (or when the predecessor is unused, for permutations).
Prune early with constraints: remaining sum below zero, too many open brackets, a queen attacking along a column or diagonal.
Record a copy of the path at each solution, and undo every state change on the way back up.
glossary: Exploring choices depth-first and undoing the last choice when it cannot lead to a solution, to try the next option.
The input for which a recursive function returns directly without recursing.
One choice at a node of the decision tree, leading to a subtree of further choices.
The sequence 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, … counting balanced bracket strings, binary tree shapes and many other structures; the n-th is about 4ⁿ / n^1.5.
The backtracking template: make a choice, recurse, then reverse the choice.
Using a choice to immediately eliminate options elsewhere, such as removing a digit from a Sudoku row's candidates.
The tree of all sequences of choices; backtracking walks it depth-first.
Exploring a graph or tree by following one path as deep as possible before backing up; backtracking is DFS over the decision tree.
Following one path all the way down before trying alternatives.
Solving overlapping subproblems once and reusing the answers; memoised backtracking becomes DP when subproblem answers are path-independent.
Minimum remaining values: in constraint search, fill the variable with the fewest legal options first, which shrinks the tree.
Skipping a branch of the decision tree because it provably cannot lead to a valid or better solution.
A function solving a problem by calling itself on smaller instances.
A program that decides whether a Boolean formula can be made true; modern solvers extend the DPLL backtracking algorithm with clause learning.
The information carried through the search (current path, used flags, remaining target) that choices modify and unchoose restores.
drill:
Design the search

"Given an array of up to 16 positive integers and k, can the array be partitioned into k subsets with equal sums?" Design a backtracking solution, its pruning, and say what you would do if it were too slow.

Answer

First checks: if sum % k ≠ 0, return false; target = sum / k; if the largest element exceeds target, return false. Sort the numbers in decreasing order — placing big numbers first fails fast. State: an array of k bucket sums. For each number in order, try putting it into each bucket whose sum plus the number is ≤ target; recurse to the next number; undo. Success when every number is placed (all buckets must then equal target). Pruning: (1) capacity — skip a bucket if it would overflow; (2) symmetry — if two buckets currently have the same sum, trying the number in the second is pointless, so skip a bucket whose sum equals an earlier bucket's sum (in particular, only try one empty bucket); (3) decreasing order, as above. These make typical inputs fast. If still too slow, switch to bitmask DP over used elements: dp[mask] = the fill level of the current bucket after using the elements in mask (or −1 if unreachable); for each mask and unused element i with dp[mask] + nums[i] ≤ target, set dp[mask | 1 << i] = (dp[mask] + nums[i]) % target. The answer is dp[full] == 0. That is O(2ⁿ · n) ≈ 10⁶ operations for n = 16 — guaranteed, unlike the search.
qa: E
Generate all subsets of a list of distinct numbers.

Backtrack with a start index: record the current path, then for each i from start to n − 1, append nums[i], recurse with start i + 1, and pop. Every node of the recursion is a subset, giving 2ⁿ subsets in O(n·2ⁿ) time including copies. An alternative iterates over bitmasks 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.
E
Generate all permutations of distinct numbers.

Keep a used array. At each depth, try every unused element: mark it used, append, recurse, then pop and unmark. Record the path when its length is n. There are n! permutations, so O(n·n!) including copies; the recursion depth is n.
E
Letter combinations of a phone number.

Depth equals the digit index; at each depth branch over the letters for that digit, append, recurse, pop. Record when the depth equals the number of digits. The output size is up to 4ⁿ, and the work is O(n·4ⁿ). Return an empty list for empty input.
M
Combination Sum: find all combinations of candidates (reusable) summing to target.

Sort candidates and backtrack with a start index and the remaining target. For each i from start, if candidates[i] exceeds the remaining target, break (sorted, so all later ones do too); otherwise append it and recurse with the same i (reuse allowed) and remaining minus it, then pop. Record when remaining hits zero.
Follow-up: Each candidate may be used once and the input has duplicates (Combination Sum II)? — Recurse with i + 1 and skip candidates[i] when i > start and it equals candidates[i − 1].
M
Subsets II: all subsets of a list with duplicates, without duplicate subsets.

Sort. In the loop over i from start, skip i when i > start and nums[i] == nums[i − 1]: choosing the second copy at the same depth would generate the same subsets as choosing the first. Deeper levels may still pick the second copy after the first, so multisets like [2, 2] are produced once.
M
Generate all valid strings of n pairs of parentheses.

Backtrack with counts of open and close used. Add '(' if open < n; add ')' if close < open. Record when the length is 2n. The pruning means only valid prefixes are ever built, so the work is proportional to the output, the n-th Catalan number of strings times their length.
M
Word Search: does a word exist in a grid via adjacent cells, each used once?

From every cell matching the first letter, DFS: if the index reaches the word's length, succeed; if out of bounds or the letter does not match, fail; otherwise mark the cell visited (for example overwrite it with '#'), recurse into the four neighbours with the next index, and restore the cell. O(R·C·4·3^(L−1)) in the worst case for a word of length L.
Follow-up: Many words at once? — Build a trie of the words and backtrack once over the grid following trie nodes (Word Search II, al15).
M
Palindrome Partitioning: all ways to split a string into palindromes.

Backtrack with a start index: for each end from start to n − 1, if s[start..end] is a palindrome, append it, recurse from end + 1, and pop. Record when start reaches n. Precompute a table isPal[i][j] with DP in O(n²) so each check is O(1); the output can be up to 2^(n−1) partitions.
M
Permutations II: all unique permutations of a list with duplicates.

Sort and use a used array. When choosing nums[i] at some depth, skip it if it is used, or if i > 0, nums[i] == nums[i − 1] and nums[i − 1] is not used. That rule forces equal values to be placed in their original relative order, so each distinct permutation is produced exactly once.
H
N-Queens: place n queens so none attack each other; return all boards.

Place one queen per row. Keep three sets: occupied columns, occupied diagonals (r − c) and occupied anti-diagonals (r + c). For each column in the current row, if it conflicts with none, add to the sets, recurse to the next row, then remove. Record the board when all rows are filled. Checking conflicts is O(1), so the cost is proportional to the explored tree, far smaller than n^n.
H
Write a Sudoku solver.

Track for each row, column and 3×3 box the set of digits used. Choose an empty cell — preferably the one with the fewest legal digits (MRV) — and try each legal digit: place it, update the three sets, recurse, and undo on failure. Return true as soon as the board is full. MRV and constant-time legality checks make typical puzzles solve in milliseconds.
Follow-up: How to make it faster still? — Constraint propagation (fill cells with a single candidate immediately) or an exact-cover formulation with Knuth's Dancing Links.
H
When does a backtracking problem become dynamic programming?

When the same subproblem is reached by different paths and its answer does not depend on the path. Word Break with backtracking re-explores the same suffix many times; memoising on the start index turns it into O(n²) DP. But generating all solutions cannot be memoised away, because the output itself is large, and problems whose state includes the whole path (used cells in a grid) have too many states to memoise.

t: Binary trees and BSTs: traversals, top-down and bottom-up recursion
sum: Traverse trees depth-first and level by level, choose between passing information down and returning it up, solve diameter, balance and maximum path sum, use the BST ordering for search, validation and k-th smallest, and handle LCA, construction and serialisation.
prereq: al13
Recursion: base case, recursive case, and trusting the recursive call; backtracking undoes state on the way back.
al8
A stack can replace recursion; Python's recursion limit is 1,000 frames.
why:
Your file system is a tree: folders contain folders and files. So is a web page (the HTML document object model), a company's reporting structure, the parsed form of every program a compiler reads, and the index that lets a database find one row among a billion. When an interviewer asks a tree question, they are testing whether you can reason about data that branches — and whether you are comfortable with the recursion that branching data invites.

Tree problems make up a large share of coding interviews, and they have a reputation for being either trivially short or baffling. "Maximum depth" is three lines. "Maximum path sum" is also about ten lines, but most candidates cannot find those ten lines under pressure. The difference is not cleverness; it is knowing a small number of reusable shapes. Almost every binary tree solution is one of: a traversal in a particular order; a recursion that passes information down to children; a recursion that returns information up to parents; or a recursion that returns one thing up while updating a global answer on the side. Binary search trees add one more idea — an ordering that lets you discard half the tree at each step.

This lesson builds those shapes in order: the vocabulary and traversal orders (depth-first and level by level, recursive and iterative); top-down versus bottom-up recursion; the "return one thing, track another" pattern behind diameter and maximum path sum; the BST property and the classic BST bug; lowest common ancestor; building a tree from traversals; and serialisation. Each is worked through with a trace on a small tree.
primer:
The mental model: a family tree, and asking your children

A binary tree is a family tree in which each person has at most two children, called left and right. The person at the top is the root; people with no children are leaves. A person's subtree is that person plus all their descendants. Two measures matter constantly: the depth of a node is how many generations below the root it is, and the height of a node is how many generations its longest line of descendants goes down.

Now the key idea. Suppose the root wants to know "how many generations does our family span?". The root does not need to look at everyone. It asks its left child "how deep does your branch go?", asks its right child the same, takes the larger answer and adds one for itself. Each child answers by asking its own children, and so on down to the leaves, whose answer is immediate. That is recursion on trees: a node's answer is computed from its children's answers. Because every subtree is itself a tree, the same function works at every level.

Two directions of information

Tree recursions move information in one of two directions, and choosing correctly is most of the design.

  • Top-down: the parent tells the child something about the path above it — "you are at depth 3", "the largest value above you is 8", "your value must lie between 2 and 9". The child uses it and passes an updated version down. Answers are usually collected at the leaves or in a shared result.
  • Bottom-up: the child tells the parent something about the subtree below it — "my subtree has height 4", "my subtree sums to 17", "my subtree is balanced". The parent combines its children's answers into its own.

Some problems need both, and the hardest ones return one value up (for the parent's use) while updating a separate global answer that involves both children. Recognising which direction a problem needs is the first question to ask.

Where the family analogy breaks: a family can have more than two children, and real trees in software often do (file systems, the HTML DOM, B-trees with hundreds of children per node). Everything in this lesson generalises — loop over the children instead of naming left and right — but binary trees dominate interviews because they keep the code short. The other break: in a family you can ask your parent a question, but a tree node usually has no pointer to its parent. Problems that need to go "up" from an arbitrary node (distance k, for instance) must first record parents themselves.

One more practical point about cost: almost every tree algorithm in this lesson visits each node a constant number of times, so it is O(n) time; the extra space is the recursion depth, O(h). Saying "O(n) time and O(h) space, where h is log n if balanced and n if degenerate" covers the complexity question for most tree problems in one sentence.
body:
Depth-first traversals: recursive and iterative

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def inorder(node, out):
    if not node: return
    inorder(node.left, out)
    out.append(node.val)          # move this line up for pre-order, down for post-order
    inorder(node.right, out)

Recursion is the clearest form, but interviews often ask for the iterative version, and Python's recursion limit makes it necessary for very deep trees. Iterative in-order uses a stack to remember the nodes whose left subtrees you are exploring:

def inorder_iter(root):
    out, stack, node = [], [], root
    while node or stack:
        while node:                 # go as far left as possible
            stack.append(node); node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()          # leftmost unvisited node
        out.append(node.val)
        node = node.right           # then its right subtree
    return out

Iterative pre-order is simpler — pop a node, record it, push its right child then its left child (so the left is processed first). Iterative post-order is the trickiest; a common trick is to do a modified pre-order (node, right, left) and reverse the output.

Level-order traversal

Breadth-first traversal visits nodes level by level, using a queue. The one technique to know is how to separate levels: read the queue's length at the start of a level, and pop exactly that many nodes.

from collections import deque
def level_order(root):
    if not root: return []
    res, q = [], deque([root])
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):          # exactly the nodes of this level
            node = q.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            if node.left: q.append(node.left)
            if node.right: q.append(node.right)
        res.append(level)
    return res

On the figure's tree this gives [[4], [2, 6], [1, 3, 5, 7]]. Variants are small edits: Right Side View takes the last value of each level; Zigzag reverses every other level; minimum depth returns the level number of the first leaf found, which BFS finds before exploring deeper levels — an advantage over DFS when the tree is lopsided.

Top-down recursion: passing information down

"Count the good nodes: a node is good if no node on the path from the root to it has a larger value." Each node needs to know the maximum value on the path above it — information that flows down.

def good_nodes(root):
    def go(node, max_above):
        if not node: return 0
        good = 1 if node.val >= max_above else 0
        m = max(max_above, node.val)
        return good + go(node.left, m) + go(node.right, m)
    return go(root, float("-inf"))

Other top-down problems: "Path Sum" (pass the remaining target down; succeed at a leaf where it reaches zero), "Path Sum II" (pass the path down and backtrack — append on entry, pop on exit, al13), "sum root-to-leaf numbers" (pass the number formed so far: cur * 10 + node.val), and BST validation (pass bounds down, below).

Bottom-up recursion: returning information up

"Is the tree height-balanced (every node's subtrees differ in height by at most one)?" A node can only decide after knowing its children's heights — information that flows up. A neat trick returns −1 to mean "unbalanced", so one function returns both the height and the verdict:

def is_balanced(root):
    def height(node):
        if not node: return 0
        l = height(node.left)
        if l == -1: return -1
        r = height(node.right)
        if r == -1 or abs(l - r) > 1: return -1
        return 1 + max(l, r)
    return height(root) != -1

This is O(n). The naive version — compute heights separately at every node — is O(n²) on a degenerate tree, because each height call walks the whole subtree again. Returning combined information in one pass is the bottom-up pattern's main advantage.

Comparison problems are bottom-up too. Same Tree: both null, or equal values and same left and same right. Symmetric Tree: compare the left subtree with the mirror of the right (left.left with right.right, left.right with right.left). Subtree of Another Tree: at each node of the big tree, run Same Tree against the small one — O(m·n) — or serialise both with null markers and use a substring search for O(m + n).

Return one thing, track another: diameter and maximum path sum

"The diameter is the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes." The longest path through a given node goes down its left side as far as possible and down its right side as far as possible: left height + right height. But the parent cannot use a path that bends at its child — a path through the parent can only continue down one side of the child. So the function returns the height (what the parent can use) and updates a global with the bent path (the candidate answer).

def diameter(root):
    best = 0
    def height(node):
        nonlocal best
        if not node: return 0
        l, r = height(node.left), height(node.right)
        best = max(best, l + r)          # path bending at this node
        return 1 + max(l, r)             # path the parent can extend
    height(root)
    return best

Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (values can be negative; a path can start and end anywhere) is the same shape with sums instead of heights. Define gain(node) = the best sum of a path that starts at node and goes down one side. A negative child gain is better ignored (take 0 instead). At each node, the best path bending there is node.val + max(0, gain(left)) + max(0, gain(right)); the gain returned to the parent is node.val + max(0, gain(left), gain(right)).

def max_path_sum(root):
    best = float("-inf")
    def gain(node):
        nonlocal best
        if not node: return 0
        l = max(0, gain(node.left)); r = max(0, gain(node.right))
        best = max(best, node.val + l + r)
        return node.val + max(l, r)
    gain(root)
    return best

Trace on root −10 with children 9 and 20, where 20 has children 15 and 7: gain(9) = 9; at 20, gains 15 and 7, best = 20 + 15 + 7 = 42, return 20 + 15 = 35; at −10, l = 9, r = 35, candidate −10 + 9 + 35 = 34 < 42. Answer 42 — a path that never touches the root. Initialising best to −∞, not 0, matters for all-negative trees.

Binary search trees

A binary search tree (BST) adds an ordering: every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's key, and every key in its right subtree is larger. That makes search like binary search: compare with the node, go left or right, and discard the other subtree. Search, insert and delete each follow one root-to-leaf path, O(h). An in-order traversal visits keys in sorted order — the most useful fact about BSTs in interviews.

Validating a BST is the classic trap. Checking only left.val < node.val < right.val at each node accepts trees like 5 → (left 4, right 6 → (left 3)), where 3 sits in 5's right subtree but is smaller than 5. Every node must respect bounds from all its ancestors, which is top-down information:

def is_valid_bst(root):
    def ok(node, lo, hi):
        if not node: return True
        if not (lo < node.val < hi): return False
        return ok(node.left, lo, node.val) and ok(node.right, node.val, hi)
    return ok(root, float("-inf"), float("inf"))

The alternative is to run an in-order traversal and check that each value is strictly greater than the previous one.

K-th smallest in a BST: run the iterative in-order traversal and stop at the k-th popped node, O(h + k). LCA in a BST: walk from the root; if both p and q are smaller, go left; if both are larger, go right; otherwise the current node splits them and is the answer, O(h). Convert a sorted array to a balanced BST: the middle element is the root, recursively build each half — O(n), height ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉.

Lowest common ancestor in a general binary tree

Without the BST ordering, you cannot decide which way to go, so search both sides. The recursive function returns the node if it is p or q (or None if neither is in this subtree); if both children report a non-null result, p and q are on different sides and this node is their LCA.

def lca(node, p, q):
    if node is None or node is p or node is q:
        return node
    l, r = lca(node.left, p, q), lca(node.right, p, q)
    if l and r: return node         # p and q on different sides
    return l or r                   # both on one side, or only one found so far

O(n). It works even when p is an ancestor of q: the search returns p as soon as it reaches it, and p is indeed the LCA. (It assumes both nodes exist in the tree; if that is not guaranteed, count how many were actually found.)

Building a tree from traversals

Given pre-order [3, 9, 20, 15, 7] and in-order [9, 3, 15, 20, 7], rebuild the tree (values unique). The first pre-order value, 3, is the root. In the in-order list, everything left of 3 ([9]) is the left subtree and everything right ([15, 20, 7]) is the right subtree. The left subtree has 1 node, so the next 1 pre-order value (9) belongs to it, and the rest ([20, 15, 7]) to the right. Recurse.

def build_tree(preorder, inorder):
    idx = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}
    it = iter(preorder)
    def build(lo, hi):                      # in-order range [lo, hi)
        if lo >= hi: return None
        v = next(it)                        # next pre-order value is this root
        node = TreeNode(v)
        node.left = build(lo, idx[v])       # left first: matches pre-order
        node.right = build(idx[v] + 1, hi)
        return node
    return build(0, len(inorder))

The dictionary of in-order positions makes each split O(1), so construction is O(n). Consuming pre-order with an iterator in the same order as the recursion (root, left, right) avoids computing pre-order index ranges.

Serialisation

To store a tree as a string and rebuild it exactly, write a pre-order traversal with an explicit marker for every missing child, such as "1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#". The markers make the encoding unambiguous (a traversal without them cannot distinguish a left-only child from a right-only child). Deserialise with the same recursion: read a token; "#" means None; otherwise make a node and build its left then right subtree from the following tokens. Both directions are O(n). Level-order with markers (the format LeetCode uses to display trees) works too.

Going up: parent pointers

"All Nodes Distance K in Binary Tree" asks for nodes k edges from a target, which can be up through ancestors and then down other branches. Trees only point downwards, so first run a DFS that records each node's parent in a dict. Now the tree is effectively an undirected graph; run a BFS from the target, stepping to left, right and parent, with a visited set, for exactly k levels. This "turn the tree into a graph" move recurs whenever a problem needs to travel upwards.

Recognising the pattern

For any tree problem, ask: does each node need information from above (top-down) or from below (bottom-up)? Is the answer a single global value built from local candidates (track a global)? Is it about levels or shortest distance from the root (BFS)? Does the BST ordering let me discard subtrees? Then write the function signature first — its parameters are the top-down information and its return value is the bottom-up information.

Practice in the DSA list: Invert Binary Tree, Maximum Depth, Same Tree, Subtree of Another Tree, Diameter, Balanced Binary Tree, Level Order, Zigzag, Right Side View, Count Good Nodes, Path Sum II, Validate BST, Kth Smallest in a BST, LCA of a BST, LCA of a Binary Tree, Construct from Preorder and Inorder, All Nodes Distance K, Maximum Path Sum, Serialize and Deserialize.
deep:
Why BSTs need balancing

Inserting the keys 1, 2, 3, …, n into a plain BST in that order builds a chain where every node has only a right child: height n − 1, and every operation O(n). Self-balancing BSTs fix this by restructuring with rotations — local rearrangements of a parent and child that preserve the in-order sequence while changing heights. AVL trees keep every node's subtree heights within one of each other (height ≤ about 1.44 log₂ n); red-black trees enforce a looser colouring rule (height ≤ 2 log₂(n + 1)) with fewer rotations per update, which is why they are the usual choice in standard libraries (C++ std::map, Java TreeMap, the Linux kernel's scheduler and memory areas historically). Python has no built-in balanced BST; the third-party sortedcontainers uses a list-of-lists design instead. In interviews you are rarely asked to implement rotations, but you should know why balancing exists and what guarantee it buys.

Tree DP: returning tuples

Some bottom-up problems need more than one value from each child. "House Robber III": houses form a binary tree, adjacent (parent–child) houses cannot both be robbed; maximise the total. Each node returns a pair (best if this node is robbed, best if it is not). If robbed, its children must not be: rob = val + left.skip + right.skip. If skipped, each child may be either: skip = max(left) + max(right). The answer is the max of the root's pair. Returning a tuple per node turns what looks like an exponential choice into O(n) — this is dynamic programming on trees (al23), and the same shape solves "minimum cameras to monitor a tree" (three states per node) and "maximum independent set on a tree".

Morris traversal: O(1) extra space

Recursive and stack-based traversals use O(h) space. Morris in-order traversal uses O(1) by temporarily threading the tree: for a node with a left subtree, find its in-order predecessor (the rightmost node in the left subtree) and point that predecessor's right child back to the node. Then go left. When you later arrive back at the node through the thread, you know the left subtree is done: remove the thread, visit the node, and go right. Every edge is traversed a constant number of times, so it is O(n) time. It is a favourite "can you do it in constant space?" follow-up; the key sentence is "use the null right pointers of predecessors as temporary return links, and restore them".

Many LCA queries: binary lifting

The recursive LCA is O(n) per query. For q queries on a static tree, preprocess once: record each node's depth and its 2ᵏ-th ancestor for every k up to log n (up[k][v] = up[k − 1][up[k − 1][v]]). To answer LCA(u, v), lift the deeper node to the same depth using the binary representation of the depth difference, then lift both together from the largest k downwards while their ancestors differ; the parent of where they stop is the LCA. Preprocessing is O(n log n) and each query O(log n). The same table answers "k-th ancestor" queries, and the technique ("jump pointers at powers of two") reappears in skip lists and in sparse tables (al27).

Counting tree shapes and why recursion fits

The number of distinct binary tree shapes with n nodes is the n-th Catalan number (1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, …), the same sequence that counts balanced parenthesis strings (al13). This is not a coincidence: a tree is a root plus a left tree and a right tree, so count(n) = Σ count(i) · count(n − 1 − i), which is the Catalan recurrence. "Unique Binary Search Trees" asks exactly for this number, and "Unique Binary Search Trees II" asks you to generate them all by recursing on every possible root. The recursive definition of trees — a node with two smaller trees — is why recursion is the natural language for them.

Recursion depth and iterative post-order

A degenerate tree with 10⁵ nodes makes a recursive traversal exceed Python's default limit of 1,000 frames. Options: raise the limit with sys.setrecursionlimit (risky — the C stack can still overflow and crash the interpreter), or rewrite iteratively. For bottom-up computations that need children's results first, iterative post-order can use a stack of (node, visited_flag) pairs: push (node, False); on popping a False entry, push (node, True) then the children; on popping a True entry, all children have been processed and their results (stored in a dict) can be combined. Mentioning this when the interviewer says "the tree can have 10⁵ nodes in a line" shows awareness of the runtime, not just the algorithm.
prod:
In the interview room

Tree problems reward a clear function signature. Before coding, say what the recursive function takes (the top-down information) and what it returns (the bottom-up information), and whether a separate global is updated. "height(node) returns the height of node's subtree and updates best with the longest path bending at node" is a complete plan; the code follows in a few lines.

The common bugs are predictable. Forgetting the None base case (or handling leaves but not empty trees). Confusing height conventions (edges versus nodes) and being off by one in diameter. Validating a BST with local parent–child comparisons. Using 0 instead of −∞ as the initial best in max-path-sum. Using == on node values instead of is on node identities in LCA when values can repeat. Mutating a shared path in Path Sum II without popping. And for BFS, forgetting to snapshot len(q) before the inner loop, which mixes levels. Test on an empty tree, a single node, a left-only chain, and a tree with negative values.

Interviewers often follow up on complexity with "what if the tree is very deep?" (recursion limit; iterative traversal), "what if there are many queries?" (precompute subtree sizes, parents, or binary lifting), and "what if the BST is unbalanced?" (O(n) operations; self-balancing trees). For hard problems like max path sum, they usually ask you to explain why the return value and the global answer differ — have the "a parent can only extend a one-sided path" sentence ready.

Finally, draw. A five-node tree on the whiteboard, with the values your function returns written next to each node, is the fastest way to check a bottom-up recursion and the most convincing way to explain it.

On online assessments, tree inputs usually arrive as a level-order list with nulls (LeetCode's format) or as parent arrays and edge lists. Converting edges into an adjacency list and treating the tree as a graph rooted at node 0 is often the cleanest route, and it makes BFS and DFS from al16 directly applicable.

In real systems

Trees are everywhere in production systems. Databases index tables with B-trees and B+ trees — balanced trees with hundreds of children per node, so that a lookup among a billion rows touches only three or four disk pages (the database track covers them in depth). File systems store directories as trees, and many (ext4's htree, Btrfs, APFS) use B-tree variants internally. Browsers parse HTML into the DOM tree and lay out pages by traversing it; CSS selectors are matched by walking it. Compilers and interpreters parse source code into abstract syntax trees — Python's own ast module exposes them — and run optimisation passes as tree traversals. Git stores each commit's snapshot as a tree of tree objects, and Merkle trees (each node a hash of its children) let Git, blockchains and distributed databases like Cassandra detect differences between replicas by comparing hashes top-down. Machine-learning decision trees and gradient-boosted ensembles are, literally, binary trees evaluated root to leaf. The interview skills — choosing the traversal, passing state down, aggregating results up — are the same ones those systems use.
myths: To validate a BST, check that each node is greater than its left child and smaller than its right child.

That local check accepts invalid trees: a node deep in the left subtree can be larger than an ancestor while still being consistent with its parent. Every node must lie within bounds inherited from all its ancestors, so pass (low, high) down the recursion, or check that an in-order traversal is strictly increasing.
Tree operations are O(log n).

They are O(h), where h is the height. For a balanced tree h is about log₂ n, but an unbalanced BST built from sorted input degenerates into a linked list with h = n. Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) exist precisely to keep h logarithmic.
The diameter of a tree always passes through the root.

The longest path can lie entirely inside one subtree, for example when the root has one short branch and the other branch is bushy. That is why the diameter is computed at every node (left height plus right height) and the maximum is tracked globally.
Recursion is the only clean way to traverse a tree.

Iterative traversals with an explicit stack (DFS) or queue (BFS) are standard, avoid Python's recursion limit on deep trees, and are often asked for directly. Morris traversal even achieves in-order traversal with O(1) extra space by temporarily rewiring pointers.
Level-order traversal needs extra bookkeeping to know where each level ends.
Record the queue's length at the start of each level and pop exactly that many nodes; everything pushed during those pops belongs to the next level. No sentinels or depth tags are needed.
lab:
Build random trees, then check the bottom-up diameter and the bound-based BST validator against brute-force definitions.

  1. Save as tree_lab.py: 
    import random
from itertools import combinations

class T:
    def __init__(s, v, l=None, r=None): s.val, s.left, s.right = v, l, r

def rand_tree(n, lo=0, hi=9):
    if n == 0: return None
    k = random.randint(0, n - 1)
    return T(random.randint(lo, hi), rand_tree(k, lo, hi), rand_tree(n - 1 - k, lo, hi))

def diameter(root):
    best = 0
    def h(n):
        nonlocal best
        if not n: return 0
        a, b = h(n.left), h(n.right); best = max(best, a + b); return 1 + max(a, b)
    h(root); return best

def diameter_brute(root):                  # BFS from every node over an undirected view
    adj, stack = {}, [(root, None)]
    while stack:
        n, p = stack.pop()
        if not n: continue
        adj.setdefault(n, [])
        if p: adj[n].append(p); adj[p].append(n)
        stack += [(n.left, n), (n.right, n)]
    def far(s):
        dist, q = {s: 0}, [s]
        for u in q:
            for w in adj[u]:
                if w not in dist: dist[w] = dist[u] + 1; q.append(w)
        return max(dist.values())
    return max((far(s) for s in adj), default=0)

def valid(n, lo=float("-inf"), hi=float("inf")):
    return not n or (lo < n.val < hi and valid(n.left, lo, n.val) and valid(n.right, n.val, hi))

def inorder(n): return inorder(n.left) + [n.val] + inorder(n.right) if n else []

for _ in range(3000):
    t = rand_tree(random.randint(0, 9))
    assert diameter(t) == diameter_brute(t)
    vals = inorder(t)
    assert valid(t) == all(a < b for a, b in zip(vals, vals[1:]))
print("diameter and BST validation agree with brute force")
  2. Run it and expect the final message. The brute force computes the diameter by definition — the longest shortest path from any node — and BST validity by "in-order is strictly increasing".
  3. Replace valid with the local check n.left.val < n.val < n.right.val (guarding None children) and run again; it disagrees on trees where a deeper node violates an ancestor's bound.

What this proves: the one-pass bottom-up diameter equals the definition on every tree shape, and local BST checks are genuinely wrong, not just inelegant.
recap: A binary tree node has a value and up to two children; height is the longest root-to-leaf path, and most operations cost O(h).
Pre-order, in-order and post-order are depth-first traversals that differ only in when the node is visited relative to its subtrees; level order uses a queue and processes one level at a time.
Top-down recursion passes information from parent to child (depth so far, bounds, maximum on the path); bottom-up recursion returns information from children to parent (height, sums, is-balanced).
Many hard tree problems compute a local answer at every node from children's returned values and keep a global best, as in diameter and maximum path sum.
In a BST every key in the left subtree is smaller and every key in the right subtree is larger, so search, insert and delete follow one path, and in-order traversal is sorted.
Validate a BST by passing down (low, high) bounds, not by comparing each node only with its children.
The lowest common ancestor in a binary tree is the node where p and q are found in different subtrees (or the node is one of them); in a BST it is the first node whose value lies between p and q.
Construction from pre-order and in-order uses the pre-order's first element as the root and a hash map of in-order positions to split subtrees in O(n).
glossary: A node on the path from the root to a given node, and conversely a node in a given node's subtree.
A self-balancing BST that keeps the heights of every node's two subtrees within one of each other, using rotations.
A tree whose height is O(log n); for a binary tree often defined as every node's subtrees differing in height by at most one.
A binary tree where every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than it and every key in its right subtree is larger.
A tree in which each node has at most two children, called left and right.
Breadth-first search (level by level, with a queue) and depth-first search (one branch at a time, with recursion or a stack); level order is BFS, the three depth-first orders are DFS.
The number of edges from the root to a node.
The number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes.
Document Object Model: the tree a browser builds from an HTML page.
The number of edges (or nodes, by some conventions) on the longest path from a node down to a leaf.
Visit left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree; on a BST it yields keys in sorted order.
Visiting nodes level by level from the root, using a queue; also called breadth-first traversal.
The deepest node that has both of two given nodes as descendants (a node counts as its own descendant).
Visit left subtree, right subtree, then the node; used when a node needs its children's results first.
Visit the node, then the left subtree, then the right subtree; used for copying and serialising trees.
A node together with all its descendants.
drill:
Choose the direction

For each problem, say whether you pass information down, return it up, or both, and write the function signature. (a) Sum of all root-to-leaf numbers, where each path's digits form a number. (b) Count the subtrees whose values are all equal (uni-value subtrees). (c) The longest path where consecutive nodes differ by exactly one (Binary Tree Longest Consecutive Sequence, parent to child only). (d) Flatten the tree into a linked list in pre-order, in place.

Answer

(a) Down: go(node, cur) with cur = cur·10 + node.val; at a leaf return cur, otherwise return go(left) + go(right). (b) Up plus global: is_uni(node) -> bool; a node is uni-value if both children are uni-value (None counts) and each existing child's value equals node.val; increment a global count when true. Evaluate both children before combining, so every subtree is counted — short-circuiting with and would skip the right subtree. (c) Down is simplest: go(node, parent_val, length) where length becomes length + 1 if node.val == parent_val + 1 else 1, updating a global maximum; a bottom-up version returning "longest consecutive path starting here going down" also works. (d) Up: flatten(node) -> tail returns the last node of the flattened subtree; flatten the left and right, then splice: left_tail.right = node.right, node.right = node.left, node.left = None, and return the right tail (or left tail, or node). Alternatively the O(1)-space Morris-like loop: for each node with a left child, attach the right subtree to the rightmost node of the left subtree, move the left subtree to the right, and advance.
qa: E
Find the maximum depth of a binary tree.
Bottom-up: depth(None) = 0 and depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)). O(n) time, O(h) stack space. Iteratively, run a level-order traversal and count the levels.
E
Invert a binary tree.
Swap each node's left and right children and recurse into both (pre-order or post-order both work). O(n) time, O(h) space. Iteratively, use a queue or stack and swap children as you visit each node.
E
What do pre-order, in-order and post-order traversals produce on a BST?

In-order gives the keys in sorted order. Pre-order lists each node before its subtrees, which is the order you would insert keys to rebuild the same BST. Post-order lists children before parents, which suits deleting a tree or evaluating an expression tree.
M
Return the level-order traversal of a binary tree as a list of levels.

BFS with a deque. At the start of each level, read the queue length k; pop k nodes, recording their values and pushing their children. Those k values form one level. O(n) time, O(width) space. Right Side View records the last value of each level; zigzag reverses every other level.
M
Validate a binary search tree.

Recurse with bounds: valid(node, low, high) requires low < node.val < high, then checks the left subtree with (low, node.val) and the right with (node.val, high). Start with (−∞, +∞). Alternatively do an in-order traversal and check each value is strictly greater than the previous. O(n).
Follow-up: Why is comparing each node with its children not enough? — Tree [5, left 4, right 6 with left child 3] passes every parent–child check, but 3 is in 5's right subtree and smaller than 5.
M
Find the diameter of a binary tree.

Bottom-up height function that also updates a global best: at each node, the longest path through it has left_height + right_height edges, so best = max(best, l + r); return 1 + max(l, r) as the height. The answer is best. O(n) time.
M
Find the k-th smallest element in a BST.
In-order traversal visits keys in sorted order, so stop at the k-th visited node. Iteratively: push left children onto a stack, pop, count, then move to the right child. O(h + k) time.
Follow-up: Many queries with insertions and deletions? — Store subtree sizes in each node; then select the k-th by comparing k with the left subtree's size at each step, O(h) per query.
M
Lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a binary tree.

Recurse: if the node is None, p or q, return it. Otherwise recurse into both children. If both return non-null, p and q are on different sides, so this node is the LCA; otherwise return whichever is non-null. O(n). In a BST you can instead walk from the root: go left if both values are smaller, right if both larger, else stop — O(h).
M
Construct a binary tree from its pre-order and in-order traversals.

The first pre-order element is the root. Its position in the in-order list splits the in-order into left and right subtrees, and their sizes split the remaining pre-order. Recurse. A dict from value to in-order index makes each split O(1), so O(n) total. Values must be unique.
H
Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (a path may start and end anywhere).

Bottom-up gain(node) = the best sum of a downward path starting at node: node.val + max(0, gain(left), gain(right)), ignoring negative branches. At each node, the best path through it uses both sides: node.val + max(0, gain(left)) + max(0, gain(right)); update a global maximum with it. Return the gain. O(n). Initialise the global with −∞ so all-negative trees work.
H
Serialise and deserialise a binary tree.

Pre-order traversal writing a marker such as '#' for every null child, joined with commas. To deserialise, read tokens from an iterator: a '#' returns None; otherwise create the node and recursively build its left then right child. The null markers make the encoding unambiguous. O(n) both ways.
Follow-up: Can a BST be serialised without null markers? — Yes; its pre-order alone determines it, because the BST property tells you where each subtree ends.
H
Find all nodes at distance k from a target node.

A tree only has child pointers, but distance k can go up through ancestors. First record each node's parent with a DFS. Then BFS from the target over the undirected graph of child and parent edges, with a visited set, for k levels; the nodes at level k are the answer. O(n).

sum: Store strings character by character in a tree so every prefix is a path: insert, search and prefix queries in O(length), wildcard search, Word Search II, autocomplete, replace-with-root, and the binary trie that finds maximum XOR pairs.
