t: Union-find (disjoint set union): dynamic connectivity in near-constant time
sum: Maintain groups that merge over time with find and union: path compression and union by rank or size, component counting, cycle detection and redundant edges, Accounts Merge, equation satisfiability, stones on rows and columns, islands added online, weighted ratios and Kruskal's algorithm.
prereq: al16
Connected components and cycle detection with DFS and BFS.
al14
Trees with parent pointers; height determines the cost of walking to the root.
why:
A social network receives a stream of friendship events: Asha befriends Ben, Ben befriends Chen, Dev befriends Ema, Chen befriends Dev. After each event, the product wants to know: are two given people in the same circle? How many separate circles are there? With a few people you could redraw the groups each time. With 10 million users and 100 million events, running a BFS after every event — O(V + E) each time — would never finish.

The question has a special shape that makes it much easier than general graph search. Groups only ever merge; nobody is ever separated. And you never need the path between two people, only whether they are in the same group. A structure built exactly for that — union-find, also called disjoint set union (DSU) — answers "same group?" and performs "merge these groups" in amortised time so close to constant that, for any practical input, it is constant.

Union-find shows up in interviews in two ways. Directly: counting components, detecting the edge that creates a cycle, merging accounts that share an email, checking whether a set of equations can all be true, counting islands as land is added. And as a building block: Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm is "sort the edges, then use union-find to skip edges that would create a cycle". It is also a classic "implement this data structure" question, where interviewers look for the two optimisations that make it fast.

This lesson builds union-find from a naive version to the optimised one, explains why the two heuristics — path compression and union by rank — matter, then applies it to each problem family, including weighted union-find for ratio queries and the trick of mapping rows and columns into one id space.
primer:
The mental model: clubs with presidents

Imagine every person belongs to exactly one club, and every club has a president. To find out whether two people are in the same club, ask each of them "who is your president?" — if the answers match, they are in the same club. To merge two clubs, one president agrees to report to the other; from then on, the second president leads everyone.

The trick that makes this cheap is that nobody needs to know their president directly. Each person only knows one other person to ask — their parent — and asking repeatedly ("who do you report to?") eventually reaches someone who reports to themselves: the president, or root. That is the find operation. Merging two clubs (union) only changes one pointer: the root of one club starts pointing to the root of the other. Thousands of members join a new club with a single change, because they all reach the new president through their old one.

The danger is that the chains of "ask your parent" can get long — if every union hangs a big club under a single person, find might walk a long way. Two simple rules prevent this. Union by rank (or size): when merging, the smaller (or shorter) tree goes under the larger one, so trees stay shallow. Path compression: after find walks a path to the root, every node on that path is re-pointed straight at the root, so the next find on any of them is one step. With both rules, a long sequence of operations averages out to effectively constant time each.

Where the club analogy breaks: in a real club, people can leave. Union-find cannot split a group — there is no record of which merges created it, and path compression has erased the original structure anyway. If a problem needs to remove connections, union-find alone will not do; the deep layer covers the workarounds.

It helps to compare costs concretely. Suppose 10⁶ people and 10⁷ friendship events, with a "same circle?" query after each event. Re-running BFS after each event would cost on the order of 10⁷ × 10⁷ operations — impossible. Union-find does about 10⁷ unions and 10⁷ pairs of finds, each a handful of pointer steps: a few seconds even in Python. The gap is not a constant factor; it is the difference between an answer and no answer.

A good way to recognise union-find problems is the phrase pattern "are these in the same group?" plus "groups merge over time" — or any problem where you would otherwise re-run a connectivity search after every change.
body:
From naive to fast

The most naive version stores each element's group id directly (quick-find): find is O(1), but union must relabel every member of one group, O(n). The parent-forest version (quick-union) makes union cheap — link one root to the other — but without care the trees can become chains, making find O(n). Union by rank and path compression fix that.

class DSU:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))       # each element is its own root
        self.size = [1] * n
        self.count = n                     # number of groups

    def find(self, x):
        while self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]   # path halving
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x

    def union(self, a, b):
        ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return False                   # already together: this edge adds a cycle
        if self.size[ra] < self.size[rb]:
            ra, rb = rb, ra                # attach the smaller tree under the larger
        self.parent[rb] = ra
        self.size[ra] += self.size[rb]
        self.count -= 1
        return True

Three details are worth saying aloud. find uses path halving — each node on the path is pointed at its grandparent as the loop goes — an iterative form of compression that avoids recursion and has the same guarantees. union returns whether a merge actually happened, which many problems need (it is the cycle test). And count is maintained incrementally, so "how many groups?" is O(1). The recursive full-compression version, if parent[x] != x: parent[x] = find(parent[x]); return parent[x], is shorter but can hit Python's recursion limit on a long chain before compression has flattened it.

Trace with n = 8: union(1, 2) → root 1 gets 2 (count 7). union(3, 4) → count 6. union(2, 4): find(2) = 1, find(4) = 3, sizes equal, 3 goes under 1 (count 5). union(5, 6), union(6, 7) → 5's group {5, 6, 7} (count 3: groups {0}, {1,2,3,4}, {5,6,7}). union(3, 7): find(3) = 1 (size 4), find(7) = 5 (size 3), so 5 goes under 1 (count 2). Now find(7) walks 7 → 5 → 1 and halving shortens the path. Are 2 and 6 connected? find(2) = 1 = find(6), yes.

Counting components and spotting cycles

"Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph": create a DSU of n, union every edge, return count. "Graph Valid Tree": a tree on n nodes has exactly n − 1 edges and no cycle; check the edge count, then union every edge and fail if any union returns False (both ends already connected, so this edge would close a cycle). "Redundant Connection": a tree with one extra edge; the first edge (in input order) whose union returns False is the one to remove.

def find_redundant_connection(edges):
    dsu = DSU(len(edges) + 1)            # nodes are 1..n
    for u, v in edges:
        if not dsu.union(u, v):
            return [u, v]

These are short because union-find answers exactly the question asked. DFS can solve them too, but re-checking connectivity after each edge is where union-find's incremental nature wins.

Grouping by shared attributes: Accounts Merge

"Each account is a name and a list of emails; two accounts belong to the same person if they share any email. Merge them." The elements to group are emails. Within one account, all emails belong together, so union each email with the account's first email. Accounts that share an email become connected through it.

def accounts_merge(accounts):
    parent, owner = {}, {}
    def find(x):
        parent.setdefault(x, x)
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]; x = parent[x]
        return x
    for name, *emails in accounts:
        for e in emails:
            owner[e] = name
            parent[find(e)] = find(emails[0])      # union with the first email
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for e in owner:
        groups[find(e)].append(e)
    return [[owner[root]] + sorted(es) for root, es in groups.items()]

A dict-based parent lets emails (strings) be elements directly. This version skips union by size for brevity; with path halving it is still fast. Sorting each group dominates the cost: O(E log E) for E emails.

Equivalence first, then contradictions: equality equations

"Given equations like 'a==b' and 'b!=c' over 26 variables, can all be true at once?" Equalities define groups (equality is transitive); inequalities are constraints between groups. So: union the variables of every '==' equation first; then, for each '!=' equation, if both variables share a root, they are forced equal and the system is unsatisfiable. The order matters — checking an inequality before processing a later equality could miss a contradiction.

Mapping two kinds of things into one id space: stones

"Stones sit on a grid; a stone can be removed if another stone shares its row or column. What is the maximum number of removable stones?" Within any group of stones connected by shared rows or columns, you can remove stones one at a time (always a leaf of a spanning tree of the group) until one remains. So the answer is stones − number of groups. The neat modelling trick: instead of unioning stones with each other (O(n²) pairs), union each stone's row with its column, treating rows and columns as the elements. Two stones in the same row share that row element; two in the same column share the column element. Keep rows and columns in different id ranges (for example row r → r, column c → c + 10001).

def remove_stones(stones):
    parent = {}
    def find(x):
        parent.setdefault(x, x)
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]; x = parent[x]
        return x
    for r, c in stones:
        parent[find(r)] = find(c + 10001)
    roots = {find(x) for x in parent}
    return len(stones) - len(roots)

This "make the attributes the elements" move recurs: union people with the groups they belong to, or words with the synonyms they are equivalent to, rather than comparing every pair of items.

Online connectivity: Number of Islands II

"An R×C grid starts as water; positions are turned into land one at a time; after each, report the number of islands." Re-running flood fill after each addition is O(R·C) per step. With union-find over cell ids r·C + c: when a cell becomes land, add it as a new set (count + 1), then union it with each of its four neighbours that are already land (each union that merges two different roots does count − 1). Skip positions that are already land. Each addition costs O(α(R·C)) amortised. This is the clearest demonstration of why union-find exists: the graph grows, and the question is asked after every change.

Weighted union-find: ratios and offsets

"Evaluate Division" (a/b = 2, b/c = 3, what is a/c?) was solved with DFS in al16. Union-find can store a value on each parent link: w[x] = x / parent[x]. When find compresses x's path to the root, it multiplies the weights along the way so that w[x] becomes x / root.

parent, w = {}, {}
def find(x):
    if parent[x] != x:
        p = parent[x]
        root = find(p)
        w[x] *= w[p]               # x/p * p/root = x/root
        parent[x] = root
    return parent[x]

def union(a, b, k):                # record a / b = k
    for v in (a, b):
        if v not in parent: parent[v], w[v] = v, 1.0
    ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
    if ra != rb:
        parent[ra] = rb
        w[ra] = k * w[b] / w[a]    # ra/rb = (a/ra)^-1 * (a/b) * (b/rb)

def query(a, c):
    if a not in parent or c not in parent or find(a) != find(c): return -1.0
    return w[a] / w[c]             # (a/root) / (c/root)

For a/b = 2 and b/c = 3: after both unions, a/c = w[a] / w[c] = 6. The same idea with additive offsets answers "how far apart are these two items?" in relative-positioning problems, and with parity bits (offset mod 2) checks bipartiteness incrementally — "Possible Bipartition" with edges arriving online.

Kruskal's minimum spanning tree

A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices of a weighted undirected graph with the least total edge weight. Kruskal's algorithm is greedy: sort edges by weight and take each edge that connects two different components (union returns True), skipping those that would form a cycle. Stop after n − 1 edges.

def min_cost_connect_points(points):
    n = len(points)
    edges = sorted((abs(x1 - x2) + abs(y1 - y2), i, j)
                   for i, (x1, y1) in enumerate(points)
                   for j, (x2, y2) in enumerate(points) if i < j)
    dsu, total, used = DSU(n), 0, 0
    for w, i, j in edges:
        if dsu.union(i, j):
            total += w; used += 1
            if used == n - 1: break
    return total

Sorting dominates: O(E log E). Its correctness rests on the cut property — the lightest edge crossing any division of the vertices into two sides belongs to some MST — and on the fact that forests form a matroid, so the greedy is optimal (al12). For dense graphs like this complete one, Prim's algorithm is often better (al20).

Listing groups and their sizes

Many problems want the groups themselves at the end: the merged accounts, the members of each island, the size of the largest friend circle. Union-find does not store members, but recovering them is easy: after all unions, loop over every element, compute its root with find, and append it to a list keyed by root. That is O(n·α(n)). Sizes are even cheaper if you maintain size at the roots during union, as the DSU class does: the largest group is max(size[r] for r in roots). If you need members during the process (for example, to notify everyone in a merged group), keep a member list at each root and, on union, extend the larger list with the smaller one; each element moves at most log₂ n times (its group at least doubles each time it moves), so the total is O(n log n).

Recognising the pattern

Reach for union-find when groups merge and never split, when you need "same group?" or "how many groups?" after many merges, when an edge's arrival should be checked for creating a cycle, or when items are equivalent through shared attributes (emails, rows and columns, synonyms). If the graph is static and you also need paths or distances, BFS/DFS may be simpler.

Practice in the DSA list: Number of Connected Components, Number of Provinces, Graph Valid Tree, Redundant Connection, Accounts Merge, Satisfiability of Equality Equations, Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column, Min Cost to Connect All Points, Evaluate Division (al16), Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges in MST (al20).
deep:
Why both heuristics, and what α(n) means

Union by rank alone keeps every tree's height at most log₂ n: a tree of rank r has at least 2^r nodes, because its rank only increases when two trees of equal rank merge, doubling the minimum size. So find is O(log n). Path compression alone gives O(log n) amortised as well. Together, Tarjan proved in 1975 that m operations cost O(m·α(n)), where α is the inverse of the Ackermann function — a function that grows so fast that α(n) ≤ 4 for any n you could ever store; the first n with α(n) = 5 is a tower of exponents vastly larger than the number of atoms in the universe. The intuition: compression makes nodes skip ever-larger stretches of rank, and the number of times a node's "skip level" can increase is bounded by an iterated logarithm of an iterated logarithm, and so on. In interviews, "amortised inverse Ackermann, effectively constant" is the expected phrase; and it is worth adding that union by size works as well as by rank and is more useful in practice because the sizes are often needed anyway.

Deletions: offline reversal and rollback

Union-find cannot undo a union, because path compression destroys the information needed. Three workarounds exist. Offline reversal: if all operations are known in advance, process them backwards — start from the final state, and deletions become unions. This solves problems like "remove these edges one by one; after each removal, how many components remain?" in O((V + E)·α). Rollback DSU: drop path compression, keep union by size, and push every parent change onto a stack so the last union can be undone exactly; find becomes O(log n). Combined with a segment tree over time ("each edge exists during an interval of operations"), this gives offline dynamic connectivity in O(m log m log n). Fully dynamic connectivity structures support online insertions and deletions in polylogarithmic amortised time, but they are research-grade and rarely implemented in interviews — naming them is enough.

Kruskal versus Prim, and single-linkage clustering

Kruskal needs the edges sorted: O(E log E). It is ideal for sparse graphs given as edge lists. Prim grows one tree from a start vertex, always adding the cheapest edge leaving it, using a heap (O(E log V)) or, for dense graphs, an array of best distances scanned in O(V) per step (O(V²) total, better than sorting V²/2 edges). If you stop Kruskal early, when k components remain, the components are exactly the clusters of single-linkage hierarchical clustering with k clusters — the same algorithm used by SciPy's linkage(method="single"). That connection is a nice bridge from DSA to machine learning.

Union-find in type inference and compilers

Hindley–Milner type inference — the algorithm behind type inference in ML, OCaml, Haskell and (in spirit) parts of Rust and TypeScript — represents type variables as union-find elements. Unifying two types ("these must be the same") is a union; finding what a type variable stands for is a find. Compilers also use union-find for alias analysis (which pointers may refer to the same memory), register coalescing, and computing equivalence classes of program variables. These are examples where near-constant merges over millions of elements are essential.

Parity and bipartiteness with union-find

Store, for each node, the parity (0 or 1) of the path to its parent. find accumulates parity along the path (XOR), giving each node's parity relative to its root. Adding an edge u–v that says "u and v are on opposite sides" either links two roots with the parity chosen to make it true, or — if u and v already share a root — checks that their parities differ; if they are equal, the graph has an odd cycle and is not bipartite. This handles bipartiteness online as edges arrive, which BFS colouring cannot do without recomputation.

Percolation and connectivity thresholds

A classic simulation asks: in a grid where each cell is open with probability p, at what p does a path of open cells connect top to bottom? Opening cells one by one and union-ing with open neighbours, with two virtual nodes connected to the whole top and bottom rows, answers "does it percolate yet?" with a single find comparison after each opening. Monte Carlo runs estimate the threshold (about 0.593 for site percolation on a square grid). The same virtual-node trick — one extra element standing for "the border" or "the outside" — simplifies many grid problems, such as Surrounded Regions solved with union-find.
prod:
In the interview room

Interviewers who ask union-find usually want to see the implementation with both optimisations and a clear explanation of what each buys. Write the class with find, union that returns a boolean, and a count; say "path compression flattens trees on find; union by size keeps them shallow; together amortised inverse Ackermann". Common bugs: comparing parent[x] instead of find(x); unioning non-root nodes (parent[a] = b instead of parent[find(a)] = find(b)), which silently breaks groups; forgetting to decrement the count only on successful merges; off-by-one node numbering (1-based inputs with a 0-based array of size n); and recursive find on a long chain hitting the recursion limit. Test with repeated unions of the same pair, a union of an element with itself, and a long chain.

Recognition is the other half. The tell-tale phrases are "groups", "merge", "connected", "same component", "redundant", "equivalent", and anything where edges arrive over time. A strong answer also says when not to use union-find: if the graph is static and the question needs paths or distances, BFS is simpler; if edges are deleted, union-find needs an offline trick.

A good follow-up to anticipate: "what if the elements are strings?" (dict-based parent, created lazily); "what if there are 10⁸ elements?" (arrays of 32-bit integers rather than Python lists, or sharding by component); "can you list the members of a group?" (union-find does not store members — either group by find at the end, or keep a member list at each root and merge the smaller into the larger, which costs O(n log n) total).

On online assessments, union-find problems often hide behind stories about friend circles, network cables, or "how many groups after these operations". Reading the operations as unions and the questions as finds or counts is usually the whole insight; the implementation is the same twenty lines every time, so it is worth having them memorised.

In real systems

Union-find appears wherever equivalence classes are built incrementally. Image processing labels connected components in two passes — the first assigns provisional labels and records which labels touch in a union-find, the second replaces each label by its root — which is how OpenCV and scikit-image label blobs efficiently. Network design and clustering use Kruskal's algorithm; single-linkage clustering in SciPy is Kruskal stopped early. Entity resolution systems (deciding which customer records refer to the same person) union records that share strong identifiers such as email or phone, exactly like Accounts Merge, at the scale of billions of records in distributed versions. Compilers use union-find in type inference and alias analysis. Physics and materials simulations use it for percolation. And distributed graph systems compute connected components with label-propagation variants of the same idea, iteratively pointing each vertex at the smallest label in its neighbourhood until the labels stop changing.
myths: Union-find is just another way to do BFS.

Both can count components of a fixed graph, but union-find shines when edges arrive one at a time and you must answer 'are these connected?' or 'how many groups?' after each one. Re-running BFS after every edge costs O(V + E) each time; union-find handles each edge in nearly constant amortised time.
Path compression alone, or union by rank alone, gives O(1) operations.

Each heuristic alone gives O(log n) amortised per operation. Together they give O(α(n)) amortised, where α is the inverse Ackermann function — at most 4 for any input that fits in the universe. In practice either heuristic is usually fast enough, but interviews expect you to know both.
Union-find can remove edges or split groups.

The structure only merges. Deleting an edge could split a group, and the parent forest has no record of which edges built it. When deletions are needed, process operations offline in reverse (deletions become additions), or use more complex dynamic-connectivity structures.
parent[x] is x's group id.

parent[x] is only the next step towards the group's representative; after unions, many elements point to non-root nodes until path compression flattens them. Always compare find(x) with find(y), never parent[x] with parent[y].
Union-find only works on integer ids 0..n−1.

Any hashable element works if parent is a dictionary, created lazily on first find. Strings (emails, account names) and tuples (grid cells) are common. Mapping elements to integer ids first is an optimisation, not a requirement.
lab:
Check the DSU's component count against BFS on random graphs, and see the effect of the heuristics on tree height.

  1. Save as dsu_lab.py: 
    import random
from collections import defaultdict

class DSU:
    def __init__(s, n, compress=True, by_size=True):
        s.p, s.sz, s.count, s.c, s.b = list(range(n)), [1] * n, n, compress, by_size
    def find(s, x):
        while s.p[x] != x:
            if s.c: s.p[x] = s.p[s.p[x]]
            x = s.p[x]
        return x
    def union(s, a, b):
        ra, rb = s.find(a), s.find(b)
        if ra == rb: return False
        if s.b and s.sz[ra] < s.sz[rb]: ra, rb = rb, ra
        s.p[rb] = ra; s.sz[ra] += s.sz[rb]; s.count -= 1; return True

def bfs_components(n, edges):
    g = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v in edges: g[u].append(v); g[v].append(u)
    seen, comps = set(), 0
    for s in range(n):
        if s in seen: continue
        comps += 1; stack = [s]; seen.add(s)
        while stack:
            u = stack.pop()
            for v in g[u]:
                if v not in seen: seen.add(v); stack.append(v)
    return comps

for _ in range(2000):
    n = random.randint(1, 12)
    edges = [(random.randrange(n), random.randrange(n)) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 15))]
    d = DSU(n)
    for u, v in edges: d.union(u, v)
    assert d.count == bfs_components(n, edges)
print("DSU component counts match BFS")

def height(d, x):
    h = 0
    while d.p[x] != x: x = d.p[x]; h += 1
    return h
n = 100_000
for c, b in ((False, False), (False, True), (True, True)):
    d = DSU(n, c, b)
    for i in range(1, n): d.union(i, i - 1)    # adversarial chain of unions
    print(f"compress={c!s:5} by_size={b!s:5} max height={max(height(d, x) for x in range(0, n, 997))}")
  2. Run it. The first line confirms the counts. The height lines show the effect of the heuristics on a chain of 100,000 unions: with neither, trees grow tall (the exact height depends on which root goes under which); with union by size they stay tiny; with both, flatter still. If the no-heuristic case is slow, reduce n.

What this proves: union-find computes the same components as a graph search, and the heuristics are what keep find paths short — without them, an unlucky union order can make find walk long chains.

drill:
Pick the structure

For each scenario, choose BFS/DFS or union-find and justify it in one sentence. (a) A static road network; find the shortest route between two cities by number of roads. (b) Servers are linked one cable at a time; after each cable, report whether the network is fully connected. (c) Given 10⁵ synonym pairs, decide for 10⁵ sentence pairs whether they are equivalent word by word. (d) Cables can also be cut; after each event, report the number of connected groups, with all events known in advance. (e) Find whether a static graph is bipartite.

Answer

(a) BFS: a static graph and a shortest-path question; union-find knows nothing about paths. (b) Union-find: connections only accumulate, and "fully connected" is count == 1 after each union — O(α) per cable instead of a BFS each time. (c) Union-find over words: union each synonym pair, then two sentences are equivalent if they have the same length and find(word) matches position by position — fast, and transitive synonyms ("happy ~ glad ~ joyful") are handled automatically. (d) Union-find processed offline in reverse: start from the final set of cables, walk the events backwards turning cuts into unions, record the count at each step, and reverse the answers. (e) BFS/DFS two-colouring is simplest for a static graph; a parity union-find also works and is the better choice if edges arrive online.
qa: E
What operations does union-find support and at what cost?

find(x) returns x's group representative and union(x, y) merges their groups. With path compression and union by rank or size, any sequence of m operations on n elements costs O(m·α(n)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function, so each operation is effectively O(1) amortised. Initialisation is O(n).
E
Number of connected components given n nodes and an edge list.

Initialise each node as its own group and count = n. For each edge, if find(u) ≠ find(v), union them and decrement count. The final count is the answer. O(n + E·α(n)). DFS works too for a fixed graph, but union-find also handles edges arriving online.
E
Number of Provinces from an adjacency matrix.
Union i and j for every isConnected[i][j] = 1 with i < j, decrementing a counter from n on each successful union. O(n²·α(n)) because the matrix has n² entries. DFS over the matrix is equally valid.
M
Graph Valid Tree: are n nodes and these edges a tree?

A tree on n nodes has exactly n − 1 edges and no cycle. Check the edge count first; then union the edges, returning false if any edge joins two nodes already in the same group (that edge would close a cycle). With n − 1 edges and no cycle the graph is connected. O(n·α(n)).
M
Redundant Connection: a tree plus one extra edge; return the edge that can be removed.

Process edges in order with union-find; the first edge whose endpoints already have the same root is the one that closes the cycle, and it is the answer (the last such edge in input order, as the problem requires, is this same edge because there is exactly one extra). O(n·α(n)).
M
Accounts Merge: merge accounts that share any email.

Treat each email as an element. For each account, union every email with the account's first email. Then group emails by their root, sort each group, and attach the owner's name (store a map from email to name). O(E·α(E) + E log E) for E emails, the sort dominating.
M
Satisfiability of Equality Equations such as a==b, b!=c.

First union the two variables of every '==' equation. Then check every '!=' equation: if its two variables have the same root, the system is unsatisfiable. Processing all equalities before any inequality matters, because a later equality could connect variables that an earlier inequality separated. 26 variables, so effectively O(n).
M
Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column.

A stone can be removed if another stone shares its row or column, so within each connected group (stones linked through shared rows or columns) all but one can be removed. Answer = stones − number of groups. Union each stone's row with its column, using distinct ids for rows and columns (for example column + 10001), and count distinct roots among the used ids. O(n·α(n)).
M
Number of Islands II: land is added one cell at a time; report the island count after each addition.

Map each cell to an id r·C + c. When a cell becomes land, add it as a new set and increment the count; then union it with each land neighbour, decrementing the count for each union that merges different roots. Ignore repeated additions of the same cell. Each step is O(α(R·C)), versus O(R·C) for re-flooding.
H
Evaluate Division with weighted union-find.

Store for each variable its parent and weight[x] = x / parent[x]. find(x) compresses the path and updates weight[x] to x / root by multiplying weights along the way. To add a/b = k, find both roots ra, rb with weights wa = a/ra and wb = b/rb; link ra under rb with weight[ra] = k·wb/wa. A query a/c, if both share a root, is weight[a] / weight[c]; otherwise −1.
H
Min Cost to Connect All Points (Manhattan distances).

This is a minimum spanning tree on a complete graph. Kruskal: generate all O(n²) edges, sort by weight, and add each edge that joins different components until n − 1 edges are added — O(n² log n). For dense complete graphs Prim's algorithm with an O(n²) array scan is often faster and avoids storing all edges (al20).

Follow-up: Why is Kruskal's greedy correct? — The cut property: the lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST, and Kruskal always adds the lightest edge crossing the cut between the components it joins.
H
How would you support connectivity queries when edges can also be deleted?

Union-find cannot split sets. If all operations are known in advance, process them offline in reverse: start from the final graph, and turn deletions into unions while walking backwards, answering queries along the way. For online deletions use a dynamic connectivity structure (link-cut trees for forests, or the polylogarithmic Holm–de Lichtenberg–Thorup structure), or segment-tree-over-time with a union-find that supports rollback.

why:
A delivery app knows travel times along every road segment in a city. Between the restaurant and your door there are thousands of possible routes; the app needs the fastest one, in milliseconds, for millions of orders a day. Breadth-first search (al16) will not do: it finds the route with the fewest road segments, which might be a slow crawl through the city centre rather than a longer but much faster ring road. Once edges carry weights — minutes, kilometres, costs, latencies — "shortest" means smallest total weight, and you need different algorithms.

Interviewers love weighted shortest paths because the core algorithm, Dijkstra's, is short enough to write in a round but subtle enough to reveal understanding: why it needs a priority queue, why it fails with negative weights, how to handle outdated heap entries in Python, and how to adapt it when the "length" of a path is not a sum at all — the steepest climb on a hike, the probability that a message gets through, the highest water level you must wait for. Around Dijkstra sit three relatives you should know: Bellman-Ford for negative weights and "at most k edges" constraints, Floyd-Warshall for all pairs on small graphs, and the topological-order trick for DAGs.

A neighbouring question is different but often confused with shortest paths: not the best route between two points, but the cheapest set of links connecting everything — laying cable between offices, or connecting points on a plane. That is a minimum spanning tree, built greedily by Prim's or Kruskal's algorithm.

This lesson builds the idea of relaxation, then Dijkstra with a full trace and proof sketch, its variants, Bellman-Ford and the k-stops problem, Floyd-Warshall, and spanning trees — ending with a decision table for picking the right algorithm from the weights and the question.
primer:
The mental model: water spreading through pipes of different lengths

Imagine pouring water into one junction of a network of pipes, where each pipe takes a known time to fill. The water reaches nearby junctions first and spreads outward, but not in neat rings as in BFS: a junction at the end of one long pipe may be reached later than a junction three short pipes away. If you watched and wrote down the moment the water first arrived at each junction, you would have every junction's shortest travel time from the source. Dijkstra's algorithm simulates exactly this: it always processes next the junction the water would reach soonest.

The bookkeeping uses one idea, relaxation. Each vertex has a tentative distance — the best route found so far, initially infinity (and 0 for the source). When you process a vertex u, you look at each pipe u → v of length w and ask: is going through u faster than the best route to v I know? If dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v]. Every shortest-path algorithm is a strategy for which edges to relax, and in what order.

Dijkstra's rule is: always process the unprocessed vertex with the smallest tentative distance. A min-heap finds it quickly. Once a vertex is popped, its distance is final — provided no edge has a negative weight. That proviso is the most important fact in this lesson: with all weights non-negative, any route that has not been explored yet must pass through some vertex at least as far away as the one just popped, so it cannot be shorter.

Where the water analogy breaks: water cannot flow backwards in time, but a negative-weight edge is exactly that — arriving at a vertex earlier by taking a detour. Real costs can be negative (a cashback, a refund, an energy gain going downhill), and then Dijkstra's "first arrival is final" logic is wrong. Bellman-Ford, which keeps relaxing every edge until nothing changes, handles that case, at a higher cost.

It is worth fixing the cost model before going further. Each vertex is popped once in a useful way and each edge relaxed at most once per pop of its source, so the work is dominated by heap operations: about E pushes and pops, each O(log E). For a road network with half a million edges, that is roughly ten million elementary heap steps — well under a second in a compiled language and a few seconds in Python. Bellman-Ford on the same graph would be V × E, about 10¹¹: hopeless. The choice of algorithm is not a detail.

A second break: water spreads from one source to everywhere. If the question is "shortest distance between every pair", repeating Dijkstra from each vertex works, but for small dense graphs a different algorithm, Floyd-Warshall, is simpler and just as fast.
body:
Dijkstra's algorithm with heapq

import heapq
def dijkstra(graph, src):              # graph[u] = [(v, w), ...], w >= 0
    dist = {src: 0}
    heap = [(0, src)]
    while heap:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue                   # stale entry: a shorter path was found later
        for v, w in graph[u]:
            nd = d + w
            if nd < dist.get(v, float("inf")):
                dist[v] = nd           # relax
                heapq.heappush(heap, (nd, v))
    return dist

Python's heapq has no "decrease priority" operation, so when a vertex's distance improves, the code simply pushes a new entry. The old entry stays in the heap; when it is eventually popped, its distance is larger than the recorded best, and the d > dist[u] check skips it. This is lazy deletion. The heap can hold up to E entries, so each operation is O(log E), and since E ≤ V², log E ≤ 2 log V: the total is O(E log V).

Trace the figure's graph from S. The heap starts with (0, S). Pop S: relax A to 4 and B to 1; heap [(1, B), (4, A)]. Pop B (1): relax A to 1 + 2 = 3 (better than 4; push (3, A)) and C to 1 + 5 = 6; heap [(3, A), (4, A), (6, C)]. Pop A (3): relax C to 3 + 1 = 4 (push). Pop (4, A): stale (4 > 3), skip. Pop C (4): relax D to 7. Pop (6, C): stale. Pop D (7). Final distances: S 0, B 1, A 3, C 4, D 7.

To recover the actual route, record parent[v] = u whenever you relax, and walk back from the destination. If you only need the distance to one target, you may stop as soon as it is popped — that is when it becomes final.

Network Delay Time is Dijkstra from the source, then the maximum of the distances (or −1 if some node is missing): the last node to receive the signal determines when everyone has it.

Why it works, in one paragraph

Claim: when u is popped (and not stale), dist[u] is the true shortest distance. Suppose not: some path P to u is shorter. P starts at the source, which is finalised, and ends at u, which is not yet; let y be the first vertex on P that is not finalised, and x the vertex just before it, which is. When x was finalised, the edge x → y was relaxed, so dist[y] ≤ dist[x] + w(x, y), which is the length of P up to y. Because all weights are non-negative, that prefix is no longer than P itself, which is shorter than dist[u]. So dist[y] < dist[u], and y would have been popped before u. Contradiction. The only place non-negativity is used is "a prefix of a path is no longer than the path" — exactly what a negative edge violates.

Variants: when the path cost is not a sum

Dijkstra works for any path cost that (1) is built edge by edge and (2) never gets better when the path is extended. That covers several interview favourites.

  • Path With Minimum Effort (grid, effort = the largest height difference between consecutive cells): cost of extending is max(cost, |h[u] − h[v]|). The maximum never decreases, so it qualifies.
  • Swim in Rising Water (earliest time t such that a path exists using only cells with elevation ≤ t): cost is max(cost, elevation[v]) — a minimax path.
  • Path with Maximum Probability: cost is the product of edge probabilities, which never increases because each factor is at most 1. Use a max-heap (push negated values), or transform with −log so products become sums of non-negative numbers.

Minimax problems also have two other standard solutions — binary search on the threshold with a BFS reachability check (al7), and adding edges in increasing weight order with union-find until source and target connect (al19) — which are worth mentioning as alternatives.

Bellman-Ford: negative weights and hop limits

Bellman-Ford makes no assumptions about weights. It relaxes every edge, and repeats V − 1 times. After round i, every vertex whose shortest path uses at most i edges has its correct distance — because a shortest path in a graph without negative cycles is simple (at most V − 1 edges), V − 1 rounds suffice. If a V-th round still improves something, there is a negative cycle reachable from the source, and shortest paths are undefined (you could loop forever, getting cheaper).

def bellman_ford(n, edges, src):           # edges: (u, v, w), any sign
    INF = float("inf")
    dist = [INF] * n
    dist[src] = 0
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        changed = False
        for u, v, w in edges:
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w; changed = True
        if not changed: break              # already converged
    for u, v, w in edges:
        if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
            return None                    # negative cycle reachable
    return dist

O(V·E): much slower than Dijkstra, but general. The same round structure solves Cheapest Flights Within K Stops, where the limit is on the number of edges (k stops = at most k + 1 flights). Run exactly k + 1 rounds, and in each round relax using a copy of the previous round's distances:

def find_cheapest_price(n, flights, src, dst, k):
    INF = float("inf")
    dist = [INF] * n; dist[src] = 0
    for _ in range(k + 1):
        prev = dist[:]                     # only use paths from the last round
        for u, v, w in flights:
            if prev[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = prev[u] + w
    return -1 if dist[dst] == INF else dist[dst]

Without the copy, relaxing edges in a lucky order could chain several flights within one round and exceed the stop limit. With it, round i extends paths by exactly one more flight. This problem is a classic trap for plain Dijkstra: the cheapest route to an intermediate city might use too many stops, while a slightly more expensive route with fewer stops is the one that leads to a valid answer. If you prefer Dijkstra, the state must be (city, stops used).

Floyd-Warshall: all pairs on small graphs

When you need distances between every pair and V is small (a few hundred), Floyd-Warshall is the simplest option. Start with dist[i][j] = edge weight (∞ if none, 0 on the diagonal). Then for each vertex k, allow it as an intermediate stop: for every pair (i, j), if going i → k → j is shorter, take it.

def floyd_warshall(n, edges):
    INF = float("inf")
    d = [[0 if i == j else INF for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        d[u][v] = min(d[u][v], w)
    for k in range(n):                     # k must be the OUTER loop
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(n):
                if d[i][k] + d[k][j] < d[i][j]:
                    d[i][j] = d[i][k] + d[k][j]
    return d

After processing k, d[i][j] is the shortest path using only vertices 0..k as intermediates; after all k, it is the true shortest distance. The order of loops matters: k outermost. O(V³) time, O(V²) memory; it handles negative edges, and a negative value on the diagonal reveals a negative cycle. "Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbours at a Threshold Distance" (n ≤ 100) is a direct application: 10⁶ steps.

Minimum spanning trees: Prim and Kruskal

A minimum spanning tree picks V − 1 edges that connect every vertex with the smallest total weight. It answers "the cheapest way to connect everything", not "the shortest route between two vertices". Two greedy algorithms build it, both justified by the cut property: for any split of the vertices into two groups, the lightest edge crossing the split belongs to some MST.

Kruskal (al19): sort edges by weight; add each edge that joins two different components (union-find); stop at V − 1 edges. O(E log E).

Prim: grow one tree from any start vertex; repeatedly add the cheapest edge that connects the tree to a vertex outside it. With a heap it looks almost exactly like Dijkstra — the difference is the priority: the edge weight alone, not the distance from the source.

def prim(n, graph):                        # graph[u] = [(v, w), ...], undirected
    in_tree, total = [False] * n, 0
    heap = [(0, 0)]                        # (edge weight, vertex)
    while heap:
        w, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if in_tree[u]: continue
        in_tree[u] = True; total += w
        for v, wv in graph[u]:
            if not in_tree[v]:
                heapq.heappush(heap, (wv, v))
    return total if all(in_tree) else None   # None: graph not connected

For dense graphs such as "Min Cost to Connect All Points" (every pair of points is an edge, so E ≈ V²/2), an array-based Prim — keep best[v], the cheapest edge from the tree to each outside vertex, and scan for the minimum each step — runs in O(V²) without storing any edges, beating both heap Prim and Kruskal's sort.

Multi-source and reverse searches

Two small tricks extend Dijkstra cheaply. Multi-source: to find each vertex's distance to the nearest of several sources (the closest hospital, the nearest charging station), push every source with distance 0 at the start; one run gives the answer for all vertices, exactly like multi-source BFS on grids. Reverse graph: to find every vertex's distance to a single target in a directed graph (how long from each house to the fire station), reverse every edge and run Dijkstra from the target. Combining both directions answers "shortest path from s to t that passes through some vertex in a set": run forward from s and backward from t, then minimise d_s(v) + d_t(v) over the set.

deep:
A*: Dijkstra with a compass

When you need one target and have a good estimate of the remaining distance, A* orders the heap by g + h, where g is the distance so far and h a heuristic estimate to the target. If h never overestimates (admissible — for example, straight-line distance on a road map), the first time the target is popped its distance is optimal; if h is also consistent (h(u) ≤ w(u, v) + h(v)), each vertex is popped at most once, exactly like Dijkstra. With h = 0, A* is Dijkstra. A good heuristic focuses the search towards the target and can cut explored vertices by orders of magnitude, which is why games and robots use it. In interviews, "A* is Dijkstra plus an admissible heuristic" and an example heuristic is the expected depth.

Negative edges: Johnson's algorithm and the trouble with SPFA

For all pairs on a sparse graph with negative edges, Floyd-Warshall's O(V³) may be too slow and V runs of Bellman-Ford are worse. Johnson's algorithm runs Bellman-Ford once from a new virtual vertex connected to all others with weight 0, obtaining potentials h(v), then reweights every edge as w'(u, v) = w(u, v) + h(u) − h(v), which is non-negative and preserves shortest paths. Then it runs Dijkstra from every vertex: O(V·E log V). A popular Bellman-Ford optimisation, SPFA (only re-relax edges out of vertices whose distance changed, using a queue), is fast on random graphs but has the same O(V·E) worst case and can be forced into it by crafted inputs; competitive programmers learned this the hard way. Mentioning that you would not rely on SPFA for adversarial input is a sign of depth.

State-expanded graphs

Many hard shortest-path problems become ordinary Dijkstra on a bigger graph whose vertices carry extra information: (city, stops used) for flights with a stop limit, (cell, fuel left) for refuelling, (node, discount coupons left) for "you may halve one edge's cost", (node, time mod k) for periodic schedules. The cost is that the graph has V × (states) vertices. The modelling skill — "what must I know about my situation to decide the future?" — is the same one used for BFS with state on grids (al17) and for dynamic programming states (al21).

Road networks at scale

Plain Dijkstra on a continental road network (tens of millions of vertices) takes seconds per query — too slow for a navigation app. Production routing engines preprocess the graph. Contraction hierarchies order vertices by importance and add "shortcut" edges that skip unimportant ones; a bidirectional search that only climbs the hierarchy then answers queries in about a millisecond. Other techniques include arc flags, hub labelling and customisable route planning, which separates the graph's structure (preprocessed once) from its weights (updated with live traffic). OSRM and GraphHopper, two open-source routing engines, implement contraction hierarchies. The interview-level takeaway: Dijkstra is the core, bidirectional search halves the work, and preprocessing makes repeated queries fast.

Bidirectional Dijkstra

Running Dijkstra simultaneously from the source (forward) and the target (on the reversed graph, backward), alternating steps, explores roughly two discs of radius d/2 instead of one of radius d — about half the work on road-like graphs. The stopping rule is subtle: stop when the sum of the two heaps' minimum keys is at least the best s–t path found so far (tracked by checking, on every relaxation, whether the vertex has been reached from the other side), not merely when the searches first touch. Getting this wrong returns a slightly suboptimal path, which is a classic implementation bug.

Why the greedy MST algorithms are right

Both Prim and Kruskal rely on the cut property: take any partition of the vertices into two non-empty sets S and V − S, and let e be the lightest edge crossing it. Suppose an MST T does not contain e. Adding e to T creates a cycle, which must cross the cut at some other edge f with weight at least w(e). Replacing f with e gives a spanning tree no heavier than T, so some MST contains e. Prim applies this to the cut between the current tree and the rest; Kruskal to the cut between the two components an edge joins. The companion cycle property — the heaviest edge on any cycle is in no MST (if weights are distinct) — justifies discarding edges, and underlies the critical/pseudo-critical edge problem.
prod:
In the interview room

Dijkstra is a standard "write it from scratch" question, so practise the twelve lines until they are automatic. The common bugs: forgetting the stale-entry check (correct output, but much slower, and wrong if you also do work per pop); marking a vertex visited when it is pushed (that is BFS logic and produces wrong distances in weighted graphs); using a max-heap by accident; pushing (vertex, distance) instead of (distance, vertex), so the heap orders by vertex id; and not handling unreachable vertices (missing keys versus infinity). For Bellman-Ford with a hop limit, the classic bug is relaxing in place instead of from a copy. For Floyd-Warshall, putting the k loop inside.

Interviewers almost always ask "why does Dijkstra fail with negative weights?" — have the one-sentence answer ready (a popped vertex is assumed final, and a later negative edge can undercut it) plus a tiny counterexample: S→A weight 2, S→B weight 5, B→A weight −4; Dijkstra finalises A at 2, but the true distance is 1. Also expect "how would you speed this up for a map app?" (bidirectional search, A* with straight-line heuristic, preprocessing such as contraction hierarchies) and "what if you need the k shortest paths?" (Yen's algorithm, or Dijkstra allowing each vertex to be popped k times).

When the problem is a disguised shortest path — minimum effort, maximum probability, rising water, stops limits — say explicitly what the vertices are, what the edge cost is, and why the cost never improves when a path is extended. That justification is what separates a memorised template from understanding.

On online assessments, shortest-path problems are often stated as costs of tickets, toll roads, or network latencies with additional rules ("at most k transfers", "one discount coupon", "some roads are one-way"). Translating each rule into either a modified edge cost or an extra state dimension is the main work; the algorithm itself is usually plain Dijkstra on the transformed graph.

In real systems

Shortest-path algorithms run the internet and the roads. Link-state routing protocols such as OSPF and IS-IS flood the network topology to every router, and each router runs Dijkstra to build its forwarding table — RFC 2328 specifies the procedure. Distance-vector protocols such as RIP are distributed Bellman-Ford: routers repeatedly share their distance estimates with neighbours, which is why they converge slowly and suffer the "count to infinity" problem when links fail. Navigation services run Dijkstra-derived searches over road graphs with preprocessing (contraction hierarchies in OSRM and GraphHopper) and live traffic weights. Game engines path-find with A*. Logistics companies compute delivery routes on top of shortest-path distance matrices. Minimum spanning trees appear in network design (laying fibre or power lines), in clustering (single-linkage), and as approximations for harder problems such as the travelling salesman problem, where an MST gives a 2-approximation for metric distances.
myths: Dijkstra works with negative edge weights if you are careful.

Dijkstra finalises a vertex when it is popped, assuming no later path can be shorter. A negative edge discovered later can make a finalised vertex's distance wrong, and with lazy deletion the error can propagate or be missed entirely. Use Bellman-Ford (or a DAG order) for negative weights, and no algorithm gives meaningful shortest paths through a negative cycle.
BFS and Dijkstra are unrelated.

Dijkstra is BFS with the FIFO queue replaced by a priority queue keyed on distance. With all weights equal to 1, the priority queue pops vertices in exactly BFS order. 0-1 BFS sits in between, using a deque.
Dijkstra needs a decrease-key operation.

Python implementations push a new (distance, vertex) entry whenever a shorter distance is found, and skip entries whose distance is larger than the recorded best when they are popped. This lazy approach is simpler, and the heap holds at most O(E) entries, so the complexity stays O(E log V).
A minimum spanning tree gives shortest paths between vertices.

An MST minimises the total weight of edges connecting everything; the path between two vertices inside the MST can be much longer than their shortest path in the full graph. They answer different questions: cheapest network versus fastest route.
Cheapest Flights Within K Stops is a plain Dijkstra.

Plain Dijkstra keeps only the best distance per city, but a more expensive route with fewer stops may be the only one that fits the limit. You need state (city, stops) in Dijkstra, or Bellman-Ford run for exactly k + 1 rounds using a copy of the previous round's distances.
lab:
Cross-check Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall on random graphs, and see Dijkstra fail on a negative edge.

  1. Save as sp_lab.py: 
    import heapq, random

def dijkstra(n, edges, s):
    g = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges: g[u].append((v, w))
    dist, h = {s: 0}, [(0, s)]
    while h:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(h)
        if d > dist[u]: continue
        for v, w in g[u]:
            if d + w < dist.get(v, float("inf")): dist[v] = d + w; heapq.heappush(h, (d + w, v))
    return [dist.get(i, float("inf")) for i in range(n)]

def bellman_ford(n, edges, s):
    d = [float("inf")] * n; d[s] = 0
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        for u, v, w in edges:
            if d[u] + w < d[v]: d[v] = d[u] + w
    return d

def floyd(n, edges):
    d = [[0 if i == j else float("inf") for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges: d[u][v] = min(d[u][v], w)
    for k in range(n):
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(n):
                if d[i][k] + d[k][j] < d[i][j]: d[i][j] = d[i][k] + d[k][j]
    return d

for _ in range(500):
    n = random.randint(1, 7)
    edges = [(random.randrange(n), random.randrange(n), random.randint(0, 9)) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 15))]
    fw = floyd(n, edges)
    for s in range(n):
        assert dijkstra(n, edges, s) == bellman_ford(n, edges, s) == fw[s]
print("Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall agree on non-negative graphs")

def dijkstra_strict(n, edges, s):                  # textbook: popped = final, never revisited
    g = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges: g[u].append((v, w))
    dist, done, h = {s: 0}, set(), [(0, s)]
    while h:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(h)
        if u in done: continue
        done.add(u)
        for v, w in g[u]:
            if v not in done and d + w < dist.get(v, float("inf")):
                dist[v] = d + w; heapq.heappush(h, (d + w, v))
    return [dist.get(i, float("inf")) for i in range(n)]

neg = [(0, 1, 2), (0, 2, 5), (2, 1, -4), (1, 3, 1)]   # S=0, A=1, B=2, C=3
print("strict Dijkstra:", dijkstra_strict(4, neg, 0))
print("lazy Dijkstra:  ", dijkstra(4, neg, 0))
print("Bellman-Ford:   ", bellman_ford(4, neg, 0))
  2. Run it. The first line confirms all three algorithms agree on 500 random graphs with non-negative weights, including parallel edges and self-loops.
  3. The last three lines show the counterexample from the interview section, extended with C after A. Bellman-Ford gives A = 1 and C = 2. The strict textbook Dijkstra finalises A at 2 when it is popped and never revisits it, so it reports A = 2 and C = 3 — wrong. The lazy version happens to repair both here, because it re-processes A when a cheaper entry appears; but that repair is not guaranteed in general and, with negative edges, re-processing can blow up to exponential time on crafted graphs.

What this proves: on non-negative graphs all three agree, which validates each implementation; and negative edges invalidate Dijkstra's "popped means final" guarantee even when a particular run gets lucky.
recap: Relaxation updates dist[v] to dist[u] + w(u, v) when that is smaller; every shortest-path algorithm is a strategy for ordering relaxations.
Dijkstra pops the closest unfinished vertex from a min-heap and relaxes its edges; with non-negative weights each popped vertex is final, giving O(E log V).
In Python, use lazy deletion: push new entries on improvement and skip popped entries whose distance exceeds the recorded best.
Dijkstra adapts to other path costs that never improve by extension, such as the maximum edge on a path or a product of probabilities at most one.
Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V − 1 times, handles negative weights in O(V·E), detects negative cycles, and with a copied array per round limits the number of edges used.
Floyd-Warshall computes all-pairs shortest paths in O(V³) with the update dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]).
A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices at least total cost; Prim grows one tree with a heap and Kruskal adds sorted edges with union-find.

Choose by weights and question: BFS for unit weights, 0-1 BFS for 0/1, Dijkstra for non-negative, Bellman-Ford for negative or hop limits, Floyd-Warshall for all pairs on small graphs, topological order on DAGs.
glossary: The shortest distance between every pair of vertices.
Breadth-first search; the special case of Dijkstra when every edge weight is equal.
A single-source shortest-path algorithm that relaxes every edge V − 1 times; works with negative weights and detects negative cycles.
For any division of vertices into two sides, the lightest edge crossing it belongs to some minimum spanning tree.
Directed acyclic graph; shortest paths on a DAG are computed in topological order in O(V + E), even with negative weights.
A single-source shortest-path algorithm for non-negative weights that repeatedly finalises the closest unfinished vertex.
An all-pairs algorithm that, for each intermediate vertex k, tries routing every pair through k; O(V³).
Leaving outdated heap entries in place and ignoring them when popped instead of updating them.
A path minimising its largest edge weight rather than the sum.
A subset of edges that connects all vertices with no cycles and the least total weight.
A cycle whose edge weights sum to a negative number; going round it repeatedly makes paths arbitrarily cheap.
Open Shortest Path First: an internet routing protocol in which each router runs Dijkstra on the network map.
An MST algorithm that grows a single tree, always adding the cheapest edge from the tree to a new vertex.
Checking whether going through u gives a shorter path to v, and updating dist[v] if so.
Shortest distances from one start vertex to every other vertex.
The best distance to a vertex found so far, which may still decrease until the vertex is finalised.
drill:
Model and choose

A ride-hailing company models a city as 2 × 10⁵ intersections and 5 × 10⁵ road segments with travel times. (a) For one rider, find the fastest route from pickup to drop-off. (b) A promotion gives a free ride on at most one segment (its time counts as zero); find the fastest route with the coupon. (c) Each night, compute the travel time between all 300 depots. (d) Design the cheapest set of fibre links to connect the 300 depots given candidate link costs.

Answer

(a) Dijkstra from the pickup with early exit when the drop-off is popped: O(E log V) ≈ 5 × 10⁵ × 18 ≈ 10⁷ heap operations. For production, bidirectional Dijkstra or A* with a straight-line-distance heuristic (divided by the maximum speed so it never overestimates), and preprocessing like contraction hierarchies for millisecond queries. (b) State-expanded Dijkstra over (intersection, coupon_used ∈ {0, 1}): from state (u, 0) an edge can be taken normally to (v, 0) or for free to (v, 1); from (u, 1) only normally to (v, 1). The answer is min(dist[(t, 0)], dist[(t, 1)]). The graph doubles: still O(E log V). (c) 300 runs of Dijkstra, one per depot, O(300 · E log V) ≈ 3 × 10⁹ — heavy but feasible overnight in a compiled language; Floyd-Warshall would be O(V³) on the full 2 × 10⁵-vertex graph (far too slow), so it only applies if you first reduce to a 300 × 300 matrix, which you cannot do without the Dijkstra runs. (d) Minimum spanning tree over the depots with candidate link costs: Kruskal with union-find if candidates are a sparse list, or array-based Prim in O(300²) if every pair is a candidate. Note that (c) and (d) are different questions — travel times are shortest paths, the fibre network is an MST.
qa: E
Why can't BFS find shortest paths in a weighted graph?

BFS counts edges, not weight. A route with three cheap edges can be shorter than one expensive edge, but BFS would reach the destination through the single edge first and stop. Weighted graphs need an algorithm that processes vertices in order of accumulated weight, which is what Dijkstra's priority queue does.
E
Network Delay Time: how long until a signal from k reaches all nodes?

Run Dijkstra from k over the directed weighted edges to get every node's shortest arrival time. If some node is unreachable, return −1; otherwise return the maximum distance, since the last node to receive the signal determines the time. O(E log V).
E
What is relaxation?

For an edge u → v with weight w, relaxation checks whether dist[u] + w is less than dist[v], and if so sets dist[v] = dist[u] + w (and records u as v's parent for path reconstruction). Shortest-path algorithms differ only in the order and number of times they relax edges.
M
Implement Dijkstra's algorithm in Python and give its complexity.

dist = {src: 0}; heap = [(0, src)]. Pop (d, u); if d > dist[u], skip (stale). For each edge (v, w), if d + w < dist.get(v, ∞), set dist[v] and push (d + w, v). Each edge pushes at most once per improvement, so at most E entries: O(E log E) = O(E log V) time and O(V + E) space.
Follow-up: Why is a popped vertex final? — All weights are non-negative, so any other path to it goes through a vertex with distance at least the current one and cannot be shorter.
M
Path With Minimum Effort: minimise the largest height difference along a path in a grid.

Dijkstra where a path's cost is the maximum step rather than the sum: new cost = max(cost so far, |h[u] − h[v]|). The max never decreases when the path is extended, which is the property Dijkstra needs. Alternatively binary search the effort and test reachability with BFS, or union-find edges in increasing order until the corners connect.
M
Path with Maximum Probability.

Each edge has a success probability; the path probability is the product. Run Dijkstra with a max-heap (push negated probabilities), extending with prob × p. Multiplying by p ≤ 1 never increases the value, so a popped vertex's probability is final. Taking −log of probabilities turns it into an ordinary shortest-path problem.
M
Cheapest Flights Within K Stops.

Bellman-Ford limited to k + 1 rounds: each round, copy the distance array and relax every flight using the previous round's distances only, so each round adds at most one edge to any path. After k + 1 rounds, the destination's value is the cheapest with at most k stops. O(k·E). The copy is essential; relaxing in place could chain several flights in one round.
Follow-up: A Dijkstra version? — Use state (cost, city, stops); skip expanding when stops exceed k, and track the best stops per city instead of only the best cost.
M
Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbours at a Threshold Distance.

n ≤ 100, so compute all-pairs shortest paths with Floyd-Warshall in O(n³) = 10⁶. For each city count the others within the threshold; return the city with the smallest count, preferring the largest index on ties. Running Dijkstra from every city also works, O(n·E log n).
M
Compare Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms.

Both build a minimum spanning tree greedily. Kruskal sorts all edges and adds each that joins two components (union-find): O(E log E), good for sparse graphs given as edge lists. Prim grows one tree from a start vertex, adding the cheapest edge leaving it, with a heap in O(E log V), or with an array in O(V²), which is best for dense graphs such as complete graphs of points.
H
Prove that Dijkstra's algorithm is correct, and show where negative edges break it.

Invariant: when u is popped, dist[u] is the true shortest distance. Suppose a shorter path P exists; let y be the first vertex on P not yet finalised, with predecessor x finalised. dist[y] ≤ dist[x] + w(x, y) ≤ length(P) < dist[u], so y would have been popped before u — contradiction. The step 'length(P) is at least the length of its prefix up to y' needs non-negative weights; a negative edge after y could make P shorter than its prefix, and the argument fails.
H
Swim in Rising Water: at time t you can be in any cell with elevation ≤ t; what is the earliest time to reach the bottom-right corner?

The answer is the minimum over paths of the maximum elevation on the path — a minimax path. Dijkstra with cost = max(cost, elevation of next cell) from the top-left gives it in O(n² log n). Equivalent alternatives: binary search on t with a BFS check, or process cells in increasing elevation with union-find until the two corners join.
H
Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges in a Minimum Spanning Tree.

Compute the MST weight W with Kruskal. An edge is critical if excluding it either disconnects the graph or raises the MST weight above W. An edge is pseudo-critical if it is not critical and forcing it into the tree first (union its endpoints, add its weight, then run Kruskal on the rest) still gives weight W. With E edges this is O(E² α(V)) after one sort, fine for E ≤ 200.
