t: Dynamic programming III: intervals, bitmasks, state machines, trees and digits
sum: Richer DP states for harder problems: interval DP that chooses a split or the last action inside a range, bitmask DP over subsets, state-machine DP for stock trading with cooldowns and limits, DP on trees and on implicit DAGs, digit DP for counting numbers, and common speed-ups.
prereq: al21
The five-step recipe; finding a state that captures everything the future depends on.
al22
2D tables, and filling by increasing length for substring problems.
al14
Bottom-up tree recursion that returns values from children to parents.
al13
Bitmasks as a compact representation of a chosen subset.
why:
The DPs in the previous two lessons had natural states: an index into an array, or a pair of indices into two strings. Hard problems need more imagination. "Burst balloons in the order that maximises coins" — the value of each burst depends on which neighbours are still there, which depends on everything burst before. "Visit all 12 nodes of a graph by the shortest walk" — what matters is not only where you are but which nodes you have already seen. "Maximise trading profit with a one-day cooldown after selling" — the same price on the same day is a good or bad move depending on whether you hold a share and whether you sold yesterday. "Count numbers up to 10⁹ with no repeated digits" — you cannot loop over a billion numbers.

Each of these becomes a standard DP once you choose the right shape of state. There are a handful of shapes that cover almost every hard DP in interviews:

  • Interval DP: the state is a range [i, j], and the decision is where to split it or which element to handle last.
  • Bitmask DP: the state includes a subset of items, encoded as the bits of an integer, for problems with up to about 20 items.
  • State-machine DP: the state includes a mode (holding a share, cooling down, transactions used), with transitions between modes each step.
  • Tree DP: each node returns a small summary (a pair or triple) to its parent.
  • DP on implicit DAGs: memoised DFS when moves only go "upwards" in some quantity.
  • Digit DP: counting numbers up to N by processing digits with a "tight" flag.

This lesson teaches each shape with its signature problem, the reasoning that leads to the state, and the fill order. It ends with the most common transition speed-ups. These are the problems that separate a strong DP candidate from an average one, and they reward the habit built in al21: ask what the future depends on, and put exactly that in the state.
primer:
The mental model: choose the right "bookmark"

A DP state is a bookmark: it records where you are in the problem precisely enough that you could hand the rest of the work to someone else, and they would not need to know your history. For a single array, "I have processed the first i elements" is a good bookmark. For harder problems, the right bookmark has a different shape, and recognising the shape is most of the battle.

If the problem repeatedly merges or splits a contiguous sequence — combining stones, cutting a stick, multiplying a chain of matrices, bursting balloons — the bookmark is a range: "the answer for the piece from i to j". If the problem is about which items have been used, and there are few of them, the bookmark is a set, stored as a bitmask. If the problem walks through time with a small number of modes, the bookmark is (time, mode). If the input is a tree, the bookmark is a subtree, plus a flag about its root. If you are counting numbers, the bookmark is (digit position, whether you are still matching the upper bound, what the property needs).

A practical way to find the shape is to look at what the brute force would have to remember. A brute force for Burst Balloons tries every order and must remember which balloons are still present — but if you decide the last balloon in a range, you only need the range's two ends. A brute force for TSP tries every order and must remember the cities visited and where you are — a set and a city, which for 16 cities fits in a bitmask and an index. A brute force for stock trading simulates every buy/sell decision and must remember whether you hold a share and whether you just sold — a mode. In each case the DP state is the brute force's memory, compressed to what the future actually depends on.

Whatever the shape, the rest of the recipe from al21 is unchanged: write the recurrence by thinking about the last decision, set base cases, pick an order in which dependencies come first, and identify the answer. The order is where these shapes differ most: ranges are filled by increasing length; masks by increasing value (adding a bit makes the number larger, so subsets come before supersets); trees in post-order; implicit DAGs by memoised DFS; digits from the most significant.

Where the bookmark analogy breaks: a real bookmark is tiny, but some DP states are big — 2ⁿ masks, n² ranges, n·k (day, transactions) pairs. The cost of a DP is always (number of states) × (work per transition), and with these richer states that product is what tells you whether the approach fits the constraints. A bitmask DP for n = 25 has 3.3 × 10⁷ masks, and multiplying by n for a "last element" makes it too slow; the constraints usually stop at 16–20 for exactly that reason.
body:
Interval DP: split points

The classic is matrix chain multiplication: multiplying matrices A₁A₂…Aₙ, where the order of multiplication (the parenthesisation) changes the cost dramatically. dp[i][j] = the minimum cost to multiply Aᵢ..Aⱼ. The last multiplication splits the chain at some k: (Aᵢ..Aₖ)(Aₖ₊₁..Aⱼ), costing dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + rows(Aᵢ)·cols(Aₖ)·cols(Aⱼ). Try every k. Every term is a shorter range, so fill by increasing length:

for length in range(2, n + 1):
    for i in range(0, n - length + 1):
        j = i + length - 1
        dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j] + cost(i, k, j) for k in range(i, j))

n² states × n choices of k = O(n³). Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick is the same shape: sort the cut positions, add the stick's ends, and let dp[i][j] be the minimum cost of making all cuts strictly between positions cuts[i] and cuts[j]. The first cut k in that piece costs the piece's length, cuts[j] − cuts[i], and leaves two independent pieces: dp[i][j] = cuts[j] − cuts[i] + min(dp[i][k] + dp[k][j]).

Interval DP: the last action — Burst Balloons

Bursting balloon k earns v[left]·v[k]·v[right], where left and right are its current neighbours. If you choose the first balloon to burst in a range, the neighbours of the rest depend on everything that happens later — the subproblems are tangled. Flip the question: which balloon in the open range (i, j) is burst last? When it bursts, every other balloon in (i, j) is gone, so its neighbours are exactly i and j — known boundaries. And the balloons on its left, between i and k, are burst before it with k standing as their right wall; likewise on the right. The two sides are independent.

def max_coins(nums):
    v = [1] + nums + [1]
    n = len(v)
    dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for gap in range(2, n):                   # j - i
        for i in range(0, n - gap):
            j = i + gap
            dp[i][j] = max(dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + v[i] * v[k] * v[j]
                           for k in range(i + 1, j))
    return dp[0][n - 1]

On [3, 1, 5, 8] the answer is 167 (burst 1, 5, 3, 8: 3·1·5 + 3·5·8 + 1·3·8 + 1·8·1 = 15 + 120 + 24 + 8). Padding with 1s turns the edges into ordinary boundaries. The general lesson: when "first choice" tangles the subproblems, try "last choice" — it often fixes the boundary conditions.

Bitmask DP: subsets as states

When a problem asks for the best ordering or assignment of a small number of items (n ≤ 20), the state "which items are already used" is a subset, stored as an integer mask whose bit i is 1 if item i is used. Adding item i is mask | (1 << i); testing it is mask >> i & 1. Because adding a bit always makes the number larger, iterating masks from 0 upwards processes every subset before its supersets — a valid fill order.

Travelling salesman (Held–Karp): dp[mask][v] = the shortest path that starts at city 0, visits exactly the cities in mask, and ends at v. Transition: dp[mask | 1 << u][u] = min(dp[mask][v] + dist[v][u]) for u not in mask. The answer closes the tour: min over v of dp[full][v] + dist[v][0]. That is 2ⁿ·n states with n transitions each, O(2ⁿ·n²) — about 1.7 × 10⁷ for n = 16, compared with 15! ≈ 1.3 × 10¹² orderings.

Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes (unweighted graph, n ≤ 12) is the same idea with BFS instead of a min-DP, because every edge costs 1: BFS over (node, mask) states, starting from every node with its own bit set, and stop at the first full mask.

Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets needs only the mask: dp[mask] = how full the current bucket is after placing exactly the elements in mask (or −1 if impossible). Placing element i is allowed if it fits in the current bucket: dp[mask | bit] = (dp[mask] + nums[i]) % target. When the bucket fills exactly, the modulo resets it to 0 for the next bucket. The answer is dp[full] == 0. O(2ⁿ·n).

def can_partition_k(nums, k):
    total = sum(nums)
    if total % k: return False
    target, n = total // k, len(nums)
    dp = [-1] * (1 << n); dp[0] = 0
    for mask in range(1 << n):
        if dp[mask] < 0: continue
        for i in range(n):
            if not mask >> i & 1 and dp[mask] + nums[i] <= target:
                nxt = mask | 1 << i
                if dp[nxt] < 0:
                    dp[nxt] = (dp[mask] + nums[i]) % target
    return dp[-1] == 0

State-machine DP: the stock family

Six "Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock" problems are one idea: the state is (day, mode), and each day each mode takes the best of the transitions into it (the figure). With one transaction, track the best "hold" (−min price so far) and "sold". With unlimited transactions, hold = max(hold, sold − p), sold = max(sold, hold + p). With a fee, subtract it on selling. With a cooldown, add a third mode for "sold today":

def max_profit_cooldown(prices):
    hold, sold, rest = float("-inf"), 0, 0
    for p in prices:
        hold, sold, rest = max(hold, rest - p), hold + p, max(rest, sold)
    return max(sold, rest)

All three new values are computed from the old ones in one tuple assignment, so no state reads a value already updated today. Trace [1, 2, 3, 0, 2]: the best plan is buy 1, sell 2, cool down, buy 0, sell 2 = 3.

With at most k transactions, the mode includes a counter: buy[t] and sell[t] for t = 1..k, where buy[t] = max(buy[t], sell[t−1] − p) and sell[t] = max(sell[t], buy[t] + p). O(n·k). If k ≥ n/2, the limit cannot bind (you can never make more than n/2 transactions), so fall back to the unlimited version in O(n).

Tree DP: return a tuple

On trees, the natural order is post-order: compute children first, then the parent. When one value per node is not enough, return a small tuple. House Robber III (no parent and child both robbed): each node returns (best with this node robbed, best with it not robbed).

def rob_tree(root):
    def go(node):
        if not node: return (0, 0)
        l, r = go(node.left), go(node.right)
        rob = node.val + l[1] + r[1]                 # children must be skipped
        skip = max(l) + max(r)                       # children free to choose
        return (rob, skip)
    return max(go(root))

Binary Tree Cameras (minimum cameras so every node is watched by itself, its parent or a child) uses three states per node: "has a camera", "covered without a camera", "not covered (needs the parent to cover it)". A greedy version of the same idea places cameras at parents of uncovered leaves. More generally, any "choose a set of nodes with constraints between neighbours" problem on a tree is a tree DP with a few states per node, O(n).

DP on implicit DAGs: memoised DFS

Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix: from any cell, move to a 4-neighbour with a strictly larger value; find the longest path. There is no obvious fill order — the longest path from a cell depends on its larger neighbours, which may be anywhere. But because moves go strictly upwards in value, there are no cycles: the moves form a DAG. Memoised DFS computes each cell's answer once, recursing into neighbours as needed.

from functools import cache
def longest_increasing_path(m):
    R, C = len(m), len(m[0])
    @cache
    def best(r, c):
        return 1 + max([best(nr, nc) for nr, nc in ((r+1, c), (r-1, c), (r, c+1), (r, c-1))
                        if 0 <= nr < R and 0 <= nc < C and m[nr][nc] > m[r][c]],
                       default=0)
    return max(best(r, c) for r in range(R) for c in range(C))

O(R·C) states with four transitions each. No visited set is needed — strictness rules out returning to a cell. On a large grid the recursion can be deep (a long increasing path), so an iterative alternative is to sort cells by value and process them in decreasing order, or peel cells with no larger neighbours level by level (Kahn's algorithm, al18).

Digit DP: counting numbers up to N

"How many integers in [1, N] have property P?", with N up to 10¹⁸. You cannot enumerate them, but you can build them digit by digit. The state is (position, tight, extra), where tight says whether the digits chosen so far equal N's prefix — if so, the next digit cannot exceed N's digit at this position; if not, any digit 0–9 is allowed. "extra" is whatever the property needs: a count of 1s so far, a mask of digits used, the remainder modulo something.

from functools import cache
def count_no_repeat(N):                    # numbers in [1, N] with all distinct digits
    digits = list(map(int, str(N)))
    @cache
    def go(pos, tight, mask, started):
        if pos == len(digits):
            return 1 if started else 0
        limit = digits[pos] if tight else 9
        total = 0
        for d in range(limit + 1):
            if started and mask >> d & 1: continue          # repeated digit
            now_started = started or d != 0
            total += go(pos + 1, tight and d == limit,
                        mask | (1 << d) if now_started else mask, now_started)
        return total
    return go(0, True, 0, False)

The started flag handles leading zeros (007 is really 7, and its zeros should not count as repeated digits). States: positions × 2 × 2¹⁰ × 2 — tiny. "Numbers with Repeated Digits" is N minus this count. "Number of Digit One" can be done with a general digit DP (extra = number of 1s so far) or with the per-position formula in the Q&A.

Speeding up transitions

Sometimes the state is right but each transition loops over many previous states. Three common fixes keep the same DP and make transitions cheaper. Prefix sums: if dp[i] = Σ dp[j] over a range of j, maintain a prefix-sum array of dp so the range sum is O(1). Monotonic deque: if dp[i] = a[i] + max(dp[j]) over a sliding window of j, keep a deque of candidate indices with decreasing dp values (al6) — Jump Game VI and Constrained Subsequence Sum are O(n) this way. Binary search: if the best j is the last one satisfying some sorted condition, find it with bisect, as in weighted interval scheduling (al11) and the tails array of LIS (al21).

Recognising the shape

Merging or splitting contiguous pieces, or "the order in which elements are removed" → interval DP (try "last action" if "first" tangles). Few items (≤ 20) and "which have been used" matters → bitmask DP. Time steps with modes (holding, cooling, transactions) → state machine. Tree input with neighbour constraints → tree DP with a tuple per node. Moves that only go up in some quantity → memoised DFS on the implicit DAG. Counting numbers up to a huge N with a digit property → digit DP.

Practice in the DSA list: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown, Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV, House Robber III, Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix, Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets, Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes, Burst Balloons, Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick, Number of Digit One, Palindrome Partitioning (al13).
deep:
Why "last action" untangles interval problems

An interval DP is valid only if the subproblems for the two sides are independent: the best way to handle the left part must not depend on choices made on the right. In Burst Balloons, if k bursts first, then the left part's rightmost balloon later has a neighbour from the right part — the sides interact. If k bursts last, then for every balloon on the left, k is a wall that is still standing, so the right part is invisible to it. Many problems share this structure ("remove boxes", "strange printer", "minimum score triangulation of a polygon"), and the move from "what happens first" to "what happens last" is the recurring insight. A good test: after fixing your decision k, can you describe the left and right subproblems using only i, k and j? If yes, the decomposition works.

The limits of bitmask DP

Bitmask DP is exponential, so constraints decide everything. 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶ masks is comfortable; with a "last element" dimension, 2²⁰ × 20 = 2 × 10⁷ states is fine in a compiled language and borderline in Python; with an n² transition, Held–Karp TSP is practical up to n ≈ 15–18 in Python. Iterating only over submasks of a mask (sub = (sub - 1) & mask) visits all pairs (mask, submask) in O(3ⁿ) total — the cost of "partition a set into groups" DPs. When n is around 40, split the set in half and meet in the middle (al13). Seeing "n ≤ 16" or "n ≤ 20" in the constraints of an optimisation problem is a strong hint that bitmask DP is intended.

Rerooting: tree DP for every root

Some tree problems ask for an answer for every node as the root — for example, the sum of distances from each node to all others. Running a tree DP from every root is O(n²). Rerooting does it in O(n): first a post-order pass computes subtree information for one root (subtree sizes and the sum of distances within each subtree); then a pre-order pass moves the root from a parent to each child, adjusting the answer with a formula — for sum of distances, moving the root from p to child c changes it by (n − size[c]) − size[c], because size[c] nodes get one step closer and the rest one step farther. "Sum of Distances in Tree" is the classic interview hard for this technique.

Classic DP optimisations, briefly

Beyond prefix sums and monotonic deques, competitive programming has a toolbox for speeding up specific recurrence shapes. Knuth's optimisation reduces some O(n³) interval DPs (such as optimal binary search trees) to O(n²) when the best split point is monotone. Divide-and-conquer optimisation applies when the best transition index is monotone across i. The convex hull trick handles transitions of the form min over j of (m_j·x_i + b_j) in O(log n) or amortised O(1). These are rarely required in interviews, but recognising "the best split point moves monotonically" and saying that it could reduce the complexity is a strong signal in a senior loop.

Profile DP: bitmasks over a moving frontier

Tiling problems ("how many ways to tile a 3 × n board with dominoes?", "count ways to place non-attacking kings on a grid") use a bitmask not for a set of items but for the shape of a frontier: which cells of the current column are already filled by pieces sticking out of the previous column. The DP walks column by column (or cell by cell, the "broken profile" variant), and transitions enumerate how pieces can be placed given the incoming profile. For a board of height h there are 2^h profiles, so this works for small h and any length. It is the same idea as bitmask DP — compress the exact information the future depends on into the bits of an integer — applied to geometry.

Choosing between top-down and bottom-up for rich states

With rich states, memoisation often wins on clarity: digit DP and memoised DFS on implicit DAGs are much easier to write top-down because the reachable states are irregular. Bottom-up wins when the fill order is simple (intervals by length, masks by value), when recursion depth is a risk, and when you want to compress memory (stock problems collapse to a handful of variables). In Python, top-down with @cache also carries a hashing cost per call, so a bottom-up loop over a dense table can be several times faster for the same state count — worth mentioning if performance is tight.
prod:
In the interview room

Hard DP rounds are graded on whether you can name the state and justify it. Say the shape explicitly: "this is interval DP; dp[i][j] is the best for the open range between i and j; I'll choose the last balloon burst". If you cannot find the shape, write the brute-force recursion and look at its arguments — then ask which of them can be compressed (a set into a bitmask, a path into a range, a history into a mode). Interviewers often give credit for a correct memoised recursion even if you do not reach the optimal tabulation.

Common bugs: filling an interval table in the wrong order (reading a range that is not computed yet); forgetting padding or boundary elements (Burst Balloons without the 1s); bitmask precedence errors in Python (mask >> i & 1 works because >> binds tighter than &, but mask & 1 << i also works for the same reason — when in doubt, add parentheses); updating stock states in place so that a buy and a sell happen on the same day; recursion depth in memoised DFS on large grids; and in digit DP, mishandling leading zeros. Test on the smallest inputs and on one with known answer from the problem statement.

State the complexity as states × transitions and check it against the constraints out loud: "n ≤ 300, interval DP is O(n³) = 2.7 × 10⁷, fine" or "n ≤ 16, 2¹⁶ × 16 × 16 ≈ 1.7 × 10⁷, fine". That habit reassures interviewers that you chose the approach for a reason.

On online assessments, the constraints are usually the strongest hint for these shapes. n ≤ 500 with a "merge" or "remove" story suggests interval DP; n ≤ 20 with "assign" or "visit all" suggests bitmask DP; N up to 10¹⁸ with a counting question about digits suggests digit DP; a tree with up to 10⁵ nodes suggests tree DP in O(n). Reading the constraints before the story often reveals the intended state.

Finally, when stuck in the room, it is fine to say "I think this is an interval DP but I'm not sure whether to choose the first or the last action — let me test both on the example". Working one small example by hand with each choice usually reveals which decomposition keeps the sides independent.

In real systems

These DP shapes appear in practical systems. Interval DP underlies optimal parenthesisation in database query planners and in tensor libraries: numpy.einsum_path and the opt_einsum package choose the order of contractions in a chain of tensor products, a direct descendant of matrix chain multiplication, which matters for the cost of large ML computations. Parsing with context-free grammars (the CYK algorithm) is interval DP over spans of a sentence. Bitmask DP appears in vehicle routing for small fleets, in chip design, and in exact solvers for small travelling-salesman instances. State-machine DPs are the Viterbi algorithm in speech recognition and the hidden Markov models in bioinformatics. Tree DP is used in phylogenetics (Felsenstein's algorithm computes likelihoods over evolutionary trees) and in compilers for optimal instruction selection over expression trees. Reinforcement learning's value iteration is a state-machine DP over environment states.
myths: Interval DP always splits at the first chosen element.

For many problems the right decision is the element processed last inside the interval, not first. In Burst Balloons, choosing which balloon bursts last in (i, j) makes its neighbours at that moment exactly i and j, so the two sides become independent. Choosing the first balloon leaves neighbours that depend on later choices.
Bitmask DP is just brute force.

Brute force over orderings of n items is n!; bitmask DP stores one answer per subset (and possibly a last element), 2ⁿ·n states. For n = 16 that is about a million states instead of 2 × 10¹³ orderings. It is exponential, but in a way that fits the small n these problems specify.
Stock problems each need a separate clever trick.

They are one state machine: each day you either hold a share or not (plus extra state for cooldown, fee or transactions used). Write the transitions for buy, sell and rest, and every variant is the same few lines with a different state.
Memoised DFS cannot handle cycles, so it is useless on grids.

It is useless on graphs with cycles, but many grid problems have an implicit ordering that removes cycles. In Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix you may only move to strictly larger values, so the graph of moves is a DAG and memoised DFS gives each cell's answer exactly once.
Digit DP is an advanced competition-only topic.

Its core is simple: count numbers up to N with a property by walking N's digits left to right, carrying a flag for 'still equal to N's prefix so far' plus whatever the property needs. Problems like 'count numbers ≤ N with no repeated digits' or 'how many 1s appear in 1..N' are standard interview hards.
lab:
Verify three of the shapes against brute force on small inputs.

  1. Save as dp3_lab.py: 
    import random
from itertools import permutations
from functools import cache

def burst_dp(nums):
    v = [1] + nums + [1]; n = len(v); dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for gap in range(2, n):
        for i in range(n - gap):
            j = i + gap
            dp[i][j] = max(dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + v[i] * v[k] * v[j] for k in range(i + 1, j))
    return dp[0][n - 1]

def burst_brute(nums):
    best = 0
    for order in permutations(range(len(nums))):
        alive, coins = list(range(len(nums))), 0
        for b in order:
            p = alive.index(b)
            left = nums[alive[p - 1]] if p > 0 else 1
            right = nums[alive[p + 1]] if p + 1 < len(alive) else 1
            coins += left * nums[b] * right; alive.pop(p)
        best = max(best, coins)
    return best

def stock_cooldown(prices):
    hold, sold, rest = float("-inf"), 0, 0
    for p in prices: hold, sold, rest = max(hold, rest - p), hold + p, max(rest, sold)
    return max(sold, rest)

def stock_brute(prices):
    @cache
    def go(i, holding, cool):
        if i == len(prices): return 0
        best = go(i + 1, holding, False)                       # do nothing
        if holding: best = max(best, prices[i] + go(i + 1, False, True))
        elif not cool: best = max(best, -prices[i] + go(i + 1, True, False))
        return best
    return go(0, False, False)

def distinct_digits_count(N):
    return sum(len(set(str(x))) == len(str(x)) for x in range(1, N + 1))

for _ in range(300):
    nums = [random.randint(1, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 6))]
    assert burst_dp(nums) == burst_brute(nums), nums
    prices = [random.randint(0, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 10))]
    assert stock_cooldown(prices) == stock_brute(prices), prices
print("interval DP and state-machine DP match brute force")
print("distinct-digit numbers up to 1000:", distinct_digits_count(1000))
  2. Run it. Burst Balloons is checked against every bursting order; the cooldown state machine against a direct memoised search over (day, holding, in cooldown).
  3. The last line gives a reference value (738) for numbers in [1, 1000] with all distinct digits. Paste the body's count_no_repeat into the file and check that it returns the same number for 1000 and a few random N.

What this proves: "last balloon burst" covers every possible order, and the three-state machine captures exactly the cooldown rule — two of the hardest recurrences in this lesson, confirmed by exhaustive search.
recap: Interval DP defines dp[i][j] over a contiguous range and tries every split point or every 'last action' k inside it, filling by increasing length: typically O(n³).
In Burst Balloons, choosing the last balloon k in (i, j) gives dp[i][j] = max(dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + v[i]·v[k]·v[j]).
Bitmask DP stores answers per subset, often with a last element: dp[mask][v], giving 2ⁿ·n states for n up to about 20.
Stock-trading problems are state machines over (day, holding, extra state); each day applies buy, sell or rest transitions.
Tree DP returns a small tuple from each child, such as (best if this node is used, best if not), combining them in post-order.
Memoised DFS solves DP on implicit DAGs, such as strictly increasing paths in a grid.
Digit DP counts numbers up to N by processing digits with a 'tight' flag that limits the next digit to N's digit.
Speed-ups such as prefix sums, monotonic deques and binary search reduce the cost of transitions without changing the state.
glossary: An integer whose bits represent membership of items in a set; bit i set means item i is included.
Breadth-first search, used for unweighted bitmask searches like visiting all nodes; and directed acyclic graph, the structure that makes memoised DFS valid.
Dynamic programming whose state includes a subset of items encoded as a bitmask.
Counting numbers in a range with some digit property by processing digits one at a time with a 'tight' flag.
Dynamic programming over contiguous ranges [i, j], combining answers for sub-ranges.
Choosing the parenthesisation of a product of matrices that minimises scalar multiplications; the classic interval DP.
Depth-first search that caches each node's result, computing DP over an implicit DAG.
Processing a node after its children, so children's DP values are available.
DP whose state includes a mode (such as holding or not holding) with transitions between modes.
In digit DP, whether the digits chosen so far equal the bound's prefix, which limits the next digit.
Finding the shortest route visiting every city once; solved exactly for small n by bitmask DP in O(2ⁿ·n²).
Dynamic programming on a tree where each node's value is computed from its children's values.
drill:
Name the shape, then the state

For each problem, name the DP shape and define the state in one sentence. (a) Merge piles of stones in a row, two adjacent piles at a time, each merge costing the sum of the two piles; minimise the total cost. (b) Assign n ≤ 15 workers to n jobs, one each, minimising total cost from a cost matrix. (c) A robot on a number line receives commands; each day it may hold position, or move, but cannot move two days in a row; maximise reward. (d) Count integers in [1, N] (N ≤ 10¹⁵) whose digit sum is divisible by 7. (e) In a tree, choose the maximum-weight set of nodes such that no two chosen nodes are adjacent.

Answer

(a) Interval DP: dp[i][j] = the minimum cost to merge piles i..j into one pile; the last merge combines the merged left part i..k with the merged right part k+1..j, costing dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + sum(i..j) (prefix sums make the range sum O(1)). O(n³). (b) Bitmask DP: dp[mask] = the minimum cost of assigning the first popcount(mask) workers to the jobs in mask; worker number popcount(mask) takes some job not in mask. O(2ⁿ·n) ≈ 5 × 10⁵ for n = 15. (c) State machine: dp[day][moved_yesterday ∈ {0, 1}] with transitions "hold" (to state 0) and "move" (only from state 0, to state 1); O(days). (d) Digit DP: state (position, tight, digit_sum mod 7, started); count completions where the final remainder is 0. About 16 × 2 × 7 × 2 states with 10 transitions each. (e) Tree DP: each node returns (best if chosen, best if not chosen); chosen = weight + Σ child.not_chosen, not chosen = Σ max(child.chosen, child.not_chosen). O(n) — the tree version of House Robber.
qa: E
How do you represent and manipulate a subset as a bitmask?

Use an integer whose bit i is 1 when item i is in the subset. Test membership with (mask >> i) & 1, add an item with mask | (1 << i), remove it with mask & ~(1 << i), and the full set of n items is (1 << n) − 1. Iterating mask from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 visits every subset, and every subset before its supersets, which is a valid DP order.
E
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with unlimited transactions: why is it a state machine?

Each day you are either holding a share or not, and the best profit in each mode depends only on yesterday's two values: hold = max(hold, free − price), free = max(free, hold + price). Answer free at the end. Equivalently, sum every positive day-to-day increase. O(n), O(1) space.
M
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown.

Three states per day: hold (own a share), sold (sold today, so tomorrow is a cooldown), rest (not holding, free to buy). Transitions: hold = max(hold, rest − price); sold = hold_prev + price; rest = max(rest, sold_prev). Answer max(sold, rest) at the end. O(n) time, O(1) space.
M
House Robber III: houses form a binary tree; adjacent (parent–child) houses cannot both be robbed.

Post-order DFS returning a pair per node: rob = node.val + left.skip + right.skip, skip = max(left.rob, left.skip) + max(right.rob, right.skip). The answer is max of the root's pair. O(n) time, O(h) stack.
M
Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix.

Moves go to strictly larger neighbours, so the move graph is a DAG. Memoised DFS: longest(r, c) = 1 + max(longest(nr, nc)) over larger neighbours. Each cell is computed once, so O(R·C). Alternatively peel cells in increasing order of value (topological order) and count levels.
Follow-up: Why no visited set? — There can be no cycle along strictly increasing values, so a path never returns to a cell.
M
Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets with bitmask DP.

dp[mask] = the fill level of the current bucket after placing the elements in mask, or −1 if unreachable. For each reachable mask and unused i with dp[mask] + nums[i] ≤ target, set dp[mask | 1 << i] = (dp[mask] + nums[i]) % target. The answer is dp[full] == 0. O(2ⁿ·n), which is about 10⁶ for n = 16.
M
What is interval DP, and how do you fill the table?

The state is a contiguous range dp[i][j]; the recurrence tries each split or last action k between i and j and combines dp[i][k] and dp[k][j] (or dp[k + 1][j]) with a cost for the combination. Because every term is a shorter range, fill by increasing length, or by i decreasing and j increasing. Typical cost O(n³).
H
Burst Balloons.

Pad the array with 1 at both ends. dp[i][j] = maximum coins from bursting every balloon strictly between i and j. Choose k as the last balloon burst in (i, j); at that moment its neighbours are i and j, so dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + v[i]·v[k]·v[j]. Fill by increasing gap. O(n³).
Follow-up: Why last, not first? — If k bursts first, the neighbours of the remaining balloons change depending on later choices, so the subproblems are not independent.
H
Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick.

Sort the cut positions and add 0 and n as ends. dp[i][j] = the minimum cost to make all cuts strictly between positions cuts[i] and cuts[j]. The first cut k in that piece costs its length cuts[j] − cuts[i], plus dp[i][k] + dp[k][j]. Fill by increasing gap. O(m³) for m cuts.
H
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV with at most k transactions.

State machine with a transaction counter: buy[t] = max(buy[t], sell[t − 1] − price), sell[t] = max(sell[t], buy[t] + price), for t from 1 to k, each day. Answer sell[k]. O(n·k). If k ≥ n/2 the limit never binds; sum every positive day-to-day increase in O(n).
H
Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes in an unweighted graph (n ≤ 12).

BFS over states (node, visited mask), starting from every node with its own bit set at distance 0. The first state whose mask is full gives the answer. There are n·2ⁿ states and each expands to its neighbours: O(2ⁿ·n²). This is TSP-style bitmask search with BFS because edges are unweighted.
H
Count how many times the digit 1 appears in all numbers from 1 to n.

Count per digit position. For position with place value p, split n into high = n // (10p), cur = (n // p) % 10, low = n % p. Ones contributed at this position: high·p, plus p if cur > 1, plus low + 1 if cur == 1. Sum over positions: O(log n). A general digit DP (position, count so far, tight) also works.
H
Palindrome Partitioning II: the minimum cuts to split a string into palindromes.

Precompute isPal[i][j] by increasing length in O(n²). Then cuts[j] = the minimum cuts for s[:j + 1] = 0 if s[0..j] is a palindrome, else min(cuts[i − 1] + 1) over i with s[i..j] a palindrome. O(n²) overall. Expanding around centres can fill the cuts array without the full table.
H
How would you speed up a DP whose transition is a max over a sliding range of previous states?

If dp[i] = a[i] + max(dp[j]) for j in [i − k, i − 1], keep a monotonic deque of indices with decreasing dp values, popping indices that leave the window from the front and dominated ones from the back. Each transition becomes O(1) amortised, so O(n) instead of O(n·k). Similar tricks use prefix sums for range sums and binary search when the best j moves monotonically.

t: Bit manipulation: binary tricks, XOR puzzles and bitsets
sum: How integers look in binary and two's complement, the operators and identities that matter (x & (x−1), x & −x, XOR cancellation), counting and reversing bits, the Single Number family, adding without +, range AND, subsets as masks, and bitsets as fast boolean arrays — with Python's unbounded-integer caveats.
prereq: al4
XOR-based and counting approaches to finding unique elements were previewed alongside hash maps.
al13
Subsets of n items can be enumerated as the integers 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.
why:
A file on a Unix system has permissions like rwxr-x---: read, write and execute for the owner, the group and everyone else. The system stores all nine flags in the bits of one small integer, and checking "can the group execute this?" is a single AND with a mask. A database answers "customers who are in Mumbai AND bought in the last week AND have opted into email" by AND-ing three bitmaps of millions of bits each — one CPU instruction handles 64 customers at a time. A chess engine stores the position of all white pawns as one 64-bit integer, one bit per square, and computes all their possible captures with two shifts and an AND.

Bit manipulation is the art of treating an integer as a row of 32 or 64 independent switches and operating on all of them at once. In interviews it appears in three ways. There are direct puzzles — Single Number, Missing Number, Counting Bits, Reverse Bits, Sum of Two Integers, Bitwise AND of a Range — each solved by one or two identities. There are bitmasks as compact sets, which you have already used for subsets (al13) and bitmask DP (al23). And there are optimisations, where packing booleans into bits makes a dynamic programme or a set operation many times faster.

The good news is that a small toolkit covers almost all of it: how numbers look in binary and two's complement, the five operators, and a handful of identities — x & (x − 1) clears the lowest set bit, x & −x isolates it, a ^ a = 0. This lesson builds that toolkit, applies it to each classic problem with a trace, and points out the traps specific to Python, whose integers never overflow and whose ~x does not mean what it means in C.
primer:
The mental model: a row of light switches

Picture a row of light switches, numbered from the right starting at 0. Switch i, when on, contributes 2ⁱ to the total. The number 13 is switches 3, 2 and 0 on: 8 + 4 + 1, written 1101 in binary. Every non-negative integer is exactly one pattern of switches. Bitwise operators act on every switch position independently and simultaneously:

OperatorRule per positionExample (12 op 10 = 1100 op 1010)
AND &1 if both are 11000 = 8
OR |1 if either is 11110 = 14
XOR ^1 if they differ0110 = 6
NOT ~flip (see two's complement below)~12 = −13 in Python
shift << k, >> kmove every bit k places12 << 1 = 24, 12 >> 2 = 3

With these, single switches are easy to handle. Test bit i: (x >> i) & 1. Turn it on: x | (1 << i). Turn it off: x & ~(1 << i). Flip it: x ^ (1 << i).

Negative numbers: two's complement

Computers store signed integers in two's complement: to negate x, flip all its bits and add one. In 8 bits, 5 is 00000101 and −5 is 11111011. The top bit acts as the sign. Two consequences matter constantly. First, ~x = −x − 1 (flipping is "negate and subtract one"). Second, x & −x isolates the lowest set bit: −x flips every bit above the lowest 1 of x and keeps that 1 and the zeros below it, so AND-ing leaves only that single bit.

Where the light-switch analogy breaks: real switch panels have a fixed number of switches, but Python integers have unlimited precision. There is no 32nd bit that falls off when you shift left, no overflow, and negative numbers behave as if they had infinitely many leading 1s. So ~5 is −6, not 4294967290, and 1 << 100 is a perfectly good integer. Most interview problems assume 32-bit integers; in Python you emulate that by AND-ing with 0xFFFFFFFF (32 ones) and, if a signed result is wanted, converting values of 2³¹ or more back to negatives with x − (1 << 32). We will need this for Sum of Two Integers and Single Number II.

It also helps to remember a few values by sight: 0xFF is eight 1s (255), 0xFFFFFFFF is thirty-two 1s (4,294,967,295), 2¹⁰ ≈ 10³, 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶, 2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹, and 2³¹ − 1 = 2,147,483,647 is the largest signed 32-bit integer. These come up whenever you reason about masks, overflow or whether a value fits in a bitmask.

A last piece of intuition: XOR is "addition without carrying" — 1 ^ 1 = 0 drops the carry that ordinary addition would produce. That one view explains both the XOR cancellation tricks and the carry-based addition algorithm below.
body:
The toolkit, in one place

(x >> i) & 1          # bit i of x
x | (1 << i)           # set bit i
x & ~(1 << i)          # clear bit i
x ^ (1 << i)           # toggle bit i
x & (x - 1)            # clear the lowest set bit
x & -x                 # isolate the lowest set bit
(1 << n) - 1           # n ones: the full set of n items
x.bit_length()         # number of bits needed (position of highest 1, plus 1)
x.bit_count()          # number of 1 bits (Python 3.10+)
a ^ a == 0, a ^ 0 == a # XOR cancels and is its own inverse

Learn these as phrases. In an interview you should be able to say "clear the lowest set bit with x & (x − 1)" without deriving it, then explain the derivation if asked.

Powers of two and counting bits

A power of two has exactly one set bit. Clearing it leaves zero, so n > 0 and n & (n − 1) == 0 tests it. The n > 0 guard matters: 0 & −1 is 0 too, and 0 is not a power of two.

Counting set bits (the popcount) can loop over all bit positions, but Kernighan's method loops once per set bit:

def hamming_weight(n):
    count = 0
    while n:
        n &= n - 1          # drop the lowest 1
        count += 1
    return count

For 44 (101100): 44 → 40 → 32 → 0, three iterations. Counting Bits asks for the popcount of every number from 0 to n. Recomputing each is O(n log n); a DP over integers is O(n). Shifting i right by one drops its lowest bit, so bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1). Or remove the lowest set bit: bits[i] = bits[i & (i − 1)] + 1. Both read an already-computed smaller index.

XOR cancellation: Single Number and Missing Number

XOR has three properties that make it a cancellation machine: a ^ a = 0, a ^ 0 = a, and order does not matter (it is commutative and associative). XOR a list where every value appears twice except one, and every pair vanishes:

def single_number(nums):
    x = 0
    for v in nums:
        x ^= v
    return x

[4, 1, 2, 1, 2]: 4 ^ 1 ^ 2 ^ 1 ^ 2 = 4 ^ (1 ^ 1) ^ (2 ^ 2) = 4. O(n) time and O(1) space — the reason interviewers ask it is to see whether you know XOR, since a hash set is the obvious O(n)-space answer. Missing Number (n distinct numbers from 0..n, one missing) XORs all indices 0..n together with all values: every present number cancels with its own index, and the missing one remains.

Two unique numbers: split by a differing bit

"Every number appears twice except two; find both." XOR everything and you get x = a ^ b — not either number, but their difference pattern. Since a ≠ b, x has at least one set bit, and at any set bit of x, a and b differ. Take the lowest one, d = x & −x, and split all numbers into two groups by whether they have that bit. a and b land in different groups; every duplicate pair lands together in one group. XOR each group separately:

def single_number_iii(nums):
    x = 0
    for v in nums: x ^= v
    d = x & -x                       # a bit where the two singles differ
    a = 0
    for v in nums:
        if v & d: a ^= v
    return [a, x ^ a]

This works with negative numbers in Python too, because Python's & and − follow two's complement with infinite sign extension.

Three of each: count bits modulo 3

"Every number appears three times except one." XOR no longer cancels triples. Look at one bit position: among the tripled numbers, the count of 1s at that position is a multiple of 3, so the total count modulo 3 is exactly the unique number's bit there. Do this for all 32 positions:

def single_number_ii(nums):
    result = 0
    for i in range(32):
        if sum((v >> i) & 1 for v in nums) % 3:
            result |= 1 << i
    return result - (1 << 32) if result >= 1 << 31 else result   # back to signed

The final line converts a 32-bit two's complement pattern back to a Python negative number. A cleverer O(n) version keeps two variables, ones and twos, as a per-bit counter that cycles 0 → 1 → 2 → 0: ones = (ones ^ v) & ~twos; twos = (twos ^ v) & ~ones. After all numbers, ones holds the bits that appeared once (mod 3) — the answer. It is worth knowing exists; the bit-count version is easier to explain.

Reversing bits

Reverse a 32-bit unsigned integer: take bits off the right of n and push them onto the right of the result, 32 times.

def reverse_bits(n):
    r = 0
    for _ in range(32):
        r = (r << 1) | (n & 1)
        n >>= 1
    return r

Looping exactly 32 times (not "while n") matters: the zeros in the high positions of n must become zeros in the low positions of r, and stopping as soon as n reaches zero would leave r too short — reversing 1 would give 1 instead of 2³¹. The interview follow-up "called millions of times?" has two answers: a 256-entry table of reversed bytes, combining four lookups; or the divide-and-conquer swap — swap the 16-bit halves, then the bytes within each half, then the nibbles, pairs and single bits, each with a mask and two shifts, five steps in total.

Adding without +

"Sum of Two Integers" forbids + and −. Binary addition at each position produces a sum bit (a XOR b, ignoring carry) and a carry bit (a AND b) that moves one place left. So repeat: compute the carry-free sum and the carries, then add those two numbers the same way, until there are no carries.

def get_sum(a, b):
    MASK, MAX = 0xFFFFFFFF, 0x7FFFFFFF
    while b & MASK:
        a, b = (a ^ b) & MASK, ((a & b) << 1) & MASK
    a &= MASK
    return a if a <= MAX else ~(a ^ MASK)        # reinterpret as signed 32-bit

Trace 5 + 3: a = 101, b = 011 → sum 110, carry 010 → sum 100, carry 100 → sum 000, carry 1000 → sum 1000, carry 0. Result 8. In a fixed-width language, the carry eventually shifts out of the top and the loop ends. In Python, without the mask, adding a negative number sends the carry marching left forever, because negative numbers have infinitely many 1s. Masking to 32 bits restores the fixed width, and the last line turns a pattern with the top bit set back into a negative Python integer (~(a ^ MASK) equals a − 2³²).

AND over a range

"Bitwise AND of all numbers from left to right." Iterating could be 2³¹ steps. Think per bit: if left and right differ at some bit position, then somewhere between them that bit goes from 0 to 1 or wraps, and in fact every lower position takes both values; the AND of a range that contains both a 0 and a 1 at a position is 0 there. So only the common binary prefix of left and right survives.

def range_bitwise_and(left, right):
    shift = 0
    while left != right:
        left >>= 1; right >>= 1; shift += 1
    return left << shift

For [5, 7] = [101, 111]: the common prefix is 1, followed by two zeros → 100 = 4. O(log right).

Masks as sets

A bitmask represents a subset of up to ~60 items in one integer: union is |, intersection &, difference a & ~b, membership a test of one bit, size a popcount. Enumerating all subsets of n items is for mask in range(1 << n). Enumerating all submasks of a given mask — every subset of a subset — uses a neat loop that visits each exactly once:

sub = mask
while sub:
    ...                       # process sub
    sub = (sub - 1) & mask    # next smaller submask
# (process the empty submask separately if needed)

Subtracting one flips the lowest set bit and the bits below it; AND-ing with mask throws away bits not in the mask, giving the next smaller subset. Summed over all masks of n bits, this visits 3ⁿ (mask, submask) pairs — the cost of DPs that partition a set into groups. Masks also encode small state in searches: keys collected in a maze (al17), visited nodes in TSP (al23), letters present in a word ("maximum product of word lengths" checks that two words share no letters with a single AND of their 26-bit masks).

Bitsets: many booleans per operation

A Python integer can act as a bitset of any length: bit s is one boolean. Operations on it run in C over 30- or 64-bit chunks, so one Python-level operation processes thousands of booleans. The classic use is subset-sum feasibility: "which sums can a subset of these numbers make?".

def can_reach(nums, target):
    bits = 1                         # only sum 0 is reachable at first
    for x in nums:
        bits |= bits << x            # every reachable s makes s + x reachable
    return (bits >> target) & 1 == 1

The shift-and-OR is the whole 0/1 knapsack inner loop (al22) in one expression, and in Python it is typically tens of times faster than iterating over a list. The same idea speeds up "which pairs of rows share a 1" (AND two bitsets and test for non-zero), graph reachability with adjacency rows as bitsets, and Floyd–Warshall-style transitive closure.

Checking letters and flags with masks

A 26-bit mask summarises which letters a word contains, and many string questions become one AND or one comparison. Two words share no letters when their masks AND to zero. A word is a permutation of the letters available on a keyboard row when its mask is a subset of the row's mask: word_mask & ~row_mask == 0. "Count the strings that can be rearranged into a palindrome" uses a parity mask instead: toggle bit c for every occurrence of letter c (XOR), and the string qualifies when at most one bit remains set — m & (m − 1) == 0. The same parity-mask idea, combined with prefix XORs and a hash map, counts substrings in which every vowel appears an even number of times (al3): two prefixes with the same parity mask bound such a substring.

Recognising the pattern

Think bits when the problem mentions XOR, binary, powers of two, "appears twice/three times", "without using + or ×", flags or permissions, small sets of items, or when a boolean DP or set operation is too slow. Then reach for the toolkit: cancellation with XOR, per-bit counting, lowest-set-bit tricks, masks as sets, or a bitset.

Practice in the DSA list: Single Number, Number of 1 Bits, Counting Bits, Missing Number, Reverse Bits, Single Number II, Sum of Two Integers, Bitwise AND of Numbers Range, Maximum XOR of Two Numbers (al15), Subsets via bitmasks (al13).
deep:
Two's complement, precisely

In n-bit two's complement, the bit pattern b represents b if the top bit is 0 and b − 2ⁿ if it is 1. That single rule explains everything: addition and subtraction work identically for signed and unsigned numbers (the hardware does not care), −x = 2ⁿ − x = ~x + 1, the range is −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1, and the most negative number has no positive counterpart (−(−128) overflows back to −128 in 8 bits). Overflow is "wrapping modulo 2ⁿ", which is defined behaviour for unsigned integers in C but undefined for signed ones — a real source of security bugs. Python sidesteps it by having no fixed width; conceptually, a Python negative number is a two's complement pattern with infinitely many leading 1s, which is why &, |, ^ and shifts behave consistently on negatives.

Popcount and friends in hardware

Modern CPUs implement several of this lesson's operations as single instructions: popcount (POPCNT on x86), count leading zeros (LZCNT) and count trailing zeros (TZCNT), which give the position of the highest and lowest set bit. Compilers expose them as built-ins, and Python's int.bit_count() and int.bit_length() use them. Without hardware support, popcount on a 64-bit word can be done in about a dozen operations by summing bits in parallel: add adjacent bits, then adjacent pairs, then nibbles, using masks like 0x5555… and 0x3333… — the "SWAR" (SIMD within a register) technique from Hacker's Delight. Knowing that popcount is O(1) in practice justifies treating bitmask DP transitions as constant time.

XOR as linear algebra

XOR is addition modulo 2 in each bit, so a set of numbers is a set of vectors over the field with two elements, and XOR-ing a subset is a linear combination. This view solves "maximum XOR of any subset": build a linear basis (Gaussian elimination over bits, keeping at most one basis vector per leading bit), then greedily XOR basis vectors into the answer from the top bit down. It also answers "can x be formed as an XOR of some subset?" and "how many distinct subset XORs are there?" (2^rank). These are competitive-programming staples and occasionally appear as hard interview questions; recognising XOR as linear algebra is the key.

Gray code and other orderings

The Gray code orders all n-bit numbers so that consecutive ones differ in exactly one bit: g = i ^ (i >> 1). It appears in rotary encoders (a mis-read between positions is off by one position, not wildly wrong), in error-tolerant communications, and in enumerating subsets so that each step adds or removes exactly one element — which lets some search algorithms update a running total in O(1) per subset. The inverse transformation recovers i from g by XOR-ing all right shifts. A "Gray Code" interview question is a direct application of the formula.

Bitboards: a whole board in one integer

Chess engines represent a position as a dozen 64-bit integers, one per piece type and colour, with bit i set if such a piece stands on square i. All white pawns' forward moves are (white_pawns << 8) & empty; their captures to one side are a shift by 7 or 9 with a mask that removes wrap-around across the board's edge. Sliding pieces use precomputed attack tables indexed by "magic" multiplications of the occupied-squares mask. One machine instruction then updates 64 squares at once, which is why bitboard engines like Stockfish evaluate tens of millions of positions per second. The general lesson is that when a state is a small grid of booleans, packing it into machine words turns loops over cells into single arithmetic operations.

When bit tricks hurt

Bit hacks can make code unreadable and, in high-level languages, slower than the obvious version, because the interpreter overhead dominates. In Python, bin(x).count("1") or x.bit_count() beats a hand-written Kernighan loop; a set of small integers is often clearer than a bitmask unless you need hashing or speed. Use bit manipulation where it is the natural model (flags, masks as DP state, XOR puzzles) or where it buys a real speed-up (bitsets), and explain it with a comment. Interviewers value correct, readable code over cleverness for its own sake.
prod:
In the interview room

Bit problems are short, so precision and explanation decide the score. The frequent bugs: operator precedence (in Python, & binds looser than == and comparisons, so x & 1 == 0 means x & (1 == 0) — always parenthesise: (x & 1) == 0); forgetting the n > 0 guard in power-of-two checks; looping "while n" instead of exactly 32 times in Reverse Bits; and, above all, assuming 32-bit overflow in Python, which leads to infinite loops in carry-based addition and wrong signs in Single Number II. Say explicitly when you are emulating 32 bits and why.

Expect "explain why that works" for every trick. Have the one-line justifications ready: x & (x − 1) — "subtracting one flips the lowest 1 and everything below it"; x & −x — "two's complement keeps the lowest 1 and flips everything above"; XOR cancellation — "a ^ a = 0, order does not matter". Interviewers are checking understanding, not memory.

Offer the non-bit alternative too: a Counter for Single Number II, arithmetic sum for Missing Number, a loop for popcount. Then explain what the bit version buys (O(1) space, or speed). That shows judgement.

On online assessments, bit problems sometimes hide behind constraints like "values up to 10⁹ and n up to 10⁵, find the pair maximising a ^ b" or "answer queries about subsets of at most 20 features". Recognising that 10⁹ fits in 30 bits (so per-bit reasoning is cheap) or that 20 features fit in a mask is often the whole trick.

When an interviewer asks for O(1) space on a counting problem (Single Number II, Find the Duplicate), per-bit counting is a reliable fallback: there are only 32 bit positions, so counting each position across the array is O(32·n) time and constant extra memory, and it adapts to "appears k times" for any k by taking counts modulo k.

In real systems

Bits are the native language of systems software. Unix file permissions (chmod 750) are three groups of three bits; network software tests and sets flags in packet headers with masks, and IP routing compares addresses under subnet masks (a /24 network is the top 24 bits). Feature flags and capability sets are often bitfields. Databases and search engines use bitmap indexes: Roaring Bitmaps, used by Apache Lucene, Spark, Druid and many others, compress sparse bitsets and perform AND/OR across millions of documents in microseconds. Bloom filters are a bit array plus hashing (al4). Chess and other board-game engines represent positions as bitboards — one 64-bit integer per piece type — and generate moves with shifts and masks, which is a major reason they search millions of positions per second. Hash functions and random-number generators (xorshift, FNV, MurmurHash) are built from XORs, shifts and multiplications. Compression formats pack variable-length codes into bit streams. The interview identities are the everyday tools of all of these.
myths: Bit tricks are only for low-level programmers.

They show up in everyday interview problems (Single Number, Counting Bits, subsets as masks), in bitmask DP, in permission flags, in network masks and in database bitmap indexes. A handful of identities covers almost all of them.
In Python, ~x flips the bits of a 32-bit number.

Python integers have unlimited precision, so ~x is −x − 1, not a 32-bit flip. To emulate fixed-width behaviour, mask with 0xFFFFFFFF and convert values above 0x7FFFFFFF back to negatives when a signed result is needed.
Right-shifting a negative number divides it by two exactly.

Arithmetic right shift rounds towards negative infinity: −7 >> 1 is −4, while integer division truncating towards zero (as in C, Java and Python's int(−7 / 2)) gives −3. Python's −7 // 2 is also −4, matching the shift. Be explicit when negatives are possible.
Counting set bits needs a loop over all 32 bits.

x & (x − 1) clears the lowest set bit, so a loop that applies it until x is 0 runs once per set bit (Kernighan's method). Python 3.10+ has int.bit_count(), and CPUs have a single popcount instruction.
XOR tricks only work when exactly one element is unique.

With two unique elements, XOR everything to get a ^ b, pick any set bit of that result (they differ there), and split the numbers into two groups by that bit; XOR each group to recover a and b. With 'every element appears three times except one', count each bit position modulo 3.
lab:
Verify the classic tricks against straightforward versions, including negative numbers.

  1. Save as bits_lab.py: 
    import random
from collections import Counter

def get_sum(a, b):
    MASK, MAX = 0xFFFFFFFF, 0x7FFFFFFF
    while b & MASK:
        a, b = (a ^ b) & MASK, ((a & b) << 1) & MASK
    a &= MASK
    return a if a <= MAX else ~(a ^ MASK)

def single_ii(nums):
    r = 0
    for i in range(32):
        if sum((v >> i) & 1 for v in nums) % 3: r |= 1 << i
    return r - (1 << 32) if r >= 1 << 31 else r

def single_iii(nums):
    x = 0
    for v in nums: x ^= v
    d, a = x & -x, 0
    for v in nums:
        if v & d: a ^= v
    return sorted([a, x ^ a])

def range_and(l, r):
    s = 0
    while l != r: l >>= 1; r >>= 1; s += 1
    return l << s

for _ in range(2000):
    a, b = random.randint(-1000, 1000), random.randint(-1000, 1000)
    assert get_sum(a, b) == a + b
    pool = random.sample(range(-50, 50), 5)
    u = pool[0]; nums = [u] + [v for v in pool[1:] for _ in range(3)]; random.shuffle(nums)
    assert single_ii(nums) == u
    x, y = pool[:2]; nums = [x, y] + [v for v in pool[2:] for _ in range(2)]
    assert single_iii(nums) == sorted([x, y])
    l = random.randint(0, 200); r = random.randint(l, 260)
    want = l
    for v in range(l, r + 1): want &= v
    assert range_and(l, r) == want
    n = random.randint(0, 10**6)
    assert all([n & (n - 1) == n - (n & -n), bin(n).count("1") == n.bit_count()])
print("bit tricks match direct computation, including negatives")
  2. Run it (Python 3.10+ for bit_count). Every check compares a trick with the obvious computation: real addition, a Counter-free unique search, a full range AND.
  3. Remove the & MASK from the loop in get_sum and call get_sum(-1, 1): it never terminates in Python, because the carry keeps moving left through infinitely many sign bits. Press Ctrl+C.

What this proves: the identities hold for negative numbers in Python's two's-complement model, and fixed-width masking is required exactly where an algorithm relies on bits falling off the top.
recap: An integer is a sum of powers of two; bit i is (x >> i) & 1, and AND, OR, XOR, NOT and shifts operate on all bits at once.
Negative integers use two's complement: −x equals ~x + 1, so x & −x isolates the lowest set bit.
x & (x − 1) clears the lowest set bit; it tests powers of two (result 0) and counts set bits one per iteration.
XOR is its own inverse (a ^ a = 0, a ^ 0 = a), so XOR-ing a list cancels pairs and leaves the unpaired value.
Counting Bits fills bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1) in O(n).
Addition without + repeats: sum = a ^ b, carry = (a & b) << 1, until the carry is 0; in Python mask to 32 bits.
The AND of all numbers in [left, right] is their common binary prefix followed by zeros.
A Python integer can serve as a bitset: bits |= bits << x performs a whole subset-sum update in one operation.
glossary: Bitwise operation: a result bit is 1 only if both input bits are 1.
A binary digit, 0 or 1; bit i of x has value 2ⁱ.
An integer used as a set of flags or a subset, one bit per element.
A compact boolean array stored in the bits of machine words, so many booleans are processed per operation.
Processor instructions that count set bits, leading zeros and trailing zeros of a word in one step.
The bit with value 1 (bit 0); the 'lowest set bit' is the least significant bit that is 1.
A value used with AND, OR or XOR to select, set or flip particular bits.
Bitwise operation that flips every bit; in Python, ~x equals −x − 1.
Bitwise operation: a result bit is 1 if either input bit is 1.
The number of 1 bits in an integer, also called the Hamming weight.
Moving all bits left or right by k positions; x << k multiplies by 2ᵏ and x >> k floors division by 2ᵏ.
SIMD within a register: processing several small fields packed in one machine word in parallel with ordinary arithmetic and masks.
The standard representation of signed integers, in which −x is ~x + 1 and the top bit indicates the sign.
Exclusive or: a result bit is 1 if the input bits differ; a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a.
drill:
Use bits to save memory or time

(a) "Maximum Product of Word Lengths": find the maximum len(a) × len(b) over pairs of words that share no letters; there are up to 1,000 words of up to 1,000 letters. (b) "Find the Duplicate Number" in an array of n + 1 values in 1..n with O(1) extra space and without modifying the array — give a bit-based solution as an alternative to Floyd's cycle detection. (c) Count the subsets of 25 items whose total weight is at most W, for many different W values up to 10⁶.

Answer

(a) Precompute a 26-bit mask per word (bit c set if letter c appears) in O(total letters). Two words share no letters exactly when mask[i] & mask[j] == 0, an O(1) check, so all pairs cost O(n²) = 10⁶ checks instead of comparing letter sets. Words with the same mask can be collapsed, keeping only the longest. (b) For each bit position i (about log₂ n of them), count how many array values have bit i set and how many numbers in 1..n have it set; if the array's count is larger, the duplicate has bit i set (the extra copies push the count up). Assemble the duplicate bit by bit: O(n log n) time, O(1) space. Floyd's algorithm is O(n), but this is a valid alternative that only uses counting. (c) 2²⁵ ≈ 3.4 × 10⁷ subsets is too many to enumerate per query. Meet in the middle (al13): split the items into halves of 12 and 13, enumerate each half's subset weights (4,096 and 8,192 of them, using bitmasks), and sort the second list. For a query W, for each weight s in the first list, count the second-list weights ≤ W − s with bisect, and add up: about 4,096 binary searches per query. With many queries, sort both lists and use a two-pointer sweep per query instead (O(4,096 + 8,192) each), or, since W ≤ 10⁶, precompute for every W the answer with a counting array over all pairwise sums processed in sorted order.
qa: E
Single Number: every element appears twice except one.

XOR all elements. Pairs cancel because a ^ a = 0, XOR is commutative and associative, and a ^ 0 = a, so the result is the unpaired element. O(n) time, O(1) space, versus O(n) space for a set or counter.
E
Check whether n is a power of two.
n > 0 and n & (n − 1) == 0. A power of two has exactly one set bit, and subtracting one turns that bit off and all lower bits on, so the AND is zero. For n ≤ 0 the answer is false.
E
Count the set bits of an integer.

Kernighan's method: while n, n &= n − 1 and count, one iteration per set bit. Or in Python bin(n).count('1') or n.bit_count() (3.10+). For Number of 1 Bits with a 32-bit unsigned input, all of these work directly because Python integers are non-negative here.
E
Missing Number: an array contains n distinct numbers from 0..n; find the missing one.

XOR all indices 0..n and all values; every present number cancels with its index, leaving the missing one. Alternatively n(n+1)/2 − sum(nums), which is safe in Python but can overflow in fixed-width languages.
M
Counting Bits: return the number of set bits for every i from 0 to n.
bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1): i has the same bits as i // 2 shifted left, plus its lowest bit. Or bits[i] = bits[i & (i − 1)] + 1 (remove the lowest set bit). O(n) time, a DP over integers.
M
Single Number II: every element appears three times except one.

For each of the 32 bit positions, count how many numbers have that bit set; the count modulo 3 is the unique number's bit. Reassemble, and in Python convert from 32-bit two's complement if the sign bit is set. O(32·n). The ones/twos state machine (ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos; twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones) does it in O(n) with two variables.
M
Find the two numbers that appear once when every other number appears twice.

XOR everything to get x = a ^ b, which is non-zero. Take its lowest set bit, d = x & −x; a and b differ at that bit. Split all numbers by whether they have bit d and XOR each group: the groups yield a and b. O(n) time, O(1) space.
M
Reverse the bits of a 32-bit unsigned integer.

Loop 32 times: result = (result << 1) | (n & 1); n >>= 1. For many calls, reverse bytes with a 256-entry lookup table, or swap halves, then quarters, and so on with masks (divide and conquer) in 5 steps.
M
Sum of Two Integers without + or −.

XOR gives the sum without carries and (a & b) << 1 gives the carries; repeat with a = sum, b = carry until carry is 0. In Python, mask every step with 0xFFFFFFFF to emulate 32 bits and convert the result back to negative if it exceeds 0x7FFFFFFF, otherwise negative inputs loop forever.
Follow-up: Why does it terminate in fixed width? — The carry shifts left each round, so after at most 32 rounds it is shifted out.
M
Bitwise AND of all numbers in [left, right].

Any bit position where left and right differ has, somewhere in between, both a 0 and a 1 in that position, so it becomes 0; only the common binary prefix survives. Shift both right until equal, counting shifts, then shift back left. Or clear right's lowest set bit while right > left. O(log right).
H
Maximum XOR of two numbers in an array without a trie.

Build the answer bit by bit from the top: assume the next bit can be 1 (candidate = answer | 1 << b), put all prefixes (num >> b) in a set, and check whether some prefix p has p ^ candidate_prefix in the set. If so keep the bit. O(32·n). A binary trie (al15) is the alternative.
H
How would you speed up subset-sum feasibility in Python?

Use one Python integer as a bitset where bit s means 'sum s is reachable': start with bits = 1 and for each x do bits |= bits << x; the answer is (bits >> target) & 1. Each update processes all sums in machine-word chunks inside C, often tens of times faster than a list DP, while keeping O(n · target / 64) word operations.
