t: Math for coding interviews: modular arithmetic, fast power, gcd, primes, combinatorics and randomness
sum: The number theory and counting tools that coding problems assume: arithmetic modulo 10⁹ + 7 and modular inverses, binary exponentiation, Euclid's gcd, sieves and factorisation, nCr with precomputed factorials, digit manipulation and cycle detection, recurring decimals, and correct random sampling and shuffling.
prereq: al2
Constraints up to 10¹⁸ call for O(log n) or O(1) per query; pseudo-polynomial algorithms fail on huge values.
al24
Binary representation and shifts; e >> 1 and e & 1 walk an exponent's bits.
al5
Floyd's fast and slow pointers detect a cycle in a sequence with O(1) memory.
why:
"Return the number of ways, modulo 10⁹ + 7." Many counting problems end with that sentence, and many candidates lose points there — not on the algorithm, but on the arithmetic: dividing residues directly, forgetting to reduce after a multiplication, getting negative results from a subtraction. Other problems give an n up to 10¹⁵ and ask for something that obviously needs n steps, which is only possible with a closed formula and fast exponentiation. Still others are about gcds, primes, digits, or recurring decimals, or ask you to shuffle or sample "uniformly at random" — where a plausible-looking implementation is subtly biased.

None of this is advanced mathematics. It is a toolkit of a dozen facts and five or six algorithms that every competitive programmer and most strong interviewees know cold: modular arithmetic and inverses, binary exponentiation, Euclid's algorithm, the sieve of Eratosthenes, combinations with precomputed factorials, cycle detection in number sequences, long division with remainder tracking, and the correct algorithms for shuffling, weighted picking and reservoir sampling.

A useful way to see the whole lesson is as a set of answers to one question: "the obvious method needs a huge number or a huge loop — what is the shortcut?" Huge results are tamed by working with remainders. Huge exponents are tamed by squaring. Huge gcd computations are tamed by Euclid's remainders. Huge prime searches are tamed by sieving. Huge counting problems are tamed by formulas with factorials. Each shortcut is a few lines of code once you know it exists.

The payoff is large for the effort. These tools turn up inside dynamic programming (counts modulo a prime), inside hashing and string matching (al26 builds rolling hashes on modular arithmetic), in system-design follow-ups (sampling a stream, weighted load balancing), and as standalone easy and medium questions. This lesson presents each tool with the reasoning behind it, a trace, and the language-specific pitfalls that make otherwise correct code fail.
primer:
The mental model: clock arithmetic

On a 12-hour clock, 9 o'clock plus 5 hours is 2 o'clock: you add and then keep only the remainder after dividing by 12. That is modular arithmetic, and the modulus is 12. The remarkable property that makes it useful is that you can take remainders at any point without changing the final remainder: (9 + 5) mod 12 = ((9 mod 12) + (5 mod 12)) mod 12. The same holds for subtraction and multiplication. So a count that would be a 500-digit number can be tracked as its remainder modulo 10⁹ + 7 the whole way through, by reducing after every addition and multiplication.

Division is the exception. On a 12-hour clock, "half of 4 o'clock" could be 2 or 8 — division is not even well defined. With a prime modulus p it works, but not by dividing the remainders. Instead, every non-zero number b has a modular inverse b⁻¹, with b · b⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p), and dividing by b means multiplying by b⁻¹. Fermat's little theorem gives a formula: b⁻¹ = b^(p−2) mod p. Computing that power for p ≈ 10⁹ needs the second tool of this lesson.

The second mental model is "big numbers want logarithms". Whenever an input can be as large as 10⁹ or 10¹⁸ and the naive method loops that many times, look for a method that halves the problem each step: binary exponentiation for powers, Euclid's algorithm for gcds (which shrinks the numbers at least by half every two steps), binary search for roots (al7). If a problem says "n up to 10¹⁵", it is promising you an O(log n) solution exists.

Where the clock analogy breaks: a clock has no negative hours, but programs compute differences, and remainders of negative numbers depend on the language. Python always returns a remainder with the sign of the modulus, so (3 − 5) % 7 is 5 — exactly the clock answer. Java and C++ return −2. When a subtraction can go negative in those languages, add the modulus before reducing: ((a − b) % m + m) % m. Even in Python, it is a habit worth showing, because interviewers know code gets ported.

Two small facts about Python save time in interviews: pow(b, e, m) is built in and fast, and integers never overflow, so you can check a modular computation against the exact one on small inputs (compute the true answer with big integers, then reduce it) — a quick way to debug a wrong answer in a counting problem.

Finally, keep floating point out of exact problems. 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in binary floating point, and math.sqrt of a large perfect square can come out one off when converted to int. For exact integer roots use math.isqrt; for fractions use integers (numerator and denominator reduced by their gcd) or Python's fractions.Fraction.
body:
Modular arithmetic, done right

MOD = 10**9 + 7
add = (a + b) % MOD
sub = (a - b) % MOD                 # Python: always non-negative; elsewhere add MOD first
mul = a * b % MOD
div = a * pow(b, MOD - 2, MOD) % MOD   # Fermat inverse; MOD must be prime and b % MOD != 0
inv = pow(b, -1, MOD)               # Python 3.8+: modular inverse directly

Reduce after every operation. In a DP that counts paths, write dp[i] = (dp[i − 1] + dp[i − 2]) % MOD, not a reduction at the very end. In Python the final answer would be the same, but intermediate numbers with thousands of digits make each step slow; in fixed-width languages, they overflow. Why 10⁹ + 7? It is prime (so inverses exist for every non-zero residue), it is larger than 10⁹ (so answers have room), and the product of two residues is below 2⁶³ (so a 64-bit multiply never overflows before the reduction). 998244353 is the other common choice, picked for number-theoretic transforms.

Binary exponentiation

To compute bᵉ, write e in binary. b¹³ = b⁸ · b⁴ · b¹ because 13 = 1101₂. The powers b, b², b⁴, b⁸ come from repeated squaring, and you multiply in the ones whose bit is set (the figure). Iteratively:

def power(b, e, m):
    result = 1
    b %= m
    while e > 0:
        if e & 1:                    # this bit contributes b^(2^k)
            result = result * b % m
        b = b * b % m                # next power of two
        e >>= 1
    return result

O(log e) multiplications. Python's built-in pow(b, e, m) does exactly this in C; use it in real code, but be ready to write the loop. Pow(x, n) for floating-point x and possibly negative n is the same loop without the modulus: if n < 0, replace x with 1/x and n with −n. Count Good Numbers (n up to 10¹⁵) is a closed form, 5^⌈n/2⌉ · 4^⌊n/2⌋ mod p, computed with two fast powers. Super Pow (aᵇ mod 1337 where b is given as an array of digits) uses aᵇ = (a^(b without its last digit))¹⁰ · a^(last digit), recursing over the digits with fast power at each step.

The same squaring idea works for anything you can multiply associatively. Raising a 2×2 matrix to the n-th power computes the n-th Fibonacci number in O(log n) — the standard answer to "can you compute fib(10¹⁸) mod p?" — and the technique generalises to any linear recurrence.

gcd, lcm and Euclid

The greatest common divisor of a and b equals the gcd of b and a mod b, because any common divisor of a and b also divides a − qb = a mod b, and vice versa. Repeat until the second number is 0:

def gcd(a, b):
    while b:
        a, b = b, a % b
    return a

Trace gcd(48, 18): (48, 18) → (18, 12) → (12, 6) → (6, 0) → 6. Each two steps at least halve the larger number, so it is O(log min(a, b)) — even for 18-digit numbers, under a hundred steps. lcm(a, b) = a // gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to keep numbers small). Python provides math.gcd and math.lcm.

gcd shows up in surprising places. "Greatest Common Divisor of Strings": if s + t == t + s, both are repetitions of a common block, and its length is gcd(len(s), len(t)); otherwise there is none. Reducing fractions — for example, the slope between two points as (dy/g, dx/g) with a sign convention — makes equal slopes hash equally in "max points on a line". "Water jug" problems (can you measure exactly z litres with jugs of x and y?) are answered by Bézout's identity: yes exactly when z is a multiple of gcd(x, y) and z ≤ x + y.

The extended Euclidean algorithm also returns integers x, y with ax + by = gcd(a, b). When gcd(b, m) = 1, the x in bx + my = 1 is the inverse of b modulo m — this is how inverses are computed when the modulus is not prime.

Primes: trial division and sieves

To test one number n, trial division up to √n suffices: if n = a · b with a ≤ b, then a ≤ √n. That is O(√n) — fine up to about 10¹². To find all primes up to n ("Count Primes"), the sieve of Eratosthenes is far better: start with every number from 2 marked prime; for each i that is still marked, cross out its multiples starting from i·i (smaller multiples were already crossed out by smaller primes).

def count_primes(n):
    if n < 3: return 0
    is_p = bytearray([1]) * n
    is_p[0] = is_p[1] = 0
    i = 2
    while i * i < n:
        if is_p[i]:
            is_p[i*i::i] = bytearray(len(range(i*i, n, i)))   # cross out multiples
        i += 1
    return sum(is_p)

The total work is n · (1/2 + 1/3 + 1/5 + …) over primes up to √n, which is O(n log log n) — almost linear. The slice assignment crosses out a whole arithmetic progression in C. For factorising many numbers up to n, a variant stores each number's smallest prime factor; then any number factorises by repeatedly dividing by its smallest prime factor, O(log n) steps.

Counting: combinations modulo a prime

"Unique Paths" in an m×n grid is C(m + n − 2, m − 1); many counting problems reduce to binomial coefficients. For exact values with small n, math.comb is fine. For many queries modulo a prime with n up to 10⁶, precompute factorials and inverse factorials once:

def build(n, MOD=10**9 + 7):
    fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % MOD
    inv = [1] * (n + 1)
    inv[n] = pow(fact[n], MOD - 2, MOD)          # one Fermat inverse
    for i in range(n, 0, -1):
        inv[i - 1] = inv[i] * i % MOD            # 1/(i-1)! = i / i!
    return fact, inv

def ncr(n, r, fact, inv, MOD=10**9 + 7):
    if r < 0 or r > n: return 0
    return fact[n] * inv[r] % MOD * inv[n - r] % MOD

Only one modular exponentiation is needed; the rest of the inverse factorials follow by multiplying back down. Each query is then O(1). Pascal's triangle (C(n, r) = C(n − 1, r − 1) + C(n − 1, r)) avoids inverses entirely and works for any modulus, but costs O(n²). Other counting staples: the number of subsets of n items is 2ⁿ; arrangements of n items with repeated groups is n! divided by the factorials of the group sizes; the Catalan numbers C(2n, n)/(n + 1) count balanced bracket sequences and binary tree shapes (al13, al14).

Digits: plus one, happy numbers, big multiplication

Digit problems test careful iteration. Plus One (a number as a list of digits): walk from the right, turning 9s into 0s while carrying; if you run off the front, prepend a 1 (999 → 1000). Happy Number: replace n by the sum of the squares of its digits repeatedly; is 1 reached? The values quickly drop below a few hundred (a number with d digits maps to at most 81·d), so the sequence must eventually repeat. Detect the cycle with a set of seen values, or with Floyd's fast and slow pointers (al5) for O(1) memory — the same algorithm as linked-list cycle detection, applied to the function n → digit-square-sum(n).

Multiply Strings forbids converting to integers, so implement grade-school multiplication: an array of m + n digits; digit i of a times digit j of b adds into position i + j + 1 (indexing from the left), carrying into i + j. Strip leading zeros. O(m·n). Reverse Integer and String to Integer (atoi) add a 32-bit overflow check — in Python, compare against 2³¹ − 1 and −2³¹ explicitly, since nothing overflows by itself.

Recurring decimals: remainders reveal the cycle

"Fraction to Recurring Decimal": 4/333 = 0.(012). Do long division by hand and notice what determines the next digit: only the current remainder. So if a remainder ever repeats, the digits from its first occurrence will repeat forever. Record the position at which each remainder first appeared:

def fraction_to_decimal(num, den):
    if num == 0: return "0"
    sign = "-" if (num < 0) ^ (den < 0) else ""
    num, den = abs(num), abs(den)
    q, r = divmod(num, den)
    out, seen = [sign + str(q)], {}
    if r == 0: return out[0]
    out.append(".")
    while r and r not in seen:
        seen[r] = len(out)               # where this remainder's digit goes
        q, r = divmod(r * 10, den)
        out.append(str(q))
    if r:                                # repeated remainder: insert parentheses
        out.insert(seen[r], "(")
        out.append(")")
    return "".join(out)

There are fewer than den possible remainders, so the loop runs at most den times. The sign handling (XOR of the two signs) and the zero case are the usual traps.

Randomness: weighted picks, shuffles and reservoirs

Random Pick with Weight: index i should be returned with probability w[i] / Σw. Lay the weights end to end on a line of length total = Σw, draw a uniform integer r in [1, total], and find which segment contains it: the first prefix sum ≥ r, found with bisect_left. O(n) setup, O(log n) per pick.

import random, bisect, itertools
class Solution:
    def __init__(self, w):
        self.prefix = list(itertools.accumulate(w))
    def pickIndex(self):
        r = random.randint(1, self.prefix[-1])
        return bisect.bisect_left(self.prefix, r)

Shuffle: the Fisher–Yates algorithm fills positions from the end. For i from n − 1 down to 1, choose j uniformly from 0..i and swap a[i] with a[j]. Every permutation arises from exactly one sequence of choices (n choices, then n − 1, …), so each has probability 1/n!. The tempting alternative — swap each a[i] with a random index from the whole array — produces nⁿ equally likely choice sequences, and since nⁿ is not divisible by n! for n ≥ 3, some permutations must be more likely than others. For n = 3: 27 sequences over 6 permutations cannot be uniform.

Reservoir sampling picks a uniform random element from a stream whose length you do not know (a linked list, a log file, a network feed) in one pass. Keep the first item; at the i-th item, replace the kept one with probability 1/i. The figure shows why it is uniform. For a sample of k items, keep the first k, and at item i (i > k) replace a uniformly chosen reservoir slot with probability k/i. "Linked List Random Node" and "Random Pick Index" (uniform among indices of a target value) are direct applications.

Recognising the pattern

"Modulo 10⁹ + 7" → reduce every step, inverses for division, precomputed factorials for combinations. "n up to 10¹⁵" → closed form plus fast power, or matrix power for recurrences. gcd, lcm, fractions, divisibility, "measure exactly" → Euclid. Primes up to n → sieve. Digit sequences that might loop → cycle detection. "Uniformly at random", "with probability proportional to", "from a stream" → Fisher–Yates, prefix sums with bisect, reservoir sampling.

Practice in the DSA list: Plus One, Happy Number, Greatest Common Divisor of Strings, Pow(x, n), Count Primes, Multiply Strings, Fraction to Recurring Decimal, Super Pow, Random Pick with Weight, Count Good Numbers, Unique Paths (al22, also a binomial coefficient).
deep:
Why Fermat's inverse works, and when it does not

Fermat's little theorem says that for prime p and b not divisible by p, b^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Multiply both sides by b⁻¹: b^(p−2) ≡ b⁻¹. Two conditions are essential. The modulus must be prime — for composite m, use the extended Euclidean algorithm, and the inverse exists only if gcd(b, m) = 1. And b must not be a multiple of p: dividing by something congruent to 0 is meaningless, which matters in nCr when n ≥ p (then factorials contain p, and you need Lucas' theorem, which computes C(n, r) mod p from the base-p digits of n and r). Euler's theorem generalises Fermat: b^φ(m) ≡ 1 (mod m) when gcd(b, m) = 1, where φ(m) counts integers below m coprime to it — the basis of RSA.

The Chinese remainder theorem

If you know x mod 3 = 2, x mod 5 = 3 and x mod 7 = 2, then x mod 105 is determined (it is 23). In general, for pairwise coprime moduli, the remainders modulo each determine the remainder modulo their product, and an efficient construction uses modular inverses. It appears in problems about cyclic schedules ("when do these three periodic events coincide?"), in computing with very large numbers by working modulo several primes in parallel, and in cryptography. Interviews rarely require the construction, but recognising "coincidence of periodic events" as CRT (or lcm, when the offsets are all zero) is useful.

Primality testing for big numbers

Trial division is hopeless for 18-digit numbers (√10¹⁸ = 10⁹ divisions). The Miller–Rabin test checks whether n behaves like a prime with respect to a few bases a, using fast modular exponentiation: write n − 1 = 2ˢ·d and check whether a^d ≡ 1 or a^(2ʳd) ≡ −1 for some r. For 64-bit integers, a specific small set of bases makes the test deterministic. Pollard's rho algorithm factors large composites using — once again — Floyd's cycle detection, on the sequence x → x² + c mod n. These are well beyond typical interviews, but they show how the basic tools (fast power, cycle detection) compose into serious algorithms.

Bias in naive random number use

Uniform randomness is easy to break. random.randint(0, 2**32) % n is biased whenever n does not divide the range, because some remainders occur one extra time; libraries avoid this with rejection sampling (draw again if the value falls in the incomplete last block). Generating "rand7() from rand5()" works the same way: combine two calls into a uniform number in 0..24, accept it only if it is below 21, and return it mod 7. Shuffling with sorted(a, key=lambda _: random.random()) is uniform in practice (ties have negligible probability) but O(n log n); the classic bug is sorting with a random comparator, which is biased and can break some sort implementations. For security-sensitive randomness (tokens, keys), use the secrets module, not random, whose Mersenne Twister generator is predictable from its outputs.

Matrix exponentiation for linear recurrences

Any sequence defined by a fixed linear recurrence — Fibonacci (f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2)), tribonacci, the number of ways to tile a 2×n board, the number of length-n strings avoiding a pattern described by a small automaton — can be written as "state vector × fixed matrix = next state vector". Raising the k×k matrix to the n-th power with binary exponentiation computes the n-th term in O(k³ log n). For Fibonacci, [[1, 1], [1, 0]]ⁿ contains f(n + 1), f(n) and f(n − 1), so f(10¹⁸) mod p needs about 60 2×2 matrix multiplications. When an interviewer follows up a DP with "now n is 10¹⁸", this is usually the answer they want, provided the DP's transition does not depend on n.

Floating point and exactness

Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so equality tests and accumulated sums drift: summing 0.1 ten times gives 0.9999999999999999. Exact problems should stay in integers — compare fractions by cross-multiplying, represent money in cents, use math.isqrt for integer square roots (int(math.sqrt(n)) can be off by one for n near 10¹⁶ and above), and use fractions.Fraction or decimal.Decimal when rational or decimal exactness is required. When floats are unavoidable (geometry, probabilities), compare with a tolerance and say so.
prod:
In the interview room

Math-flavoured problems are graded on correctness at the edges. The common bugs: dividing residues directly instead of multiplying by an inverse; reducing only at the end (slow in Python, overflow elsewhere); negative remainders when porting to other languages; forgetting the sign or zero cases in Fraction to Recurring Decimal and in Pow(x, n) with negative n; off-by-one bounds in sieves (crossing out from 2i instead of i², or looping i while i < n instead of i·i < n — correct but slower); and biased shuffles. Test with 0, 1, negative inputs, the largest allowed input, and a case where the modulus actually matters.

Interviewers often probe understanding: "why 10⁹ + 7?", "why can you not divide modulo p?", "prove your shuffle is uniform", "why is Euclid's algorithm logarithmic?", "what if the stream length is unknown?". Each has a two-sentence answer in this lesson; practise saying them. For randomness questions, giving the probability argument (the telescoping product for reservoir sampling, the n! sequences for Fisher–Yates) is what distinguishes a strong answer.

When n is huge, say the closed form first and then the algorithm: "the answer is 5^⌈n/2⌉ · 4^⌊n/2⌋, and I'll compute each power with binary exponentiation in O(log n)". Interviewers appreciate seeing the mathematical simplification separated from the implementation.

On online assessments, the most common math-related failures are not conceptual but mechanical: a missing modulus on one line of a DP, an intermediate product that overflows in Java, or a floating-point comparison that fails on one hidden test. A final pass over your code checking every multiplication and subtraction for "is this reduced?" takes a minute and catches most of them.

Finally, keep the toolkit's limits in mind out loud: "Fermat's inverse needs a prime modulus", "the sieve needs O(n) memory, so for n = 10¹⁰ I would use a segmented sieve", "Fisher–Yates needs a good random source". Stating the precondition with the technique is the senior habit.

In real systems

This toolkit underpins a lot of infrastructure. Hash tables and hash functions use modular arithmetic, often with prime moduli, and rolling hashes for string matching and deduplication (al26) update hash values modulo a large prime in O(1). Public-key cryptography is modular exponentiation and inverses at scale: RSA encrypts with c = mᵉ mod n using exactly binary exponentiation, and computes its private key with the extended Euclidean algorithm. Checksums such as the Luhn algorithm on credit-card numbers and ISBN check digits are modular arithmetic on digits. Data platforms sample huge streams with reservoir sampling to compute approximate statistics or keep representative logs; load balancers route requests with weighted random choice; A/B testing systems assign users to variants by hashing user ids modulo the number of buckets; and online games and card apps must shuffle with Fisher–Yates (a widely reported 1999 online-poker flaw came from a shuffle with too little randomness, which let attackers predict hands).
myths: (a / b) mod p equals (a mod p) / (b mod p).

Division does not distribute over the modulus. You must multiply by the modular inverse of b: a · b^(p−2) mod p when p is prime (Fermat's little theorem), or the inverse from the extended Euclidean algorithm otherwise. Integer-dividing residues gives wrong answers.
Taking the modulus only at the end is fine in Python because integers never overflow.

It is correct but can be very slow: intermediate products grow to thousands of digits, and every multiplication gets slower. Reduce modulo p after each operation to keep numbers small. In Java or C++ you must reduce early anyway, or 64-bit values overflow.
The remainder of a negative number is always non-negative.

It depends on the language. Python's % returns a result with the sign of the divisor (−7 % 3 == 2), but C, C++, Java and JavaScript return a result with the sign of the dividend (−7 % 3 == −1). Ported code needs ((a % m) + m) % m.
Shuffling by swapping each element with a random position gives a uniform shuffle.

Swapping element i with a random index in the whole array produces n^n equally likely outcomes, which cannot divide evenly among the n! permutations, so some orderings are more likely. Fisher–Yates swaps element i with a random index in i..n−1, giving each permutation probability exactly 1/n!.
Checking primes up to n needs trial division of every number.

The sieve of Eratosthenes marks all composites up to n in O(n log log n) by crossing out multiples of each prime starting from its square. For a single number, trial division up to √n suffices; for very large single numbers, probabilistic tests like Miller–Rabin are used.
lab:
Check the toolkit against Python's built-ins and against brute-force probability counts.

  1. Save as math_lab.py: 
    import random, math
from collections import Counter
from itertools import permutations

MOD = 10**9 + 7
def power(b, e, m):
    r, b = 1, b % m
    while e:
        if e & 1: r = r * b % m
        b = b * b % m; e >>= 1
    return r

def gcd(a, b):
    while b: a, b = b, a % b
    return a

fact = [1] * 2001
for i in range(1, 2001): fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % MOD
inv = [1] * 2001; inv[2000] = pow(fact[2000], MOD - 2, MOD)
for i in range(2000, 0, -1): inv[i - 1] = inv[i] * i % MOD

for _ in range(2000):
    b, e = random.randint(0, 10**12), random.randint(0, 10**12)
    assert power(b, e, MOD) == pow(b, e, MOD)
    n = random.randint(0, 2000); r = random.randint(0, n)
    assert fact[n] * inv[r] % MOD * inv[n - r] % MOD == math.comb(n, r) % MOD
    a, c = random.randint(1, 10**9), random.randint(1, 10**9)
    assert math.gcd(a, c) == gcd(a, c)
print("fast power, nCr mod p and gcd agree with the built-ins")

def fisher_yates(a):
    a = a[:]
    for i in range(len(a) - 1, 0, -1):
        j = random.randint(0, i); a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    return tuple(a)
def naive(a):
    a = a[:]
    for i in range(len(a)):
        j = random.randint(0, len(a) - 1); a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
    return tuple(a)
for f in (fisher_yates, naive):
    c = Counter(f([1, 2, 3]) for _ in range(60000))
    print(f.__name__, sorted(round(v / 600) / 100 for v in c.values()))
  2. Run it. The first message confirms the hand-written fast power, the factorial-table nCr and Euclid against pow, math.comb and math.gcd.
  3. The two shuffle lines show the frequency of each of the six permutations of [1, 2, 3]. Fisher–Yates gives six values near 0.17 (1/6); the naive shuffle gives three permutations near 0.19 and three near 0.15 — the bias predicted by 27 sequences over 6 outcomes (5/27 and 4/27).

What this proves: the toolkit's algorithms match the library versions, and the shuffle bias is real and measurable, not a theoretical nicety.
recap: Addition, subtraction and multiplication commute with taking remainders, so reduce after every step; division needs a modular inverse.
For prime p, the inverse of b is b^(p−2) mod p by Fermat's little theorem; Python's pow(b, -1, p) computes inverses directly from 3.8.
Binary exponentiation computes bᵉ in O(log e) multiplications by squaring the base and multiplying it in for each set bit of e.
Euclid's algorithm gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) runs in O(log min(a, b)); lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) · b.
The sieve of Eratosthenes finds all primes up to n in O(n log log n); a smallest-prime-factor sieve factorises any number up to n in O(log n).
nCr mod p is fact[n] · invfact[r] · invfact[n − r] after O(n) precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials.
Long division with a map from remainder to position detects the repeating part of a fraction; digit-sum sequences cycle and Floyd's algorithm detects it.
Use Fisher–Yates for uniform shuffles, reservoir sampling for uniform samples from streams, and prefix sums with binary search for weighted random picks.
glossary: Computing a power by repeated squaring, using the binary digits of the exponent; O(log e) multiplications.
The number of ways to choose r items from n without order: n! / (r! (n − r)!).
For pairwise coprime moduli, remainders modulo each determine the remainder modulo their product.
Two integers whose greatest common divisor is 1.
Computing gcd(a, b) by repeatedly replacing (a, b) with (b, a mod b) until b is 0.
Euclid's algorithm that also finds integers x and y with ax + by = gcd(a, b); gives modular inverses.
For prime p and b not divisible by p, b^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p), so b^(p−2) is the inverse of b.
An in-place shuffle that swaps each position i with a uniformly random position from i to the end.
The largest integer dividing both numbers.
Arithmetic on remainders after division by a modulus m, like hours on a clock.
A number b⁻¹ such that b · b⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod m); it exists exactly when gcd(b, m) = 1.
An integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself.
A public-key cryptosystem whose encryption and decryption are modular exponentiations and whose key setup uses modular inverses.
Choosing k items uniformly from a stream of unknown length in one pass with O(k) memory.
Finding all primes up to n by crossing out multiples of each prime.
drill:
Count, then compute

"A rectangular grid has m rows and n columns (m, n ≤ 10⁶). A robot moves only right or down from the top-left to the bottom-right. How many paths are there modulo 10⁹ + 7? Now add: the robot must pass through a given cell (r, c). And: there are 100 forbidden cells it must avoid." Give an efficient method for each.

Answer

All paths: a path is a sequence of (m − 1) down moves and (n − 1) right moves, so the count is C(m + n − 2, m − 1). With m, n up to 10⁶, a DP table of 10¹² cells is impossible; precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to 2 × 10⁶ in O(m + n) and answer in O(1). Through (r, c): paths from the start to (r, c) times paths from (r, c) to the end: C(r + c, r) · C((m − 1 − r) + (n − 1 − c), m − 1 − r), both from the same tables. Avoiding 100 forbidden cells: sort the forbidden cells by (row, column) and add the target as a final "cell". Let bad[i] = the number of paths from the start to forbidden cell i that avoid every earlier forbidden cell: bad[i] = paths(start, i) − Σ over j before i that can reach i of bad[j] · paths(j, i). The answer is the same formula evaluated for the target. That is O(k²) binomial evaluations for k forbidden cells — 10⁴ — plus the factorial precomputation. This inclusion–exclusion by "first forbidden cell hit" is a standard technique, and it shows how combinatorics plus modular inverses solves grid problems far beyond what a DP table could hold.
qa: E
Why do problems ask for answers modulo 10⁹ + 7?

The true answer can be astronomically large (counts of paths or arrangements), so the problem asks for its remainder modulo a prime that fits comfortably in 32 bits. 10⁹ + 7 is prime, so every non-zero residue has an inverse, and the product of two residues stays below 2⁶³, so 64-bit arithmetic never overflows before reduction.
E
Compute gcd and lcm of two numbers.

Euclid: while b: a, b = b, a % b; return a. Each step at least halves the larger number every two steps, so O(log min(a, b)). lcm(a, b) = a // gcd(a, b) * b, dividing first to keep intermediate values small. Python has math.gcd and math.lcm.
E
Count the primes below n.

Sieve of Eratosthenes: a boolean array of size n, initially true from 2; for each i from 2 while i·i < n, if i is still marked prime, cross out multiples of i starting from i·i. Count what remains. O(n log log n) time, O(n) space.
M
Implement Pow(x, n) for integer n, possibly negative.

Binary exponentiation: while n > 0, if n is odd multiply the result by x; square x; halve n. For negative n, compute with x = 1/x and n = −n. O(log |n|) multiplications. With floats, the result has rounding error but no overflow concern in Python.
Follow-up: Modular version? — The same loop with every multiplication reduced mod m; Python's pow(b, e, m) does it.
M
Compute nCr modulo 10⁹ + 7 for many queries with n up to 10⁶.

Precompute fact[i] for i up to n and invfact[n] = pow(fact[n], p − 2, p), then invfact[i − 1] = invfact[i] · i going down. Each query is fact[n] · invfact[r] · invfact[n − r] mod p, O(1). Precomputation is O(n). Pascal's triangle is O(n²) and fine only for small n.
M
Fraction to Recurring Decimal.

Handle the sign and the integer part, then do long division on the remainder: multiply by 10, emit the next digit, and record the position at which each remainder first appeared. When a remainder repeats, the digits from its first position onward repeat forever, so insert the parentheses there. If the remainder becomes 0, the decimal terminates. O(length of the period) ≤ O(denominator).
M
Happy Number: does repeatedly summing the squares of the digits reach 1?

The sequence of values eventually either reaches 1 or enters a cycle (the values quickly fall below a few hundred). Detect a cycle with a set of seen values or with Floyd's fast and slow pointers, which uses O(1) memory. O(log n) per step.
M
Multiply two non-negative integers given as strings.

Grade-school multiplication into an array of length m + n: digit i of a times digit j of b contributes to position i + j + 1 (indexing from the left), with carries propagated to i + j. Strip leading zeros at the end. O(m·n). Python's big integers would do it in one line, but the question asks for the algorithm.
M
Random Pick with Weight.

Build prefix sums of the weights. To pick, draw an integer r uniformly in [1, total] and return the first index whose prefix sum is ≥ r (bisect_left). Index i is chosen with probability w[i] / total. O(n) preprocessing, O(log n) per pick. For many picks with static weights, the alias method gives O(1) per pick.
H
Shuffle an array uniformly.

Fisher–Yates: for i from n − 1 down to 1, pick j uniformly in [0, i] and swap a[i] and a[j]. Each permutation results from exactly one sequence of choices, and there are n! such sequences, each with probability 1/n!. The common bug, picking j from the whole array each time, gives n^n outcomes that cannot be spread evenly over n! permutations.
H
Sample one element uniformly from a linked list or stream of unknown length in one pass.

Reservoir sampling: keep the first element; at the i-th element (1-based), replace the kept element with probability 1/i. By induction, after i elements each has been kept with probability 1/i. For k samples, keep the first k and replace a random one of them with probability k/i at element i. O(1) or O(k) memory.
Follow-up: Prove it for k = 1. — Element j survives if chosen at step j (probability 1/j) and not replaced later: Π over i > j of (1 − 1/i) = j/n, giving 1/j · j/n = 1/n.
H
Count Good Numbers: digits at even indices must be even (5 choices) and at odd indices prime (4 choices); count strings of length n up to 10¹⁵ modulo 10⁹ + 7.

There are ceil(n/2) even positions and floor(n/2) odd positions, so the answer is 5^ceil(n/2) · 4^floor(n/2) mod p. With n up to 10¹⁵ you cannot loop; binary exponentiation computes each power in about 50 multiplications. This is the typical shape of 'count with a huge n': find a closed form, then use fast power.
refs: Fast power, its variants and applications such as matrix exponentiation.
Inverses via extended Euclid and Fermat, and computing all inverses up to n in O(n).
The sieve, its complexity, and the linear sieve with smallest prime factors.
Python docs — built-in pow and math module
pow(base, exp, mod), modular inverses with exp = −1 (3.8+), math.gcd, math.comb and math.isqrt.
Donald Knuth — The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 2, section 3.4.2
Random sampling and shuffling, including the algorithms now called Fisher–Yates and reservoir sampling.

t: String matching: KMP, the Z-function and rolling hashes
sum: Find patterns in text in linear time: why naive matching is O(n·m), the prefix (failure) function and KMP, the Z-function, Rabin–Karp rolling hashes with collision handling, and their applications — periods, shortest palindrome, longest happy prefix, repeated DNA, longest duplicate substring and rotations.
prereq: al4
Hashing whole substrings costs O(length) each; rolling hashes fix that.
al25
Arithmetic modulo a large prime; reduce after every operation.
al7
Binary search on the answer when 'a duplicate of length L exists' is monotone in L.
why:
Every editor has "find", every log viewer has search, and every genome pipeline looks for short DNA patterns inside billions of letters. The simplest method — line the pattern up at each position of the text and compare character by character — is what most people write first, and on ordinary English it is fast. But consider searching for "aaaaab" in a text of a million "a"s. At every position, the comparison matches five characters before failing on the sixth, and then the method shifts by one and starts again from scratch. For a pattern of length m and text of length n, that is about n·m comparisons. The naive method keeps throwing away what it just learned: after matching "aaaaa", it already knows the next text characters are "aaaa" — yet it re-reads them.

Linear-time string matching is about not throwing that knowledge away. KMP precomputes, from the pattern alone, how far it can safely shift after a mismatch, so the text pointer never moves backwards. The Z-function computes, for every position, how long a prefix of the string matches there, reusing earlier matches. Rabin–Karp takes a different route: it compares numbers instead of strings, using a hash of each text window that can be updated in O(1) as the window slides.

These algorithms matter in interviews beyond "implement strStr". The KMP prefix function directly answers questions about a string's structure — its smallest period, whether it is a repetition, its longest prefix that is also a suffix, its longest palindromic prefix. Rolling hashes solve "repeated DNA sequences" and, with binary search, "longest duplicate substring". This lesson develops each tool from the naive method, with traces, and explains the pitfalls — especially the hash collisions that make rolling-hash solutions fail on adversarial tests.
primer:
The mental model: never re-read the text

Imagine reading a long scroll through a narrow slot, looking for a particular phrase. Each time you fail to match, you must decide where the phrase could next begin. The naive approach rewinds the scroll to one character after the last starting point — you re-read text you have already seen. A smarter reader asks: "of the characters I just matched, is there a later point where the phrase could already be partly underway?" If the pattern is "abcabd" and you matched "abcab" before failing, the last two characters "ab" are also the start of the pattern — so you can continue as if "ab" were already matched, without moving the scroll back at all.

That question — "what is the longest piece at the end of what I matched that is also a beginning of the pattern?" — depends only on the pattern, not on the text, so it can be precomputed for every possible amount matched. The answer is the prefix function (also called the failure function or LPS, for "longest proper prefix which is also suffix"): lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of it. A prefix that is also a suffix is called a border.

A second way to think about the same knowledge is the Z-function: for each position i of a string, z[i] is how many characters starting at i agree with the start of the string. Searching for a pattern P in a text T then becomes computing Z of P + "#" + T (the "#" is a character in neither) and reporting positions where z equals len(P).

The third idea abandons character comparison: give each window of the text a numeric fingerprint (a hash) that can be updated in O(1) when the window slides, and compare fingerprints. If the fingerprints differ, the strings differ; if they match, the strings are probably equal — and you verify. That is Rabin–Karp.

To put numbers on the difference: searching a 10⁶-character text for a 10⁴-character pattern that keeps almost matching costs the naive method about 10¹⁰ character comparisons — minutes in Python. KMP, Z and Rabin–Karp all do about 2 × 10⁶ steps. On friendly text all three methods look equally fast, which is exactly why the worst case has to be reasoned about rather than measured on examples.

Where the scroll analogy breaks: a real reader keeps a memory of the text, but KMP keeps only one number — how much of the pattern is currently matched. All the cleverness lives in the pattern's precomputed table. Rolling hashes break the analogy differently: they do not "read" the text in the human sense at all, which is why they need a verification step that the comparison-based algorithms do not.
body:
The naive method and its worst case

def naive_find(t, p):
    for i in range(len(t) - len(p) + 1):
        if t[i:i + len(p)] == p:      # O(m) comparison
            return i
    return -1

O(n·m) in the worst case: text "aaa…a" (n characters), pattern "aa…ab" (m characters). Every alignment matches m − 1 characters before failing. For n = 10⁶ and m = 10⁴ that is 10¹⁰ character comparisons. (Python's slicing and comparison run in C, which hides the cost on small inputs, but not the growth.)

The prefix function

lps[i] = the length of the longest proper prefix of p[0..i] that is also a suffix of p[0..i]. For p = "aabaaab":

ip[0..i]longest borderlps[i]
0a(none; proper means shorter)0
1aaa1
2aab—0
3aabaa1
4aabaaaa2
5aabaaaaa2
6aabaaabaab3

Computing it naively per position is O(m²) or worse. The linear algorithm extends the previous border when possible and, when not, falls back to the next-shorter border — which is the longest border of the current border, already stored in the table:

def prefix_function(p):
    lps = [0] * len(p)
    k = 0                                 # length of the current border
    for i in range(1, len(p)):
        while k and p[i] != p[k]:
            k = lps[k - 1]                # fall back to a shorter border
        if p[i] == p[k]:
            k += 1                        # extend the border by one character
        lps[i] = k
    return lps

Trace i = 5 in "aabaaab": the previous border has length k = 2 ("aa"). p[5] = 'a' and p[2] = 'b' differ, so fall back to k = lps[1] = 1 ("a"); now p[5] = 'a' equals p[1] = 'a', so k becomes 2. lps[5] = 2. At i = 6, p[6] = 'b' equals p[2] = 'b', so k = 3. The fallback is safe because any border of p[0..i] minus its last character is a border of p[0..i−1], and the borders of a string, from longest to shortest, are exactly the chain lps[k − 1], lps[lps[k − 1] − 1], …. Linear time: k grows by at most one per iteration and every fallback shrinks it, so the total number of fallbacks is at most m.

KMP search

Scan the text once with j = the number of pattern characters currently matched. On a match, advance j; on a mismatch, fall back with j = lps[j − 1] (the text pointer stays put); when j reaches m, report a match and fall back to continue searching for overlapping matches.

def kmp_find_all(t, p):
    lps, j, out = prefix_function(p), 0, []
    for i, ch in enumerate(t):
        while j and ch != p[j]:
            j = lps[j - 1]
        if ch == p[j]:
            j += 1
        if j == len(p):
            out.append(i - len(p) + 1)
            j = lps[j - 1]                # allow overlapping matches
    return out

O(n + m) time, O(m) extra space. An equivalent formulation computes the prefix function of p + "#" + t directly: positions where the value equals m mark the ends of matches. Either is fine in an interview; the combined-string version means you only write one loop.

What the prefix function tells you about a string

The last value, lps[−1], is the longest proper prefix of s that is also a suffix. Three interview problems are just that number:

  • Longest Happy Prefix: return s[:lps[−1]].
  • Smallest period: p = len(s) − lps[−1]. If a border of length b exists, s is "periodic with period n − b": shifting by n − b lines it up with itself. The longest border gives the smallest period.
  • Repeated Substring Pattern (is s a repetition of a shorter block?): yes exactly when lps[−1] > 0 and len(s) is divisible by the smallest period. "abcabcabc": lps[−1] = 6, period 3, 9 % 3 = 0 → yes. "abcab": lps[−1] = 2, period 3, 5 % 3 ≠ 0 → no.

Shortest Palindrome ("add the fewest characters in front of s to make it a palindrome") needs the longest palindromic prefix of s; everything after it must be mirrored at the front. A prefix of s is a palindrome exactly when it equals the corresponding suffix of reverse(s). So build lps for s + "#" + reverse(s): the final value is the length k of the longest prefix of s that matches a suffix of reverse(s) — the longest palindromic prefix. The answer is reverse(s[k:]) + s. The "#" separator stops a border from spanning both halves.

The Z-function

z[i] = the length of the longest substring starting at i that is also a prefix of s (z[0] is conventionally n or 0). For "aabxaab": z = [−, 1, 0, 0, 3, 1, 0]. The linear algorithm keeps the interval [l, r) — the rightmost window known to match a prefix — and reuses it:

def z_function(s):
    n = len(s); z = [0] * n
    l = r = 0                                # s[l:r] matches s[0:r-l]
    for i in range(1, n):
        if i < r:
            z[i] = min(r - i, z[i - l])      # reuse what is known inside the window
        while i + z[i] < n and s[z[i]] == s[i + z[i]]:
            z[i] += 1                        # extend by direct comparison
        if i + z[i] > r:
            l, r = i, i + z[i]
    return z

Inside [l, r), the substring starting at i is a copy of the substring starting at i − l (since s[l:r] copies the prefix), so z[i − l] is a lower bound, capped at r − i because beyond r nothing is known. Every iteration of the inner while loop that succeeds pushes r to the right, so the total work is O(n). To search for P in T, compute z of P + "#" + T and report every i where z[i] == len(P) (the match starts at i − len(P) − 1 in T).

Rabin–Karp and rolling hashes

A polynomial hash treats a string as a number in base B, reduced modulo a large prime M: hash(s) = (s[0]·B^(m−1) + s[1]·B^(m−2) + … + s[m−1]) mod M. The key property is that sliding a window by one character updates the hash in O(1):

new_hash = ((old_hash - t[i] * B^(m-1)) * B + t[i + m]) mod M

— remove the outgoing character's contribution, shift everything up one power, and add the incoming character.

def rabin_karp(t, p, B=911382323, M=(1 << 61) - 1):
    n, m = len(t), len(p)
    if m > n: return -1
    high = pow(B, m - 1, M)
    hp = ht = 0
    for i in range(m):
        hp = (hp * B + ord(p[i])) % M
        ht = (ht * B + ord(t[i])) % M
    for i in range(n - m + 1):
        if hp == ht and t[i:i + m] == p:          # verify on a hash match
            return i
        if i + m < n:
            ht = ((ht - ord(t[i]) * high) * B + ord(t[i + m])) % M
    return -1

Expected O(n + m). The verification step costs O(m) only on hash matches, which for random-looking data are almost always true matches. The modulus here is a 61-bit Mersenne prime, which makes accidental collisions extremely rare; with a modulus near 10⁹ and millions of windows, collisions become likely (see the deep layer), so verification or a second hash is essential.

Applications of rolling hashes

Repeated DNA Sequences: every 10-letter substring that occurs more than once. With only four letters, encode each in 2 bits; a window of 10 letters is a 20-bit integer, updated by code = ((code << 2) | letter) & ((1 << 20) − 1). That is a perfect (collision-free) rolling hash. Count codes in a dict and report those seen twice.

Longest Duplicate Substring: the longest substring appearing at least twice. If a duplicate of length L exists, a duplicate of length L − 1 exists too (drop a character), so "a duplicate of length L exists" is monotone — binary search on L (al7). For each candidate L, roll a hash over all windows of length L and look for a repeated hash, verifying actual equality for candidate pairs. O(n log n) expected. It is a showcase of combining patterns: binary search on the answer, a sliding window, and hashing.

Comparing substrings in O(1): precompute prefix hashes H[i] = hash(s[:i]) and powers of B. Then hash(s[l:r]) = (H[r] − H[l]·B^(r−l)) mod M, and any two substrings can be compared in O(1) (probabilistically). This answers many queries such as "do s[a:b] and s[c:d] match?", "longest common prefix of two suffixes" (binary search with hash comparisons) and "is s[l:r] a palindrome?" (compare with the prefix hashes of the reversed string).

Rotations and repeated copies

Rotate String: goal is a rotation of s exactly when len(goal) == len(s) and goal occurs in s + s — every rotation of s appears as a window of s + s. Repeated String Match: the fewest copies of a whose concatenation contains b. Any match must fit in ⌈len(b)/len(a)⌉ copies, or one more copy if the match begins partway through a; test those two with a linear search, else −1.

Palindromes in linear time: Manacher, briefly

Longest Palindromic Substring is O(n²) with expand-around-centre (al22). Manacher's algorithm makes it O(n) with the same idea as the Z-function: keep the rightmost palindrome found so far, and for a new centre inside it, the mirror centre's radius gives a lower bound, so you only expand beyond what is known. Implementations insert a separator between characters ("#a#b#a#") so odd and even lengths are handled uniformly. It is rarely required in interviews, but knowing that the Z-style "reuse the rightmost known window" trick has a palindrome version is a good senior aside.

Wildcards and approximate matching

Real searches often allow uncertainty. A pattern with single-character wildcards ("a?c") breaks KMP's border logic, because a wildcard matches different characters at different alignments; simple approaches split the pattern at wildcards and search for the pieces, or use bit-parallel algorithms (Shift-Or, also called Bitap) that keep a bitmask of "partial match states" per text character and handle wildcards and character classes naturally. Approximate matching ("occurrences with at most k mismatches or edits") extends Bitap with k + 1 bitmasks, which is how the classic agrep tool worked, or uses the edit-distance DP (al22) restricted to a band. These are rarely interview questions in full, but they explain why "fuzzy find" in editors feels instant: bit-parallelism processes 64 pattern positions per machine instruction.

Recognising the pattern

Use a linear-time matcher when a problem searches for a pattern in a long text with worst-case guarantees, or asks about a string's self-overlap: periods, repetitions, longest prefix-suffix, palindromic prefixes (KMP or Z). Use rolling hashes when you must compare many substrings of the same length (sliding windows, duplicate detection) or arbitrary substrings in O(1) after preprocessing — and always handle collisions.

Practice in the DSA list: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String, Rotate String, Repeated String Match, Repeated DNA Sequences, Longest Happy Prefix, Shortest Palindrome, Longest Duplicate Substring, Longest Palindromic Substring (al22).
deep:
Why KMP is linear, precisely

In the search loop, i (the text index) increases by exactly one per iteration, and j (characters matched) increases by at most one per iteration. Each execution of j = lps[j − 1] strictly decreases j. Since j never goes below zero, the total number of decreases over the whole run is at most the total number of increases, which is at most n. So the inner while loop runs at most n times in total, and the search is O(n); the prefix function's construction is O(m) by the same argument. This is the aggregate method from al2, and it is the answer to the common follow-up "the while loop inside the for loop — is it quadratic?".

KMP as an automaton, and Aho–Corasick

The prefix function defines a finite automaton with states 0..m (characters matched) and transitions for each character: on a match go to j + 1, otherwise follow failure links until a match or 0. Precomputing the full transition table (m × alphabet) makes each text character a single table lookup, which is how some hardware and high-throughput matchers work. Building the same structure on a trie of many patterns — failure links pointing to the longest proper suffix that is a prefix of some pattern — gives the Aho–Corasick automaton (al15), which finds all occurrences of thousands of patterns in one pass over the text. It is the standard engine for multi-keyword search, antivirus signatures and intrusion detection.

Collision probability and anti-hash tests

For two fixed different strings and a random base, a polynomial hash modulo a prime M collides with probability at most about m/M. But in "find any repeated window" you compare N windows pairwise, and by the birthday effect the expected number of colliding pairs is about N²/(2M). With N = 10⁶ windows and M ≈ 10⁹, that is around 500 false collisions — certain trouble without verification. With M = 2⁶¹ − 1 it is about 2 × 10⁻⁷. Worse, with a fixed known base and modulus (or with "natural overflow" modulo 2⁶⁴ in C++), testers can construct strings that collide deliberately — the Thue–Morse sequence breaks any hash modulo 2⁶⁴. The defences are a random base chosen at run time, a large prime modulus or two independent moduli, and verification on matches when correctness matters more than speed.

Suffix arrays and the LCP array

A suffix array lists the starting positions of all suffixes of a string in sorted order; the LCP array gives the longest common prefix of each adjacent pair. Together they answer many string questions deterministically: the longest repeated substring is the maximum LCP value; the number of distinct substrings is n(n+1)/2 − Σ LCP; pattern search is a binary search over the sorted suffixes. Construction is O(n log n) with prefix doubling (sorting by the first 1, 2, 4, … characters using ranks) or O(n) with SA-IS, and Kasai's algorithm computes LCP in O(n). Bioinformatics and full-text indexes (the FM-index used in genome aligners like BWA and Bowtie) build on them. In interviews, naming the suffix array as the deterministic alternative to binary-search-plus-hashing for Longest Duplicate Substring shows breadth.

Prefix-function automata for counting strings

A harder family asks "how many strings of length n over an alphabet do not contain a given pattern?" or "contain it exactly k times?". Build the KMP automaton of the pattern (states 0..m, with a transition for every character computed from the failure links), then run a DP over (length so far, automaton state): from each state, each character leads to the next state, and reaching state m means the pattern appeared. That is O(n · m · alphabet), and with matrix exponentiation over the automaton (al25) it handles n up to 10¹⁸. It is a beautiful combination of string matching and dynamic programming, and it also underlies counting with several forbidden patterns via Aho–Corasick.

What real libraries use

Production string search rarely uses textbook KMP. GNU grep relies on Boyer–Moore-style algorithms, which compare from the end of the pattern and can skip ahead by up to m characters on a mismatch — sublinear on typical text — together with a DFA engine for regular expressions. CPython's str.find historically used a simplified Boyer–Moore–Horspool with a bloom-filter skip, and since Python 3.10 switches to the Crochemore–Perrin two-way algorithm for longer needles, which guarantees linear time with constant extra memory. Knowing that the built-in is linear-time is why "just use in" is acceptable in real code, while implementing KMP or Z remains the expected interview demonstration.
prod:
In the interview room

String-algorithm questions reward a crisp definition and a clean loop. State the definition first ("lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of p[0..i] that is also a suffix"), trace it on a short pattern, then write the code. The common bugs: forgetting that "proper" excludes the whole string (lps[0] = 0); using if instead of while for the fallback, which only tries one shorter border; not falling back after a full match, which misses overlapping occurrences; omitting the separator in s + "#" + t tricks, which lets borders span both parts; and, for rolling hashes, negative values before the modulus in languages where % can return negatives, forgetting to precompute B^(m−1), and skipping verification. Test with a pattern longer than the text, an empty pattern if allowed, all-equal characters, and overlapping matches ("aaa" in "aaaaa" occurs three times).

Expect "why is it linear?" (the aggregate argument), "how would you handle many patterns?" (Aho–Corasick or a trie), and, for hashing, "what about collisions?" (verify, or double hash, plus the birthday estimate). When a problem can be solved with either KMP or hashing, choose the one you can write correctly under pressure and mention the other; interviewers care more about correctness and justification than about the specific technique.

On online assessments, string-matching problems often disguise themselves as "how many times does this pattern occur in this long log", "the smallest block that repeats to form this string", or "the longest prefix that also appears at the end". Each maps to one of the identities in this lesson; recognising the identity is usually the hard part.

Finally, remember the separator rule for every concatenation trick (s + "#" + t, p + "�" + t): the separator must be a character that cannot occur in either string, or borders and Z-values can run across the boundary and report false matches. In Python, a character outside the input alphabet such as "�" is a safe choice for text problems.

In real systems

Rolling hashes are a workhorse of data infrastructure. rsync synchronises files over a network by computing a cheap rolling checksum of every window of the local file and comparing it against block checksums sent from the remote side, confirming candidates with a strong hash — Tridgell and Mackerras's 1996 report describes the design. Backup and deduplication systems (and tools like restic and borg) split files into chunks at positions where a rolling hash of the last few dozen bytes hits a target pattern ("content-defined chunking"), so inserting a byte only changes nearby chunks. Plagiarism detectors such as MOSS fingerprint documents with Rabin hashes and the winnowing algorithm. Search tools combine Boyer–Moore skipping, automata and SIMD scanning; antivirus engines and network intrusion detection systems (Snort, Suricata) run Aho–Corasick over traffic; and genome aligners index reference genomes with suffix-array-based FM-indexes to find billions of short reads. The interview ideas — reuse what you have matched, hash windows incrementally, verify on collision — are exactly their design principles.
myths: Naive substring search is O(n) in practice, so linear-time algorithms are academic.

On ordinary text the naive method is fast, but on inputs with long partial matches — 'aaaa…ab' searched in 'aaaa…a' — it does O(n·m) work. Interview problems and online judges include exactly these inputs. KMP, Z and rolling hashes guarantee linear time.
KMP's prefix function is the same as counting matching prefixes.

lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of it — a border, not a count. For 'aabaaab' it is [0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 2, 3]. Getting the definition exactly right is what makes the rest of the algorithm work.
A rolling-hash match proves the strings are equal.

Different strings can share a hash. With a modulus near 10⁹ and many comparisons, collisions become likely (the birthday effect), and adversarial tests can force them for a known modulus and base. Verify the actual characters on a hash match, or use two independent hashes.
Python's 'in' operator for strings is naive.

CPython's string search combines several techniques; since Python 3.10 it uses the Crochemore–Perrin two-way algorithm for longer patterns, which guarantees linear time. In interviews you still implement KMP or Z to show the idea, but in real code use the built-in.
The Z-function and KMP solve different problems.

Both compute, in linear time, how the pattern matches against itself, and either can do pattern search: KMP via the failure function, Z via the Z-array of pattern + separator + text. Many problems can be solved with either; pick the one you can write correctly.
lab:
Check KMP, Z-search and Rabin–Karp against Python's own search on random and adversarial strings.

  1. Save as string_lab.py: 
    import random

def prefix_function(p):
    lps, k = [0] * len(p), 0
    for i in range(1, len(p)):
        while k and p[i] != p[k]: k = lps[k - 1]
        if p[i] == p[k]: k += 1
        lps[i] = k
    return lps

def kmp_all(t, p):
    lps, j, out = prefix_function(p), 0, []
    for i, ch in enumerate(t):
        while j and ch != p[j]: j = lps[j - 1]
        if ch == p[j]: j += 1
        if j == len(p): out.append(i - j + 1); j = lps[j - 1]
    return out

def z_all(t, p):
    s = p + "\0" + t; n = len(s); z = [0] * n; l = r = 0
    for i in range(1, n):
        if i < r: z[i] = min(r - i, z[i - l])
        while i + z[i] < n and s[z[i]] == s[i + z[i]]: z[i] += 1
        if i + z[i] > r: l, r = i, i + z[i]
    return [i - len(p) - 1 for i in range(len(p) + 1, n) if z[i] == len(p)]

def builtin_all(t, p):
    out, i = [], t.find(p)
    while i != -1: out.append(i); i = t.find(p, i + 1)
    return out

for _ in range(3000):
    t = "".join(random.choices("ab", k=random.randint(0, 30)))
    p = "".join(random.choices("ab", k=random.randint(1, 5)))
    assert kmp_all(t, p) == z_all(t, p) == builtin_all(t, p), (t, p)
print("KMP and Z find exactly the same occurrences as str.find")

s = "abcabcabc"; lps = prefix_function(s); period = len(s) - lps[-1]
print("lps", lps, "smallest period", period, "repetition:", lps[-1] > 0 and len(s) % period == 0)
  2. Run it. The random tests use a two-letter alphabet, which creates many overlapping and partial matches — the cases where off-by-one errors in fallbacks show up.
  3. Check the last line: lps of "abcabcabc" is [0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], the smallest period is 3, and it is a repetition. Try "abcab" and "aaaa".
  4. Change the while in kmp_all's fallback to if and rerun: the random tests start failing (patterns such as "bbbba" miss matches), because a single fallback cannot walk the whole chain of shorter borders.

What this proves: both linear-time matchers agree with the built-in on every occurrence, including overlaps, and the full fallback chain is necessary.
recap: Naive matching restarts after a mismatch and can take O(n·m); linear algorithms reuse what the partial match already revealed.
The prefix function lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of p[0..i] that is also a suffix of it.
KMP scans the text once; on a mismatch it falls back to j = lps[j − 1] instead of moving backwards in the text, giving O(n + m).
The smallest period of a string s is len(s) − lps[−1]; s is a repetition of a block exactly when that period divides len(s) and is shorter than s.
The Z-function z[i] is the length of the longest substring starting at i that matches a prefix of the string; Z on pattern + '#' + text finds every match.
A polynomial rolling hash updates a window's hash in O(1) by removing the outgoing character and adding the incoming one, modulo a large prime.
On a hash match, compare the characters (or use two hashes) because collisions happen.
Binary search on length plus a rolling hash finds the longest duplicate substring in O(n log n) expected.
glossary: A string that is both a proper prefix and a suffix of another string, such as 'ab' in 'abcab'.
With N possible hash values, collisions become likely after about √N items, far fewer than N.
Deterministic finite automaton: a state machine with exactly one transition per state and input character; KMP can be compiled into one.
Another name for the KMP prefix function: where to continue matching after a mismatch.
A linear-time pattern-matching algorithm that never moves backwards in the text, using the prefix function.
For a suffix array, the lengths of the longest common prefixes of adjacent suffixes in sorted order.
A linear-time algorithm for the longest palindromic substring that reuses palindromes found so far.
A shift p such that s[i] = s[i + p] for all valid i; the smallest period is len(s) − lps[−1].
A string hash computed as Σ s[i]·Bⁿ⁻¹⁻ⁱ mod M for a base B and modulus M.
For each position, the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix of the string up to that position.
A prefix shorter than the whole string.
Pattern matching by comparing rolling hashes of text windows with the pattern's hash.
A hash of a sliding window that can be updated in O(1) when the window moves by one character.
The starting positions of all suffixes of a string, sorted lexicographically.
For each position i, the length of the longest substring starting at i that equals a prefix of the string.
drill:
Pick the tool

For each task, choose KMP/Z or rolling hashes (or both) and outline the solution. (a) Given a string of length 10⁵, find its shortest prefix that, repeated (possibly with a partial copy at the end), reproduces the string. (b) Given two strings of length 10⁵, find the length of their longest common substring. (c) Count the distinct substrings of a string of length 5,000. (d) For 10⁵ queries (l1, r1, l2, r2), decide whether s[l1:r1] == s[l2:r2].

Answer

(a) KMP: the answer is the prefix of length len(s) − lps[−1] (the smallest period); a partial final copy is allowed, so no divisibility check is needed. O(n). (b) Binary search on the length L (a common substring of length L implies one of length L − 1); for each L, put the rolling hashes of all length-L windows of the first string in a set and check the second string's windows against it, verifying hits. O((n + m) log n) expected. A suffix automaton or a suffix array of a + "#" + b gives deterministic O(n log n) or O(n). (c) With n = 5,000 there are about 12.5 million substrings; for each length L, roll hashes over the n − L + 1 windows and add them to a set (or use a 64-bit pair of hashes to make collisions negligible), summing distinct counts: O(n²) hash operations, about 1.25 × 10⁷. Deterministically, a suffix array gives n(n+1)/2 − Σ LCP in O(n log n). (d) Precompute prefix hashes and powers once in O(n); each query compares (lengths first, then) hash(s[l1:r1]) and hash(s[l2:r2]) in O(1) — use two moduli or a 61-bit modulus so 10⁵ comparisons are effectively collision-free.
qa: E
Find the first occurrence of a needle in a haystack.

In production, haystack.find(needle). In an interview, show a linear algorithm: build KMP's prefix function for the needle and scan the haystack once, or compute the Z-function of needle + '#' + haystack and return the first i with z[i] = len(needle). Both are O(n + m). Mention that naive matching is O(n·m) in the worst case.
E
Rotate String: is goal a rotation of s?

goal is a rotation of s exactly when the lengths match and goal occurs in s + s, because s + s contains every rotation of s as a substring. The containment check is O(n) with KMP or the built-in search.
M
Compute the KMP prefix function and explain its complexity.

lps[0] = 0; keep k = length of the current border. For i from 1, while k > 0 and p[i] != p[k], set k = lps[k − 1]; if p[i] == p[k], k += 1; lps[i] = k. k increases by at most one per step and every fallback decreases it, so the total number of fallbacks is at most n: O(n) overall.
Follow-up: Why is falling back to lps[k − 1] safe? — The next-longest border of p[0..i−1] is the longest border of its longest border, so no shorter candidate is skipped.
M
Repeated Substring Pattern: is s a repetition of a shorter block?
Let p = len(s) − lps[−1], the smallest period. s is a repetition exactly when lps[−1] > 0 and len(s) % p == 0. An alternative trick: s is a repetition if s occurs in (s + s)[1:−1]. Both O(n).
M
Repeated DNA Sequences: all 10-letter substrings occurring more than once.

Slide a window of length 10 and keep a rolling hash, or encode each letter in 2 bits so the window is a 20-bit integer updated by shift, OR and mask. Count windows in a dict and report those seen twice. O(n). Hashing each 10-character slice directly is also O(n) because the length is a constant, but the rolling version generalises to long windows.
M
Longest Happy Prefix: the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix.
That is exactly lps[−1] of the KMP prefix function: return s[:lps[−1]]. O(n). A rolling hash comparing prefix and suffix hashes for each length from n − 1 down also works in O(n) expected.
M
How does the Rabin–Karp rolling hash update work?

With hash(s[i..i+m−1]) = Σ s[i+j]·B^(m−1−j) mod M, moving the window right subtracts the outgoing character times B^(m−1), multiplies by B and adds the incoming character, all mod M. Precompute B^(m−1) mod M. Each update is O(1), so all windows are hashed in O(n).
Follow-up: How do you choose B and M? — A large prime M (around 10⁹ or a 61-bit prime) and a random base in [256, M − 1], so adversarial inputs cannot be prepared in advance.
M
Repeated String Match: the fewest copies of a so that b is a substring.

b can only fit if the repeated string is at least len(b) long, so try q = ceil(len(b)/len(a)) and q + 1 copies — one extra copy covers a match that starts partway through a. Check containment with a linear-time search. If neither works, return −1.
H
Shortest Palindrome: add the fewest characters in front of s to make it a palindrome.

The answer keeps the longest palindromic prefix of s and prepends the reverse of the rest. Find that prefix with KMP: build lps for s + '#' + reverse(s); the final value is the length of the longest prefix of s that equals a suffix of reverse(s), i.e. the longest palindromic prefix. Return reverse(s[k:]) + s. O(n).
H
Longest Duplicate Substring.

If a duplicate of length L exists, so does one of length L − 1, so binary search on L. For a candidate L, hash every length-L window with a rolling hash and look for a repeated hash, verifying candidate matches by comparing the substrings (or using two moduli). O(n log n) expected. A suffix array with the LCP array gives a deterministic O(n log n) solution.
H
Explain the Z-function algorithm.

Keep the rightmost interval [l, r) known to match a prefix. For each i < r, the value z[i − l] tells you a lower bound: z[i] ≥ min(r − i, z[i − l]). Then extend by direct comparison past r if possible, updating [l, r). Every successful comparison moves r forward, so the total work is O(n).
H
Why can hashing-based solutions fail on judges, and how do you make them robust?

With a fixed, publicly known base and modulus, testers can construct different strings with equal hashes, and even random inputs collide often with a 32-bit modulus once you compare millions of hashes. Use a random base, a large modulus (a 61-bit Mersenne prime, or two independent moduli), and verify equality on a hash match when correctness matters. The expected collision count with N hashes and modulus M is about N²/(2M).

t: Range queries: Fenwick trees, segment trees, lazy propagation and sparse tables
sum: Answer range sums, minimums and counts while the data changes: why prefix sums break under updates, Fenwick (binary indexed) trees, segment trees for any associative operation, lazy propagation for range updates, sparse tables for static range minimum, coordinate compression, and the counting problems they solve.
prereq: al3
Prefix sums answer static range sums in O(1); a single update forces O(n) recomputation.
al24
x & −x isolates the lowest set bit; binary decomposition of an index.
al14
Binary trees, recursion on left and right children, height log₂ n for a balanced tree.
why:
A trading dashboard shows the total volume traded in any time window a user selects, while new trades keep arriving. A game keeps a leaderboard of a million players and must answer "how many players have a score below 4,250?" every time someone looks at their rank, while scores change every second. A calendar service must report, after each new booking, the maximum number of meetings overlapping at any moment. All three combine two kinds of operation on the same data: queries over a range and updates.

Prefix sums (al3) answer range sums in O(1), but they are frozen: change one element and every later prefix changes, an O(n) rebuild. Recomputing each range query from scratch is the opposite trade — O(1) updates, O(n) queries. With a million elements and a million mixed operations, either extreme costs on the order of 10¹² steps. The structures in this lesson meet in the middle: O(log n) for both, so a million operations take around twenty million steps.

The two workhorses are the Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree), a dozen lines of code for prefix sums with point updates, and the segment tree, which handles any associative operation — sums, minimums, maximums, gcds — over arbitrary ranges, and with lazy propagation supports updates to whole ranges too. For data that never changes, a sparse table answers range minimums in O(1). Combined with coordinate compression, these structures also solve counting problems that do not look like range queries at first: smaller elements after each position, inversions, range sums within bounds.

This lesson builds each structure from the idea behind it, with a trace, and then applies them to the interview hards that require them. It is the most "advanced" lesson in this track, but each structure rests on one simple idea: precompute answers for a well-chosen family of ranges, and answer any query by combining a few of them.
primer:
The mental model: a company's reporting hierarchy

Imagine a company where each team leader knows the total sales of their team, each department head knows the total for their teams, and the CEO knows the company total. To find the sales of any group of consecutive teams, you do not ask every salesperson; you ask a few managers whose groups exactly cover the range — a department head here, a couple of team leaders at the edges. When one salesperson closes a deal, only the people above them in the hierarchy — their team leader, department head and the CEO — need to update their totals. Both questions and updates touch only a handful of people, about one per level of the hierarchy.

A segment tree is exactly that hierarchy built over array positions: the root covers the whole array, each node's two children cover its left and right halves, and each node stores the combined value (sum, min, …) of its range. A tree over n positions has about log₂ n levels, so any range can be covered by O(log n) nodes and any point update changes O(log n) nodes.

A Fenwick tree is a cleverer, flatter version of the same idea for prefix sums. It uses a single array where entry i stores the sum of a block of positions ending at i, whose length is the lowest set bit of i (al24). Those blocks are arranged so that any prefix [1, i] is tiled by at most log₂ i of them, found by repeatedly removing the lowest set bit of i, and any position is contained in at most log₂ n of them, found by repeatedly adding the lowest set bit.

The cost argument is worth making concrete. With n = 10⁶ positions, a segment tree has about 2 × 10⁶ nodes and depth 20. A point update rewrites 20 node values; a range query combines at most about 40 node values (two partial nodes per level). Compare that with recomputing a range sum over up to a million elements, or rebuilding a million prefix sums after each update. Both structures turn "touch everything" into "touch one node per level", which is the same logarithmic trick as binary search and heaps, applied to ranges.

Where the company analogy breaks: real managers can summarise anything about their teams, but these structures can only summarise with an operation that combines two summaries into the summary of the union — an associative operation like sum, min, max or gcd. "The median sales of a team" cannot be combined from two halves' medians, so a plain segment tree cannot answer range medians. And for Fenwick trees, the operation must also be invertible (subtraction undoes addition) to answer arbitrary ranges as prefix(r) − prefix(l − 1).

Choosing a structure

NeedStructureQueryUpdate
Range sums, no updatesprefix sums (al3)O(1)O(n) rebuild
Range min/max, no updatessparse tableO(1)none (static)
Prefix or range sums, point updatesFenwick treeO(log n)O(log n)
