Range updates and range queriessegment tree + lazyO(log n)O(log n)
Range add, point queryFenwick on a difference arrayO(log n)O(log n)

The last row reuses the difference-array idea from al3: adding v to a[l..r] is two point updates (+v at l, −v at r + 1) in a Fenwick tree over differences, and a[i] is the prefix sum up to i.

The Fenwick tree

Use 1-based positions. Let lowbit(i) = i & −i, the value of i's lowest set bit (al24). Entry tree[i] holds the sum of a over the block (i − lowbit(i), i]. So tree[8] covers positions 1–8, tree[6] covers 5–6, tree[7] covers just 7.

class Fenwick:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.t = [0] * (n + 1)              # 1-based

    def add(self, i, delta):                # a[i] += delta, i is 1-based
        while i <= self.n:
            self.t[i] += delta
            i += i & -i                     # next block that contains i

    def prefix(self, i):                    # sum of a[1..i]
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += self.t[i]
            i -= i & -i                     # strip the block just used
        return s

    def range_sum(self, l, r):              # sum of a[l..r]
        return self.prefix(r) - self.prefix(l - 1)

Trace prefix(7): 7 = 111₂ → add tree[7] (block 7..7), strip lowbit → 6 = 110₂ → add tree[6] (block 5..6), strip → 4 = 100₂ → add tree[4] (block 1..4), strip → 0. Three blocks tile 1..7. Trace add(5, δ): 5 = 101₂ → tree[5], add lowbit → 6 = 110₂ → tree[6], → 8 = 1000₂ → tree[8], → 16 > n stops. Those are exactly the blocks containing position 5.

"Range Sum Query — Mutable" is a Fenwick tree plus a copy of the array (to turn "set a[i] to v" into "add v − a[i]"). Building by n calls to add is O(n log n); an O(n) build adds each tree[i] into tree[i + lowbit(i)] once in a left-to-right pass. Remember the 1-based indexing: convert at the boundary (i + 1) and nowhere else.

Counting with a Fenwick tree over values

Many counting problems become range queries if the Fenwick tree is indexed by value instead of position. Count of Smaller Numbers After Self: for each element, how many elements to its right are smaller? Scan from right to left; keep a Fenwick tree where count[v] is the number of already-seen elements (all to the right) with value v. For each element, the answer is prefix(v − 1); then add 1 at v.

Values can be up to 10⁴ in magnitude, or 10⁹ in other problems, and negative. Coordinate compression fixes that: sort the distinct values and replace each by its 1-based rank. Only the order matters for "smaller than", so ranks give the same answers.

def count_smaller(nums):
    ranks = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(nums)))}
    fw, out = Fenwick(len(ranks)), []
    for v in reversed(nums):
        r = ranks[v]
        out.append(fw.prefix(r - 1))     # seen elements with smaller rank
        fw.add(r, 1)
    return out[::-1]

Trace [5, 2, 6, 1]: ranks 1→1, 2→2, 5→3, 6→4. From the right: 1 (rank 1) → 0 smaller, add; 6 (rank 4) → prefix(3) = 1, add; 2 (rank 2) → prefix(1) = 1, add; 5 (rank 3) → prefix(2) = 2. Reversed: [2, 1, 1, 0]. O(n log n). Counting inversions (pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j]) is the same scan, summing the answers. Reverse Pairs (a[i] > 2·a[j]) queries for values above 2·a[j], which needs the doubled values included in the compression, or merge sort with a two-pointer count per merge.

Count of Range Sum applies the same tool to prefix sums: the subarray i..j has sum P[j + 1] − P[i], so count pairs of prefix values whose difference lies in [lower, upper]. Scan prefixes left to right, and for each P[j] query how many earlier prefixes lie in [P[j] − upper, P[j] − lower] — a range count in a Fenwick tree over compressed prefix values — then insert P[j]. This is the "inequality between pairs of prefixes needs a sorted structure" situation flagged in al3.

The segment tree

A segment tree works for any associative operation. A clean recursive version stores node values in an array of size 4n, with node 1 as the root and children 2k and 2k + 1:

class SegTree:                                 # range minimum, point update
    def __init__(self, a):
        self.n = len(a); self.t = [float("inf")] * (4 * self.n)
        self._build(1, 0, self.n - 1, a)
    def _build(self, k, lo, hi, a):
        if lo == hi: self.t[k] = a[lo]; return
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        self._build(2 * k, lo, mid, a); self._build(2 * k + 1, mid + 1, hi, a)
        self.t[k] = min(self.t[2 * k], self.t[2 * k + 1])
    def update(self, i, v, k=1, lo=0, hi=None):
        if hi is None: hi = self.n - 1
        if lo == hi: self.t[k] = v; return
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if i <= mid: self.update(i, v, 2 * k, lo, mid)
        else: self.update(i, v, 2 * k + 1, mid + 1, hi)
        self.t[k] = min(self.t[2 * k], self.t[2 * k + 1])
    def query(self, l, r, k=1, lo=0, hi=None):  # min of a[l..r]
        if hi is None: hi = self.n - 1
        if r < lo or hi < l: return float("inf")      # disjoint
        if l <= lo and hi <= r: return self.t[k]       # fully covered
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        return min(self.query(l, r, 2 * k, lo, mid),
                   self.query(l, r, 2 * k + 1, mid + 1, hi))

Three cases in the query make it O(log n): a node completely outside the range contributes the identity (∞ for min, 0 for sum); a node completely inside contributes its stored value without recursing; only nodes that partially overlap recurse, and there are at most two such nodes per level. Changing min and the identity gives range sum, max, gcd, or a product modulo p. An iterative bottom-up version — leaves at indices n..2n − 1, parent of i at i // 2 — is shorter and faster and is worth learning if you use segment trees often (see the references).

Lazy propagation: range updates

"Add v to every element in [l, r]" would touch up to n leaves. Lazy propagation applies the update to whole nodes instead: when a node's range is completely inside [l, r], update its stored value as if all its leaves had changed (for sums: add v × length; for max: add v) and record v in the node's lazy tag, meaning "my children still owe this addition". Only when a later operation needs to go below that node do you push the tag: apply it to both children (their values and their tags) and clear it.

def push(k, lo, mid, hi):                       # range add, range sum version
    if lazy[k]:
        for c, a, b in ((2 * k, lo, mid), (2 * k + 1, mid + 1, hi)):
            t[c] += lazy[k] * (b - a + 1)
            lazy[c] += lazy[k]
        lazy[k] = 0

def range_add(l, r, v, k, lo, hi):
    if r < lo or hi < l: return
    if l <= lo and hi <= r:
        t[k] += v * (hi - lo + 1); lazy[k] += v; return
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    push(k, lo, mid, hi)
    range_add(l, r, v, 2 * k, lo, mid); range_add(l, r, v, 2 * k + 1, mid + 1, hi)
    t[k] = t[2 * k] + t[2 * k + 1]

Queries push tags on the way down in the same way. Both operations still visit O(log n) nodes. The same pattern supports range assignment (tag = "set everything to x"), range max with range add (My Calendar III: +1 on each booking's interval, then the root's max), and range assignment with range max (Falling Squares: query the max height over a square's span, then assign max + side to that span). Coordinate compression keeps the tree small when the coordinates are large; a "dynamic" segment tree that creates nodes only when needed is the alternative when coordinates are not known in advance.

Sparse tables: O(1) range minimum on static data

If the array never changes, precompute the minimum of every range whose length is a power of two: sp[0][i] = a[i], and sp[k][i] = min(sp[k−1][i], sp[k−1][i + 2^(k−1)]) — the range of length 2ᵏ starting at i is two halves of length 2^(k−1). That is O(n log n) values. A query [l, r] picks k = floor(log₂(r − l + 1)), the largest power of two that fits, and covers the range with two blocks of that length, one starting at l and one ending at r:

def query(l, r):
    k = (r - l + 1).bit_length() - 1
    return min(sp[k][l], sp[k][r - (1 << k) + 1])

The two blocks overlap, which is fine for min because min(x, x) = x — the operation is idempotent. For sums, overlap would double-count, so sparse tables are only for idempotent operations (min, max, gcd, bitwise AND/OR). O(1) per query makes them ideal for many queries on static data, such as LCA via Euler tour (al14) or the "minimum over a sliding range" step inside other algorithms.

Merge sort as a counting tool

Counting inversions, smaller-after-self, reverse pairs and range sums can also be done during merge sort. While merging two sorted halves, every time an element from the right half is placed before remaining left-half elements, it is smaller than all of them — that count is the number of inversions it forms across the halves. Variations count pairs satisfying a[i] > 2·a[j] with a separate two-pointer pass before each merge. The complexity is O(n log n), the same as a Fenwick tree, and it needs no compression. Which to use is a matter of taste; Fenwick trees are easier to adapt to online queries, merge sort to pair-counting with arbitrary conditions.

Recognising the pattern

Reach for these structures when a problem mixes range queries with updates, when the constraints (n and q up to 10⁵) rule out O(n) per operation, or when a counting problem asks "how many earlier/later elements are smaller/larger/in a range" — that is a Fenwick tree over compressed values. Static range minimum suggests a sparse table; range updates suggest lazy propagation.

Practice in the DSA list: Range Sum Query — Mutable, Count of Smaller Numbers After Self, Reverse Pairs, Count of Range Sum, My Calendar III, Falling Squares, Longest Increasing Subsequence II, Range Sum Query 2D (al3, static version).
deep:
Why the Fenwick tree works

Write a prefix length i in binary, say 13 = 1101₂ = 8 + 4 + 1. The prefix [1, 13] splits into consecutive blocks of lengths 8, 4 and 1: [1, 8], [9, 12], [13, 13]. Those are exactly the blocks stored at tree[8], tree[12] and tree[13], because tree[j] covers the block of length lowbit(j) ending at j. Removing the lowest set bit of 13 gives 12, then 8, then 0 — walking those blocks from right to left. For updates, the blocks containing position p are those tree[j] with j ≥ p and j − lowbit(j) < p; adding the lowest set bit repeatedly enumerates exactly them. Both walks visit at most one index per bit, O(log n). The structure is implicit — no pointers, no node objects — which is why it is so compact and cache-friendly.

Fenwick variants: range updates and 2D

A Fenwick tree over a difference array supports range add and point query. Supporting range add and range sum needs two Fenwick trees: maintain B1 and B2 so that prefix(i) = B1.prefix(i) · i − B2.prefix(i); a range add of v on [l, r] does B1.add(l, v), B1.add(r + 1, −v), B2.add(l, v·(l − 1)), B2.add(r + 1, −v·r). It is a neat algebraic trick and an alternative to lazy segment trees for sums. A 2D Fenwick tree nests the loops over rows and columns to answer rectangle sums under point updates in O(log R · log C) — "Range Sum Query 2D — Mutable".

Order statistics with a Fenwick tree

A Fenwick tree counting values acts as a dynamic multiset with rank queries: the rank of x is prefix(x). The inverse — the k-th smallest — can be found in O(log V) by binary lifting: start at position 0, and for each power of two from the largest down, if pos + step ≤ V and tree[pos + step] < k, move to pos + step and subtract tree[pos + step] from k. Because tree[pos + step] is exactly the count in the next block, the walk descends the implicit tree like a binary search. This gives leaderboards ("what score is the 1000th best?") and sliding-window medians with O(log V) operations.

Square-root decomposition and offline tricks

When an operation is not associative or the update is awkward for a segment tree, splitting the array into about √n blocks of √n elements, each with a precomputed summary, gives O(√n) per operation — for n = 10⁵ about 300 steps, often fast enough and much simpler. Mo's algorithm orders offline range queries so that moving from one range to the next adds and removes few elements, answering q queries in O((n + q)√n) for problems like "number of distinct values in a range" that resist segment trees. Offline processing more generally — sorting queries by their right endpoint and sweeping — turns many hard online problems into a Fenwick tree sweep; "count distinct values in [l, r]" is solved by sweeping r and keeping, per value, only its last occurrence marked in a Fenwick tree.

Choosing what a node stores

The real design question for a new segment-tree problem is "what summary of a range lets me combine two adjacent ranges into the summary of their union?". For sums it is the sum; for minimums the minimum. For "longest run of 1s in a range with flips", a node needs the length of its longest run, its longest prefix run, its longest suffix run and its length — the run across the boundary is the left child's suffix run plus the right child's prefix run. For "number of inversions in a range", a node would need more than a few numbers, which is a sign that a segment tree is the wrong tool. Practise by writing the merge function first; if you can write it in a few lines, the rest of the segment tree is boilerplate.

Beyond the basics

Segment trees extend in many directions. Storing a richer summary per node (best prefix sum, best suffix sum, best subarray sum, total) answers "maximum subarray sum in a range with updates" — the merge of two children combines those four numbers. Persistent segment trees keep every past version by copying only the O(log n) nodes an update changes, enabling queries on historical states and "k-th smallest in a range" in O(log n). Segment trees over time support offline dynamic connectivity with a rollback union-find (al19). For interviews, the essential skills are the three basic structures, lazy propagation for range updates, and the ability to say what summary a node must store for a new query.
prod:
In the interview room

Range-query structures are long enough that bugs hide easily, so structure your answer: name the operations needed ("point update and range sum"), pick the simplest structure that supports them (Fenwick unless you need min/max or range updates), state the complexity, and then code. The common bugs: mixing 0-based and 1-based indices in a Fenwick tree (convert once at the API boundary); forgetting that "set a[i] = v" is "add v − a[i]"; querying prefix(l) instead of prefix(l − 1) for a range starting at l; segment tree arrays that are too small (allocate 4n); wrong identity values (0 for sums, ∞ for min); forgetting to push lazy tags before recursing, or pushing with the wrong length; and compressing coordinates without including every value you will query (Reverse Pairs needs 2·a[j]).

Test with a single element, a full-range query, a query on one position, and an update followed by a query that includes and excludes the updated position. If time allows, compare against a brute-force array on random operations — the lab does exactly that.

Interviewers often accept a simpler solution first. If n is small (≤ 10³), say so and offer the O(n²) or sorted-list approach, then describe the O(n log n) structure. For problems like Count of Smaller Numbers After Self, mentioning both the Fenwick and the merge-sort solutions shows breadth. And if a problem only needs static data, a sparse table or prefix sums is the better answer — reaching for a segment tree when prefix sums suffice is a mild negative signal.

On online assessments, the tell-tale constraint is "n, q ≤ 10⁵ (or 2 × 10⁵) with updates between queries". Any per-operation O(n) loop times out at 10¹⁰ total work, which is the cue for a Fenwick or segment tree.

A last interview tip: write the brute-force version alongside the structure (a plain list with O(n) operations) and mention that you would fuzz one against the other. It costs two minutes, and it is exactly how experienced engineers gain confidence in index-heavy code.

In real systems

Peter Fenwick designed his structure in 1994 for arithmetic coding, where a compressor must maintain cumulative frequencies of symbols that change as it adapts — the original "prefix sums with updates" application. Leaderboards need rank queries over changing scores: Redis sorted sets implement them with skip lists whose links store span lengths, which is the same "combine a few precomputed range counts" idea in linked form, giving O(log n) ZRANK. Time-series databases and monitoring systems store pre-aggregated rollups at several resolutions (per minute, hour, day) so a dashboard query over an arbitrary window combines a few coarse buckets with a few fine ones — a segment tree over time in spirit. Order books in trading systems maintain aggregate quantities over price levels for fast "volume up to price p" queries. Game engines and geographic systems use segment-tree and interval-tree variants for collision and range searches, and database engines use similar hierarchical summaries (zone maps, min/max per block) to skip data that cannot match a range predicate.
myths: Segment trees are only for competitive programming.

They appear in interview hards (Count of Smaller Numbers After Self, Range Sum Query — Mutable, My Calendar III, Falling Squares) and in real systems that aggregate over ranges with updates. More importantly, the idea — precompute answers for a hierarchy of ranges and combine O(log n) of them — is a standard design tool.
A Fenwick tree can answer range minimum queries as easily as sums.

Fenwick trees rely on subtraction: a range sum is prefix(r) − prefix(l − 1). Minimum has no inverse, so a Fenwick tree can only give prefix minimums (and only under updates that decrease values). For range minimum with updates, use a segment tree; for static data, a sparse table.
Lazy propagation is a different data structure.

It is a segment tree that postpones work: a range update marks whole nodes with a pending change instead of updating every leaf, and pushes the change down only when a later query or update needs the children. It keeps range updates at O(log n).
You need a segment tree whenever values change.

If you only need prefix or range sums with point updates, a Fenwick tree is shorter, faster and uses n + 1 integers. If updates are rare and queries many, recomputing prefix sums can even be acceptable. Choose the simplest structure that supports the operations.
Large values (up to 10⁹) make Fenwick and segment trees impossible.

When only the relative order matters — counting smaller elements, inversions, overlapping intervals — replace each value by its rank among the distinct values (coordinate compression). The structure then has size equal to the number of distinct values, at most n.
lab:
Fuzz the Fenwick tree and a segment tree against a plain list with random updates and queries.

  1. Save as range_lab.py: 
    import random

class Fenwick:
    def __init__(s, n): s.n, s.t = n, [0] * (n + 1)
    def add(s, i, d):
        i += 1
        while i <= s.n: s.t[i] += d; i += i & -i
    def prefix(s, i):                      # sum of a[0..i-1]
        r = 0
        while i > 0: r += s.t[i]; i -= i & -i
        return r

class SegMin:
    def __init__(s, a):
        s.n = len(a); s.t = [float("inf")] * (2 * s.n)
        s.t[s.n:] = a
        for i in range(s.n - 1, 0, -1): s.t[i] = min(s.t[2 * i], s.t[2 * i + 1])
    def set(s, i, v):
        i += s.n; s.t[i] = v
        while i > 1: i //= 2; s.t[i] = min(s.t[2 * i], s.t[2 * i + 1])
    def query(s, l, r):                    # min of a[l..r-1]
        res, l, r = float("inf"), l + s.n, r + s.n
        while l < r:
            if l & 1: res = min(res, s.t[l]); l += 1
            if r & 1: r -= 1; res = min(res, s.t[r])
            l //= 2; r //= 2
        return res

for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 40); a = [random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(n)]
    fw, sg = Fenwick(n), SegMin(a)
    for i, v in enumerate(a): fw.add(i, v)
    for _ in range(200):
        i = random.randrange(n); v = random.randint(-9, 9)
        fw.add(i, v - a[i]); sg.set(i, v); a[i] = v
        l = random.randrange(n); r = random.randint(l + 1, n)
        assert fw.prefix(r) - fw.prefix(l) == sum(a[l:r])
        assert sg.query(l, r) == min(a[l:r])
print("Fenwick sums and segment-tree minimums match a plain list")
  2. Run it; expect the final message after 60,000 random update/query pairs. The segment tree here is the compact iterative version: leaves at n..2n − 1, parent of i at i // 2, and a half-open query [l, r).
  3. Change fw.prefix(l) to fw.prefix(l + 1) in the sum check and rerun: it fails immediately, the classic off-by-one at a range's left edge.

What this proves: both structures stay exactly consistent with the array under arbitrary interleavings of updates and queries — the property that makes them safe to rely on — and fuzzing against a brute-force list is the fastest way to catch index errors.
recap: Prefix sums give O(1) range sums but O(n) updates; range-query structures balance both at O(log n).
A Fenwick tree stores at index i the sum of the range of length i & −i ending at i; prefix queries strip lowest bits and updates add them, each O(log n).
A range sum on a Fenwick tree is prefix(r) − prefix(l − 1), so it needs an invertible operation such as addition.
A segment tree stores the combined value of each node's range, for any associative operation; queries combine O(log n) nodes that exactly cover the range.
Lazy propagation stores pending range updates at internal nodes and pushes them down only when needed, keeping range updates O(log n).
A sparse table precomputes minimums of all power-of-two ranges in O(n log n) and answers static range minimum in O(1) using two overlapping blocks.
Coordinate compression maps large values to ranks so value-indexed structures stay small.
Counting problems such as smaller-after-self and inversions scan the array while querying and updating a Fenwick tree indexed by value.
glossary: An operation where grouping does not matter: (a ∘ b) ∘ c = a ∘ (b ∘ c); sum, min, max and gcd are associative.
Replacing values by their rank among the sorted distinct values.
An array-based structure supporting prefix sums and point updates in O(log n), using lowest-set-bit arithmetic.
An operation where combining a value with itself changes nothing, such as min(x, x) = x; required for overlapping blocks in sparse tables.
Lowest common ancestor in a tree; static LCA queries reduce to range minimum queries over an Euler tour, which a sparse table answers in O(1).
A pair i < j with a[i] > a[j]; the number of inversions measures how unsorted an array is.
Deferring range updates in a segment tree by tagging nodes and pushing tags to children only when needed.
Changing a single element of the array.
Asking for an aggregate (sum, min, max, count) over a contiguous range of positions.
Changing every element in a contiguous range, such as adding v to positions l..r.
A binary tree over array positions where each node stores the aggregate of its range.
A table of answers for all ranges whose length is a power of two, for static arrays.
Splitting an array into about √n blocks with precomputed block summaries, giving O(√n) operations.
drill:
Choose and justify

For each scenario, choose a structure and give the cost per operation. (a) A static array of 10⁶ temperatures; 10⁶ queries for the coldest reading between two days. (b) An array of 10⁵ stock prices that change; queries for the total over a range. (c) The same array, but updates are "add x to every price in [l, r]" and queries are "maximum price in [l, r]". (d) A stream of 10⁵ scores; after each new score, report how many earlier scores are strictly higher. (e) 10⁵ integers and 10⁵ offline queries "how many distinct values are in a[l..r]?".

Answer

(a) Sparse table: O(n log n) ≈ 2 × 10⁷ preprocessing, O(1) per query; no updates are needed, and min is idempotent so overlapping blocks are fine. (b) Fenwick tree: O(log n) point update and O(log n) range sum via two prefix queries. (c) Segment tree with lazy propagation: range add tags and range max queries, O(log n) each; a Fenwick tree cannot do range max. (d) Fenwick tree over compressed scores (compress offline if all scores are known; otherwise a Fenwick tree over the value range or a balanced tree / SortedList): for each score, answer seen − prefix(rank) (elements with rank greater than it), then add 1 at its rank. O(log n). (e) Offline sweep: sort queries by r; sweep i from left to right, and for value a[i], if it was seen before at position p, do fw.add(p, −1); then fw.add(i, +1) and record last[a[i]] = i. Each value is now marked only at its last occurrence up to i, so for queries with r = i the answer is fw.range_sum(l, r). O((n + q) log n). This "keep only the last occurrence" trick is a standard way to count distinct elements in ranges.
qa: E
Why not just use prefix sums when the array changes?

Prefix sums answer a range sum in O(1), but changing one element changes every later prefix, costing O(n) per update. With q updates and queries mixed, that is O(n·q). A Fenwick or segment tree makes both operations O(log n), so the total is O((n + q) log n).
E
What can a segment tree compute that a Fenwick tree cannot easily?

Any associative operation over arbitrary ranges — minimum, maximum, gcd, the maximum subarray sum of a range — because it combines node values directly rather than subtracting prefixes. Fenwick trees need an inverse operation for arbitrary ranges, so they are natural for sums and counts. Segment trees also support lazy range updates cleanly.
M
Implement Range Sum Query — Mutable.

A Fenwick tree of size n + 1: update(i, delta) does i += 1 and while i ≤ n: tree[i] += delta; i += i & −i. prefix(i) sums tree entries while stripping lowest bits: while i > 0: s += tree[i]; i −= i & −i. For set(i, value), apply delta = value − current, keeping a copy of the array. sumRange(l, r) = prefix(r + 1) − prefix(l). Both operations O(log n).
M
Explain how a Fenwick tree's indices work.

Using 1-based positions, tree[i] covers the range (i − lowbit(i), i], where lowbit(i) = i & −i. A prefix sum up to i walks i → i − lowbit(i), visiting O(log n) disjoint ranges that tile [1, i]. An update at i walks i → i + lowbit(i), visiting exactly the O(log n) nodes whose ranges contain i.
Follow-up: How do you build in O(n)? — For each i, add tree[i] into tree[i + lowbit(i)] once, left to right.
M
Count of Smaller Numbers After Self.

Compress values to ranks. Scan from right to left with a Fenwick tree over ranks that counts how many elements of each rank have been seen. For each element, the answer is prefix(rank − 1) — the count of already-seen (to the right) elements with smaller rank — then add 1 at its rank. O(n log n). Merge sort with index tracking is an alternative.
M
Count inversions in an array.

Either merge sort, counting at each merge how many elements of the right half jump ahead of remaining left-half elements, or a Fenwick tree over compressed values: scan left to right, and for each element add the number of earlier elements greater than it (seen − prefix(rank)). Both O(n log n).
M
What is a sparse table and when is it the best choice?

For a static array, sparse[k][i] = min of a[i..i + 2ᵏ − 1], built in O(n log n) from sparse[k][i] = min(sparse[k−1][i], sparse[k−1][i + 2ᵏ⁻¹]). A query [l, r] takes k = floor(log₂(r − l + 1)) and returns min(sparse[k][l], sparse[k][r − 2ᵏ + 1]) — two overlapping blocks, fine because min is idempotent. O(1) per query; no updates.
H
Range add and range sum with a segment tree: how does lazy propagation work?

Each node stores the sum of its range and a pending addition tag. A range update that fully covers a node adds v × length to its sum and v to its tag, without visiting children. Before descending into a node's children (for a partial update or query), push the tag down: add it to each child's sum (times the child's length) and tag, then clear it. Each operation visits O(log n) nodes.
H
My Calendar III: after each booking, report the maximum number of overlapping bookings.

With up to a few hundred bookings, a sorted map of +1/−1 deltas swept after each booking is O(n) per booking and fine. For large inputs, compress all endpoints (or use a dynamic segment tree over [0, 10⁹)) with lazy range add (+1 on [start, end)) and a max query over the whole range: O(log n) per booking.
H
Count of Range Sum: count pairs (i, j) with lower ≤ sum(nums[i..j]) ≤ upper.

With prefix sums P, count pairs i < j with lower ≤ P[j] − P[i] ≤ upper, i.e. P[j] − upper ≤ P[i] ≤ P[j] − lower. Scan j left to right with a Fenwick tree over compressed prefix values, querying the count of earlier P[i] in that window, then insert P[j]. Or merge sort with two moving pointers per merge. O(n log n).
H
Falling Squares: squares drop onto a line and stack; report the tallest height after each drop.

Compress all left and right edges. For each square, query the maximum height over its covered range, then assign height = that maximum + side to the range, and record the global maximum. That needs a segment tree with range-max query and range-assign lazy updates. O(n log n). With n ≤ 1000, an O(n²) scan over previous squares also passes.
H
How would you find the k-th smallest element in a dynamic multiset of integers up to 10⁶?

Use a Fenwick tree over values counting occurrences, and binary-lift on it: start at position 0 and, for step sizes from the highest power of two down, move forward by the step if the count in that block is less than k (subtracting it from k). The final position + 1 is the answer. Insert and delete are point updates; each operation is O(log V).

why:
"Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put." "Design a set that supports insert, delete and getRandom, each in O(1)." "Design a snapshot array." "Design an iterator over a nested list." These "design a class" questions are a fixture of coding interviews, and they test something different from algorithm puzzles. There is rarely a clever idea to discover. Instead, you must meet several complexity targets at once — and no single standard structure meets them all. A hash map finds keys in O(1) but has no order. A linked list moves nodes in O(1) but cannot find them. An array picks a random element in O(1) but deletes from the middle in O(n). The answer is always a combination, kept consistent on every operation.

These questions also mirror real engineering more closely than most interview problems. Every web service has caches with eviction policies; databases keep versions of data for snapshots; operating systems and message brokers use ring buffers; every collection library has iterators. Interviewers like the format because it reveals how you decompose requirements, choose building blocks, reason about invariants, and handle edge cases — exactly what you do when designing a component at work.

This lesson gives a method for any design question, then applies it to the classics: LRU and LFU caches, the O(1) randomised set, snapshot arrays and time-versioned keys, browser history, circular queues, lazy iterators (peeking, nested-list flattening, BST traversal), the All O'one structure, and a miniature Twitter feed. Each design is presented with the invariant that ties its parts together, because a forgotten update to one part is the bug interviewers see most.
primer:
The mental model: a toolbox and a requirements list

Think of a carpenter given a list of jobs and a toolbox. No single tool does every job, but each job is easy with the right tool, and the craft is choosing a small set of tools that covers the list. In data-structure design, the jobs are the operations with their required complexities, and the tools are the primitives you already know:

PrimitiveCheap atExpensive at
hash map / setfind, insert, delete by key — O(1)order, min/max, random element
dynamic arrayindex access, append, pop end, random element — O(1)insert/delete in the middle — O(n)
doubly linked listinsert/remove a known node, move to front/back — O(1)find a node — O(n)
heapmin/max O(1), push/pop O(log n)find/delete arbitrary — O(n)
sorted list + bisectsearch, predecessor — O(log n)insert in the middle — O(n)
balanced tree / SortedListordered ops — O(log n)constants and memory
deque / ring bufferpush/pop at both ends — O(1)middle access

The pattern behind most O(1) designs is a hash map that points into an ordered structure. The map provides "find it in O(1)"; the ordered structure (a linked list, an array, a list of buckets) provides "the oldest", "the most frequent", "a random one" or "the next" in O(1). The map stores, for each key, its exact position in the ordered structure, so the two can be updated together.

A method for any design question

  1. List the operations and their targets. Write them down: get O(1), put O(1), evict least recent O(1).
  2. Find the hardest pair. Usually two operations that no single primitive supports together (find by key and find the oldest; delete by value and pick at random).
  3. Combine primitives so each operation is cheap in at least one of them, and make one point into the other.
  4. State the invariant that ties them together, in one sentence.
  5. Walk every operation and check it maintains the invariant, including edge cases (capacity 0 or 1, updating an existing key, removing the last element).

Most designs in this lesson are variations on three shapes: map + linked list (LRU, LFU's buckets, All O'one), map + array (randomised set, snapshot histories, circular buffers), and stack of pending work (iterators). Recognising which shape a new question needs is usually the moment it becomes easy.

Where the toolbox analogy breaks: a carpenter's tools are independent, but data structures in a design share data, and every update must touch all of them. Forgetting to delete a key from the map when its node is evicted, or to update the moved element's index after a swap, leaves the structures disagreeing — a bug that often surfaces only several operations later. The invariant in step 4 is your defence: after writing each method, re-read it against the invariant.
body:
LRU cache

Operations: get(key) and put(key, value), both O(1), evicting the least recently used key when over capacity. The hardest pair is "find by key" (hash map) and "find and move the oldest" (ordered list). Combine a dict from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered by recency, using sentinel head and tail nodes:

class Node:
    __slots__ = ("key", "val", "prev", "next")
    def __init__(self, key=0, val=0):
        self.key, self.val, self.prev, self.next = key, val, None, None

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap, self.map = capacity, {}
        self.head, self.tail = Node(), Node()        # sentinels
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head

    def _unlink(self, n):
        n.prev.next, n.next.prev = n.next, n.prev

    def _push_front(self, n):
        n.prev, n.next = self.head, self.head.next
        self.head.next.prev = n
        self.head.next = n

    def get(self, key):
        n = self.map.get(key)
        if n is None: return -1
        self._unlink(n); self._push_front(n)        # now most recent
        return n.val

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.map:
            n = self.map[key]; n.val = value
            self._unlink(n); self._push_front(n)
            return
        n = Node(key, value)
        self.map[key] = n; self._push_front(n)
        if len(self.map) > self.cap:
            lru = self.tail.prev                    # least recent
            self._unlink(lru); del self.map[lru.key]

Each node stores its key so that eviction can delete the map entry — a detail that is easy to forget. Trace capacity 2: put(1, 1), put(2, 2) → list 2, 1. get(1) → list 1, 2. put(3, 3) → list 3, 1, 2, over capacity, evict 2. get(2) → −1. In Python, collections.OrderedDict implements the same structure: move_to_end(key) on access and popitem(last=False) to evict. Interviewers usually accept it after you explain what it does internally, or ask you to write the linked list.

LFU cache

Evict the least frequently used key, breaking ties by least recently used. Now there are two orderings: by frequency, and by recency within a frequency. The O(1) design keeps:

  • key → (value, freq),
  • freq → OrderedDict of keys with that frequency (insertion order = recency within the bucket),
  • min_freq, the smallest frequency present.
from collections import defaultdict, OrderedDict
class LFUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap, self.kv, self.buckets, self.min_freq = capacity, {}, defaultdict(OrderedDict), 0

    def _touch(self, key):                          # increment a key's frequency
        val, f = self.kv[key]
        del self.buckets[f][key]
        if not self.buckets[f]:
            del self.buckets[f]
            if self.min_freq == f: self.min_freq += 1
        self.buckets[f + 1][key] = None
        self.kv[key] = (val, f + 1)

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.kv: return -1
        self._touch(key)
        return self.kv[key][0]

    def put(self, key, value):
        if self.cap == 0: return
        if key in self.kv:
            self.kv[key] = (value, self.kv[key][1]); self._touch(key); return
        if len(self.kv) == self.cap:
            old, _ = self.buckets[self.min_freq].popitem(last=False)   # LFU, then LRU
            if not self.buckets[self.min_freq]: del self.buckets[self.min_freq]
            del self.kv[old]
        self.kv[key] = (value, 1); self.buckets[1][key] = None
        self.min_freq = 1                           # a new key always has frequency 1

The subtle parts: min_freq only ever increases by one when its bucket empties during a touch (the touched key moves to min_freq + 1, so that bucket exists), and it resets to 1 on every new insertion. Capacity 0 must be handled explicitly. Everything is O(1).

Insert, delete and getRandom in O(1)

getRandom needs an array (pick a random index). Delete by value needs a hash map (find it). But deleting from the middle of an array is O(n). The trick: order does not matter, so move the last element into the deleted slot and pop the end.

import random
class RandomizedSet:
    def __init__(self):
        self.vals, self.pos = [], {}               # pos[v] = index of v in vals
    def insert(self, v):
        if v in self.pos: return False
        self.pos[v] = len(self.vals); self.vals.append(v); return True
    def remove(self, v):
        if v not in self.pos: return False
        i, last = self.pos[v], self.vals[-1]
        self.vals[i], self.pos[last] = last, i      # move last into the hole
        self.vals.pop(); del self.pos[v]
        return True
    def getRandom(self):
        return random.choice(self.vals)

The order of the two lines in remove matters when v is itself the last element: setting pos[last] = i and then deleting pos[v] (the same key) leaves the map correct. With duplicates allowed, map each value to a set of indices and perform the same swap, updating the moved value's index set.

Versioned data: Snapshot Array and Time Map

Snapshot Array: set(index, val), snap() returning a snapshot id, and get(index, snap_id) returning the value at that snapshot. Copying the array on each snap is O(n). Store history per index instead: a list of (snap_id, value) changes. set appends (current_snap, val), or overwrites the last entry if it already belongs to the current snapshot. get binary-searches the last change with snap_id ≤ the requested id.

import bisect
class SnapshotArray:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.hist = [[(-1, 0)] for _ in range(n)]   # (snap_id, value); -1: initial 0
        self.snap_id = 0
    def set(self, i, v):
        h = self.hist[i]
        if h[-1][0] == self.snap_id: h[-1] = (self.snap_id, v)
        else: h.append((self.snap_id, v))
    def snap(self):
        self.snap_id += 1
        return self.snap_id - 1
    def get(self, i, sid):
        h = self.hist[i]
        k = bisect.bisect_right(h, (sid, float("inf"))) - 1
        return h[k][1]

set and snap are O(1); get is O(log k) for k changes at that index; memory is proportional to the number of sets. Time Based Key-Value Store is the same design keyed by strings with timestamps (al7). This "append-only history plus binary search" structure is how databases implement multi-version reads, in simplified form.

Bounded and navigable sequences

Circular queue (fixed capacity k): an array of size k, a head index and a size. The tail position is (head + size) % k. Tracking the size, rather than separate head and tail indices alone, removes the ambiguity between "full" and "empty" when head and tail coincide.

class MyCircularQueue:
    def __init__(self, k): self.a, self.head, self.size, self.k = [0] * k, 0, 0, k
    def enQueue(self, x):
        if self.size == self.k: return False
        self.a[(self.head + self.size) % self.k] = x; self.size += 1; return True
    def deQueue(self):
        if self.size == 0: return False
        self.head = (self.head + 1) % self.k; self.size -= 1; return True
    def Front(self): return self.a[self.head] if self.size else -1
    def Rear(self): return self.a[(self.head + self.size - 1) % self.k] if self.size else -1

Browser History: visit(url), back(steps), forward(steps). Keep an array of pages, a current index and an end index. visit writes at current + 1 and sets end = current (logically discarding forward history without deleting anything); back and forward clamp current within [0, end]. All O(1). The two-stack version is simpler to describe but costs O(steps) per navigation.

Lazy iterators

An iterator should produce one element per call without precomputing everything. The pattern: keep a stack of pending work, and on each call do just enough to expose the next element.

BST Iterator (in-order, next and hasNext): keep the stack of nodes on the path of left children (the iterative in-order traversal of al14, spread across calls).

class BSTIterator:
    def __init__(self, root):
        self.stack = []; self._push_left(root)
    def _push_left(self, node):
        while node: self.stack.append(node); node = node.left
    def next(self):
        node = self.stack.pop()
        self._push_left(node.right)              # next smallest lies down the right subtree's left spine
        return node.val
    def hasNext(self):
        return bool(self.stack)

A single next can push many nodes, but every node is pushed once and popped once over the whole traversal: amortised O(1) per call, O(h) memory. Flatten Nested List Iterator keeps a stack of iterators over the nested lists; hasNext descends into lists until an integer is exposed (or everything is exhausted), buffering it for next. Doing the descent in hasNext (rather than next) matters because empty nested lists like [[]] must make hasNext return false. Peeking Iterator caches one element ahead of the underlying iterator so peek can return it without consuming it; fill the cache in the constructor.

All O'one: buckets of keys in a linked list

inc(key), dec(key), getMaxKey(), getMinKey(), all O(1). Counts change by exactly one, so a key only ever moves to a neighbouring count. Keep a doubly linked list of buckets in increasing count order, each bucket holding the set of keys with that count, and a map from key to its bucket. inc moves a key from its bucket to the next one (creating a bucket with count + 1 immediately after if it does not exist) and deletes the old bucket if it becomes empty. dec moves it to the previous bucket (or removes the key at count 1). The minimum key is any key in the first bucket and the maximum any key in the last. It is the LFU idea — frequency buckets — with direct access to both extremes.

A tiny Twitter: merging feeds

postTweet(user, tweet), follow, unfollow, and getNewsFeed(user) returning the 10 most recent tweets from the user and the people they follow. Store each user's tweets in a list with a global increasing timestamp, and followees in a set. The feed is a k-way merge of reverse-chronological lists (al10): push the newest tweet of each relevant user into a max-heap, pop the newest overall, and push that user's next older tweet; stop after 10.

import heapq, itertools
from collections import defaultdict
class Twitter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.clock = itertools.count()
        self.tweets = defaultdict(list)             # user -> [(time, id)]
        self.follows = defaultdict(set)
    def postTweet(self, u, tid):
        self.tweets[u].append((next(self.clock), tid))
    def follow(self, a, b):
        if a != b: self.follows[a].add(b)
    def unfollow(self, a, b):
        self.follows[a].discard(b)
    def getNewsFeed(self, u):
        heap = []
        for v in self.follows[u] | {u}:
            if self.tweets[v]:
                i = len(self.tweets[v]) - 1
                t, tid = self.tweets[v][i]
                heap.append((-t, tid, v, i))
        heapq.heapify(heap); feed = []
        while heap and len(feed) < 10:
            _, tid, v, i = heapq.heappop(heap); feed.append(tid)
            if i:
                t, nid = self.tweets[v][i - 1]
                heapq.heappush(heap, (-t, nid, v, i - 1))
        return feed

Cost O(F + 10 log F) for F followees. Guarding follow against following yourself and using discard (not remove) for unfollow avoids common errors.

Rate limiting and hit counting

"Design a hit counter: hit(timestamp) and getHits(timestamp) returning hits in the last 300 seconds." A deque of timestamps works (pop from the front while older than timestamp − 300), but memory grows with traffic. A fixed design uses a ring of 300 buckets indexed by timestamp % 300, each storing (the second it represents, count): on a hit, if the bucket's stored second is stale, reset it; getHits sums buckets whose stored second is within the window. Memory is O(300) regardless of traffic and each operation is O(300) or O(1) with a running total. It is the sliding-window counter from al6 expressed as a data-structure design, and the same ring-of-buckets idea underlies rate limiters and per-second metrics in monitoring agents.

Recognising the pattern

"Design a class with operations X, Y, Z in O(…)" means: list the operations, find the conflicting pair, and combine primitives — usually a hash map pointing into an ordered structure (linked list, array, buckets, per-key history). Then state the invariant and check every operation against it.

Practice in the DSA list: LRU Cache, LFU Cache, Insert Delete GetRandom O(1), Snapshot Array, Time Based Key-Value Store, Design Browser History, Design Circular Queue, Peeking Iterator, Online Stock Span, All O`one Data Structure, Design Twitter, Min Stack (al8).
deep:
Amortised bounds in iterator designs

Lazy iterators trade a uniform per-call cost for a good average. The BST iterator's next can push h nodes, but the total pushes over a full traversal is n, so n calls cost O(n): amortised O(1). The same aggregate argument (al2) justifies the nested-list iterator. In an interview, state both bounds: "worst case O(h) for a single call, amortised O(1), memory O(h)". If an application needs a hard per-call bound (real-time systems), a structure with threaded pointers (Morris-style, al14) or a precomputed array may be preferable, at the cost of memory or mutation.

Thread safety and real caches

Interview caches are single-threaded; real ones are not. A naive LRU guarded by one lock serialises every read, because even get modifies the list. Production designs reduce contention by sharding the cache into many independent LRUs keyed by hash, by recording accesses in per-thread buffers that are applied to the list in batches (Caffeine's design in Java), or by abandoning exact LRU. Redis, for instance, approximates LRU by sampling a handful of keys and evicting the oldest among them, which avoids maintaining a global list at all; its LFU mode uses a small logarithmic counter per key with decay. CPU caches use pseudo-LRU with a few bits per set. Knowing that "exact LRU is a hash map plus linked list, and real systems approximate it for concurrency and memory" is a strong senior answer to the usual follow-up.

Expiry and lazy deletion

Caches often need time-to-live expiry as well as size-based eviction. Scanning for expired entries is O(n); the usual techniques are lazy deletion — check an entry's expiry when it is read and treat it as missing if stale — plus a background sweep that samples keys or walks a min-heap (or timing wheel) ordered by expiry time. The heap approach has the stale-entry issue from al10: when a key is refreshed, its old heap entry remains and must be skipped when popped. Memcached and Redis both combine lazy expiry on access with periodic active expiry.

Versioning, copy-on-write and persistence

Snapshot Array stores per-element histories. An alternative for snapshotting whole structures is copy-on-write: share the data between versions and copy only what an update changes. Persistent data structures (persistent arrays as trees, persistent segment trees, the hash array mapped tries behind Clojure's and Scala's immutable maps) give every version O(log n) access while sharing almost all memory. Databases implement snapshot isolation with multi-version concurrency control, keeping several versions of each row with transaction timestamps — conceptually the (version, value) lists of this lesson, plus garbage collection of versions no transaction can see.

Choosing between exactness and memory

Several designs have cheaper approximate versions that production systems prefer. Exact LFU needs per-key counters and buckets; Redis's LFU keeps an 8-bit logarithmic counter per key and decays it over time, trading precision for a fixed tiny footprint. Exact distinct counts need a set; HyperLogLog estimates them in kilobytes. Exact top-k needs counts for every key; Count-Min sketches plus a small heap approximate it (al10). In an interview, deliver the exact design first, then mention where you would approximate at scale and what you would lose — that shows judgement about real constraints rather than only puzzle-solving.

Testing designs: model-based fuzzing

Design bugs usually involve sequences of operations, which hand-written tests miss. The effective technique is model-based testing: implement a trivially correct but slow reference ("a list of keys in recency order" for LRU, "a Python set and a random.choice over list(set)" for the randomised set), generate random sequences of operations, and compare outputs after each operation. A few thousand random sequences of length 50 find almost every invariant violation. Libraries like Hypothesis automate this with stateful testing. Mentioning it — and doing it in the lab — shows how you would gain confidence in a design beyond the examples.
prod:
In the interview room

Start by restating the operations and targets, then name the combination before writing code: "a dict from key to node and a doubly linked list by recency; the invariant is that the map and the list contain the same keys". Interviewers grade the decomposition as much as the code. Ask about edge cases up front: capacity 0, updating an existing key, behaviour on missing keys, whether values can repeat.

The common bugs are bookkeeping slips: not storing the key in the node (so eviction cannot delete the map entry); forgetting to move an updated key to the front in put; deleting from the map but not the list, or vice versa; updating the moved element's index after the pop instead of before in RandomizedSet; mishandling the case where the removed element is the last one; min_freq not reset on insert in LFU; hasNext that does not handle empty nested lists; and off-by-one errors in circular indices. After writing each method, re-check it against the invariant line by line.

Expect scale follow-ups: "how would this work with multiple threads?" (locks, sharding, approximate eviction), "the cache is distributed across machines" (consistent hashing of keys to nodes, each running a local LRU), "values are large" (store sizes and evict by total bytes, not count), and "the feed has celebrity users" (hybrid push/pull fan-out). Having one or two sentences for each turns a coding question into a small system-design conversation, which senior interviewers appreciate.

On online assessments, design problems are graded by hidden sequences of calls, often including the edge cases above. A quick local test that replays the example sequence and a few hand-made edge sequences (capacity 1, repeated puts of the same key, removing the last element) catches most failures before submission.

A final habit for these rounds: once the code is written, walk one complete scenario out loud through all structures at once — "put a, put b, get a, put c at capacity 2: map has a and c, list is c then a, b was evicted from both". Saying the state of every structure after each step is the fastest way to catch the forgotten update before the interviewer does.

In real systems

These designs are everywhere. Python's own functools.lru_cache is a dict plus a circular doubly linked list, exactly this lesson's LRU. Memcached uses per-slab LRU lists; Redis offers approximated LRU and LFU eviction policies by sampling; CDNs and browsers cache objects with LRU-like policies plus expiry; database buffer pools use LRU variants (often with "midpoint insertion" or clock algorithms) to keep hot pages in memory. Ring buffers are the backbone of high-throughput systems: the Linux kernel's io_uring and network drivers use them to pass work between producer and consumer without locking, and the LMAX Disruptor built a trading platform on a single ring buffer. Versioned key-value storage with timestamps is how databases provide snapshot reads (MVCC) and how systems like Bigtable store multiple cell versions. Social feeds are built from per-user timelines merged or precomputed exactly as in the Twitter design, with hybrid fan-out for accounts with huge follower counts.
myths: An LRU cache needs a heap of access times.

A heap gives O(log n) and makes 'touch an existing key' awkward. A hash map from key to node plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency gives O(1) for get, put and eviction: the map finds the node, the list moves it to the front or removes the back.
Deleting from the middle of a list is O(1) if you know the index.

In an array-backed list (a Python list) deleting at an index shifts every later element: O(n). The O(1) trick for unordered collections is to swap the element with the last one and pop the end, updating the moved element's stored index.
Snapshot Array should copy the array on every snap.

Copying costs O(n) per snapshot and O(n · snaps) memory. Store, for each index, only the changes as (snap_id, value) pairs; a lookup binary-searches the latest change at or before the requested snapshot. Snap becomes O(1) and memory is proportional to the number of writes.
An iterator should materialise everything in its constructor.

Flattening a huge nested list or traversing a large tree up front costs O(n) memory and delays the first result. A lazy iterator keeps only a stack of positions and produces the next element on demand, with amortised O(1) per call and memory proportional to the nesting depth or tree height.
Design questions are about clever algorithms.

They are mostly about bookkeeping: choosing two or three standard structures whose combination supports every operation within the target complexity, and keeping them consistent on every update. Most bugs are a forgotten update to one of the structures.
lab:
Model-based fuzzing: compare the LRU cache and the randomised set against slow reference implementations on random operation sequences.

  1. Save as design_lab.py, pasting the LRUCache (with Node) and RandomizedSet classes from the body above the following code: 
    import random

class SlowLRU:                                   # reference model: list in recency order
    def __init__(self, cap): self.cap, self.order, self.vals = cap, [], {}
    def get(self, k):
        if k not in self.vals: return -1
        self.order.remove(k); self.order.append(k); return self.vals[k]
    def put(self, k, v):
        if k in self.vals: self.order.remove(k)
        self.order.append(k); self.vals[k] = v
        if len(self.order) > self.cap: del self.vals[self.order.pop(0)]

for _ in range(2000):
    cap = random.randint(1, 4); a, b = LRUCache(cap), SlowLRU(cap)
    for _ in range(50):
        k = random.randint(0, 6)
        if random.random() < 0.5:
            assert a.get(k) == b.get(k)
        else:
            v = random.randint(0, 99); a.put(k, v); b.put(k, v)
print("LRU matches the reference model")

for _ in range(2000):
    rs, model = RandomizedSet(), set()
    for _ in range(50):
        v = random.randint(0, 6)
        if random.random() < 0.5: assert rs.insert(v) == (v not in model); model.add(v)
        else: assert rs.remove(v) == (v in model); model.discard(v)
        assert sorted(rs.vals) == sorted(model) and all(rs.vals[i] == x for x, i in rs.pos.items())
print("RandomizedSet stays consistent with a plain set")
  2. Run it and expect both messages. Each trial replays 50 random operations against a trivially correct model; the second check also verifies the invariant "pos[x] is x's index in vals" after every operation.
  3. Introduce a bug — for example, delete del self.map[lru.key] in LRUCache.put, or, in RandomizedSet.remove, move del self.pos[v] above the line that updates self.pos[last] (which breaks removing the last element) — and rerun. The fuzzer reports a mismatch within a few trials.

What this proves: random operation sequences against a slow model catch the bookkeeping bugs that make design questions hard, far more reliably than a few hand-written calls.
recap: Start a design question by listing every operation with its target complexity; then pick structures so that each operation is cheap in at least one of them.
Keep an explicit invariant tying the structures together, and update every structure in every operation.
LRU cache: hash map from key to node plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency, with sentinels; every operation is O(1).
LFU cache: map from key to (value, frequency), map from frequency to an insertion-ordered set of keys, and a running minimum frequency.
O(1) insert, delete and getRandom: a list of values plus a map from value to index, deleting by swapping with the last element.
Versioned data stores per-key lists of (version, value) and answers historical reads with binary search.
Circular buffers use a fixed array with a head index and a size, wrapping with modulo.
Lazy iterators keep a stack of pending work and do just enough on each call, giving amortised O(1) next.
glossary: Constant average cost per operation over a sequence, even if a single call occasionally does more work.
Binary search tree; its in-order traversal yields keys in sorted order, which the BST iterator produces lazily.
A fixed-size array used as a queue whose indices wrap around with modulo arithmetic.
Removing an entry from a full cache to make room for a new one.
A condition that must hold between operations, such as 'every key in the map has exactly one node in the list'.
An object that produces elements one at a time through next() and hasNext().
Least frequently used: evict the entry accessed the fewest times, breaking ties by least recent use.
Least recently used: evict the entry whose last access is oldest.
Doing work only when its result is needed.
Multi-version concurrency control: databases keep several timestamped versions of each row so readers see a consistent snapshot.
A Python dict subclass with O(1) move_to_end and popitem from either end, implemented with a doubly linked list.
A dummy node at the head or tail of a linked list that removes edge cases for empty lists and end insertions.
A saved version of a data structure's state that can be read later.
Time to live: how long a cache entry remains valid before it expires.
Deleting from an unordered array in O(1) by moving the last element into the hole and shrinking the array.
drill:
Design under new requirements

"Design a cache with capacity C supporting get(key) and put(key, value, ttl_seconds), O(1) average per operation. Entries expire ttl seconds after their last put. When full, evict the least recently used entry among those not yet expired; expired entries should be removed first." Describe the structures, the invariant, and how expiry is handled.

Answer

Start from LRU: a dict key → node (storing key, value and expires_at) and a doubly linked list by recency with sentinels. Add expiry with lazy deletion: get checks expires_at against the current time and, if expired, unlinks the node, deletes the key and returns a miss — O(1). For "expired entries removed first" when the cache is full, keep a min-heap of (expires_at, key, version) alongside: on put, push a new entry and bump the key's version so older heap entries become stale. Before evicting, pop heap entries while the top is stale (version mismatch or key gone) — and if the top is expired, remove that key instead of the LRU one. The heap makes put O(log C) rather than strictly O(1); if O(1) is mandatory, use a timing wheel (buckets of keys by expiry second, swept as time advances) for amortised O(1). Invariant: every live key appears exactly once in the dict and once in the list; the heap may hold stale entries but never misses a live key's current expiry. Edge cases: put on an existing key refreshes both value and TTL and moves it to the front; capacity 0; a key that expires between a get's lookup and its return (use one timestamp per call). At scale, add a periodic sampler that removes expired keys so memory does not fill with dead entries that are never read — the approach Redis uses.

Design a stack with O(1) push, pop, top and getMin.

Store (value, minimum so far) pairs: push computes min(value, previous minimum); getMin reads the top pair's minimum. All O(1). Alternatively keep a second stack of minimums, pushing only when the new value is at most the current minimum and popping when the popped value equals it.
E
Design a circular queue with a fixed capacity.

A fixed array, a head index and a size. enQueue writes at (head + size) % capacity and increments size if not full; deQueue advances head = (head + 1) % capacity and decrements size if not empty; Front reads array[head], Rear reads array[(head + size − 1) % capacity]. All O(1). Tracking size avoids the ambiguity between full and empty when head equals tail.

Design browser history with visit, back(steps) and forward(steps).

An array of pages, a current index and a logical end. visit writes the page at current + 1, sets current and end there (discarding forward history in O(1) without deleting elements); back moves current to max(0, current − steps); forward to min(end, current + steps). All O(1). Two stacks also work, at O(steps) per move.
M
Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put.

A dict from key to node and a doubly linked list of nodes from most to least recently used, with head and tail sentinels. get: if present, unlink the node, relink it after head, return the value. put: if present, update and move to front; otherwise create a node at the front, add it to the dict, and if over capacity remove the node before tail and delete its key from the dict. Every step is O(1).
Follow-up: In Python, simpler? — OrderedDict: move_to_end(key) on access and popitem(last=False) to evict.
M
Design Insert Delete GetRandom O(1).

A list of values and a dict from value to its index. insert appends and records the index. remove looks up the index, moves the last value into that slot, updates the moved value's index, pops the end and deletes the removed key. getRandom returns random.choice(list). All O(1) average.
Follow-up: Duplicates allowed? — Map each value to a set of indices; on removal take any index from its set, swap with the last element, and fix the moved element's index set.

Design Snapshot Array with set, snap and get(index, snap_id).

For each index keep a list of (snap_id, value) changes, starting with (0, 0). set appends (current_snap, value), or overwrites the last entry if it has the same snap_id. snap returns current_snap and increments it. get binary-searches the last entry with snap_id ≤ the requested id. set and snap O(1), get O(log k), memory proportional to the number of sets.

Design an iterator that flattens a nested list.

Keep a stack of iterators. hasNext: while the stack is non-empty, look at the next element of the top iterator; if the iterator is exhausted pop it; if the element is a list push an iterator over it; if it is an integer, buffer it and return true. next returns the buffered integer. Each element is pushed and handled once, so amortised O(1) per call, with memory proportional to the nesting depth.
M
Design a BST iterator with next and hasNext in amortised O(1) and O(h) memory.

Keep a stack holding the path of left children from the current position. Initialise by pushing the root and all its left descendants. next pops a node, then pushes its right child and all of that child's left descendants, and returns the popped value. Each node is pushed and popped once over the full traversal, so amortised O(1); the stack never exceeds the height.
M
Design a Peeking Iterator.

Wrap the underlying iterator and cache one element ahead. peek returns the cached element; next returns it and refills the cache from the underlying iterator; hasNext reports whether a cached element exists. All O(1). The cache must be filled in the constructor so peek works before the first next.
H
Design an LFU cache with O(1) get and put.

Maintain key → (value, freq), freq → OrderedDict of keys (insertion order = recency within that frequency), and min_freq. On access, remove the key from its frequency bucket, add it to freq + 1, and if the old bucket was min_freq and is now empty, increment min_freq. On insert of a new key into a full cache, evict the first key of the min_freq bucket, then insert the new key with freq 1 and set min_freq = 1. All O(1).

Design the All O'one data structure: inc, dec, getMaxKey and getMinKey, all O(1).

A doubly linked list of buckets in increasing count order, each bucket holding a set of keys with that count, plus a map from key to its bucket. inc moves a key to the next bucket (creating a bucket with count + 1 right after if needed) and deletes its old bucket if empty; dec does the reverse or removes the key at count 1. Min and max keys come from the first and last buckets. All O(1).
H
Design a simplified Twitter: postTweet, follow, unfollow and getNewsFeed (10 most recent tweets from the user and followees).

Store each user's tweets as a list of (timestamp, id) with a global increasing counter, and each user's followees as a set. getNewsFeed pushes the latest tweet of each relevant user into a max-heap keyed by timestamp, then pops up to 10 times, pushing the next older tweet of the popped user each time — a k-way merge of reverse-chronological lists. O(F + 10 log F) for F followees.
Follow-up: At scale? — Fan-out on write (push tweets into followers' precomputed feeds) for most users, fan-out on read for celebrity accounts with millions of followers.
